CV-025.stem_html:
A 66-year-old woman is hospitalized with pneumonia. On day 3 she has two brief episodes of lightheadedness. Telemetry shows runs of polymorphic ventricular tachycardia in which the QRS axis twists around the baseline, each lasting 10–15 seconds and stopping on its own. Medications are levofloxacin, ondansetron and haloperidol for delirium.

On physical examination, blood pressure is 124/70 mm Hg and pulse rate is 64/min. She is awake and oriented. Between episodes, the ECG shows sinus rhythm with a corrected QT interval of 590 ms.

Potassium3.4 mEq/L
Magnesium1.6 mg/dL
CV-025.lead: In addition to stopping QT-prolonging drugs and replacing potassium, which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
CV-025.explain_html:
Correct answer: B Torsades de pointes

Torsades de pointes is polymorphic VT with a "twisting" axis that occurs on a background of a long QT interval. Here the cause is acquired: three QT-prolonging drugs (levofloxacin, ondansetron, haloperidol) plus hypokalemia and hypomagnesemia, in an older woman.

IV magnesium sulfate (2 g) is first-line even when the serum magnesium is normal; it suppresses the early afterdepolarizations that trigger torsades. Then:

  • Stop all QT-prolonging drugs and correct potassium to ≥4.0 mEq/L (ideally 4.5–5.0) and magnesium to ≥2.0 mg/dL.
  • If torsades recurs, increase the heart rate (bradycardia and pauses lengthen the QT): temporary transvenous overdrive pacing or isoproterenol.
  • Unsynchronized defibrillation if it degenerates into sustained VT/VF.

Why not the others

  • (A) Intravenous lidocaine — Lidocaine (class IB) does not prolong QT and can be tried in refractory cases, but magnesium is first-line.
  • (C) Oral metoprolol — Beta-blockers are used for congenital long QT syndrome, but in acquired long QT they slow the rate and can promote pause-dependent torsades.
  • (D) Intravenous procainamide — Procainamide (class IA) prolongs the QT interval and is contraindicated in torsades.
  • (E) Intravenous amiodarone — Amiodarone prolongs the QT interval and can worsen torsades. It is used for monomorphic VT, not for long-QT torsades.
🎓 ABIM pearl

Acquired long QT has three common culprits on the wards — "antis": anti-arrhythmics (IA, III), anti-psychotics/anti-emetics (haloperidol, ondansetron), anti-infectives (fluoroquinolones, macrolides, azoles) — plus low K and low Mg.

🎯 Educational objective

Treat torsades de pointes with intravenous magnesium, removal of QT-prolonging drugs and correction of electrolytes, followed by overdrive pacing if it recurs.

CV-026.stem_html:
A 22-year-old woman is evaluated after fainting yesterday while standing in a crowded, hot church service. She felt warm, nauseated and sweaty and her vision "grayed out" just before she fell. A friend says she was pale, had a few jerking movements of her arms for several seconds, and was fully alert within a minute. She did not bite her tongue or lose bladder control. She had a similar episode at age 16 when her blood was drawn. She takes no medications. There is no family history of sudden death.

On physical examination, blood pressure is 112/68 mm Hg supine and 110/70 mm Hg standing; pulse rate is 68/min supine and 76/min standing. Cardiac and neurologic examinations are normal. ECG is normal, with a normal QT interval.
CV-026.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
CV-026.explain_html:
Correct answer: A Vasovagal syncope

This is classic vasovagal (reflex) syncope: a trigger (prolonged standing, heat, crowding, blood draw), a prodrome of warmth, nausea, sweating and tunnel vision, rapid full recovery, and a young patient with a normal examination and ECG.

The brief jerks are convulsive syncope — common with cerebral hypoperfusion and not a sign of epilepsy. Seizures cause prolonged postictal confusion, lateral tongue biting and longer tonic-clonic activity.

The key tools in syncope are the history, examination and ECG. When these give a confident diagnosis of reflex syncope and no high-risk features are present, no further testing is needed. Management: reassurance, education about triggers, adequate fluid and salt intake, and physical counter-pressure maneuvers (leg crossing, squatting, handgrip) at the first sign of a prodrome.

Why not the others

  • (B) Electroencephalography — The brief myoclonic jerks during syncope do not indicate epilepsy; an EEG is not indicated without features of seizure.
  • (C) Tilt-table testing — Tilt-table testing can help when the diagnosis of reflex syncope is uncertain. Her history is already diagnostic.
  • (D) Echocardiography — With a normal cardiac examination and ECG and a clear reflex trigger, echocardiography has very low yield.
  • (E) 30-day ambulatory ECG monitoring — Ambulatory monitoring is for suspected arrhythmic syncope (exertional syncope, palpitations, abnormal ECG, structural heart disease).
🎓 ABIM pearl

High-risk syncope features that need cardiac work-up: syncope during exertion or while supine, no prodrome, palpitations before the event, structural heart disease, abnormal ECG (QT prolongation, Brugada pattern, preexcitation, bundle branch block) and family history of sudden death before age 50.

🎯 Educational objective

In typical vasovagal syncope with a normal examination and ECG, no further testing is needed; manage with reassurance, trigger avoidance and counter-pressure maneuvers.

CV-027.stem_html:
A 19-year-old college basketball player is evaluated after a near-syncopal episode during a game. He has had chest tightness with sprinting for several months. His uncle died suddenly at age 35.

On physical examination, blood pressure is 122/70 mm Hg and pulse rate is 62/min. There is a grade 3/6 harsh crescendo-decrescendo systolic murmur best heard at the left lower sternal border that does not radiate to the carotid arteries. The murmur becomes louder when the patient stands from a squat and during the strain phase of the Valsalva maneuver, and softer with passive leg raising. Carotid upstroke is brisk.
CV-027.lead: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
CV-027.explain_html:
Correct answer: A Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy — murmur maneuvers

A young athlete with exertional symptoms, a family history of sudden death, and a systolic murmur that gets louder when preload falls has hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy (HCM) until proven otherwise.

In HCM the hypertrophied septum and the mitral valve (systolic anterior motion) obstruct the left ventricular outflow tract. A smaller ventricle brings the septum and valve closer and worsens obstruction; a fuller ventricle reduces it. Almost every other murmur does the opposite.

Maneuver Effect on LV volume HCM murmur Aortic stenosis murmur
Valsalva (strain), standing ↓ preload Louder Softer
Squatting, leg raise ↑ preload Softer Louder
Handgrip ↑ afterload Softer Softer (AS); MR louder

The next step is echocardiography (wall thickness ≥15 mm, LVOT gradient), with cardiac MRI for risk assessment. He should avoid competitive sports until evaluated. First-degree relatives need screening.

Why not the others

  • (B) Ventricular septal defect — A VSD gives a holosystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border that gets louder with handgrip and softer with Valsalva.
  • (C) Mitral valve prolapse — Mitral valve prolapse causes a midsystolic click and late systolic murmur at the apex. Valsalva makes the click earlier and the murmur longer, but the murmur location and click differ.
  • (D) Bicuspid aortic valve stenosis — Aortic stenosis murmurs radiate to the carotids, get softer with Valsalva, and produce a delayed, weak carotid upstroke (pulsus parvus et tardus). The brisk upstroke here fits HCM.
  • (E) Pulmonic stenosis — Pulmonic stenosis is heard at the left upper sternal border, often with an ejection click, and gets louder with inspiration.
🧠 Mnemonic

Only two murmurs get louder with Valsalva: HCM and MVP ("Hypertrophic and Mitral prolapse — How Much less blood").

🎯 Educational objective

Recognize hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy by a systolic murmur that increases with maneuvers that reduce left ventricular preload (Valsalva, standing).

CV-028.stem_html:
A 56-year-old man with a known bicuspid aortic valve is evaluated during annual follow-up. He reports no dyspnea, chest pain or decreased exercise tolerance; he runs 3 miles twice a week.

On physical examination, blood pressure is 152/48 mm Hg and pulse rate is 66/min. There is a bounding carotid pulse and a grade 3/4 high-pitched decrescendo diastolic murmur at the left sternal border, heard best with the patient leaning forward.

Echocardiogram shows severe aortic regurgitation. The LVEF is 50% (60% one year ago) and the left ventricular end-systolic dimension is 48 mm. The ascending aorta measures 42 mm.
CV-028.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

choices.E: Begin nifedipine and repeat echocardiography in 6 months

CV-028.explain_html:
Correct answer: A Chronic severe aortic regurgitation

He has chronic severe aortic regurgitation and is asymptomatic, but his LVEF has fallen to ≤55%. In chronic AR the left ventricle dilates to handle the regurgitant volume; once systolic function falls, damage can become irreversible.

Indications for surgical aortic valve replacement in severe AR:

  • Symptoms, regardless of LV function.
  • Asymptomatic with LVEF ≤55% or LV end-systolic dimension >50 mm (or indexed >25 mm/m²).
  • Undergoing other cardiac surgery.
  • Reasonable with a progressive decline in LVEF or increase in LV size on serial studies.

His aorta (42 mm) is below the threshold for repair at the same operation in a bicuspid valve (≥45 mm when already having AVR).

Why not the others

  • (B) Repeat echocardiography in 1 year — Waiting risks irreversible LV dysfunction.
  • (C) Transcatheter aortic valve replacement — TAVR is not approved for native-valve pure aortic regurgitation (except in selected inoperable patients with a dedicated device) and is unsuitable for a bicuspid valve with pure AR in a 56-year-old surgical candidate.
  • (D) Exercise stress test — Exercise testing helps when symptoms are uncertain. Surgery is already indicated by the fall in LVEF.
  • (E) Begin nifedipine and repeat echocardiography in 6 months — Vasodilators treat hypertension in AR but do not delay surgery; they are not a substitute when surgical criteria are met.
🎓 ABIM pearl

The "55 rule" in regurgitant lesions — think about surgery in asymptomatic severe AR when EF ≤55%; in severe primary MR the threshold is EF ≤60% (or LVESD ≥40 mm).

🎯 Educational objective

Recommend aortic valve replacement for asymptomatic chronic severe aortic regurgitation when LVEF falls to 55% or less or the LV end-systolic dimension exceeds 50 mm.

CV-029.stem_html:
A 68-year-old man is hospitalized with 3 weeks of fevers, night sweats and fatigue. He has lost 4 kg (8.8 lb).

On physical examination, temperature is 38.4 °C (101.1 °F), blood pressure is 128/70 mm Hg, and pulse rate is 98/min. There is a new grade 2/6 holosystolic murmur at the apex. Conjunctival petechiae are present.

Three sets of blood cultures grow Streptococcus gallolyticus (formerly S. bovis biotype I). Transesophageal echocardiogram shows an 8-mm mobile vegetation on the anterior mitral leaflet. Hemoglobin is 10.8 g/dL with an MCV of 76 fL.

Appropriate intravenous antibiotic therapy is started.
CV-029.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate additional diagnostic test?
CV-029.explain_html:
Correct answer: C Streptococcus gallolyticus endocarditis

Streptococcus gallolyticus (S. bovis group) bacteremia or endocarditis has a strong association with colorectal neoplasia — adenomas or carcinoma in up to 60% of patients. The organism colonizes the colon, and disrupted mucosa over a tumor lets it into the bloodstream.

Every patient with S. gallolyticus bacteremia needs colonoscopy, even without GI symptoms. His microcytic anemia adds to the concern. The organism is also associated with chronic liver disease.

Similar "bug → hidden source" links: Clostridium septicum → colon cancer; Streptococcus anginosus group → abscesses; Fusobacterium necrophorum → Lemierre syndrome; HACEK organisms → dental source.

Why not the others

  • (A) Dental panoramic radiography — Viridans group streptococci (not S. gallolyticus) suggest a dental source.
  • (B) Abdominal ultrasonography — Liver disease is associated with S. gallolyticus, but the priority is to look for colorectal neoplasia.
  • (D) Upper endoscopy — The association is with colorectal, not upper GI, neoplasia. Microcytic anemia in an older man needs colonoscopy first.
  • (E) Echocardiography of all first-degree relatives — Infective endocarditis is not inherited; relatives do not need echocardiography.
🧠 Mnemonic

S. bovis — "bovis in the bowel" → scope the colon.

🎯 Educational objective

Perform colonoscopy in patients with Streptococcus gallolyticus (S. bovis) bacteremia or endocarditis because of the strong association with colorectal neoplasia.

CV-030.stem_html:
A 61-year-old woman with metastatic lung adenocarcinoma is brought to the emergency department with 3 days of progressive dyspnea and lightheadedness.

On physical examination, blood pressure is 86/64 mm Hg, pulse rate is 124/min, and respiration rate is 26/min. Oxygen saturation is 94% breathing ambient air. Jugular venous pressure is elevated to the angle of the jaw. Heart sounds are muffled. Systolic blood pressure falls by 18 mm Hg during inspiration. Lungs are clear.

ECG shows sinus tachycardia with low QRS voltage and beat-to-beat variation in QRS amplitude. Bedside echocardiogram shows a large circumferential pericardial effusion with diastolic collapse of the right ventricle and a plethoric inferior vena cava.
CV-030.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
CV-030.explain_html:
Correct answer: B Cardiac tamponade

This is cardiac tamponade: pericardial fluid under pressure compresses the heart and limits filling. Beck triad (hypotension, raised JVP, muffled heart sounds) + pulsus paradoxus (>10 mm Hg inspiratory fall in systolic BP) + electrical alternans (the heart swinging in the fluid) + echocardiographic RV diastolic collapse and a plethoric IVC.

Tamponade is obstructive shock. The only effective treatment is urgent drainage — pericardiocentesis (echo-guided needle) or surgical pericardial window. While preparing, give an IV fluid bolus to support preload. Malignant effusions often recur, so a drain or window may be needed later.

Why not the others

  • (A) Colchicine and ibuprofen — Anti-inflammatory therapy treats pericarditis; it does not relieve hemodynamic compromise.
  • (C) Intravenous furosemide — Diuretics lower preload and worsen tamponade physiology.
  • (D) Positive-pressure mechanical ventilation — Positive-pressure ventilation raises intrathoracic pressure, reduces venous return and can cause cardiovascular collapse in tamponade.
  • (E) Intravenous norepinephrine as definitive therapy — Vasopressors may briefly support blood pressure but do not relieve the compression.
🎓 ABIM pearl

Pulsus paradoxus is an exaggeration of normal physiology: on inspiration the RV fills, and in tamponade the septum bulges into the LV (interventricular dependence), so LV stroke volume falls. It also occurs in severe asthma/COPD, massive PE and RV infarction.

🎯 Educational objective

Treat cardiac tamponade with urgent pericardiocentesis; avoid diuretics and positive-pressure ventilation.

CV-031.stem_html:
A 64-year-old man with long-standing poorly controlled hypertension presents with sudden, severe tearing pain between his shoulder blades that began 2 hours ago.

On physical examination, blood pressure is 182/104 mm Hg in the right arm and 176/100 mm Hg in the left arm; pulse rate is 96/min. Pulses are present and equal in all four extremities. Neurologic examination is normal. There is no murmur.

CT angiography shows a dissection flap starting distal to the left subclavian artery and extending to the level of the renal arteries. The ascending aorta and arch are not involved. There is no malperfusion, rupture or periaortic hematoma. Creatinine is 1.0 mg/dL and lactate is normal.
CV-031.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate initial management?

choices.D: Intravenous esmolol followed by intravenous nicardipine as needed

CV-031.explain_html:
Correct answer: D Uncomplicated type B aortic dissection

This is an acute type B (Stanford) dissection — it spares the ascending aorta — and it is uncomplicated (no malperfusion, rupture, refractory pain or uncontrolled hypertension).

Uncomplicated type B dissection is treated medically in the ICU. The goals are to reduce shear stress (dP/dt) on the aortic wall:

  1. IV beta-blocker first (esmolol or labetalol) → heart rate <60/min.
  2. Then a vasodilator (nicardipine, clevidipine, nitroprusside) if needed → systolic BP 100–120 mm Hg, within 20 minutes.
  3. IV opioids for pain.

Type A (ascending aorta) dissection is a surgical emergency. Complicated type B dissection is treated with TEVAR (thoracic endovascular repair).

Why not the others

  • (A) Emergency open surgical repair — Open surgery is for type A dissection. Uncomplicated type B is managed medically, with endovascular repair for complications.
  • (B) Intravenous nicardipine alone — A vasodilator given without prior beta-blockade causes reflex tachycardia and increases dP/dt.
  • (C) Intravenous hydralazine — Hydralazine causes reflex tachycardia, which raises shear stress on the aortic wall.
  • (E) Heparin infusion — Anticoagulation is contraindicated in acute aortic dissection.
🧠 Mnemonic

"Rate before pressure" — beta-block first (HR <60), then vasodilate (SBP 100–120).

🎯 Educational objective

Treat acute uncomplicated type B aortic dissection medically with an intravenous beta-blocker first, then a vasodilator, to a heart rate below 60/min and systolic BP of 100–120 mm Hg.

CV-032.stem_html:
A 68-year-old man comes for a routine health maintenance visit. He feels well. He has hypertension and hyperlipidemia. He smoked one pack of cigarettes daily for 30 years and quit 8 years ago. His brother had an abdominal aortic aneurysm repaired at age 70.

On physical examination, blood pressure is 130/78 mm Hg and pulse rate is 70/min. BMI is 29. Abdominal examination shows no pulsatile mass. Femoral and pedal pulses are normal.
CV-032.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate screening test?
CV-032.explain_html:
Correct answer: C Abdominal aortic aneurysm screening

The USPSTF recommends one-time ultrasonography screening for abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA) in men aged 65 to 75 years who have ever smoked (≥100 cigarettes in a lifetime) — Grade B. Screening this group reduces AAA rupture and AAA-related death. A family history of AAA adds to his risk.

A normal aorta (<3.0 cm) needs no further screening. If an aneurysm is found, surveillance intervals depend on size, and elective repair is recommended at ≥5.5 cm in men (≥5.0 cm in women), growth >0.5 cm in 6 months, or symptoms.

Group USPSTF
Men 65–75, ever smoked One-time screen (B)
Men 65–75, never smoked Selective (C) — e.g., family history
Women who never smoked Do not screen (D)
Women 65–75 who ever smoked Insufficient evidence (I)

Why not the others

  • (A) CT angiography of the abdomen — CT exposes him to contrast and radiation; ultrasonography is accurate, safe and cheap for screening.
  • (B) No screening is indicated — He is a former smoker in the target age range, the group with the clearest benefit from screening.
  • (D) Ankle-brachial index — The ABI detects peripheral artery disease and is not recommended for screening asymptomatic adults.
  • (E) Abdominal ultrasonography every 2 years — Repeated screening after a normal study is not recommended; new large aneurysms rarely develop after a normal scan at this age.
🎓 ABIM pearl

Physical examination is not a reliable screen for AAA, especially in patients with obesity — always use ultrasonography.

🎯 Educational objective

Screen men aged 65 to 75 years who have ever smoked with a one-time abdominal ultrasound for abdominal aortic aneurysm.

CV-033.stem_html:
A 66-year-old man is evaluated for 6 months of cramping pain in his right calf that comes on after walking two blocks and resolves within 3 minutes of rest. He has hypertension, type 2 diabetes and a 40 pack-year smoking history; he quit 1 year ago. Medications are lisinopril, metformin and aspirin.

On physical examination, blood pressure is 136/78 mm Hg. Right popliteal and pedal pulses are diminished. The skin is intact without ulcers, and capillary refill is normal.

Ankle-brachial index (right)0.68
Ankle-brachial index (left)0.92
LDL cholesterol118 mg/dL
Hemoglobin A1c7.1%
CV-033.lead: In addition to continuing aspirin, which of the following is the most appropriate management?

choices.B: Begin high-intensity statin therapy and supervised exercise therapy
choices.E: Begin cilostazol and refer for angiography

CV-033.explain_html:
Correct answer: B Peripheral artery disease — claudication

He has symptomatic peripheral artery disease (PAD) with intermittent claudication — reproducible exertional calf pain relieved by rest — confirmed by a resting ABI ≤0.90. There are no signs of chronic limb-threatening ischemia (rest pain, ulcers, gangrene).

PAD is a coronary artery disease equivalent. Care has two goals:

  1. Lower cardiovascular risk: high-intensity statin, antiplatelet therapy (aspirin or clopidogrel), BP and diabetes control, smoking abstinence. Low-dose rivaroxaban (2.5 mg twice daily) plus aspirin further reduces events in selected patients (COMPASS, VOYAGER-PAD).
  2. Improve walking: supervised exercise therapy (30–45 minutes, ≥3 times weekly for ≥12 weeks) improves walking distance as much as revascularization. Cilostazol is the drug for persistent symptoms (avoid in heart failure).

Revascularization is for lifestyle-limiting claudication despite exercise and medical therapy, or for chronic limb-threatening ischemia.

ABI Meaning
>1.40 Noncompressible (calcified) vessels — use toe-brachial index
1.00–1.40 Normal
0.91–0.99 Borderline
≤0.90 PAD

Why not the others

  • (A) Begin warfarin — Full-dose warfarin adds bleeding risk without benefit in PAD.
  • (C) Refer for endovascular revascularization — Revascularization comes only after a trial of exercise and medical therapy fails, or for limb-threatening ischemia.
  • (D) Begin pentoxifylline — Pentoxifylline is no better than placebo for claudication.
  • (E) Begin cilostazol and refer for angiography — Cilostazol can be added later for persistent symptoms, but angiography is not needed unless revascularization is planned.
🎯 Educational objective

Treat intermittent claudication with high-intensity statin therapy, antiplatelet therapy, risk factor control and supervised exercise therapy before considering revascularization.

CV-034.stem_html:
A 34-year-old woman is evaluated after a work screening showed high cholesterol. She feels well and exercises regularly. She does not smoke. Her father had a myocardial infarction at age 44. She uses a copper IUD for contraception and does not plan pregnancy in the next few years.

On physical examination, blood pressure is 118/74 mm Hg. BMI is 23. There are firm nodules on both Achilles tendons. The remainder of the examination is normal.

Total cholesterol312 mg/dL
LDL cholesterol224 mg/dL
HDL cholesterol58 mg/dL
Triglycerides150 mg/dL
TSH1.6 µU/mL
Fasting glucose88 mg/dL
CV-034.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

choices.A: Recommend dietary changes and repeat lipids in 6 months
choices.B: Obtain a coronary artery calcium score
choices.D: Calculate the 10-year ASCVD risk to decide on statin therapy

CV-034.explain_html:
Correct answer: E Familial hypercholesterolemia

An LDL cholesterol ≥190 mg/dL means severe primary hypercholesterolemia. With tendon xanthomas and premature CAD in a first-degree relative, she very likely has heterozygous familial hypercholesterolemia (LDL-receptor, APOB or PCSK9 variant). Secondary causes — hypothyroidism, nephrotic syndrome, cholestatic liver disease, drugs — have been excluded.

These patients have had high LDL since birth, so their lifetime risk is high even when a 10-year score looks low. Risk calculators do not apply. Start a high-intensity statin (atorvastatin 40–80 mg or rosuvastatin 20–40 mg) to reduce LDL by ≥50% (and ideally to <100 mg/dL). Add ezetimibe and then a PCSK9 inhibitor if needed. Offer cascade screening of first-degree relatives.

She must avoid pregnancy while taking a statin; her IUD is appropriate.

Why not the others

  • (A) Recommend dietary changes and repeat lipids in 6 months — Diet alone cannot lower genetically driven LDL of this degree, and delaying therapy extends her exposure.
  • (B) Obtain a coronary artery calcium score — A calcium score helps decide on statins in borderline-to-intermediate risk. A score of zero is common in young people with FH and would falsely reassure.
  • (C) Begin ezetimibe alone — Ezetimibe lowers LDL by about 20% — not enough. It is an add-on to a statin.
  • (D) Calculate the 10-year ASCVD risk to decide on statin therapy — Pooled cohort equations are not used when LDL is ≥190 mg/dL; they underestimate risk in familial hypercholesterolemia.
🎓 ABIM pearl

Dutch Lipid Clinic criteria for FH: LDL level, tendon xanthomas, corneal arcus before age 45, and premature CAD (men <55, women <60) in the patient or first-degree relatives.

🎯 Educational objective

Start high-intensity statin therapy, without risk calculation, in adults with LDL cholesterol of 190 mg/dL or higher.

CV-035.topic: Coronary artery calcium score in borderline risk
CV-035.stem_html:
A 52-year-old man is evaluated for cardiovascular risk. He feels well. He does not smoke and has no diabetes. His blood pressure is 128/80 mm Hg without treatment. There is no family history of premature coronary disease. He is reluctant to take a "lifelong pill" unless he truly needs it.

Total cholesterol214 mg/dL
LDL cholesterol136 mg/dL
HDL cholesterol46 mg/dL
Triglycerides160 mg/dL
10-year ASCVD risk (pooled cohort equations)8.2%
CV-035.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step to guide the decision about statin therapy?
CV-035.explain_html:
Correct answer: E Coronary artery calcium score in borderline risk

His 10-year ASCVD risk is intermediate (7.5% to <20%), and he is uncertain about starting a statin. When the decision is unclear in borderline (5% to <7.5%) or intermediate risk, a coronary artery calcium (CAC) score is the best risk "tiebreaker".

CAC score Statin decision
0 Reasonable to withhold statin (reassess in 5–10 y) unless diabetes, smoking or strong family history
1–99 Favors statin, especially if age ≥55
≥100 or ≥75th percentile Start statin

A CAC of zero has a very high negative predictive value for events over the next decade. Other risk enhancers (family history of premature ASCVD, LDL ≥160, metabolic syndrome, CKD, inflammatory disease, high lipoprotein(a), high hs-CRP, South Asian ancestry, premature menopause or preeclampsia) also tip the balance toward a statin.

Why not the others

  • (A) Exercise ECG stress test — Stress testing is for symptoms; it is not recommended for risk assessment in asymptomatic adults.
  • (B) Coronary CT angiography — CCTA uses contrast and more radiation and is a test for symptomatic patients, not for risk stratification.
  • (C) High-sensitivity C-reactive protein — hs-CRP ≥2 mg/L is a risk enhancer, but it reclassifies risk far less than CAC.
  • (D) Carotid intima-media thickness ultrasonography — Carotid intima-media thickness adds little to risk prediction and is not recommended.
🎯 Educational objective

Use a coronary artery calcium score to guide statin decisions in asymptomatic adults at borderline or intermediate 10-year ASCVD risk when the decision is uncertain.

DE-001.stem_html:
A 51-year-old man comes to the office because his wife noticed that a mole on his upper back has grown and darkened over the past 6 months. It occasionally itches. He had several blistering sunburns as a child and works outdoors. He has no personal or family history of skin cancer.

On the left upper back there is a 9-mm, asymmetric pigmented macule with an irregular, notched border and several shades of brown, black and blue-gray. It looks different from his other moles. There is no palpable axillary or cervical lymphadenopathy.
DE-001.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

choices.A: Photograph the lesion and re-examine in 3 months

DE-001.explain_html:
Correct answer: C Suspected melanoma

The lesion has almost every ABCDE feature of melanoma plus the "ugly duckling" sign — it looks different from the patient's other nevi.

The best first step is a full-thickness excisional biopsy with narrow (1–3 mm) clinical margins, oriented along lymphatic drainage. The pathologist needs the whole lesion and its full depth to measure Breslow thickness — the most important prognostic factor — which then determines the definitive wide-excision margin and whether sentinel lymph node biopsy is needed.

Breslow thickness Wide excision margin
In situ 0.5–1 cm
≤1.0 mm 1 cm
1.01–2.0 mm 1–2 cm
>2.0 mm 2 cm

Why not the others

  • (A) Photograph the lesion and re-examine in 3 months — Monitoring is for lesions with low suspicion. A changing, multicolored, asymmetric lesion needs tissue now.
  • (B) Cryotherapy — Destroying the lesion leaves no tissue for diagnosis or staging.
  • (D) Wide local excision with 2-cm margins — Wide margins are chosen after histologic depth is known; excising first without diagnosis risks wrong margins and disrupts lymphatic mapping.
  • (E) Superficial shave biopsy — A superficial shave can transect the base and make accurate Breslow staging impossible. (A deep saucerization that removes the whole lesion is an acceptable alternative.)
🧠 Mnemonic

ABCDE: Asymmetry, Border irregularity, Color variation, Diameter >6 mm, Evolution (change in size, shape, color, symptoms).

🎓 ABIM pearl

Evolution is the most sensitive single feature. Nodular melanoma often lacks ABCD features — remember "EFG": Elevated, Firm, Growing for more than a month.

🎯 Educational objective

A lesion suspicious for melanoma should be removed by full-thickness excisional biopsy with narrow margins so that Breslow depth can guide definitive treatment.

DE-002.topic: Drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms (DRESS)
DE-002.stem_html:
A 58-year-old woman comes to the emergency department with 4 days of fever and a spreading itchy rash that began on her face and trunk. Allopurinol was started 5 weeks ago for recurrent gout. She has chronic kidney disease. She takes no other new medications.

Temperature is 38.9 °C (102.0 °F), blood pressure is 118/70 mm Hg and pulse is 104/min. There is facial edema and a confluent erythematous morbilliform eruption covering about 60% of the body surface. There are no blisters, skin sloughing or mucosal erosions. Tender cervical and axillary lymphadenopathy is present.

Leukocyte count14,800/µL
Eosinophils1,900/µL
Atypical lymphocytespresent
ALT342 U/L
AST266 U/L
Creatinine2.1 mg/dL (baseline 1.5 mg/dL)
DE-002.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

choices.A: Stop allopurinol and start systemic glucocorticoids
choices.B: Stop allopurinol and switch to febuxostat
choices.C: Stop allopurinol and observe without other treatment
choices.D: Continue allopurinol and add an oral antihistamine
choices.E: Continue allopurinol at a lower dose

DE-002.explain_html:
Correct answer: A Drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms (DRESS)

Fever, a widespread rash with facial edema, lymphadenopathy, eosinophilia, atypical lymphocytes and organ involvement (liver, kidney) starting 2–8 weeks after a new drug is DRESS (drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms). Mortality is up to about 10%, mostly from liver failure.

Management:

  1. Stop the culprit drug immediately — the single most important step.
  2. With significant organ involvement (as here — hepatitis and acute kidney injury), give systemic glucocorticoids (for example prednisone 0.5–1 mg/kg/day) with a slow taper over 6–12 weeks; tapering too fast causes relapse.
  3. Monitor for late complications: autoimmune thyroiditis, type 1 diabetes and reactivation of HHV-6.
Common culprits of DRESS
Allopurinol, aromatic anticonvulsants (carbamazepine, phenytoin, lamotrigine, phenobarbital)
Sulfonamides (including sulfasalazine, dapsone), minocycline, vancomycin

Why not the others

  • (B) Stop allopurinol and switch to febuxostat — Avoid any urate-lowering therapy until DRESS resolves; restarting a related drug during active disease is unsafe. Febuxostat can be considered later with specialist input.
  • (C) Stop allopurinol and observe without other treatment — Stopping the drug is necessary but not enough with hepatitis and kidney injury; systemic glucocorticoids are recommended for moderate–severe organ involvement.
  • (D) Continue allopurinol and add an oral antihistamine — Continuing the culprit drug allows ongoing immune activation and organ damage. Antihistamines only help itch.
  • (E) Continue allopurinol at a lower dose — Dose reduction does not stop an immune reaction. Allopurinol must never be given again to this patient.
🎓 ABIM pearl

Timing separates the big drug eruptions: morbilliform exanthem 1–2 weeks, SJS/TEN 4–28 days (mucosal erosions, skin detachment), DRESS 2–8 weeks (eosinophilia, organs), AGEP within days (sterile pustules).

🎯 Educational objective

DRESS presents 2–8 weeks after drugs such as allopurinol with fever, rash, eosinophilia and organ injury; stop the drug and give systemic glucocorticoids with a slow taper when organs are involved.

DE-003.stem_html:
A 38-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department with 2 days of fever, painful skin and a spreading rash. She started lamotrigine for bipolar disorder 3 weeks ago. Before the rash she had a sore throat and burning eyes.

On physical examination, temperature is 38.8 °C (101.8 °F), blood pressure is 108/64 mm Hg, and pulse rate is 118/min. There are dusky red macules and flaccid blisters on the trunk and face, with areas of epidermal detachment covering about 20% of the body surface area. Gentle lateral pressure on normal-looking skin causes the epidermis to slide off (positive Nikolsky sign). There are erosions of the lips, oral mucosa and conjunctivae.
DE-003.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.A: Stop lamotrigine and transfer to a burn unit or ICU
choices.B: Continue lamotrigine at a lower dose
choices.C: Discharge with oral prednisone and dermatology follow-up
choices.D: Start intravenous vancomycin and piperacillin-tazobactam for staphylococcal scalded skin

DE-003.explain_html:
Correct answer: A Stevens-Johnson syndrome / toxic epidermal necrolysis

Fever and a prodrome, then painful dusky skin with blisters, positive Nikolsky sign and mucosal involvement (≥2 sites), 1–3 weeks after starting a high-risk drug → Stevens-Johnson syndrome/toxic epidermal necrolysis overlap (SJS <10% BSA; overlap 10–30%; TEN >30%).

The single most important step is to stop the culprit drug immediately — earlier withdrawal lowers mortality. Then transfer to a burn unit or ICU for wound care, fluid and electrolyte management, temperature control, nutrition, infection surveillance, and urgent ophthalmology (to prevent scarring and blindness). Calculate SCORTEN for prognosis.

Adjunctive therapies such as cyclosporine or etanercept may reduce mortality; systemic glucocorticoids and IVIG are controversial.

High-risk drugs for SJS/TEN
Allopurinol (HLA-B*58:01)
Anticonvulsants — carbamazepine (HLA-B15:02), phenytoin, lamotrigine*, phenobarbital
Sulfonamides (TMP-SMX)
NSAIDs (oxicams), nevirapine

Why not the others

  • (B) Continue lamotrigine at a lower dose — The drug must be stopped permanently; continuing it at any dose causes progression and death.
  • (C) Discharge with oral prednisone and dermatology follow-up — SJS/TEN with 20% detachment needs intensive inpatient care; outpatient steroids are unsafe.
  • (D) Start intravenous vancomycin and piperacillin-tazobactam for staphylococcal scalded skin — Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome mostly affects children and adults with kidney failure and spares mucous membranes; prophylactic antibiotics are not recommended in SJS/TEN.
  • (E) Topical triamcinolone to affected areas — Topical steroids do not treat SJS/TEN and are not appropriate for extensive denuded skin.
🎯 Educational objective

In suspected SJS/TEN, immediately stop the culprit drug and transfer the patient to a burn unit or ICU with urgent ophthalmology involvement.

DE-004.stem_html:
A 44-year-old man is evaluated for a 10-year history of itchy skin plaques. He has used topical clobetasol with partial relief, but the plaques are spreading. For the past 6 months his fingers have become swollen ("like sausages"), and he has morning stiffness in his hands for 1 hour.

On physical examination, BMI is 33. There are well-demarcated erythematous plaques with silvery scale on the elbows, knees, scalp and lower back covering about 12% of body surface area. There is nail pitting and onycholysis. The second and third fingers of the right hand are diffusely swollen (dactylitis), and there is tenderness at several distal interphalangeal joints.

Rheumatoid factor and anti-CCP antibodiesnegative
Hand radiographDIP erosions
Hepatitis B and C serologiesnegative
Interferon-γ release assaynegative
DE-004.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?

choices.A: A TNF inhibitor or IL-17 inhibitor

DE-004.explain_html:
Correct answer: A Psoriasis — comorbidities and treatment

He has moderate-to-severe plaque psoriasis (>10% BSA) and psoriatic arthritis — dactylitis, DIP joint involvement, nail disease, seronegative, with erosions. Up to 30% of people with psoriasis develop psoriatic arthritis; nail disease is the strongest predictor.

With erosive arthritis plus extensive skin disease, the best choice is a biologic that treats both — a TNF inhibitor (adalimumab, etanercept, infliximab, certolizumab, golimumab) or an IL-17 inhibitor (secukinumab, ixekizumab), or an IL-23 inhibitor (guselkumab, risankizumab). Screening for TB and hepatitis B has been done. Methotrexate is an option for skin and peripheral arthritis but is less effective for dactylitis and erosive disease.

Psoriasis is a systemic inflammatory disease: screen for obesity, metabolic syndrome, diabetes, dyslipidemia, cardiovascular disease, MASLD, depression and IBD.

Why not the others

  • (B) Hydroxychloroquine — Hydroxychloroquine is ineffective for psoriatic arthritis and can trigger psoriasis flares.
  • (C) Oral prednisone taper — Systemic glucocorticoids can provoke a severe (pustular or erythrodermic) psoriasis flare when tapered.
  • (D) Higher-potency topical steroid with occlusion — Topical therapy is appropriate for limited disease (<3–5% BSA) and does not treat psoriatic arthritis.
  • (E) Narrowband UVB phototherapy alone — Phototherapy helps skin disease but does not treat erosive arthritis.
🎯 Educational objective

Treat moderate-to-severe psoriasis with erosive psoriatic arthritis with a biologic (TNF, IL-17 or IL-23 inhibitor) after screening for TB and hepatitis B, and screen for metabolic and cardiovascular comorbidities.

DE-005.topic: Basal cell carcinoma on the face
DE-005.stem_html:
A 68-year-old man with a history of extensive sun exposure as a farmer is evaluated for a slowly growing lesion on the side of his nose that occasionally bleeds. It has been present for 1 year.

On physical examination, there is a 9-mm pearly, translucent papule with rolled borders, telangiectasias and a small central ulcer on the left nasal ala. There is no lymphadenopathy.

Shave biopsy shows infiltrative basal cell carcinoma.
DE-005.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?

choices.C: Observation, because basal cell carcinoma rarely metastasizes

DE-005.explain_html:
Correct answer: E Basal cell carcinoma on the face

Basal cell carcinoma (BCC) is the most common cancer in humans. It rarely metastasizes, but it invades and destroys local tissue — especially on the central face.

Mohs micrographic surgery is the treatment of choice for high-risk BCC:

  • Location in the "H zone" of the face (nose, eyelids, lips, ears, temples) — the "mask" area
  • Aggressive histology — infiltrative, morpheaform/sclerosing, micronodular
  • Size ≥2 cm on trunk/extremities; recurrent tumors; immunosuppression

Mohs removes the tumor layer by layer with complete margin examination, giving the highest cure rate (~99%) with the most tissue sparing — crucial on the nose.

Low-risk superficial BCC on the trunk can be treated with curettage and electrodesiccation, topical imiquimod or 5-FU, cryotherapy or standard excision.

Why not the others

  • (A) Topical 5-fluorouracil — Topical 5-FU is for superficial BCC in low-risk sites, not infiltrative tumors.
  • (B) Cryotherapy — Cryotherapy lacks margin control and is used for superficial, low-risk lesions on the trunk, not infiltrative BCC on the nose.
  • (C) Observation, because basal cell carcinoma rarely metastasizes — BCC grows and destroys local tissue; untreated facial BCC can invade cartilage and bone.
  • (D) Vismodegib — Hedgehog inhibitors are for locally advanced or metastatic BCC that cannot be treated with surgery or radiation.
🎯 Educational objective

Treat high-risk basal cell carcinoma (central face, infiltrative histology) with Mohs micrographic surgery.

DE-006.stem_html:
A 29-year-old woman is evaluated for 1 week of painful red nodules on both shins. Three weeks ago she had a sore throat and fever that resolved without treatment. She takes an oral contraceptive. She has no cough, diarrhea, joint pain, abdominal pain or weight loss.

On physical examination, temperature is 37.4 °C (99.3 °F). There are several tender, warm, poorly demarcated, erythematous subcutaneous nodules on both anterior shins. There is no ulceration. The remainder of the examination is normal.
DE-006.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate initial evaluation?

choices.C: Antistreptolysin O titer and chest radiograph

DE-006.explain_html:
Correct answer: C Erythema nodosum — evaluation

Erythema nodosum (EN) — tender, red, warm subcutaneous nodules on the anterior shins that do not ulcerate and heal without scarring (bruise-like) — is a septal panniculitis, a hypersensitivity reaction to many triggers. The diagnosis is clinical; biopsy is rarely needed.

About half of cases are idiopathic, but EN is a clue to an underlying disease:

Cause Clues and tests
Streptococcal infection (most common identified cause) Recent pharyngitis — ASO, anti-DNase B
Sarcoidosis (Löfgren) Chest radiograph — hilar adenopathy
Drugs Oral contraceptives, sulfonamides, penicillins
IBD (Crohn, UC) GI symptoms
TB, fungal (coccidioidomycosis), Yersinia Exposures
Pregnancy, Behçet, lymphoma

A reasonable initial evaluation is CBC, ESR/CRP, ASO titer, chest radiograph (± TB testing). Treat the cause; NSAIDs, rest, leg elevation, and compression for symptoms. Consider stopping the oral contraceptive.

Why not the others

  • (A) Colonoscopy — Colonoscopy is indicated only with GI symptoms suggesting IBD.
  • (B) Excisional biopsy of a nodule — Biopsy is reserved for atypical lesions (ulceration, unusual locations, persistence) to exclude other panniculitides.
  • (D) No evaluation is needed — EN often signals an underlying disease; a basic evaluation is indicated.
  • (E) Interferon-γ release assay only — TB testing may be included, but the most likely triggers (streptococcal infection, sarcoidosis) are evaluated with ASO and chest radiography.
🎯 Educational objective

Evaluate erythema nodosum with ASO titers (for streptococcal infection) and a chest radiograph (for sarcoidosis), and review medications such as oral contraceptives.

DE-007.stem_html:
A 52-year-old man with type 2 diabetes is evaluated for an itchy rash in his groin and inner thighs for 2 months. A clinician prescribed a topical hydrocortisone and clotrimazole-betamethasone cream, and the rash briefly improved, then spread.

On physical examination, there are annular, erythematous plaques with a raised scaly advancing border and central clearing on the inner thighs. The scrotum is spared. There are no satellite pustules. His toenails are thick and yellow, and there is scaling between the toes.
DE-007.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate diagnostic test?

choices.A: Potassium hydroxide (KOH) preparation of scale from the border

DE-007.explain_html:
Correct answer: A Tinea — KOH preparation

Annular scaly plaques with an active scaly border and central clearing in the groin, sparing the scrotum, with onychomycosis and tinea pedis (the usual source) → tinea cruris (dermatophyte, usually Trichophyton rubrum). Topical steroids partly suppress and then spread dermatophyte infection (tinea incognito).

Confirm with a KOH preparation of scale scraped from the advancing edge: septate branching hyphae. Fungal culture can identify the species.

Tinea cruris Candidal intertrigo Erythrasma
Scrotum Spared Involved Variable
Border Raised, scaly Beefy red with satellite pustules Brown, no active border
Test KOH: hyphae KOH: pseudohyphae, yeast Wood lamp: coral-red

Treat with a topical allylamine (terbinafine) or azole for 2–4 weeks; stop topical steroids; treat the feet to prevent recurrence. Oral terbinafine for onychomycosis (after nail testing).

Why not the others

  • (B) Patch testing — Patch testing evaluates allergic contact dermatitis, which does not have central clearing with an advancing scaly border.
  • (C) Bacterial culture of the rash — Bacterial cultures do not diagnose a dermatophyte infection.
  • (D) Punch biopsy for direct immunofluorescence — Direct immunofluorescence is for autoimmune blistering diseases.
  • (E) Wood lamp examination — Wood lamp shows coral-red fluorescence in erythrasma (Corynebacterium); dermatophytes of the groin do not fluoresce.
🎯 Educational objective

Confirm tinea with a KOH preparation of scale from the advancing border showing septate hyphae, and avoid topical steroids.

EN-001.stem_html:
A 38-year-old woman comes to the office with 10 days of pain in the front of her neck that spreads to her jaw and ears. She also has palpitations, sweating and trouble sleeping. Three weeks ago she had a sore throat and cough that resolved on their own. She takes no medications.

Temperature is 37.9 °C (100.2 °F), blood pressure is 128/72 mm Hg and pulse is 108/min. The thyroid is mildly enlarged, firm and exquisitely tender to palpation. There is a fine tremor of the outstretched hands. There is no proptosis or lid lag.

TSH<0.01 µU/mL
Free T₄3.1 ng/dL
Erythrocyte sedimentation rate82 mm/h
Leukocyte count9,800/µL
24-hour radioactive iodine uptake1% (normal 10%–30%)
EN-001.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
EN-001.explain_html:
Correct answer: D Subacute (de Quervain) thyroiditis

A painful, tender thyroid after a viral illness, fever, a very high ESR, thyrotoxicosis and a near-zero radioiodine uptake is subacute granulomatous (de Quervain) thyroiditis.

The problem is leakage, not overproduction. Inflammation breaks follicles and releases stored hormone into the blood; the gland is not making new hormone, so uptake is low. The course has three phases: thyrotoxic (weeks) → hypothyroid (weeks–months) → recovery in most patients.

Treatment is supportive: a beta-blocker for adrenergic symptoms and an NSAID for pain. Use prednisone (for example 40 mg/day tapered over weeks) if pain is severe or does not respond to NSAIDs.

Low-uptake thyrotoxicosis Clue
Subacute thyroiditis Tender gland, fever, high ESR
Painless / postpartum thyroiditis Nontender, within 1 year of delivery, TPO antibodies
Exogenous thyroid hormone Low thyroglobulin, small gland
Iodine load (amiodarone, contrast) History

Why not the others

  • (A) Radioactive iodine ablation — Radioiodine is not taken up by an inflamed gland (uptake 1%) and the condition is self-limited.
  • (B) Methimazole — Thionamides block hormone synthesis. Here the gland is not synthesizing extra hormone, so methimazole does not help.
  • (C) Total thyroidectomy — Surgery has no role in a self-limited inflammatory condition.
  • (E) Levothyroxine — Levothyroxine may be needed later if the hypothyroid phase is symptomatic or persists, but it worsens the current thyrotoxic phase.
🎓 ABIM pearl

Thyroglobulin separates thyroiditis (high) from surreptitious levothyroxine use (low) — both have low uptake.

🎯 Educational objective

Subacute thyroiditis causes painful, low-uptake thyrotoxicosis from hormone leakage; treat with a beta-blocker and an NSAID (or glucocorticoids if severe), not antithyroid drugs or radioiodine.

EN-002.stem_html:
A 59-year-old man with type 2 diabetes mellitus comes for follow-up. He had an anterior myocardial infarction 2 years ago. He takes metformin 1000 mg twice daily, aspirin, atorvastatin 80 mg, metoprolol succinate and lisinopril. He has gained 4 kg (8.8 lb) over the past year despite trying to diet. He has no symptoms of heart failure.

Blood pressure is 128/78 mm Hg and BMI is 33 kg/m². Examination is normal.

Hemoglobin A1c7.9%
Creatinine1.0 mg/dL (eGFR 82 mL/min/1.73 m²)
Urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio18 mg/g
Echocardiogram (1 year ago)LV ejection fraction 55%
EN-002.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate addition to his regimen?
EN-002.explain_html:
Correct answer: D Type 2 diabetes with cardiovascular disease

In type 2 diabetes with established ASCVD, add a drug with proven cardiovascular benefit — a GLP-1 receptor agonist or an SGLT2 inhibitor — regardless of A1c and independent of metformin. These drugs lower major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) by about 12%–26% in outcome trials.

For this patient a GLP-1 receptor agonist (semaglutide, dulaglutide, liraglutide) is the best fit: it reduces MACE, lowers A1c about 1%–1.5% and causes meaningful weight loss, which he needs. An SGLT2 inhibitor would be preferred first if he had heart failure or albuminuric CKD.

Comorbidity First add
ASCVD GLP-1 RA or SGLT2 inhibitor with proven benefit
Heart failure (any EF) SGLT2 inhibitor
CKD (eGFR ≥20, albuminuria) SGLT2 inhibitor; GLP-1 RA if needed
Obesity GLP-1 RA or dual GIP/GLP-1 RA (tirzepatide)

Why not the others

  • (A) Sitagliptin — DPP-4 inhibitors are weight-neutral and safe but showed no MACE reduction in outcome trials.
  • (B) Pioglitazone — Pioglitazone causes weight gain and fluid retention (heart-failure risk) and is not a first choice for cardiovascular risk reduction.
  • (C) Glipizide — Sulfonylureas lower glucose but cause hypoglycemia and weight gain and have no cardiovascular benefit.
  • (E) Insulin glargine — Basal insulin is not needed at an A1c of 7.9% and adds weight gain and hypoglycemia; GLP-1 RAs are preferred before insulin.
🧠 Mnemonic

"Hearts love GLP, pumps love SGLT." Atherosclerosis → GLP-1 RA or SGLT2i; heart failure or kidneys → SGLT2i.

🎓 ABIM pearl

GLP-1 RAs are contraindicated with a personal or family history of medullary thyroid cancer or MEN2. Hold them before procedures with deep sedation because of delayed gastric emptying.

🎯 Educational objective

For type 2 diabetes with ASCVD, add a GLP-1 receptor agonist or SGLT2 inhibitor with proven cardiovascular benefit; favor a GLP-1 RA when weight loss is also a goal.

EN-003.stem_html:
A 46-year-old woman is evaluated for a high calcium level found on routine laboratory testing. She feels well. She has no history of kidney stones or fractures. She takes no medications or supplements other than a daily multivitamin.

Examination is normal.

Calcium11.0 mg/dL
Albumin4.2 g/dL
Phosphorus2.4 mg/dL
Parathyroid hormone (intact)94 pg/mL
25-Hydroxyvitamin D34 ng/mL
Creatinine0.8 mg/dL
24-hour urine calcium260 mg
DXA (lowest T-score)−1.6 at the distal radius
Renal ultrasoundno nephrolithiasis or nephrocalcinosis
EN-003.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

choices.E: Observation with annual calcium and creatinine measurement

EN-003.explain_html:
Correct answer: B Primary hyperparathyroidism

High calcium with an inappropriately normal or high PTH means primary hyperparathyroidism (most often a single adenoma). A 24-hour urine calcium of 260 mg excludes familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia (FHH), which has very low urinary calcium.

Surgery cures the disease and is recommended for symptomatic patients and for asymptomatic patients who meet any of the criteria below. She is younger than 50, so she should have a parathyroidectomy even though she feels well — young patients face decades of bone and kidney damage.

Surgery for asymptomatic PHPT if any of:
Serum calcium >1 mg/dL above the upper limit of normal
Age <50
Osteoporosis (T-score ≤ −2.5 at spine, hip or distal radius) or vertebral fracture
eGFR <60 mL/min, nephrolithiasis or nephrocalcinosis, or urine calcium >250 mg/day (women) / >300 mg/day (men) with high stone risk

Why not the others

  • (A) Hydrochlorothiazide — Thiazides raise serum calcium by increasing distal tubular calcium reabsorption and would worsen hypercalcemia.
  • (C) Cinacalcet — Cinacalcet lowers serum calcium in patients who cannot or will not have surgery; it does not improve bone density or cure the disease.
  • (D) Alendronate — Bisphosphonates protect bone in patients who cannot have surgery, but they do not treat the cause; her bone density is not in the osteoporotic range.
  • (E) Observation with annual calcium and creatinine measurement — Observation is reasonable only when no surgical criterion is met. Her age alone is an indication.
🎓 ABIM pearl

Order imaging (sestamibi, 4D-CT or ultrasound) after deciding on surgery — to localize the gland for the surgeon, not to make the diagnosis.

🎯 Educational objective

Primary hyperparathyroidism is diagnosed biochemically; parathyroidectomy is indicated for asymptomatic patients who are younger than 50 or have marked hypercalcemia, osteoporosis, or kidney involvement.

EN-004.stem_html:
A 66-year-old woman comes for follow-up of osteoporosis. Five years ago a DXA scan showed a lumbar spine T-score of −2.6 and a total hip T-score of −2.2, and she started alendronate weekly. She has taken it consistently. She has never had a fracture and has not fallen. She does not smoke, drinks rarely, and takes no glucocorticoids. She walks daily and takes calcium in food and vitamin D 1000 units daily.

Height is unchanged from 5 years ago. Examination is normal.

DXA today — lumbar spine T-score−2.1
DXA today — total hip T-score−1.9
Calcium9.4 mg/dL
25-Hydroxyvitamin D36 ng/mL
Creatinine0.8 mg/dL
EN-004.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

choices.C: Stop alendronate and repeat DXA in 2–3 years

EN-004.explain_html:
Correct answer: C Osteoporosis — bisphosphonate drug holiday

Bisphosphonates bind to bone and keep working for years after they are stopped. After 5 years of oral therapy (3 years of IV zoledronic acid), reassess fracture risk.

She is now at lower risk: no fractures, hip T-score above −2.5, no new risk factors. For such patients, a drug holiday of 2–3 years is recommended — it keeps most of the benefit and lowers the rare but serious risks of long-term use: atypical femoral fracture and osteonecrosis of the jaw. Restart therapy when bone density falls or a fracture occurs.

After 5 y oral / 3 y IV bisphosphonate Plan
Low risk (no fracture, hip T > −2.5) Drug holiday, reassess in 2–3 years
High risk (hip T ≤ −2.5, fracture before or on therapy) Continue up to 10 y oral / 6 y IV, or switch

Why not the others

  • (A) Add teriparatide to alendronate — Anabolic therapy is for very high risk (recent fracture, T ≤ −3.0, multiple fractures). Combining with a bisphosphonate is not standard.
  • (B) Switch to denosumab — Denosumab is a strong option for high-risk patients, but it has no lasting effect — once started, it should not be stopped without follow-up therapy. Not needed here.
  • (D) Continue alendronate for another 5 years — Ten years of therapy is for patients who stay at high risk. In low-risk patients, extended therapy adds little fracture benefit and more atypical femoral fractures.
  • (E) Switch to raloxifene — Raloxifene is weaker (vertebral only) and raises the risk of venous thromboembolism and hot flashes. No reason to switch.
🎓 ABIM pearl

Never take a holiday from denosumab. Stopping it causes rapid bone loss and rebound multiple vertebral fractures — always follow it with a bisphosphonate.

🎯 Educational objective

After 5 years of oral bisphosphonate therapy, offer a 2–3-year drug holiday to women at lower fracture risk (no fracture, hip T-score above −2.5); continue or switch therapy for those at high risk.

EN-005.stem_html:
A 74-year-old woman comes to the office because of 2 weeks of fatigue and mild unsteadiness. Six weeks ago hydrochlorothiazide was added to her amlodipine for hypertension. She drinks about 2 L of fluid per day. She has no vomiting, diarrhea, headache or confusion.

Blood pressure is 132/76 mm Hg without orthostatic change, and pulse is 76/min. Mucous membranes are moist, jugular venous pressure is normal, and there is no edema. She is alert and oriented, and neurologic examination is normal.

Sodium124 mEq/L (6 months ago 139 mEq/L)
Potassium3.3 mEq/L
Serum osmolality262 mOsm/kg H₂O
Glucose96 mg/dL
Creatinine0.8 mg/dL
Urine osmolality410 mOsm/kg H₂O
Urine sodium58 mEq/L
TSH1.8 µU/mL
Cortisol (8 AM)16 µg/dL
EN-005.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.B: Continue hydrochlorothiazide and restrict fluids to 1 L/day

EN-005.explain_html:
Correct answer: A Thiazide-induced hyponatremia

She has hypotonic hyponatremia (osmolality 262) with mild symptoms that began after starting a thiazide. Thiazides act in the distal convoluted tubule, where they impair the kidney's ability to make dilute urine while leaving the medullary concentrating gradient intact. Older women with low body mass are at highest risk, usually within the first weeks of therapy.

The fix is to stop the thiazide (and replace potassium). Sodium usually recovers over days to weeks. She should not be rechallenged with a thiazide — the problem tends to recur. A different antihypertensive class (for example an ACE inhibitor or ARB) can be used.

Correct slowly: limit the rise to ≤8 mEq/L in 24 hours in high-risk patients (hypokalemia, alcohol use, malnutrition, advanced liver disease) to avoid osmotic demyelination syndrome.

Why not the others

  • (B) Continue hydrochlorothiazide and restrict fluids to 1 L/day — Fluid restriction alone while continuing the offending drug leaves the cause in place.
  • (C) Intravenous 0.9% saline, 2 L over 12 hours — Isotonic saline helps hypovolemic hyponatremia; she is euvolemic, and with a urine osmolality of 410 the saline load can be partly excreted as concentrated urine, retaining free water.
  • (D) Start tolvaptan — Tolvaptan is for persistent euvolemic or hypervolemic hyponatremia when other measures fail; it risks overly rapid correction and liver injury, and the cause here is reversible.
  • (E) Intravenous 3% saline 100-mL bolus — Hypertonic saline boluses are for severe symptoms (seizures, obtundation, respiratory distress). She is alert with mild symptoms.
🎓 ABIM pearl

Hyponatremia + hypokalemia in an older woman = think thiazide first. Hypokalemia also accelerates sodium rise when K⁺ is replaced (K⁺ shifts into cells, Na⁺ out) — watch the overcorrection.

🎯 Educational objective

Thiazide-induced hyponatremia with mild symptoms is treated by stopping the thiazide, correcting potassium, and avoiding rapid sodium correction.

EN-006.stem_html:
A 71-year-old woman is evaluated after routine testing showed an abnormal TSH level. She feels well and has no fatigue, cold intolerance, constipation or weight gain. She has hypertension treated with amlodipine. She is not planning pregnancy.

On physical examination, blood pressure is 132/76 mm Hg and pulse rate is 70/min. BMI is 25. The thyroid gland is normal in size without nodules. The remainder of the examination is normal.

TSH7.2 µU/mL (repeated 2 months later, 6.8 µU/mL)
Free thyroxine (T₄)1.1 ng/dL (normal)
Thyroid peroxidase antibodiespositive
LDL cholesterol112 mg/dL
EN-006.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

choices.C: Measure TSH again in 6 to 12 months

EN-006.explain_html:
Correct answer: C Subclinical hypothyroidism

She has subclinical hypothyroidism: an elevated TSH with a normal free T₄, confirmed on repeat testing. Her TSH is below 10 µU/mL, she has no symptoms, and she is older.

In the TRUST trial (adults ≥65 years with TSH 4.6–19.9), levothyroxine did not improve symptoms, quality of life or fatigue. TSH normally drifts upward with age, so a mildly high TSH in an older adult may be physiologic.

Monitor TSH every 6–12 months — positive TPO antibodies mean a higher chance (about 4% per year) of progression to overt hypothyroidism.

Treat subclinical hypothyroidism when
TSH ≥10 µU/mL
Pregnancy or planning pregnancy (any TSH above trimester range)
Younger patient with clear symptoms (trial of therapy)
Goiter or progressive rise in TSH

Why not the others

  • (A) Begin levothyroxine, 25 µg/d — Low-dose levothyroxine does not help asymptomatic older adults with TSH <10 µU/mL and risks overtreatment (atrial fibrillation, bone loss).
  • (B) Obtain thyroid ultrasonography — Her gland is normal on examination. Ultrasonography is for nodules or goiter, not for evaluating an abnormal TSH.
  • (D) Begin liothyronine (T₃) — Liothyronine is not used for routine replacement because of its short half-life and peaks of T₃.
  • (E) Begin levothyroxine, 1.6 µg/kg/d — Full replacement dosing is for overt hypothyroidism, and an older adult would start low even then.
🎓 ABIM pearl

Before diagnosing subclinical hypothyroidism, repeat the TSH in 2–3 months — transient elevations are common during recovery from illness (nonthyroidal illness) and after thyroiditis.

🎯 Educational objective

Do not treat asymptomatic subclinical hypothyroidism with a TSH below 10 µU/mL in older adults; monitor TSH periodically.

📚 Read more in Wardology🦋 Thyroid disease in the office →

EN-007.stem_html:
A 29-year-old woman who is 8 weeks pregnant is evaluated for palpitations, heat intolerance and a 3-kg (6.6-lb) weight loss over 2 months. She has no nausea or vomiting.

On physical examination, blood pressure is 128/66 mm Hg and pulse rate is 112/min. There is a diffusely enlarged, nontender thyroid with a bruit. Mild bilateral proptosis is present. She has a fine tremor.

TSH<0.01 µU/mL
Free thyroxine (T₄)3.9 ng/dL (normal for trimester, 0.8–1.8)
TSH receptor antibodies (TRAb)elevated
EN-007.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?

choices.C: Propranolol alone until the second trimester

EN-007.explain_html:
Correct answer: E Hyperthyroidism in early pregnancy

Diffuse goiter with a bruit, proptosis and positive TSH receptor antibodies mean Graves disease, not gestational transient thyrotoxicosis (which has no goiter or eye disease, negative TRAb and usually hyperemesis).

In the first trimester, the antithyroid drug of choice is propylthiouracil (PTU). Methimazole is teratogenic in weeks 6–10 (aplasia cutis, choanal/esophageal atresia, omphalocele). After the first trimester many experts switch to methimazole because PTU can cause severe hepatotoxicity.

Use the lowest dose that keeps free T₄ at or slightly above the upper limit of normal — antithyroid drugs cross the placenta and can cause fetal hypothyroidism and goiter. A beta-blocker can be used briefly for symptoms.

Situation Drug
First trimester / planning pregnancy PTU
Second and third trimesters Methimazole
Thyroid storm PTU (also blocks T₄→T₃ conversion)
Everyone else Methimazole

Why not the others

  • (A) Total thyroidectomy now — Thyroidectomy is reserved for failure or intolerance of drug therapy and, if needed, is done in the second trimester.
  • (B) Radioactive iodine ablation — Radioactive iodine is absolutely contraindicated in pregnancy; it destroys the fetal thyroid after 10–12 weeks.
  • (C) Propranolol alone until the second trimester — Beta-blockers help symptoms but do not treat the hyperthyroidism, and long-term use in pregnancy is linked to fetal growth restriction.
  • (D) Methimazole — Methimazole causes congenital malformations when taken during organogenesis in the first trimester.
🧠 Mnemonic

"PTU for the Pregnant first Trimester; Methimazole for the More common rest."

🎯 Educational objective

Treat Graves hyperthyroidism in the first trimester of pregnancy with propylthiouracil, switching to methimazole after the first trimester.

EN-008.stem_html:
A 54-year-old woman is evaluated for a neck lump she noticed while putting on a necklace. She reports mild palpitations. She has no hoarseness, dysphagia or history of neck irradiation. There is no family history of thyroid cancer.

On physical examination, pulse rate is 94/min. There is a 2.5-cm firm, mobile nodule in the left thyroid lobe. There is no cervical lymphadenopathy.

TSH0.08 µU/mL
Free thyroxine (T₄)1.7 ng/dL (normal, 0.8–1.8)
Thyroid ultrasonography2.4-cm solid isoechoic nodule with smooth margins and no microcalcifications
EN-008.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate next diagnostic test?

choices.D: CT scan of the neck with contrast

EN-008.explain_html:
Correct answer: E Thyroid nodule with low TSH

The first step in any thyroid nodule is a TSH. When the TSH is low, the nodule may be autonomously functioning ("hot"), and hot nodules are almost never malignant. Obtain a radionuclide (I-123 or technetium) uptake scan:

  • Hot nodule (takes up tracer, rest of gland suppressed) → no biopsy; treat the subclinical/overt hyperthyroidism (radioiodine, surgery or antithyroid drug).
  • Cold or indeterminate nodule → proceed to FNA according to ultrasound features.

When the TSH is normal or high, skip the scan and decide on FNA by ultrasound pattern and size (e.g., high-suspicion nodule ≥1 cm, low-suspicion ≥1.5 cm).

Why not the others

  • (A) Serum calcitonin — Routine calcitonin measurement (for medullary cancer) is not recommended in the United States.
  • (B) Fine-needle aspiration biopsy — Biopsy of a hyperfunctioning nodule is unnecessary and the cytology can look falsely suspicious ("follicular"). Scan first when TSH is low.
  • (C) Serum thyroglobulin — Thyroglobulin is a tumor marker after thyroidectomy for differentiated cancer; it does not distinguish benign from malignant nodules.
  • (D) CT scan of the neck with contrast — CT adds nothing to ultrasonography for nodule characterization, and iodinated contrast can worsen hyperthyroidism and interfere with a later radionuclide scan.
🎯 Educational objective

In a patient with a thyroid nodule and a low TSH, obtain a radionuclide scan; a hyperfunctioning nodule does not need biopsy.

EN-009.stem_html:
A 63-year-old man with type 2 diabetes is hospitalized for community-acquired pneumonia. At home he takes metformin, 1000 mg twice daily, and sitagliptin. He is eating full meals. Since admission 24 hours ago he has received sliding-scale regular insulin alone, and his point-of-care glucose values have been 248, 286, 302 and 264 mg/dL.

On physical examination, temperature is 37.8 °C (100.0 °F). He weighs 90 kg (198 lb). Other vital signs are normal.

Hemoglobin A1c8.9%
Creatinine1.0 mg/dL
Anion gap10 mEq/L
EN-009.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate insulin regimen?

choices.A: Neutral protamine Hagedorn (NPH) insulin twice daily without prandial insulin
choices.C: Continue sliding-scale insulin and increase the scale
choices.D: Basal insulin glargine, 0.2 units/kg/d, plus prandial rapid-acting insulin and correction doses

EN-009.explain_html:
Correct answer: D Inpatient hyperglycemia — basal-bolus insulin

Sliding-scale insulin alone treats hyperglycemia only after it happens and is associated with worse control; guidelines discourage it as the sole regimen. In a noncritically ill patient who is eating, use scheduled basal-bolus insulin:

  • Total daily dose ≈ 0.3–0.5 units/kg (lower, 0.2–0.3, if older, low eGFR or poor intake). For 90 kg at ~0.4 units/kg → ~36 units/d.
  • Half as basal (glargine or detemir once daily) — about 0.2 units/kg, half as prandial rapid-acting insulin split over meals.
  • Plus correction doses for highs.
  • Target glucose 140–180 mg/dL.

If the patient is not eating, use basal insulin plus correction only ("basal-plus") — RABBIT 2 trials. Before discharge, his A1c of 8.9% means he needs intensified home therapy.

Why not the others

  • (A) Neutral protamine Hagedorn (NPH) insulin twice daily without prandial insulin — NPH without mealtime coverage will not control postprandial hyperglycemia and causes more hypoglycemia between meals.
  • (B) Continuous intravenous insulin infusion — IV insulin infusions are for critical illness, DKA/HHS or perioperative settings, not for a stable patient eating meals.
  • (C) Continue sliding-scale insulin and increase the scale — Sliding-scale insulin alone is reactive and leads to persistent hyperglycemia and swings. A bigger scale does not fix the problem.
  • (E) Resume metformin and sitagliptin — Oral agents are usually held in hospitalized patients with acute illness; they act slowly and can't be titrated quickly. Metformin carries a lactic acidosis risk if kidney function or perfusion worsens.
🎯 Educational objective

Treat hyperglycemia in noncritically ill hospitalized patients who are eating with scheduled basal-bolus insulin plus correction doses, targeting 140–180 mg/dL, rather than sliding-scale insulin alone.

EN-010.stem_html:
A 58-year-old man is evaluated after a CT scan done for suspected kidney stones showed a 2.4-cm left adrenal mass. The mass is homogeneous, has smooth borders and has an unenhanced attenuation of 6 Hounsfield units. He has hypertension controlled with amlodipine. He reports no headaches, palpitations, sweating or weight gain.

On physical examination, blood pressure is 134/82 mm Hg and pulse rate is 72/min. BMI is 27. There are no striae, plethora or proximal muscle weakness.

Potassium4.3 mEq/L
Glucose (fasting)96 mg/dL
EN-010.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in evaluation?

choices.C: 1-mg overnight dexamethasone suppression test and plasma free metanephrines
choices.E: Repeat CT scan in 6 months only

EN-010.explain_html:
Correct answer: C Adrenal incidentaloma

Every adrenal incidentaloma raises two questions:

  1. Is it malignant? A homogeneous mass <4 cm with ≤10 Hounsfield units on unenhanced CT is a benign lipid-rich adenoma. No further imaging is needed.
  2. Is it hormonally active? Test every incidentaloma for: - Autonomous cortisol secretion → 1-mg overnight dexamethasone suppression test (morning cortisol >1.8 µg/dL is abnormal). - Pheochromocytoma → plasma free (or 24-h urine) metanephrines — can be skipped in a clearly lipid-rich adenoma (≤10 HU), but most still test. - Primary aldosteronism → aldosterone/renin only if hypertension or hypokalemia (he has hypertension, so add this).

Surgery is for hormonally active tumors or masses with suspicious imaging (>4 cm, heterogeneous, >20 HU).

Why not the others

  • (A) Adrenal biopsy — Biopsy cannot distinguish adrenal adenoma from carcinoma and risks hypertensive crisis if the mass is a pheochromocytoma. It is used only when metastasis is suspected and pheochromocytoma has been excluded.
  • (B) MRI of the adrenal glands — The unenhanced CT has already characterized the lesion as lipid-rich; MRI would not change management.
  • (D) No further evaluation — Up to 1 in 3 adrenal incidentalomas have mild autonomous cortisol secretion, which is linked to hypertension, diabetes and osteoporosis. All need hormonal testing.
  • (E) Repeat CT scan in 6 months only — The imaging is already diagnostic of a benign adenoma; follow-up CT adds nothing. Hormonal evaluation is what is missing.
🎓 ABIM pearl

The "rule of 4s and 10s": <4 cm and <10 HU = benign; >4 cm or >20 HU (or washout delayed) = suspicious.

🎯 Educational objective

Evaluate every adrenal incidentaloma for cortisol excess with a 1-mg dexamethasone suppression test and for pheochromocytoma with metanephrines, plus aldosterone and renin if hypertension or hypokalemia is present.

EN-011.stem_html:
A 38-year-old woman is evaluated for 4 months of fatigue, nausea, salt craving, lightheadedness on standing and a 6-kg (13.2-lb) weight loss. She has hypothyroidism treated with levothyroxine.

On physical examination, blood pressure is 98/62 mm Hg supine and 82/54 mm Hg standing; pulse rate is 88/min supine and 112/min standing. There is hyperpigmentation of the palmar creases and buccal mucosa.

Sodium129 mEq/L
Potassium5.6 mEq/L
Glucose68 mg/dL
Creatinine1.2 mg/dL
Morning (8 AM) serum cortisol4 µg/dL
EN-011.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate test to confirm the diagnosis?

choices.C: Cosyntropin (ACTH) stimulation test with plasma ACTH

EN-011.explain_html:
Correct answer: C Primary adrenal insufficiency

Hyperpigmentation, orthostatic hypotension, hyponatremia, hyperkalemia and hypoglycemia in a woman with autoimmune hypothyroidism point to primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison disease), most often autoimmune in high-income countries.

A morning cortisol <5 µg/dL strongly suggests adrenal insufficiency (>15–18 µg/dL makes it unlikely). Confirm with the cosyntropin stimulation test: give 250 µg IV/IM; a peak cortisol <18 µg/dL (<14–15 µg/dL with newer specific assays) confirms the diagnosis. A high plasma ACTH shows the problem is in the adrenal gland (primary).

Primary (adrenal) Secondary (pituitary)
ACTH High Low/normal
Hyperpigmentation Yes No
Aldosterone Low → hyperkalemia Normal (renin–angiotensin intact)
Treatment Hydrocortisone + fludrocortisone Hydrocortisone only

Next step after confirmation: 21-hydroxylase antibodies. If she becomes unstable, give hydrocortisone 100 mg IV immediately — do not wait for test results.

Why not the others

  • (A) Late-night salivary cortisol — Late-night salivary cortisol screens for Cushing syndrome — the opposite problem.
  • (B) MRI of the pituitary gland — Pituitary MRI is for secondary adrenal insufficiency. Hyperpigmentation and hyperkalemia point to a primary adrenal cause.
  • (D) Insulin tolerance test — The insulin tolerance test is the reference test for the HPA axis but is risky (hypoglycemia, seizures) and is rarely used, especially in someone already hypoglycemic.
  • (E) Adrenal CT scan — Adrenal imaging is for patients with negative 21-hydroxylase antibodies (looking for TB, hemorrhage, metastases). It does not confirm adrenal insufficiency.
🎓 ABIM pearl

Thyroid hormone before steroids is dangerous. In a patient with both hypothyroidism and possible adrenal insufficiency, replace cortisol first — starting levothyroxine alone speeds cortisol clearance and can precipitate adrenal crisis.

🎯 Educational objective

Confirm suspected primary adrenal insufficiency with a cosyntropin stimulation test and an elevated plasma ACTH level.

EN-012.stem_html:
A 41-year-old woman is evaluated for weight gain of 12 kg (26.4 lb) over a year, new hypertension, easy bruising and difficulty climbing stairs. She takes no glucocorticoids by any route, including inhaled, topical or injected. Her menses have become irregular.

On physical examination, blood pressure is 156/94 mm Hg. BMI is 33. She has facial plethora, supraclavicular fat pads, wide (>1 cm) purple striae on the abdomen and proximal muscle weakness of the hip flexors. Several ecchymoses are present on her forearms.

Potassium3.4 mEq/L
Fasting glucose132 mg/dL
EN-012.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate initial diagnostic test?

choices.D: Late-night salivary cortisol on two occasions

EN-012.explain_html:
Correct answer: D Cushing syndrome — screening

Easy bruising, facial plethora, proximal myopathy and wide purple striae are the most specific features of Cushing syndrome (obesity, hypertension and diabetes are common but nonspecific). Exogenous glucocorticoids have been excluded.

Step 1 — prove cortisol excess with one or more of three first-line tests (do at least two):

  • Late-night salivary cortisol ×2 — loss of the normal nighttime cortisol nadir
  • 1-mg overnight dexamethasone suppression test — morning cortisol >1.8 µg/dL is abnormal
  • 24-hour urine free cortisol ×2

Step 2 — localize only after cortisol excess is confirmed: plasma ACTH (low → adrenal; normal/high → pituitary or ectopic), then pituitary MRI, high-dose dexamethasone testing or inferior petrosal sinus sampling as needed.

Why not the others

  • (A) Plasma ACTH level — ACTH localizes the cause, but only after hypercortisolism is confirmed.
  • (B) Random serum cortisol — Random cortisol varies with stress and time of day and cannot confirm or exclude the diagnosis.
  • (C) Morning serum cortisol — A single morning cortisol is neither sensitive nor specific for Cushing syndrome; cortisol is normally highest in the morning.
  • (E) MRI of the pituitary gland — Imaging before biochemical confirmation is a classic error — pituitary incidentalomas are present in about 10% of healthy adults.
🧠 Mnemonic

Cushing work-up = "Prove it, then find it." Biochemistry first, imaging last.

🎯 Educational objective

Screen for Cushing syndrome with late-night salivary cortisol, a 1-mg overnight dexamethasone suppression test or 24-hour urine free cortisol before measuring ACTH or imaging.
