EN-013.stem_html:
A 45-year-old man is evaluated for 6 months of episodic pounding headaches, sweating and palpitations lasting 10–20 minutes. Blood pressure during an episode in the emergency department was 210/118 mm Hg.

On physical examination, blood pressure is 162/98 mm Hg and pulse rate is 102/min. He is thin and tremulous.

Plasma free normetanephrine is 8 times the upper limit of normal. CT shows a 4.2-cm heterogeneous left adrenal mass with an unenhanced attenuation of 38 Hounsfield units. Laparoscopic adrenalectomy is planned in 3 weeks.
EN-013.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate preoperative treatment?

choices.A: No preoperative medication; control blood pressure intraoperatively
choices.E: Doxazosin, followed by propranolol after several days

EN-013.explain_html:
Correct answer: E Pheochromocytoma — preoperative preparation

Episodic headache, sweating and palpitations with paroxysmal hypertension, markedly elevated metanephrines and a dense, heterogeneous adrenal mass = pheochromocytoma.

Surgery without preparation can cause a hypertensive crisis when the tumor is handled. Preoperative care (7–14 days):

  1. Alpha-blockade first — phenoxybenzamine or a selective α₁-blocker (doxazosin, prazosin); a calcium channel blocker is an add-on or alternative.
  2. High-sodium diet and fluids to re-expand the contracted plasma volume.
  3. Beta-blocker only after adequate alpha-blockade (usually 3–4 days later) to control tachycardia.

Targets before surgery: seated BP <130/80 mm Hg, mild orthostasis, heart rate 60–70/min.

Why not the others

  • (A) No preoperative medication; control blood pressure intraoperatively — Unprepared surgery carries a high risk of intraoperative hypertensive crisis, arrhythmia and death.
  • (B) Metoprolol, followed by doxazosin — A beta-blocker first removes β₂-mediated vasodilation and leaves α-mediated vasoconstriction unopposed — a hypertensive crisis and acute heart failure can follow.
  • (C) Labetalol alone — Labetalol has much more beta- than alpha-blocking activity and can cause paradoxical hypertension; it is not a substitute for alpha-blockade.
  • (D) Hydrochlorothiazide — Diuretics worsen the volume contraction that is already present in pheochromocytoma.
🧠 Mnemonic

"Alpha before Beta" — as in the alphabet.

🎓 ABIM pearl

About 1 in 3 pheochromocytomas and paragangliomas are hereditary (MEN2, VHL, NF1, SDHx). Offer genetic testing to all patients.

🎯 Educational objective

Before resection of a pheochromocytoma, start alpha-adrenergic blockade with volume repletion and add a beta-blocker only after adequate alpha-blockade.

EN-014.stem_html:
A 27-year-old woman is evaluated for 8 months of amenorrhea and a milky nipple discharge. She would like to become pregnant in the next year. She takes no medications, including antipsychotics, metoclopramide or opioids.

On physical examination, vital signs are normal. Visual fields are full to confrontation. Expressible galactorrhea is present bilaterally.

Urine pregnancy testnegative
Prolactin186 ng/mL
TSH1.9 µU/mL
Creatinine0.7 mg/dL
MRI of the pituitary7-mm pituitary adenoma without optic chiasm compression
EN-014.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?

choices.B: Observation with repeat MRI in 1 year

EN-014.explain_html:
Correct answer: C Prolactinoma

She has a microprolactinoma (<10 mm) causing hypogonadism (amenorrhea) and galactorrhea. Pregnancy, hypothyroidism, kidney failure and dopamine-blocking drugs have been excluded. A prolactin level >150–200 ng/mL is almost always due to a prolactinoma.

Dopamine agonists are first-line for prolactinomas of any size, even macroadenomas with visual field defects: they normalize prolactin, restore ovulation and shrink the tumor. Cabergoline is preferred over bromocriptine — it is more effective and better tolerated.

Once she conceives, the dopamine agonist is usually stopped (microadenomas rarely grow in pregnancy). Very high doses (as used in Parkinson disease) are linked to cardiac valve disease; prolactinoma doses carry little risk.

Why not the others

  • (A) Transsphenoidal surgery — Surgery is second-line — for intolerance or resistance to dopamine agonists, or apoplexy.
  • (B) Observation with repeat MRI in 1 year — Observation is reasonable only for an asymptomatic microprolactinoma. Her hypogonadism and wish for pregnancy need treatment.
  • (D) Pituitary radiation therapy — Radiation is reserved for aggressive tumors resistant to medical therapy and surgery; it causes hypopituitarism.
  • (E) Combined oral contraceptive pill — Oral contraceptives restore menses and protect bone in women who do not want pregnancy, but they do not restore fertility, which is her goal.
🎓 ABIM pearl

Two traps with high prolactin: the "hook effect" (a giant macroadenoma with falsely normal-ish prolactin — ask the lab to dilute the sample) and stalk effect (a nonfunctioning macroadenoma compressing the stalk, with prolactin usually <100–150 ng/mL — surgery, not cabergoline).

🎯 Educational objective

Treat a symptomatic prolactinoma with a dopamine agonist, preferably cabergoline.

She takes no medications, including antipsychotics, metoclopramide or opioids. On physical examination, vital signs are normal. Visual fields are full to confrontation. Expressible galactorrhea is present bilaterally. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?

EN-015.stem_html:
A 48-year-old man is evaluated for 1 year of low libido, decreased morning erections and fatigue. He takes no medications or supplements and does not use anabolic steroids or opioids. He drinks alcohol rarely.

On physical examination, BMI is 28. Testicular volume is normal. There is no gynecomastia. Visual fields are full.

A total testosterone level drawn at 4:00 PM last week was 230 ng/dL (reference, 264–916 ng/dL).
EN-015.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.C: Measure fasting morning total testosterone on another day
choices.E: Obtain MRI of the pituitary gland

EN-015.explain_html:
Correct answer: C Male hypogonadism — diagnosis

Testosterone has a diurnal rhythm (highest in the early morning) and is lowered by food, acute illness and sleep loss. An afternoon value can be falsely low.

The diagnosis of male hypogonadism requires consistent symptoms plus unequivocally low testosterone on at least two fasting morning (7–10 AM) samples. Use free testosterone (by equilibrium dialysis) if SHBG may be altered (obesity, diabetes, aging, liver disease, HIV).

After confirmation, measure LH and FSH:

  • High LH/FSH → primary (testicular) — karyotype if Klinefelter suspected.
  • Low or normal LH/FSH → secondary — check prolactin, iron studies, other pituitary hormones; pituitary MRI if testosterone <150 ng/dL, other pituitary deficits, high prolactin or mass symptoms.

Why not the others

  • (A) Begin testosterone gel — Testosterone should not be started on a single afternoon value; treatment without confirmation exposes him to erythrocytosis, infertility and unnecessary lifelong therapy.
  • (B) Obtain karyotype analysis — Karyotyping is for primary hypogonadism with small testes (suspected Klinefelter syndrome). His testicular volume is normal.
  • (D) Measure estradiol level — Estradiol is measured when gynecomastia is present; it does not establish the diagnosis of hypogonadism.
  • (E) Obtain MRI of the pituitary gland — Imaging is premature before biochemical confirmation and gonadotropin measurement.
🎓 ABIM pearl

Exogenous testosterone suppresses spermatogenesis. In a man who wants children, treat secondary hypogonadism with clomiphene or hCG instead.

🎯 Educational objective

Confirm male hypogonadism with two fasting morning testosterone measurements before evaluation of the cause or treatment.

EN-016.stem_html:
A 67-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes is evaluated during a routine visit. She takes metformin, 1000 mg twice daily, and her hemoglobin A1c is 7.0%. She has hypertension treated with lisinopril. She has no history of heart failure or atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease.

On physical examination, blood pressure is 128/76 mm Hg. BMI is 31.

Creatinine1.5 mg/dL
eGFR38 mL/min/1.73 m² (42 mL/min/1.73 m² 3 months ago)
Urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio260 mg/g
Potassium4.6 mEq/L
EN-016.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate change in her diabetes therapy?

choices.B: Stop metformin and begin insulin glargine
choices.C: Continue metformin at the current dose
choices.D: Reduce metformin to 500 mg twice daily and add an SGLT2 inhibitor

EN-016.explain_html:
Correct answer: D Metformin and kidney function

Metformin is cleared by the kidney. FDA labeling:

eGFR (mL/min/1.73 m²) Metformin
≥45 Full dose
30–44 Do not start; if already taking, reduce dose (max ~1000 mg/d)
<30 Contraindicated

Her eGFR is 38, so halve the metformin dose. She also has diabetic kidney disease with albuminuria. An SGLT2 inhibitor (e.g., empagliflozin, dapagliflozin) slows CKD progression and reduces cardiovascular events and heart failure, independent of glucose lowering, and is recommended when eGFR is ≥20. Continue the ACE inhibitor; a GLP-1 receptor agonist (semaglutide, FLOW trial) or finerenone can be added for further kidney protection.

Why not the others

  • (A) Stop metformin and begin glipizide — Sulfonylureas cause hypoglycemia, especially with low eGFR, and have no kidney benefit. Glipizide is the safest of the class in CKD but is not the best choice here.
  • (B) Stop metformin and begin insulin glargine — Metformin can still be continued at a reduced dose; her A1c is near goal, and insulin adds hypoglycemia and weight gain without organ protection.
  • (C) Continue metformin at the current dose — Full-dose metformin is not recommended at an eGFR below 45 because of drug accumulation and lactic acidosis risk.
  • (E) Stop metformin and begin pioglitazone — Pioglitazone causes fluid retention and weight gain and offers no kidney protection.
🎯 Educational objective

Reduce the metformin dose when eGFR falls to 30–44 mL/min/1.73 m², stop it below 30, and add an SGLT2 inhibitor in patients with type 2 diabetes and albuminuric CKD.

EN-017.stem_html:
A 24-year-old man with type 1 diabetes is brought to the emergency department with 2 days of vomiting, abdominal pain and polyuria. He ran out of insulin 3 days ago.

On physical examination, temperature is 37.2 °C (99.0 °F), blood pressure is 102/64 mm Hg, pulse rate is 118/min, and respiration rate is 28/min with deep breaths. Mucous membranes are dry. He is drowsy but oriented.

One liter of 0.9% saline has been infused.

Sodium132 mEq/L
Potassium3.1 mEq/L
Chloride96 mEq/L
Bicarbonate8 mEq/L
Glucose520 mg/dL
β-Hydroxybutyrate7.2 mmol/L
Arterial pH7.08
Creatinine1.6 mg/dL
EN-017.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.B: Switch intravenous fluid to 5% dextrose in water
choices.C: Give intravenous potassium chloride and hold insulin until potassium is ≥3.3 mEq/L
choices.E: Begin intravenous regular insulin infusion at 0.1 units/kg/h

EN-017.explain_html:
Correct answer: C DKA — potassium before insulin

He has severe DKA (pH <7.0–7.24, bicarbonate <10, anion gap 28, ketonemia). Despite the low serum potassium, total body potassium is profoundly depleted — lost through osmotic diuresis and vomiting.

Insulin drives potassium into cells. Starting insulin with a potassium of <3.3 mEq/L can cause life-threatening hypokalemia, arrhythmias and respiratory muscle weakness.

Serum K⁺ (mEq/L) Action
<3.3 Hold insulin; give 20–40 mEq KCl/h until ≥3.3
3.3–5.2 Start insulin; add 20–30 mEq K⁺ to each liter of fluid
>5.2 Start insulin; no K⁺; recheck every 2 h

Then: IV insulin infusion, fluids, add dextrose when glucose falls below 250 mg/dL (keep insulin running until the anion gap closes), and overlap basal subcutaneous insulin by 1–2 hours before stopping the drip.

Why not the others

  • (A) Give intravenous sodium bicarbonate — Bicarbonate does not improve outcomes in DKA unless pH is <6.9–7.0, and it worsens hypokalemia.
  • (B) Switch intravenous fluid to 5% dextrose in water — Dextrose is added when glucose falls to about 250 mg/dL. He still needs isotonic saline for volume and potassium replacement.
  • (D) Give subcutaneous insulin glargine — Subcutaneous basal insulin is not adequate initial therapy for severe DKA and also lowers potassium.
  • (E) Begin intravenous regular insulin infusion at 0.1 units/kg/h — Insulin is the definitive treatment, but starting it with a potassium of 3.1 mEq/L risks fatal hypokalemia.
🧠 Mnemonic

"K before I" — potassium ≥3.3 before insulin.

🎯 Educational objective

In DKA with a serum potassium below 3.3 mEq/L, replace potassium and hold insulin until potassium is at least 3.3 mEq/L.

EN-018.topic: Euglycemic DKA from an SGLT2 inhibitor
EN-018.stem_html:
A 56-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes is evaluated on postoperative day 2 after laparoscopic cholecystectomy for nausea, vomiting and malaise. She has eaten little since surgery. Her diabetes medications are metformin and empagliflozin; both were continued until the morning of surgery.

On physical examination, blood pressure is 112/68 mm Hg, pulse rate is 106/min, and respiration rate is 26/min. The abdomen is soft with healing port sites.

Sodium138 mEq/L
Potassium4.6 mEq/L
Chloride104 mEq/L
Bicarbonate12 mEq/L
Glucose186 mg/dL
Lactate1.1 mmol/L
Creatinine0.9 mg/dL
Arterial pH7.21
Urinalysis3+ glucose, 3+ ketones
EN-018.lead: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

choices.C: Normal anion gap acidosis from saline infusion

EN-018.explain_html:
Correct answer: E Euglycemic DKA from an SGLT2 inhibitor

She has an anion gap metabolic acidosis (gap = 138 − 104 − 12 = 22), ketonuria, a normal lactate — and a glucose of only 186 mg/dL. This is euglycemic DKA, a known complication of SGLT2 inhibitors.

Mechanism: SGLT2 inhibitors make the kidney spill glucose, which keeps the blood glucose deceptively near normal. Lower glucose → lower insulin and higher glucagon → lipolysis and ketogenesis. Triggers include surgery, fasting, acute illness, reduced insulin doses and alcohol.

Treat like DKA — fluids, IV insulin with dextrose from the start (because glucose is not high), potassium as needed — and stop the SGLT2 inhibitor.

Prevention: hold SGLT2 inhibitors 3 days before surgery (4 days for ertugliflozin) and during acute illness ("sick day rules").

Why not the others

  • (A) Lactic acidosis from metformin — Lactate is normal, so metformin-associated lactic acidosis is excluded.
  • (B) Alcoholic ketoacidosis — Alcoholic ketoacidosis follows binge drinking with poor intake; there is no alcohol history here.
  • (C) Normal anion gap acidosis from saline infusion — The anion gap is elevated (22), so this is not a hyperchloremic normal anion gap acidosis.
  • (D) Postoperative starvation ketosis — Starvation ketosis causes only mild acidosis (bicarbonate rarely <18 mEq/L), not a pH of 7.21.
🎓 ABIM pearl

Check β-hydroxybutyrate and a blood gas in any patient taking an SGLT2 inhibitor who has nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain or malaise — even if the glucose is normal.

🎯 Educational objective

Recognize euglycemic DKA in a patient taking an SGLT2 inhibitor who has an anion gap acidosis and ketosis with near-normal glucose, and hold these drugs 3 days before surgery.

EN-019.topic: Hypoglycemia in a patient without diabetes
EN-019.stem_html:
A 34-year-old nurse is brought to the emergency department after she was found confused at work. Her glucose by fingerstick was 32 mg/dL, and her symptoms resolved with intravenous dextrose. She has had two similar episodes in the past month. She does not have diabetes. Her mother has type 2 diabetes treated with glyburide and insulin.

Blood was drawn during the hypoglycemic episode, before dextrose was given.

Glucose34 mg/dL
Insulin48 µU/mL (elevated)
C-peptide<0.1 ng/mL (low)
Proinsulinlow
β-Hydroxybutyratelow
Sulfonylurea screennegative
EN-019.lead: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
EN-019.explain_html:
Correct answer: A Hypoglycemia in a patient without diabetes

Hypoglycemia with Whipple triad (symptoms, low glucose, relief with glucose). The key is the pattern of insulin and C-peptide during the episode.

Pancreatic beta cells cleave proinsulin into insulin + C-peptide in equal amounts. Pharmaceutical insulin contains no C-peptide. So high insulin with suppressed C-peptide = exogenous insulin. In a health care worker with access to insulin, this is factitious hypoglycemia.

Cause Insulin C-peptide Proinsulin Sulfonylurea screen
Exogenous insulin ↑ ↓ ↓ −
Sulfonylurea/meglitinide ↑ ↑ ↑ +
Insulinoma ↑ ↑ ↑ −
Non-insulin mediated (IGF-2 tumor, adrenal insufficiency, sepsis) ↓ ↓ ↓ −

Why not the others

  • (B) Surreptitious sulfonylurea use — Sulfonylureas stimulate endogenous secretion, raising C-peptide; the screen is also negative.
  • (C) Adrenal insufficiency — Adrenal insufficiency causes hypoglycemia with suppressed (not high) insulin.
  • (D) Insulin autoimmune syndrome — Insulin autoimmune syndrome causes very high insulin levels with elevated (not suppressed) C-peptide.
  • (E) Insulinoma — Insulinoma secretes endogenous insulin, so C-peptide and proinsulin are elevated.
🧠 Mnemonic

"C-peptide = Calling card of the pancreas." No calling card → the insulin came from a syringe.

🎯 Educational objective

In hypoglycemia, high insulin with suppressed C-peptide and proinsulin indicates exogenous insulin administration.

EN-020.stem_html:
A 60-year-old man with type 2 diabetes is evaluated during a routine visit. His hemoglobin A1c is 5.6%, down from 8.2% 6 months ago, even though he has not changed his diet or medications (metformin and glipizide). His home glucose meter readings average 190 mg/dL with several readings above 250 mg/dL; the meter is accurate when checked against a laboratory glucose.

Three months ago he had a gastrointestinal bleed from a duodenal ulcer and received 3 units of packed red blood cells. He now takes oral iron.

Hemoglobin11.6 g/dL
Reticulocyte count4.8%
Fasting plasma glucose182 mg/dL
EN-020.lead: Which of the following best explains the discrepancy between his hemoglobin A1c and his glucose values?

choices.A: Glycation of hemoglobin is reduced by oral iron
choices.C: Red blood cell transfusion and increased red cell turnover lower the A1c
choices.D: Metformin directly interferes with the A1c assay
choices.E: Hypoglycemic episodes overnight lower the average glucose

EN-020.explain_html:
Correct answer: C Falsely low hemoglobin A1c

Hemoglobin A1c reflects glucose exposure over the lifespan of the red cell (~120 days). Anything that shortens red cell survival or adds new red cells gives glucose less time to glycate hemoglobin and falsely lowers A1c:

  • Blood loss and transfusion (transfused donor cells were never exposed to his glucose)
  • Hemolysis, reticulocytosis, recovery from iron/B12/folate deficiency (young red cells)
  • Erythropoiesis-stimulating agents, late pregnancy, CKD on ESA

Things that falsely raise A1c: iron deficiency (older red cells live longer), asplenia, B12/folate deficiency before treatment.

When A1c and glucose disagree, trust the glucose — use continuous glucose monitoring or fructosamine (glycated albumin, reflects ~2–3 weeks).

Why not the others

  • (A) Glycation of hemoglobin is reduced by oral iron — Iron replacement leads to a burst of young red cells (reticulocytosis), which lowers A1c, but the main effect here is transfusion plus blood loss — iron itself does not block glycation.
  • (B) Uremia causes carbamylation of hemoglobin — Carbamylated hemoglobin in severe uremia can interfere with some older assays, but his kidney function is not described as impaired and modern assays are not affected.
  • (D) Metformin directly interferes with the A1c assay — Metformin does not interfere with A1c measurement.
  • (E) Hypoglycemic episodes overnight lower the average glucose — His meter readings are high, not low. Hidden hypoglycemia would not explain an A1c this far below his measured glucose.
🎯 Educational objective

Hemoglobin A1c is falsely low when red blood cell survival is shortened or new red cells are added (blood loss, transfusion, hemolysis, reticulocytosis).

EN-021.stem_html:
A 46-year-old woman is evaluated for 6 months of diffuse bone pain and difficulty rising from a chair. She had a Roux-en-Y gastric bypass 8 years ago and stopped taking her supplements 4 years ago. She has dark skin and rarely goes outdoors.

On physical examination, there is tenderness over the ribs and tibias and proximal muscle weakness. She walks with a waddling gait.

Calcium8.2 mg/dL
Phosphorus2.1 mg/dL
Alkaline phosphatase340 U/L
Parathyroid hormone168 pg/mL
25-hydroxyvitamin D6 ng/mL
Creatinine0.7 mg/dL
EN-021.lead: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
EN-021.explain_html:
Correct answer: B Osteomalacia

Osteomalacia is defective mineralization of newly formed bone, most often from severe vitamin D deficiency. Her risks: gastric bypass (malabsorption), stopped supplements, dark skin and little sun.

The biochemical pattern:

  • Very low 25-hydroxyvitamin D
  • Low-normal calcium and low phosphorus (poor absorption + PTH-driven phosphaturia)
  • High PTH (secondary hyperparathyroidism)
  • High alkaline phosphatase (active, but failing, bone formation)

Clinically: diffuse bone pain and tenderness, proximal myopathy, waddling gait; radiographs may show Looser zones (pseudofractures). Treat with high-dose vitamin D (e.g., 50,000 IU weekly) plus calcium, then maintenance.

Why not the others

  • (A) Osteoporosis — Osteoporosis is painless until fracture and has normal calcium, phosphorus, alkaline phosphatase and PTH.
  • (C) Polymyalgia rheumatica — PMR causes shoulder and hip girdle stiffness with high inflammatory markers, not bone tenderness with mineral abnormalities.
  • (D) Primary hyperparathyroidism — Primary hyperparathyroidism causes high calcium. Her calcium is low with high PTH — secondary hyperparathyroidism.
  • (E) Paget disease of bone — Paget disease raises alkaline phosphatase but has normal calcium, phosphorus and vitamin D; pain is focal, not diffuse with myopathy.
🎯 Educational objective

Recognize osteomalacia by bone pain, proximal myopathy, low vitamin D, low phosphorus, high PTH and high alkaline phosphatase.

EN-022.stem_html:
A 66-year-old man with squamous cell carcinoma of the lung is admitted with 1 week of confusion, constipation, polyuria and poor oral intake.

On physical examination, blood pressure is 104/62 mm Hg and pulse rate is 104/min. Mucous membranes are dry. He is drowsy but arousable and oriented to person only.

Calcium15.2 mg/dL
Albumin3.6 g/dL
Phosphorus2.2 mg/dL
Creatinine1.6 mg/dL (baseline 0.9 mg/dL)
Parathyroid hormone6 pg/mL (low)
PTH-related peptideelevated
EN-022.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate initial treatment?

choices.D: Intravenous isotonic saline, calcitonin and zoledronic acid

EN-022.explain_html:
Correct answer: D Hypercalcemia of malignancy

Severe (>14 mg/dL), symptomatic hypercalcemia of malignancy from PTH-related peptide (humoral hypercalcemia — classic for squamous cell cancers). PTH is appropriately suppressed.

Three tools, three speeds:

Treatment Onset Role
IV isotonic saline (200–300 mL/h) Hours Corrects volume depletion; hypercalcemia causes nephrogenic DI
Calcitonin (4 IU/kg SC/IM q12h) 4–6 h Quick bridge; tachyphylaxis after 48 h
Zoledronic acid 4 mg IV (or pamidronate) 2–4 days Durable; blocks osteoclasts
Denosumab Days If bisphosphonate-refractory or eGFR too low

Zoledronic acid needs dose adjustment or avoidance in severe kidney injury; denosumab can be used instead. Loop diuretics only after volume is restored and only if overload develops.

Why not the others

  • (A) Furosemide alone — Furosemide before volume repletion worsens dehydration and kidney injury; it is not routinely recommended.
  • (B) Oral prednisone — Glucocorticoids work for calcitriol-mediated hypercalcemia (lymphoma, granulomatous disease), not PTHrP-mediated disease.
  • (C) Cinacalcet — Cinacalcet lowers PTH secretion in parathyroid disease; it does not treat PTHrP-mediated hypercalcemia.
  • (E) Hemodialysis — Dialysis is for severe hypercalcemia with kidney failure or heart failure that cannot tolerate saline.
🎓 ABIM pearl

Three mechanisms of hypercalcemia of malignancy — PTHrP (squamous, kidney, bladder, breast), osteolytic metastases (breast, myeloma), calcitriol (lymphoma).

🎯 Educational objective

Treat severe symptomatic hypercalcemia of malignancy with intravenous isotonic saline, calcitonin and a bisphosphonate (or denosumab).

EN-023.stem_html:
A 36-year-old man is evaluated for mild hypercalcemia found on routine testing. He feels well. He has no kidney stones, fractures or bone pain. His father and sister were told they have "high calcium" but never had treatment.

Examination is normal.

Calcium10.9 mg/dL
Phosphorus2.8 mg/dL
Parathyroid hormone62 pg/mL (reference, 10–65)
25-hydroxyvitamin D34 ng/mL
Creatinine0.9 mg/dL
24-hour urine calcium52 mg
Calcium-to-creatinine clearance ratio0.006
EN-023.lead: Which of the following is the most likely cause of his hypercalcemia?

choices.C: Inactivating mutation of the calcium-sensing receptor

EN-023.explain_html:
Correct answer: C Familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia

Familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia (FHH) is an autosomal dominant disorder, usually from a heterozygous inactivating mutation of the calcium-sensing receptor (CaSR).

The parathyroid gland and kidney "read" calcium as lower than it really is. So:

  • The parathyroids keep secreting PTH at a higher calcium set point → mild hypercalcemia with normal or slightly high PTH.
  • The kidney reabsorbs calcium avidly → low urine calcium.

The key test is the calcium-to-creatinine clearance ratio: <0.01 suggests FHH; >0.02 suggests primary hyperparathyroidism. Family history and lifelong asymptomatic hypercalcemia support the diagnosis; genetic testing confirms it.

FHH is benign and needs no treatment. Parathyroidectomy does not cure it — so the main importance is avoiding unnecessary surgery.

Why not the others

  • (A) PTH-related peptide secretion — PTHrP-mediated hypercalcemia occurs with malignancy and suppresses PTH.
  • (B) Parathyroid adenoma — A parathyroid adenoma causes primary hyperparathyroidism, which typically has normal or high urine calcium (ratio >0.02).
  • (D) Vitamin D intoxication — Vitamin D intoxication raises 25-hydroxyvitamin D (often >150 ng/mL) and suppresses PTH.
  • (E) Excess calcitriol from granulomas — Granulomatous disease causes PTH-independent hypercalcemia with suppressed PTH and high urine calcium.
🎯 Educational objective

Familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia is caused by inactivating calcium-sensing receptor mutations and is identified by a calcium-to-creatinine clearance ratio below 0.01; it does not require surgery.

ET-001.stem_html:
A 58-year-old woman comes to the office with 1 week of brief spells of intense spinning. They happen when she rolls over in bed to the right, lies down, or tilts her head back to reach a high shelf, and each lasts less than a minute. She has mild nausea during spells but no hearing loss, tinnitus, ear fullness, headache, double vision, slurred speech or weakness. Between spells she feels normal.

Vital signs are normal. Hearing is grossly normal. With the patient turned to the right during the Dix–Hallpike maneuver, after a 5-second delay, she develops vertigo with upbeating, torsional nystagmus toward the right ear that fades after 20 seconds. Testing to the left is negative. The rest of the neurologic examination, including gait, is normal.
ET-001.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?

choices.D: Vestibular rehabilitation exercises as the only treatment

ET-001.explain_html:
Correct answer: A Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo

Brief positional vertigo with a positive Dix–Hallpike — latency of a few seconds, upbeating torsional nystagmus, fatigable, lasting <1 minute — is benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV) of the right posterior semicircular canal. Loose otoconia (calcium carbonate crystals) drift into the canal and move with gravity when the head changes position.

Treat with a canalith repositioning maneuver (Epley) in the office. It moves the crystals back into the utricle and cures about 80% of patients after one to three maneuvers.

Positional nystagmus Peripheral (BPPV) Central (worrisome)
Latency Yes (2–20 s) None
Duration <1 min Persistent
Fatigability Yes No
Direction Upbeat-torsional (posterior canal) Pure vertical (often downbeat), changes direction
Other signs None Ataxia, diplopia, dysarthria

Why not the others

  • (B) Oral prednisone taper — Glucocorticoids may help acute vestibular neuritis (continuous vertigo for days), not positional vertigo.
  • (C) MRI of the brain — Classic BPPV with a typical Dix–Hallpike and normal neurologic examination does not need imaging.
  • (D) Vestibular rehabilitation exercises as the only treatment — Vestibular rehabilitation is an add-on for persistent imbalance; repositioning is the first-line cure.
  • (E) Meclizine daily for 4 weeks — Vestibular suppressants do not fix BPPV, delay central compensation and cause sedation and falls. Use them at most briefly for severe nausea.
🎓 ABIM pearl

Continuous vertigo for days with nystagmus at rest calls for HINTS (head impulse, nystagmus, test of skew) to separate vestibular neuritis from posterior circulation stroke.

🎯 Educational objective

Posterior-canal BPPV is diagnosed with the Dix–Hallpike maneuver and treated with canalith repositioning (Epley); avoid routine imaging and vestibular suppressants.

ET-002.stem_html:
A 52-year-old woman is evaluated for hearing loss in her left ear that she noticed on waking 2 days ago, with a feeling of fullness and ringing. She has no ear pain, discharge, vertigo or recent upper respiratory infection. She has no neurologic symptoms.

On physical examination, the ear canals and tympanic membranes are normal. On Weber testing, the sound lateralizes to the right (unaffected) ear. Rinne test is positive (air conduction > bone conduction) in both ears. Cranial nerves are otherwise normal.
ET-002.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.E: Urgent audiometry and oral glucocorticoids, with MRI of the internal auditory canals

ET-002.explain_html:
Correct answer: E Sudden sensorineural hearing loss

Interpret the tuning-fork tests:

  • Weber lateralizes away from the affected ear → the affected ear has sensorineural loss (in conductive loss, Weber lateralizes toward the bad ear).
  • Rinne positive (AC > BC) in the affected ear → no conductive loss.

Sudden sensorineural hearing loss (SSNHL) — ≥30 dB over 3 consecutive frequencies within 72 hours — is an otologic emergency. Most cases are idiopathic (viral, vascular, autoimmune theories).

AAO-HNS 2019:

  • Confirm with audiometry promptly.
  • Oral glucocorticoids (e.g., prednisone 1 mg/kg/d, max 60 mg, for 7–14 days) within 2 weeks of onset; intratympanic steroids as salvage or alternative.
  • MRI of the internal auditory canals with gadolinium to exclude vestibular schwannoma (found in 1–5% of SSNHL).
  • Do not order routine CT or broad lab panels; antivirals and vasodilators are not recommended.

Why not the others

  • (A) Oral amoxicillin — Antibiotics treat acute otitis media, which causes conductive loss with an abnormal tympanic membrane.
  • (B) Intranasal glucocorticoid spray and decongestants — Nasal steroids and decongestants are for eustachian tube dysfunction, which causes conductive symptoms.
  • (C) Reassurance and follow-up in 1 month — Delay reduces the chance of recovery; steroids work best within 2 weeks.
  • (D) Ear irrigation — Irrigation treats cerumen impaction, which causes conductive loss and is visible on otoscopy.
🧠 Mnemonic

Weber: "Sensorineural — Sound goes to the Sound ear. Conductive — goes to the Clogged ear."

🎯 Educational objective

Treat sudden sensorineural hearing loss as an emergency with prompt audiometry and oral glucocorticoids, and obtain MRI to exclude vestibular schwannoma.

GE-001.stem_html:
A 78-year-old woman comes for an annual visit. She has fallen twice in the past year while walking in her home — once tripping on a rug, once turning quickly in the kitchen — without serious injury. She now worries about falling and walks less. She has hypertension treated with amlodipine and takes no sedatives or other medications. Her eyeglasses were updated 6 months ago.

Blood pressure is 132/74 mm Hg supine and 130/72 mm Hg standing, without symptoms. Corrected visual acuity is 20/30 in both eyes. She needs to push with her arms to rise from a chair. The Timed Up and Go test takes 16 seconds (normal <12 seconds) with a slow, cautious gait. Sensation and reflexes in the feet are normal.

25-Hydroxyvitamin D34 ng/mL
Hemoglobin13.1 g/dL
TSH2.2 µU/mL
GE-001.lead: Which of the following is the most effective intervention to reduce her risk of further falls?

choices.B: Advise her to limit walking to reduce exposure
choices.E: Exercise program with balance and strength training

GE-001.explain_html:
Correct answer: E Fall prevention

She screens positive for fall risk: two falls, fear of falling, slow Timed Up and Go and proximal leg weakness (needs arms to rise). Orthostatic hypotension, poor vision, medications and vitamin D deficiency are not the problem here.

The single best-proven intervention for community-dwelling older adults is exercise — especially programs that combine balance, gait and strength training (for example physical therapy, Otago, tai chi). Exercise reduces falls by about 20%–35%. Add a home safety assessment (rugs, lighting, grab bars).

Multifactorial assessment and intervention is also recommended for patients at high risk.

Why not the others

  • (A) Hip protectors — Hip protectors may reduce hip fractures in nursing-home residents with good adherence; they do not prevent falls.
  • (B) Advise her to limit walking to reduce exposure — Restricting activity worsens deconditioning and fear of falling and increases fall risk.
  • (C) Vitamin D 2000 units daily — In older adults without vitamin D deficiency, supplementation does not prevent falls (USPSTF recommends against it for this purpose).
  • (D) Stop amlodipine — Her blood pressure is well controlled without orthostatic drop; amlodipine is not contributing to her falls.
🧠 Mnemonic

Fall risk review — "I HATE FALLING": Inflammation of joints, Hypotension (orthostatic), Auditory/visual impairment, Tremor, Equilibrium problems, Foot problems, Arrhythmia, Leg-length mismatch, Lack of conditioning, Illness, Nutrition, Gait disturbance.

🎓 ABIM pearl

The "STEADI" approach: ask every patient ≥65 three questions — fallen in the past year? feel unsteady? worry about falling? A yes leads to gait, strength and balance testing.

🎯 Educational objective

Exercise programs with balance and strength training are the most effective intervention to prevent falls in community-dwelling older adults; vitamin D does not prevent falls in those without deficiency.

GE-002.stem_html:
An 82-year-old man is brought to the office by his daughter because he has been confused for 4 days. He has mild Alzheimer dementia and normally manages his own dressing and meals. Since earlier this week he has been drowsy during the day, awake and agitated at night, and at times does not recognize his grandson. Oxybutynin was started 6 days ago for urinary urgency. Other medications are donepezil and lisinopril.

Temperature is 37.0 °C (98.6 °F), blood pressure is 128/70 mm Hg and pulse is 84/min. He is inattentive and cannot name the months backward. Mucous membranes are dry. There is no focal neurologic deficit and no suprapubic tenderness; bladder scan shows 90 mL.

Glucose, sodium, calcium and creatininenormal
Complete blood countnormal
Urinalysisno leukocytes or nitrite
GE-002.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
GE-002.explain_html:
Correct answer: D Drug-induced delirium (anticholinergic)

Acute onset of fluctuating inattention and altered consciousness = delirium (superimposed on dementia). The timing points to a cause: oxybutynin, a strongly anticholinergic drug, started 2 days before symptoms. Anticholinergics cross the blood–brain barrier and directly worsen cognition — and they oppose donepezil.

The most effective treatment of delirium is to find and remove the cause. Stop oxybutynin; confusion usually clears over days. Use nondrug measures (reorientation, sleep hygiene, glasses and hearing aids, family presence). If urgency still needs treatment, try behavioral therapy or a β₃-agonist (mirabegron, vibegron) rather than another antimuscarinic.

Oxybutynin is on the AGS Beers Criteria list of drugs to avoid in older adults — especially with dementia.

Why not the others

  • (A) Noncontrast CT of the head — There is no trauma, focal deficit or anticoagulation, and a clear drug cause is present; imaging is low-yield.
  • (B) Lorazepam as needed for agitation — Benzodiazepines worsen delirium (except in alcohol or benzodiazepine withdrawal).
  • (C) Haloperidol at bedtime — Antipsychotics do not shorten delirium and add risks (falls, QT prolongation, higher mortality in dementia). Reserve them for severe agitation that endangers the patient.
  • (E) Add memantine — Memantine treats moderate–severe Alzheimer disease, not delirium.
🧠 Mnemonic

Anticholinergic toxicity — "Mad as a hatter, dry as a bone, blind as a bat, red as a beet, hot as a hare, full as a flask."

🎓 ABIM pearl

Common anticholinergic culprits in older adults: diphenhydramine and other first-generation antihistamines, oxybutynin, tolterodine, tricyclic antidepressants, paroxetine, cyclobenzaprine.

🎯 Educational objective

Delirium in older adults is often drug-induced; stop strongly anticholinergic drugs such as oxybutynin and use nonpharmacologic measures rather than antipsychotics or benzodiazepines.

📚 Read more in Wardology🌀 Delirium →

  2. Marcantonio ER. Delirium in hospitalized older adults. N Engl J Med 2017;377:1456.

GE-003.stem_html:
A 72-year-old woman is evaluated before elective cataract surgery under topical anesthesia. She has hypertension, type 2 diabetes and stable coronary artery disease with a drug-eluting stent placed 4 years ago. She has no chest pain or dyspnea. She gardens and climbs two flights of stairs without symptoms. Medications are aspirin, metoprolol, lisinopril, metformin and atorvastatin.

On physical examination, blood pressure is 132/78 mm Hg and pulse rate is 64/min. Cardiac and lung examinations are normal.
GE-003.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate preoperative management?

choices.A: Electrocardiogram, chest radiograph and basic metabolic panel
choices.E: Proceed with surgery without further testing

GE-003.explain_html:
Correct answer: E Preoperative evaluation — low-risk surgery

Preoperative cardiac evaluation follows a stepwise approach (ACC/AHA 2024):

  1. Is the surgery emergent? → proceed.
  2. Active cardiac condition (ACS, decompensated HF, significant arrhythmia, severe valve disease)? → evaluate/treat first.
  3. Surgical risk: cataract surgery is a low-risk procedure (<1% risk of major adverse cardiac events), as are endoscopy and superficial procedures.
  4. If elevated risk: functional capacity ≥4 METs (climbing two flights of stairs) → proceed.

Routine preoperative tests do not improve outcomes for cataract surgery, even in older patients with comorbidities (NEJM 2000 trial). ECG, chest radiograph, echo and stress testing are indicated only for specific findings.

Continue beta-blockers, statins and aspirin (stopping aspirin in a patient with a stent raises thrombosis risk; cataract surgery has minimal bleeding). Hold metformin the day of surgery only if fasting or receiving contrast.

Why not the others

  • (A) Electrocardiogram, chest radiograph and basic metabolic panel — Routine laboratory tests and imaging do not change management or outcomes for low-risk procedures.
  • (B) Stop aspirin 7 days before surgery — Aspirin should be continued in patients with coronary stents for low-bleeding-risk procedures like cataract surgery.
  • (C) Pharmacologic stress test — Stress testing is reserved for elevated-risk surgery in patients with poor or unknown functional capacity when it would change management.
  • (D) Transthoracic echocardiography — Echocardiography is indicated for unexplained dyspnea, a new murmur or suspected change in heart failure, not routinely.
🎯 Educational objective

Proceed without preoperative testing for low-risk surgery such as cataract extraction, and continue aspirin, beta-blockers and statins.

  2. Schein OD, et al. The value of routine preoperative medical testing before cataract surgery. N Engl J Med 2000;342:168.

GE-004.topic: Urge urinary incontinence in an older woman
GE-004.stem_html:
An 80-year-old woman is evaluated for 1 year of sudden, strong urges to urinate with leakage before she reaches the bathroom, 3–4 times daily, and nocturia twice nightly. She has mild cognitive impairment, hypertension and osteoarthritis. Medications are amlodipine and acetaminophen. She drinks four cups of coffee daily.

On physical examination, there is no pelvic organ prolapse. A cough stress test is negative.

Urinalysisnormal
Postvoid residual volume40 mL
GE-004.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate initial treatment?

choices.B: Bladder training, timed voiding and reducing caffeine

GE-004.explain_html:
Correct answer: B Urge urinary incontinence in an older woman

Urge incontinence (overactive bladder): a sudden, compelling need to void with leakage. Infection is excluded and the postvoid residual is normal (<100–150 mL), so this is not overflow.

First-line treatment is behavioral (ACP, AUA):

  • Bladder training — scheduled voiding with gradually longer intervals, urge-suppression techniques
  • Timed/prompted voiding (especially with cognitive impairment)
  • Pelvic floor muscle training
  • Reduce caffeine and evening fluids; weight loss

If medication is needed: in older adults, especially with cognitive impairment, prefer β₃-agonists (mirabegron, vibegron). Antimuscinics (oxybutynin) are on the Beers list — strongly anticholinergic, they worsen cognition and increase dementia risk.

Type Mechanism First-line
Stress Urethral hypermobility/sphincter weakness Pelvic floor muscle training
Urge Detrusor overactivity Bladder training
Overflow Obstruction / underactive detrusor (high PVR) Treat cause; catheterization
Functional Mobility/cognition Prompted voiding, environment

Why not the others

  • (A) Oxybutynin — Oxybutynin is highly anticholinergic and can worsen her cognitive impairment; behavioral therapy comes first.
  • (C) Pelvic floor surgery (midurethral sling) — Midurethral slings treat stress incontinence, not urge incontinence.
  • (D) Tamsulosin — Tamsulosin relaxes the bladder outlet in men with BPH; it does not treat urge incontinence.
  • (E) Indwelling urinary catheter — Indwelling catheters cause infection and are not a treatment for urge incontinence.
🎯 Educational objective

Treat urge urinary incontinence first with bladder training, timed voiding and caffeine reduction, and prefer β₃-agonists over anticholinergics in older adults if medication is needed.

GE-005.stem_html:
A 76-year-old man is brought by his daughter for 1.5 years of gradually worsening memory. He repeats questions, missed several bills and recently got lost driving to a familiar store. He is still independent in bathing and dressing. He has no hallucinations, falls, tremor or urinary incontinence. His mood is good. Medications are amlodipine and atorvastatin.

On physical examination, vital signs are normal. MoCA score is 20/30, with deficits in delayed recall and executive function. Neurologic examination is otherwise normal. Gait is normal.
GE-005.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate initial evaluation?

choices.D: Serum vitamin B₁₂, TSH and brain imaging (MRI or CT)
choices.E: Lumbar puncture for CSF amyloid and tau

GE-005.explain_html:
Correct answer: D Dementia evaluation

He has a progressive decline in memory and executive function affecting instrumental activities of daily living (finances, driving) → mild dementia, most likely Alzheimer disease.

The standard (AAN) evaluation for reversible or contributing causes:

  • Vitamin B₁₂ and TSH (plus CBC, metabolic panel; others such as syphilis or HIV only if risk factors)
  • Structural brain imaging once — MRI (preferred) or noncontrast CT — to look for subdural hematoma, tumor, normal-pressure hydrocephalus, strokes
  • Screen for depression ("pseudodementia"), hearing and vision loss, sleep apnea, and medications (anticholinergics, benzodiazepines)

Biomarkers (amyloid PET, CSF amyloid/tau, plasma p-tau217) are used when the diagnosis is uncertain or when anti-amyloid therapy (lecanemab, donanemab) is being considered — not as first-line routine tests. APOE genotyping is not a diagnostic test (it informs risk of ARIA with anti-amyloid therapy).

Treatment: cholinesterase inhibitors (donepezil) for mild-to-moderate AD; address driving safety, advance care planning and caregiver support.

Why not the others

  • (A) Amyloid PET scan — Amyloid PET confirms amyloid pathology in selected patients (e.g., anti-amyloid therapy candidates) but is not part of the initial evaluation.
  • (B) Electroencephalography — EEG is for suspected seizures or prion disease (rapidly progressive dementia with myoclonus), not typical slowly progressive memory loss.
  • (C) APOE genotyping — APOE ε4 raises Alzheimer risk but neither confirms nor excludes the diagnosis.
  • (E) Lumbar puncture for CSF amyloid and tau — CSF biomarkers are reserved for atypical or uncertain cases or treatment eligibility.
🎯 Educational objective

Evaluate new cognitive impairment with vitamin B₁₂, TSH and one-time structural brain imaging, plus screening for depression, sensory loss and offending medications.

GE-006.stem_html:
An 84-year-old woman with advanced dementia who is bedbound is admitted from a nursing home with pneumonia. Nursing staff note a sacral wound.

On examination, there is a 4 × 3 cm wound over the sacrum with full-thickness skin loss. Subcutaneous fat is visible in the wound bed, with some granulation tissue and a small amount of slough. Bone, tendon and muscle are not visible or palpable. There is no undermining. The surrounding skin is intact.
GE-006.lead: Which of the following is the stage of this pressure injury?
GE-006.explain_html:
Correct answer: C Pressure injury staging

Pressure injury staging (NPIAP 2016):

Stage Definition
1 Intact skin with nonblanchable erythema
2 Partial-thickness loss; exposed dermis (pink, moist; or intact/ruptured serum-filled blister) — no fat
3 Full-thickness skin loss; fat visible; granulation, slough, eschar may be present; no fascia, muscle, tendon or bone
4 Full-thickness skin and tissue loss with exposed or palpable fascia, muscle, tendon, ligament, cartilage or bone
Unstageable Base obscured by slough or eschar so depth cannot be confirmed
Deep tissue injury Intact or nonintact skin with persistent nonblanchable deep red, maroon or purple discoloration

Visible fat without deeper structures = stage 3. The small amount of slough does not obscure the depth.

Management: pressure redistribution (repositioning every 2 hours, support surfaces), moisture management, nutrition, wound care (debridement of necrotic tissue), and pain control. Do not reverse-stage as wounds heal.

Why not the others

  • (A) Stage 1 — Stage 1 has intact skin with nonblanchable redness.
  • (B) Stage 2 — Stage 2 is partial-thickness loss with exposed dermis; fat is not visible.
  • (D) Stage 4 — Stage 4 requires exposed or palpable bone, tendon, muscle or fascia.
  • (E) Unstageable — A wound is unstageable only when slough or eschar hides the base so depth cannot be determined; here the depth is visible.
🎯 Educational objective

A pressure injury with full-thickness skin loss and visible subcutaneous fat, but no exposed bone, tendon, muscle or fascia, is stage 3.

GE-007.stem_html:
An 82-year-old man is evaluated after two episodes in the past month of sweating, shakiness and confusion in the late morning; once he fell. He lives alone. He has type 2 diabetes, CKD (eGFR 38 mL/min/1.73 m²) and benign prostatic hyperplasia. Medications are glyburide, 10 mg twice daily; metformin, 500 mg twice daily; tamsulosin; lisinopril; and diphenhydramine at night for sleep.

On physical examination, blood pressure is 128/72 mm Hg without orthostatic change. He has mild cognitive impairment.

Hemoglobin A1c6.1%
Fingerstick glucose during last episode48 mg/dL
GE-007.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate change to his medications?

choices.B: Increase metformin to 1000 mg twice daily
choices.E: Add a bedtime snack and keep the current regimen

GE-007.explain_html:
Correct answer: A Deprescribing — Beers criteria

He is having recurrent hypoglycemia with a fall from glyburide — a long-acting sulfonylurea with active renally cleared metabolites, accumulating with his CKD. His A1c of 6.1% is too low for an older adult with cognitive impairment who lives alone (ADA target <8.0%, or <7.0–7.5% for healthy older adults).

The AGS Beers Criteria list as potentially inappropriate in older adults:

  • Sulfonylureas — all as first- or second-line (hypoglycemia); glyburide and glimepiride worst
  • First-generation antihistamines (diphenhydramine) — strongly anticholinergic: confusion, falls, urinary retention (risky with BPH), constipation
  • Benzodiazepines and Z-drugs, sliding-scale insulin, PPIs >8 weeks without indication, and others

Deprescribe: stop glyburide (his A1c will remain near goal on metformin alone, which is fine at eGFR 30–44 with dose limits), and stop diphenhydramine (use CBT-I or sleep hygiene). If more glucose-lowering is needed later, choose low-hypoglycemia agents (DPP-4 inhibitor, SGLT2 inhibitor, GLP-1 RA).

Why not the others

  • (B) Increase metformin to 1000 mg twice daily — Metformin is capped at 1000 mg/d at an eGFR of 30–44.
  • (C) Switch tamsulosin to doxazosin — Doxazosin is a nonselective α-blocker that causes more orthostatic hypotension and falls than tamsulosin.
  • (D) Switch glyburide to insulin glargine — Insulin adds hypoglycemia risk and is unnecessary at an A1c of 6.1%.
  • (E) Add a bedtime snack and keep the current regimen — A snack does not remove the cause; glyburide will keep causing hypoglycemia, and his glycemic target is overtreated.
🎯 Educational objective

Deprescribe Beers-list medications such as glyburide and diphenhydramine in older adults, and relax glycemic targets to avoid hypoglycemia.

GI-001.stem_html:
A 58-year-old man comes to discuss the results of an upper endoscopy done for 10 years of frequent heartburn. He takes omeprazole 20 mg daily, which controls his symptoms well. He has no dysphagia, weight loss or bleeding. He is a former smoker.

Endoscopy showed salmon-colored mucosa extending 4 cm above the gastroesophageal junction without nodules or ulceration. Biopsies show intestinal metaplasia with goblet cells and no dysplasia, confirmed by a second gastrointestinal pathologist.
GI-001.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

choices.A: Continue omeprazole and repeat endoscopy in 6 months
choices.B: Continue omeprazole and repeat endoscopy in 3 years
choices.D: Radiofrequency ablation of the Barrett segment
choices.E: Stop omeprazole because symptoms are controlled

GI-001.explain_html:
Correct answer: B Barrett esophagus without dysplasia

Barrett esophagus is columnar metaplasia of the distal esophagus (with goblet cells) caused by chronic acid reflux. It is the precursor of esophageal adenocarcinoma, but the risk without dysplasia is low — roughly 0.2%–0.5% per year.

For nondysplastic Barrett, management is:

  • Daily PPI (reduces inflammation; may lower progression).
  • Surveillance endoscopy with biopsies: every 3 years for segments ≥3 cm, every 5 years for segments <3 cm.

Ablation is reserved for dysplasia. The pathway escalates with the grade of dysplasia:

Biopsy Plan
No dysplasia, ≥3 cm PPI + EGD every 3 years
No dysplasia, <3 cm PPI + EGD every 5 years
Indefinite for dysplasia Optimize PPI, repeat EGD in 6 months
Low-grade dysplasia (confirmed) Endoscopic eradication therapy (or surveillance every 12 months)
High-grade dysplasia / intramucosal cancer Endoscopic resection of nodules + ablation

Why not the others

  • (A) Continue omeprazole and repeat endoscopy in 6 months — A 6-month interval is for "indefinite for dysplasia" after optimizing acid suppression, not for nondysplastic Barrett.
  • (C) Refer for esophagectomy — Esophagectomy is reserved for invasive cancer beyond the mucosa that cannot be treated endoscopically.
  • (D) Radiofrequency ablation of the Barrett segment — Ablation is for confirmed dysplasia; in nondysplastic Barrett, ablation risks (stricture, bleeding) outweigh the small benefit.
  • (E) Stop omeprazole because symptoms are controlled — Patients with Barrett esophagus should stay on a PPI even when symptoms are controlled.
🎓 ABIM pearl

Screening endoscopy for Barrett is suggested in patients with chronic GERD plus ≥3 risk factors: male sex, age >50, White race, central obesity, smoking, or a first-degree relative with Barrett or esophageal adenocarcinoma.

🎯 Educational objective

Nondysplastic Barrett esophagus is managed with a daily PPI and surveillance endoscopy every 3 years (segment ≥3 cm) or 5 years (segment <3 cm); ablation is for dysplasia.

GI-002.stem_html:
A 44-year-old woman was diagnosed with a duodenal ulcer 4 weeks ago when she presented with epigastric pain. Biopsies were positive for Helicobacter pylori. She completed 14 days of bismuth quadruple therapy (omeprazole, bismuth subsalicylate, tetracycline and metronidazole) 2 weeks ago. She is still taking omeprazole 40 mg daily and now has no pain.

Examination is normal. Hemoglobin is 12.9 g/dL.
GI-002.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate way to confirm eradication of H. pylori?

choices.A: Repeat upper endoscopy with biopsy now
choices.C: No testing is needed because her symptoms resolved
choices.E: Urea breath test at least 4 weeks after antibiotics, after holding omeprazole for 2 weeks

GI-002.explain_html:
Correct answer: E Helicobacter pylori — test of cure

Every patient treated for H. pylori should have a test of cure — resistance (especially to clarithromycin and metronidazole) makes treatment failure common, and symptom relief does not prove eradication.

Use a test of active infection: urea breath test, stool antigen, or biopsy-based tests. Two timing rules prevent false-negative results, because PPIs, bismuth and antibiotics suppress the bacteria without killing them:

  • At least 4 weeks after finishing antibiotics and bismuth.
  • PPI held for 1–2 weeks before testing (an H₂ blocker can cover symptoms).

Uncomplicated duodenal ulcer does not need repeat endoscopy. (Gastric ulcers are different — they often need repeat endoscopy to exclude cancer.)

Why not the others

  • (A) Repeat upper endoscopy with biopsy now — Endoscopy is not needed to confirm cure after an uncomplicated duodenal ulcer; a noninvasive test is preferred.
  • (B) Serum H. pylori IgG antibody now — Antibodies stay positive for months to years after cure, so serology cannot confirm eradication. It only proves past exposure.
  • (C) No testing is needed because her symptoms resolved — Symptom resolution does not mean the bacteria are gone; persistent infection risks recurrent ulcer and bleeding.
  • (D) Urea breath test now — Testing now is too soon after antibiotics and while on a PPI — both cause false-negative results.
🧠 Mnemonic

Test of cure "4 and 2": 4 weeks off antibiotics/bismuth, 2 weeks off PPI.

🎓 ABIM pearl

First-line therapy in the US is now bismuth quadruple therapy for 14 days when clarithromycin susceptibility is unknown. Vonoprazan-based dual or triple therapy is an alternative.

🎯 Educational objective

Confirm H. pylori eradication with a urea breath test, stool antigen or biopsy at least 4 weeks after antibiotics and 1–2 weeks after stopping PPIs; serology cannot confirm cure.

GI-003.stem_html:
A 38-year-old man comes to establish care. He feels well. His father was diagnosed with colorectal cancer at age 46 and is alive after surgery and chemotherapy. No other relatives have had cancer. The patient has no rectal bleeding, change in bowel habits or weight loss.

Examination is normal. Complete blood count is normal.
GI-003.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate colorectal cancer screening plan?

choices.A: Stool DNA–FIT test now and every 3 years
choices.B: Begin screening at age 45 with colonoscopy every 10 years
choices.C: Colonoscopy now and every 5 years if normal
choices.D: Begin screening at age 45 with annual fecal immunochemical testing
choices.E: CT colonography now and every 10 years

GI-003.explain_html:
Correct answer: C Colorectal cancer screening — family history

Average-risk adults begin screening at 45. Family history changes both when and how.

With one first-degree relative diagnosed before age 60 (or two at any age), screening is by colonoscopy, starting at age 40 or 10 years before the relative's age at diagnosis, whichever comes first, and repeated every 5 years. His father was 46 → start at 36. He is already 38, so the first colonoscopy is due now.

Family history Start Test & interval
None (average risk) 45 Colonoscopy q10y, FIT q1y, stool DNA–FIT q1–3y, CT colonography q5y, sigmoidoscopy q5y
1 FDR <60 y, or ≥2 FDRs any age 40 or 10 y before youngest diagnosis Colonoscopy q5y
1 FDR ≥60 y 40 Average-risk tests and intervals

Why not the others

  • (A) Stool DNA–FIT test now and every 3 years — Stool DNA–FIT is not recommended for screening people with a first-degree relative diagnosed young.
  • (B) Begin screening at age 45 with colonoscopy every 10 years — Starting at 45 is too late and the 10-year interval is too long for his risk.
  • (D) Begin screening at age 45 with annual fecal immunochemical testing — Age 45 and annual FIT are for average-risk adults. His family history moves him to colonoscopy, starting earlier.
  • (E) CT colonography now and every 10 years — CT colonography is an average-risk option. In higher-risk patients, colonoscopy is preferred because it allows biopsy and polypectomy.
🎓 ABIM pearl

Ask whether the relative's tumor was tested for mismatch repair deficiency. A deficient tumor raises concern for Lynch syndrome, which needs genetic counseling and colonoscopy every 1–2 years starting at age 20–25.

🎯 Educational objective

A first-degree relative with colorectal cancer before age 60 calls for colonoscopy every 5 years starting at age 40 or 10 years before the relative's diagnosis, whichever is earlier.

GI-004.topic: Cirrhosis — primary prophylaxis of variceal bleeding
GI-004.stem_html:
A 57-year-old man with alcohol-associated cirrhosis comes for follow-up. He has not had alcohol for 18 months. He has never had ascites, encephalopathy or gastrointestinal bleeding. Screening upper endoscopy last week showed large esophageal varices without red wale signs or stigmata of recent bleeding.

Blood pressure is 122/74 mm Hg and pulse is 82/min. There is mild splenomegaly and no ascites.

Platelets88,000/µL
Albumin3.7 g/dL
Bilirubin, total1.2 mg/dL
INR1.2
Creatinine0.9 mg/dL
GI-004.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment to prevent variceal bleeding?

choices.A: No treatment; repeat endoscopy in 1 year

GI-004.explain_html:
Correct answer: E Cirrhosis — primary prophylaxis of variceal bleeding

Large varices that have never bled need primary prophylaxis. The options are a nonselective beta-blocker (NSBB) or endoscopic band ligation. NSBBs are now preferred in compensated cirrhosis because they also lower the risk of first decompensation (ascites), not just bleeding.

Carvedilol is the NSBB of choice: it blocks β₁ (lowers cardiac output), β₂ (unopposed α-constriction of splanchnic vessels → less portal inflow) and α₁ (lowers intrahepatic resistance). It lowers portal pressure more than propranolol. Typical dose 6.25 mg daily, increasing to 12.5 mg daily as tolerated.

Stop or reduce NSBBs if systolic BP falls below 90 mm Hg, or with refractory ascites plus hypotension, AKI or spontaneous bacterial peritonitis.

Why not the others

  • (A) No treatment; repeat endoscopy in 1 year — Large varices carry a high bleeding risk (mortality ~15%–20% per bleed); waiting without treatment is not appropriate.
  • (B) Transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt (TIPS) — TIPS is for bleeding that cannot be controlled or recurs despite therapy, and for refractory ascites — not for primary prophylaxis.
  • (C) Isosorbide mononitrate — Nitrates alone do not prevent variceal bleeding and can worsen hypotension and renal perfusion.
  • (D) Metoprolol — Metoprolol is β₁-selective. It lacks the β₂ effect that reduces splanchnic flow, so it does not lower portal pressure enough.
🎓 ABIM pearl

Patients who cannot take a beta-blocker get band ligation every 2–8 weeks until varices are eradicated. Once on carvedilol, no repeat endoscopy is needed to "check" the varices.

🎯 Educational objective

Prevent the first variceal bleed in cirrhosis with large varices with a nonselective beta-blocker — carvedilol is preferred — or band ligation if beta-blockers cannot be used.

📚 Read more in Wardology🍺 Decompensated cirrhosis →

GI-005.stem_html:
A 48-year-old woman was admitted 3 days ago with severe epigastric pain radiating to the back and vomiting. Lipase was 2,400 U/L. She received intravenous lactated Ringer solution and analgesics. Today she is hungry, her pain is gone, and she is eating a low-fat diet without discomfort. She drinks alcohol rarely.

Temperature is 37.0 °C (98.6 °F), blood pressure is 124/78 mm Hg and pulse is 80/min. The abdomen is soft with mild epigastric tenderness.

Admission ALT312 U/L
Today ALT96 U/L
Bilirubin, total (today)0.9 mg/dL
Triglycerides140 mg/dL
Calcium9.1 mg/dL
Right upper quadrant ultrasoundmultiple gallstones; common bile duct 5 mm; no pericholecystic fluid
GI-005.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.A: Start imipenem to prevent infected necrosis
choices.C: Discharge home and arrange elective cholecystectomy in 6–8 weeks

GI-005.explain_html:
Correct answer: E Gallstone pancreatitis

This is mild acute biliary pancreatitis: gallstones, an early transaminase spike (ALT >150 U/L in the first 48 hours strongly suggests a gallstone cause), and normal triglycerides and calcium. A stone passed through the ampulla and caused pancreatitis.

The key decision is timing of cholecystectomy. After mild gallstone pancreatitis, cholecystectomy during the same admission cuts the risk of recurrent biliary events — up to about 1 in 5 patients have another episode (pancreatitis, cholecystitis, colic) while waiting weeks for surgery.

Severe necrotizing pancreatitis is the exception: surgery is delayed until collections resolve or mature (usually >6 weeks).

Why not the others

  • (A) Start imipenem to prevent infected necrosis — Prophylactic antibiotics do not prevent infected necrosis and are not recommended in acute pancreatitis.
  • (B) Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP) before discharge — ERCP is for cholangitis or persistent biliary obstruction. Her bilirubin is normal and the duct is not dilated, so the stone has passed.
  • (C) Discharge home and arrange elective cholecystectomy in 6–8 weeks — Delaying cholecystectomy in mild disease leaves a high early risk of recurrent pancreatitis and other gallstone complications.
  • (D) Start ursodeoxycholic acid and discharge — Ursodiol dissolves stones slowly and incompletely and does not prevent recurrent pancreatitis; it is for patients who cannot have surgery.
🎓 ABIM pearl

The two most common causes of acute pancreatitis are gallstones and alcohol. Check triglycerides (cause if >1000 mg/dL) and calcium in every first episode.

🎯 Educational objective

After mild gallstone pancreatitis, perform cholecystectomy during the same admission; reserve ERCP for cholangitis or ongoing biliary obstruction.

📚 Read more in Wardology🔥 Acute pancreatitis →

GI-006.stem_html:
A 32-year-old woman is evaluated for 8 months of bloating, loose stools and fatigue. She has lost 3 kg (6.6 lb). She has autoimmune hypothyroidism treated with levothyroxine. She eats a regular diet that includes bread and pasta daily.

On physical examination, vital signs are normal. BMI is 20. There is a pruritic papulovesicular rash on the extensor surfaces of both elbows. The abdomen is mildly distended and nontender.

Hemoglobin10.9 g/dL
MCV76 fL
Ferritin6 ng/mL
Albumin3.6 g/dL
Aminotransferasesmildly elevated (ALT 58 U/L)
GI-006.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate initial diagnostic test?

choices.B: Stool culture and ova and parasites
choices.D: Tissue transglutaminase IgA antibody with total IgA level

GI-006.explain_html:
Correct answer: D Celiac disease — serologic testing

Diarrhea, bloating, weight loss, iron deficiency anemia unresponsive to diet, mildly raised aminotransferases, autoimmune thyroid disease and dermatitis herpetiformis (itchy vesicles on the extensor surfaces) point to celiac disease.

The best initial test is tissue transglutaminase IgA (tTG-IgA) plus a total IgA level. Selective IgA deficiency is 10–15 times more common in celiac disease and causes a false-negative tTG-IgA; if IgA is low, use deamidated gliadin peptide IgG or tTG-IgG.

The patient must be eating gluten when tested. A positive serology is confirmed with upper endoscopy and duodenal biopsies (villous atrophy, crypt hyperplasia, intraepithelial lymphocytes) before lifelong gluten-free diet.

Why not the others

  • (A) HLA-DQ2/DQ8 genotyping — HLA-DQ2/DQ8 testing has a high negative predictive value but poor positive predictive value (present in ~30% of the population). It helps exclude celiac disease in unclear cases, not as a first test.
  • (B) Stool culture and ova and parasites — Chronic diarrhea for 8 months with iron deficiency and a typical rash is not an infection pattern.
  • (C) Antigliadin IgG antibodies — Native antigliadin antibodies are inaccurate and no longer recommended.
  • (E) Trial of a gluten-free diet — Starting a gluten-free diet before testing makes serology and biopsy falsely negative and prevents a firm diagnosis.
🎓 ABIM pearl

Dermatitis herpetiformis is celiac disease of the skin — almost all patients have gluten-sensitive enteropathy, even without GI symptoms. Treat with gluten-free diet (plus dapsone for the rash).

🎯 Educational objective

Screen for celiac disease with tissue transglutaminase IgA and a total IgA level while the patient is eating gluten, and confirm positive results with duodenal biopsy.

GI-007.stem_html:
A 72-year-old woman is evaluated for 2 days of watery diarrhea (8 stools daily) and crampy abdominal pain. She finished a course of amoxicillin-clavulanate for sinusitis 10 days ago. She has no previous episodes of similar diarrhea.

On physical examination, temperature is 37.9 °C (100.2 °F), blood pressure is 124/72 mm Hg, and pulse rate is 96/min. The abdomen is soft with mild diffuse tenderness and normal bowel sounds.

Leukocyte count12,400/µL
Creatinine0.9 mg/dL (baseline 0.8 mg/dL)
Stool C. difficile PCRpositive
Stool C. difficile toxin EIApositive
GI-007.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
GI-007.explain_html:
Correct answer: A Clostridioides difficile infection — first episode

She has a first episode of nonsevere C. difficile infection (leukocyte count <15,000/µL and creatinine <1.5 mg/dL).

Oral fidaxomicin (200 mg twice daily for 10 days) is preferred over oral vancomycin for an initial episode (IDSA/SHEA 2021): cure rates are similar, but recurrence is lower because fidaxomicin is narrow-spectrum and spares the normal colonic flora. Oral vancomycin (125 mg four times daily for 10 days) remains an acceptable alternative.

Episode Treatment
First, nonsevere or severe Fidaxomicin (or oral vancomycin)
Fulminant (hypotension, ileus, megacolon) Oral vancomycin 500 mg QID + IV metronidazole (± rectal vancomycin); surgery consult
First recurrence Fidaxomicin (or vancomycin taper/pulse); consider bezlotoxumab
≥2 recurrences Fecal microbiota–based therapy

Why not the others

  • (B) Oral metronidazole — Metronidazole is less effective than vancomycin or fidaxomicin and is used only when those are unavailable for a nonsevere episode.
  • (C) Intravenous vancomycin — IV vancomycin is not excreted into the colon and does not treat C. difficile.
  • (D) Loperamide — Antimotility drugs are avoided in active C. difficile infection because they may precipitate toxic megacolon.
  • (E) Fecal microbiota transplantation — Fecal microbiota therapy is for multiple recurrences, not a first episode.
🎓 ABIM pearl

Test only unformed stools (≥3 in 24 hours) and do not test for cure. Many hospitalized patients are colonized — a positive PCR in formed stool is not infection.

🎯 Educational objective

Treat an initial episode of C. difficile infection with oral fidaxomicin (preferred) or oral vancomycin.

GI-008.stem_html:
A 28-year-old woman is evaluated for 1 year of recurrent lower abdominal cramping that occurs about 2 days per week. The pain is relieved by defecation and is associated with loose, frequent stools alternating with days of constipation. Symptoms worsen during stress at work. She has no rectal bleeding, nocturnal diarrhea, fever or weight loss. There is no family history of colon cancer, inflammatory bowel disease or celiac disease.

On physical examination, vital signs are normal and BMI is 24. The abdomen is soft with mild lower quadrant tenderness. Rectal examination is normal.

Complete blood countnormal
C-reactive protein1 mg/L
GI-008.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate next diagnostic step?

choices.A: CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis

GI-008.explain_html:
Correct answer: E Irritable bowel syndrome

She meets Rome IV criteria for irritable bowel syndrome (IBS): recurrent abdominal pain ≥1 day/week for ≥3 months, associated with defecation and a change in stool frequency or form — here IBS with mixed bowel habits.

IBS is a positive diagnosis, not a diagnosis of exclusion. In a young patient without alarm features (age ≥45 at onset, rectal bleeding, weight loss, nocturnal symptoms, anemia, family history of CRC/IBD/celiac), testing is limited to:

  • Celiac serology (tTG-IgA) for IBS with diarrhea or mixed
  • Fecal calprotectin (or lactoferrin) and CRP to screen for IBD
  • CBC

Colonoscopy is not needed without alarm features or an age-appropriate screening indication.

Why not the others

  • (A) CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis — Imaging has a very low yield in typical IBS and exposes her to radiation.
  • (B) Hydrogen breath test — Breath testing for small intestinal bacterial overgrowth or lactose intolerance is not part of the routine IBS evaluation.
  • (C) Upper endoscopy — She has no upper GI symptoms or alarm features that would warrant endoscopy.
  • (D) Colonoscopy with random biopsies — Colonoscopy is reserved for alarm features or age-appropriate screening. She has neither.
🧠 Mnemonic

Rome IV: pain 1 day a week for 3 months plus 2 of 3 — related to defecation, change in frequency, change in form.

🎯 Educational objective

Diagnose IBS by Rome IV criteria and, in the absence of alarm features, limit testing to celiac serology, fecal calprotectin, CRP and a CBC.

(b) hydrogen breath test — breath testing for small intestinal bacterial overgrowth or lactose intolerance is not part of the routine ibs evaluation. (c) upper endoscopy — she has no upper gi symptoms or alarm features that would warrant endoscopy. (d) colonoscopy with random biopsies — colonoscopy is reserved for alarm features or age-appropriate screening. she has neither. 🧠 mnemonic rome iv: pain 1 day a week for 3 months plus 2 of 3 — related to defecation, change in frequency, change in form. 🎯 educational objective diagnose ibs by rome iv criteria and, in the absence of alarm features, limit testing to celiac serology, fecal calprotectin, crp and a cbc. 📚 read more in wardology 🌀 diarrhea, c. difficile, celiac & ibs → references {'lacy be, et al. acg clinical guideline': 'management of irritable bowel syndrome. am j gastroenterol 2021;116:17.'}  irritable bowel syndrome

GI-009.stem_html:
A 26-year-old man with ulcerative colitis diagnosed 2 years ago is hospitalized with 10 days of 9 bloody stools daily, cramping and fatigue. He takes oral mesalamine.

On physical examination, temperature is 38.2 °C (100.8 °F), blood pressure is 112/68 mm Hg, and pulse rate is 104/min. The abdomen is mildly tender without distension or rebound; bowel sounds are present.

Hemoglobin9.8 g/dL
Leukocyte count13,600/µL
C-reactive protein64 mg/L
Albumin2.9 g/dL
Stool C. difficile PCRnegative
Abdominal radiographno colonic dilation
GI-009.lead: In addition to venous thromboembolism prophylaxis, which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?

choices.D: Increase oral mesalamine and add mesalamine enemas

GI-009.explain_html:
Correct answer: B Acute severe ulcerative colitis

He has acute severe ulcerative colitis by Truelove and Witts criteria: ≥6 bloody stools daily plus at least one sign of systemic toxicity — fever, tachycardia >90/min, hemoglobin <10.5 g/dL or high ESR/CRP. C. difficile is excluded, and there is no toxic megacolon.

First-line therapy is IV glucocorticoids (methylprednisolone 60 mg/d or hydrocortisone 100 mg three times daily). Also give pharmacologic VTE prophylaxis — IBD flares are strongly prothrombotic, even with rectal bleeding — and do flexible sigmoidoscopy to exclude CMV.

Reassess on day 3: if there is no response, start rescue therapy with infliximab or cyclosporine; colectomy if rescue fails or if perforation, megacolon or uncontrolled bleeding develops.

Why not the others

  • (A) Loperamide and oral iron — Antidiarrheals can precipitate toxic megacolon in severe colitis and should be avoided.
  • (C) Oral budesonide MMX — Budesonide MMX is for mild-to-moderate UC; it is not strong enough for a severe flare with systemic toxicity.
  • (D) Increase oral mesalamine and add mesalamine enemas — Escalating mesalamine is appropriate for mild-to-moderate disease, not acute severe colitis.
  • (E) Emergency total colectomy — Emergency colectomy is for perforation, toxic megacolon, massive hemorrhage or failure of medical rescue therapy.
🎯 Educational objective

Treat acute severe ulcerative colitis with intravenous glucocorticoids, VTE prophylaxis and exclusion of infection, with infliximab or cyclosporine rescue if there is no response by day 3.

GI-010.stem_html:
A 39-year-old woman with Crohn disease had a resection of 80 cm of terminal ileum 3 years ago. She is now evaluated for acute right flank pain radiating to the groin. Noncontrast CT shows a 5-mm obstructing stone in the right ureter. She has chronic loose, greasy stools.

Urine pH5.8
24-hour urine oxalate78 mg (reference, <45)
24-hour urine citratelow
Vitamin B₁₂168 pg/mL (low)
GI-010.lead: Which of the following is the most likely mechanism of her kidney stone?

choices.A: Increased intestinal absorption of oxalate due to fat malabsorption
choices.D: Increased urinary uric acid from rapid cell turnover

GI-010.explain_html:
Correct answer: A Crohn disease — ileal resection complications

This is enteric hyperoxaluria. After ileal resection, bile acids are lost, so fat is poorly absorbed (steatorrhea). In the gut lumen, unabsorbed fatty acids bind calcium (saponification). Normally calcium binds dietary oxalate and keeps it in the stool; without free calcium, oxalate stays soluble and is absorbed in the colon (bile acids also make the colon more permeable). The result is calcium oxalate stones.

Chronic diarrhea adds low urine volume and low citrate (bicarbonate loss → hypocitraturia).

Treatment: high fluid intake, low-fat, low-oxalate diet, calcium supplements taken with meals (to bind oxalate), and potassium citrate.

The ileum is also where vitamin B₁₂ (with intrinsic factor) and bile acids are absorbed — explaining her low B₁₂ and, if bile acids spill into the colon, bile acid diarrhea (treated with cholestyramine).

Why not the others

  • (B) Infection with urease-producing bacteria — Struvite stones form with urease-producing organisms (Proteus, Klebsiella) in alkaline urine.
  • (C) Increased hepatic production of oxalate — Hepatic overproduction occurs in rare inherited primary hyperoxaluria, not after bowel resection.
  • (D) Increased urinary uric acid from rapid cell turnover — Uric acid stones form in acidic urine and with gout or tumor lysis; her urine oxalate is high.
  • (E) Primary hyperparathyroidism — Hyperparathyroidism causes hypercalciuria and calcium stones, but the key abnormality here is hyperoxaluria from malabsorption.
🎓 ABIM pearl

Do not restrict dietary calcium in calcium oxalate stone formers — low calcium intake increases oxalate absorption and stone risk.

🎯 Educational objective

Fat malabsorption after ileal resection causes enteric hyperoxaluria because unabsorbed fatty acids bind calcium, freeing oxalate for colonic absorption.
