GI-011.stem_html:
A 45-year-old man is evaluated before starting rituximab for lymphoma. He has no symptoms of liver disease. He emigrated from Vietnam 20 years ago. He has never been vaccinated against hepatitis B.

Examination is normal.

ALT22 U/L
HBsAgnegative
Anti-HBsnegative
Anti-HBc (total)positive
HBV DNAundetectable
GI-011.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

choices.D: Give hepatitis B vaccine and proceed without prophylaxis

GI-011.explain_html:
Correct answer: B Hepatitis B serologies

Isolated anti-HBc positivity with negative HBsAg most often means resolved past HBV infection (with waning anti-HBs). The virus persists as cccDNA in the liver for life.

Rituximab (anti-CD20) is the highest-risk drug for HBV reactivation — even in HBsAg-negative, anti-HBc–positive patients, reactivation can cause fulminant hepatitis and death. Antiviral prophylaxis with entecavir or tenofovir is recommended, started before therapy and continued for at least 12–18 months after rituximab ends.

HBsAg Anti-HBc Anti-HBs Meaning
− − + Vaccinated
− + + Resolved infection (immune)
+ + (IgM) − Acute infection
+ + (IgG) − Chronic infection (>6 months)
− + − Resolved with waning anti-HBs, window period, or occult infection

Screen everyone with HBsAg, anti-HBc and anti-HBs before chemotherapy, immunosuppression, or anti-CD20 therapy.

Why not the others

  • (A) Proceed with rituximab without monitoring — Proceeding without prophylaxis or monitoring risks severe reactivation with rituximab.
  • (C) Repeat serologies in 6 months — The decision is needed now, before rituximab.
  • (D) Give hepatitis B vaccine and proceed without prophylaxis — Vaccination does not protect against reactivation of existing HBV, and he needs prophylaxis given the high-risk drug.
  • (E) Begin interferon alfa — Interferon is not used for prophylaxis and is poorly tolerated, and it would worsen cytopenias during chemotherapy.
🎯 Educational objective

Give nucleos(t)ide prophylaxis to anti-HBc–positive patients, even if HBsAg-negative, before rituximab or other high-risk immunosuppression.

GI-012.stem_html:
A 52-year-old man is evaluated after one-time screening showed a positive hepatitis C antibody. He used injection drugs 25 years ago and has not used since. He has no symptoms.

On physical examination, vital signs are normal. There are no stigmata of chronic liver disease.

ALT64 U/L
Platelet count212,000/µL
Albumin4.1 g/dL
HCV RNA2.4 million IU/mL
HBsAgnegative; anti-HBc, negative; anti-HBs, negative
HIV antibodynegative
FIB-4 index1.1
GI-012.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

choices.A: Monitor HCV RNA and treat only if ALT rises
choices.C: Repeat HCV RNA in 6 months to confirm chronic infection
choices.E: Sofosbuvir-velpatasvir for 12 weeks and hepatitis B vaccination

GI-012.explain_html:
Correct answer: E Chronic hepatitis C — treatment

A positive antibody with detectable HCV RNA confirms active hepatitis C. Every patient with chronic HCV should be treated (except those with very limited life expectancy) — treatment cures >95%, prevents cirrhosis and liver cancer, and stops transmission.

Simplified treatment for treatment-naive adults without cirrhosis (FIB-4 <3.25, no clinical cirrhosis):

  • Sofosbuvir-velpatasvir for 12 weeks, or glecaprevir-pibrentasvir for 8 weeks — pangenotypic, so genotyping is not required.
  • Before treatment: HBV serologies (DAA therapy can reactivate HBV), HIV test, drug-interaction check.
  • Confirm cure with sustained virologic response (undetectable RNA) 12 weeks after treatment.

He is not immune to hepatitis B, so vaccinate him (and against hepatitis A).

Why not the others

  • (A) Monitor HCV RNA and treat only if ALT rises — Treatment is recommended for all patients with chronic HCV, regardless of ALT or fibrosis stage.
  • (B) Liver biopsy before treatment — Noninvasive fibrosis assessment (FIB-4, elastography) has replaced biopsy for staging before HCV treatment.
  • (C) Repeat HCV RNA in 6 months to confirm chronic infection — An RNA-positive result after an infection that was acquired decades ago confirms chronic infection; there is no need to wait.
  • (D) Pegylated interferon plus ribavirin — Interferon-based regimens are obsolete — less effective and far more toxic than DAAs.
🎓 ABIM pearl

The USPSTF and CDC recommend one-time HCV screening for all adults 18–79 years, and testing during every pregnancy.

🎯 Educational objective

Treat all patients with chronic hepatitis C with a pangenotypic direct-acting antiviral regimen after checking for hepatitis B coinfection.

GI-013.stem_html:
A 47-year-old man is evaluated for fatigue, joint pains in his hands and mildly elevated aminotransferases found on routine testing. He drinks one beer a week. He takes no medications or supplements. His older brother has "liver problems".

On physical examination, vital signs are normal. BMI is 25. There is tenderness and bony swelling of the second and third metacarpophalangeal joints of both hands. The liver edge is palpable 2 cm below the costal margin.

ALT72 U/L
AST58 U/L
Fasting glucose128 mg/dL
Transferrin saturation78%
Ferritin1,480 ng/mL
Hepatitis B and C serologiesnegative
GI-013.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate next diagnostic test?
GI-013.explain_html:
Correct answer: E Hereditary hemochromatosis

Second and third MCP arthropathy, fatigue, elevated aminotransferases, hepatomegaly, new hyperglycemia and a family history of liver disease → hereditary hemochromatosis.

The screening tests are fasting transferrin saturation (>45%) and ferritin. When the transferrin saturation is elevated, the next step is HFE gene testing (C282Y/H63D). C282Y homozygosity confirms the diagnosis in most northern European patients.

Liver fibrosis assessment: if C282Y homozygous with ferritin >1000 ng/mL or raised aminotransferases, assess for advanced fibrosis (elastography/MRI; biopsy if uncertain) — he will need this. Treatment is therapeutic phlebotomy to a ferritin of 50–100 ng/mL. Screen first-degree relatives.

Why not the others

  • (A) Liver biopsy — Liver biopsy is no longer needed for diagnosis. It may be used to stage fibrosis when noninvasive tests are inconclusive, after HFE testing.
  • (B) Serum ceruloplasmin — Ceruloplasmin screens for Wilson disease, which presents in younger patients with neuropsychiatric findings and low ceruloplasmin.
  • (C) MRI of the hands — Hand imaging shows hook-like osteophytes and chondrocalcinosis but does not establish the diagnosis.
  • (D) Bone marrow biopsy — Bone marrow biopsy is not used to diagnose iron overload.
🧠 Mnemonic

Hemochromatosis = "bronze diabetes" — liver, pancreas, skin, heart, gonads and the "iron fist" (2nd/3rd MCP arthropathy).

🎯 Educational objective

In a patient with elevated transferrin saturation and ferritin, perform HFE genotyping to diagnose hereditary hemochromatosis.

GI-014.stem_html:
A 56-year-old woman is evaluated for mildly elevated aminotransferases found on routine testing. She has type 2 diabetes, hypertension and obesity. She drinks alcohol rarely. Medications are metformin, lisinopril and atorvastatin.

On physical examination, BMI is 36. There are no signs of chronic liver disease.

Ultrasonography shows a diffusely echogenic liver without masses; the spleen is normal in size.

AST48 U/L
ALT42 U/L
Platelet count168,000/µL
Albumin4.2 g/dL
Hepatitis B and C serologiesnegative
Ferritin210 ng/mL; transferrin saturation, 28%
FIB-4 index2.1
GI-014.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
GI-014.explain_html:
Correct answer: A MASLD — fibrosis risk assessment

She has metabolic dysfunction–associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) — hepatic steatosis plus cardiometabolic risk factors, with other causes excluded.

The main determinant of outcome is fibrosis stage. Use a two-step approach:

  1. FIB-4 (age, AST, ALT, platelets).
  2. Second-line test when FIB-4 is not low: vibration-controlled transient elastography (FibroScan) or ELF blood test.
FIB-4 Interpretation Next step
<1.3 Low risk of advanced fibrosis Repeat in 1–3 years
1.3–2.67 Indeterminate Elastography (or ELF)
>2.67 High risk Hepatology referral

Her FIB-4 of 2.1 is indeterminate. Diabetes makes advanced fibrosis more likely. Weight loss of 7–10%, GLP-1 receptor agonists and resmetirom (approved for MASH with F2–F3 fibrosis) are treatment options; semaglutide was also approved for MASH with fibrosis in 2025.

Why not the others

  • (B) Begin vitamin E, 800 IU/d — Vitamin E is an option for biopsy-proven MASH without diabetes, but it is not the next step and is less favored in patients with diabetes.
  • (C) Liver biopsy — Biopsy is reserved for uncertain diagnoses or discordant noninvasive tests; elastography comes first.
  • (D) Stop atorvastatin — Statins are safe in MASLD and should be continued — cardiovascular disease is the leading cause of death in these patients.
  • (E) Repeat FIB-4 index in 3 years — Repeating FIB-4 in 3 years is appropriate only if the score is low (<1.3).
🎯 Educational objective

In MASLD with an indeterminate FIB-4 index (1.3–2.67), use transient elastography to assess for advanced fibrosis.

GI-015.stem_html:
A 54-year-old woman is evaluated for 6 months of fatigue and generalized itching that is worse at night. She has hypothyroidism treated with levothyroxine. She takes no other medications or supplements and does not drink alcohol.

On physical examination, there are excoriations on her arms and back. There are xanthelasmas around both eyes. The liver is not enlarged.

Ultrasonography of the liver shows normal echotexture and no biliary dilation.

Alkaline phosphatase386 U/L
γ-Glutamyltransferase410 U/L
ALT52 U/L
Total bilirubin0.9 mg/dL
Antimitochondrial antibodypositive (titer 1:640)
Total cholesterol284 mg/dL
GI-015.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
GI-015.explain_html:
Correct answer: D Primary biliary cholangitis

A middle-aged woman with fatigue, pruritus, cholestatic liver tests (high alkaline phosphatase and GGT), normal bile ducts on imaging and a positive antimitochondrial antibody (AMA) has primary biliary cholangitis (PBC). AMA is positive in about 95% of patients; liver biopsy is not needed when AMA is positive and alkaline phosphatase is ≥1.5 times the upper limit.

Ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA), 13–15 mg/kg/d, is first-line for all patients. It slows progression and improves transplant-free survival. Assess response at 12 months; if alkaline phosphatase stays high, add a second-line drug — elafibranor or seladelpar (PPAR agonists approved in 2024; obeticholic acid is no longer favored because of liver safety concerns).

Associated problems to look for: hypothyroidism, Sjögren syndrome, osteoporosis, fat-soluble vitamin deficiency, hypercholesterolemia (xanthelasma — does not raise cardiovascular risk much).

Why not the others

  • (A) Cholestyramine alone — Cholestyramine relieves pruritus, but it does not treat the disease. UDCA is required.
  • (B) Prednisone — Glucocorticoids treat autoimmune hepatitis (high aminotransferases, anti–smooth muscle antibodies, high IgG), not PBC.
  • (C) Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography with stenting — ERCP is for large-duct obstruction (stones, strictures, PSC). Her ducts are normal.
  • (E) Liver transplantation referral — Transplantation is for decompensated cirrhosis or intractable pruritus; she has early disease.
🎓 ABIM pearl

PBC vs PSC: PBC — middle-aged woman, AMA+, small ducts (normal imaging). PSC — younger man with ulcerative colitis, "beaded" large ducts on MRCP, p-ANCA.

🎯 Educational objective

Treat primary biliary cholangitis with ursodeoxycholic acid and add a second-line agent if biochemical response is inadequate.

GI-016.stem_html:
A 23-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department 5 hours after ingesting about 40 tablets of 500-mg acetaminophen during an argument with her partner. She has had nausea and vomited once. She took no other drugs and drank no alcohol.

On physical examination, temperature is 36.8 °C (98.2 °F), blood pressure is 118/72 mm Hg, and pulse rate is 96/min. She is alert and tearful. The abdomen is soft and nontender.

4-hour acetaminophen level (drawn 4 hours after ingestion)210 µg/mL
ALT28 U/L
INR1.0
Creatinine0.7 mg/dL
GI-016.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?

choices.C: Observe and repeat liver tests in 24 hours

GI-016.explain_html:
Correct answer: E Acetaminophen overdose

She took 20 g — well above the toxic threshold (~150 mg/kg or >7.5–10 g). Her 4-hour level of 210 µg/mL is above the treatment line (150 µg/mL at 4 h) on the Rumack-Matthew nomogram. Normal ALT now means nothing — injury does not show until 24–36 hours.

N-acetylcysteine (NAC) replenishes glutathione, which detoxifies the toxic metabolite NAPQI. It is nearly 100% protective when started within 8 hours and still helps when given later, even after liver failure develops. Give IV NAC (or oral) now.

Phase Time Findings
I 0–24 h Nausea, vomiting, or nothing
II 24–72 h Rising ALT/AST, RUQ pain
III 72–96 h Peak injury: ALT >10,000, INR ↑, encephalopathy, AKI
IV >96 h Recovery or death

She also needs suicide risk assessment and psychiatric evaluation before discharge.

Why not the others

  • (A) Referral for liver transplantation — Transplant referral is for acute liver failure meeting King's College criteria (pH <7.3, or INR >6.5 + creatinine >3.4 + grade III–IV encephalopathy).
  • (B) Hemodialysis — Dialysis is for massive ingestions with coma, severe metabolic acidosis or very high levels, not for a patient who can receive NAC.
  • (C) Observe and repeat liver tests in 24 hours — Waiting for liver tests to rise wastes the time window when NAC is most effective.
  • (D) Activated charcoal only — Activated charcoal helps only within 1–2 hours of ingestion (up to 4 hours for large doses). It is not a substitute for NAC.
🎯 Educational objective

Start N-acetylcysteine for acetaminophen overdose when the serum level is above the treatment line on the nomogram, without waiting for liver enzymes to rise.

GI-017.stem_html:
A 58-year-old man with alcohol-associated cirrhosis and ascites is admitted with 2 days of abdominal discomfort and mild confusion. Medications are furosemide, spironolactone and lactulose.

On physical examination, temperature is 37.9 °C (100.2 °F), blood pressure is 102/60 mm Hg, and pulse rate is 98/min. He is jaundiced and has asterixis. The abdomen is distended with shifting dullness and mild diffuse tenderness.

Diagnostic paracentesis is performed.

Ascitic fluid neutrophil count620/µL
Ascitic fluid total protein0.9 g/dL
Serum-ascites albumin gradient1.8 g/dL
Ascitic fluid Gram stainno organisms
Serum creatinine1.4 mg/dL (baseline 0.9 mg/dL)
Total bilirubin4.6 mg/dL
GI-017.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?

choices.A: Wait for ascitic fluid culture before starting antibiotics
choices.B: Intravenous cefotaxime or ceftriaxone plus intravenous albumin

GI-017.explain_html:
Correct answer: B Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis

An ascitic fluid neutrophil count ≥250/µL in cirrhosis without a surgical source = spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP). Start treatment immediately, without waiting for cultures (which are often negative).

  1. IV third-generation cephalosporin (cefotaxime or ceftriaxone) for 5–7 days; broader coverage (e.g., piperacillin-tazobactam or a carbapenem) if nosocomial or recent antibiotics.
  2. IV albumin: 1.5 g/kg on day 1 and 1 g/kg on day 3 when creatinine >1 mg/dL, BUN >30 mg/dL or bilirubin >4 mg/dL. Albumin cut kidney failure (from about 30% to 10%) and mortality in this group. He has two of the three.
  3. Hold diuretics and nephrotoxins; avoid large-volume paracentesis during active SBP with AKI.
  4. After recovery: lifelong secondary prophylaxis (e.g., ciprofloxacin or TMP-SMX).

Why not the others

  • (A) Wait for ascitic fluid culture before starting antibiotics — Delay increases mortality; the neutrophil count alone is enough to begin therapy.
  • (C) Oral ciprofloxacin — Oral fluoroquinolone is used for prophylaxis or uncomplicated SBP without AKI, encephalopathy or shock. He has encephalopathy and kidney injury.
  • (D) Intravenous cefotaxime or ceftriaxone alone — Antibiotics without albumin miss the main way to prevent hepatorenal kidney injury in high-risk SBP.
  • (E) Large-volume paracentesis with albumin — Large-volume paracentesis does not treat infection and may worsen kidney perfusion during SBP.
🧠 Mnemonic

SBP albumin: "1.5 then 1, day 1 and day 3" — if creatinine >1, BUN >30, bilirubin >4.

🎯 Educational objective

Treat spontaneous bacterial peritonitis with an intravenous third-generation cephalosporin plus intravenous albumin on days 1 and 3 in patients with kidney dysfunction or jaundice.

GI-018.stem_html:
A 64-year-old woman with cirrhosis from MASH is brought to the emergency department by her husband for 2 days of increasing sleepiness and confusion. She has been constipated for 4 days. Her medications are furosemide and spironolactone.

On physical examination, temperature is 36.9 °C (98.4 °F), blood pressure is 112/68 mm Hg, and pulse rate is 84/min. She is drowsy, disoriented to time and place, and has asterixis. There is mild ascites. There are no focal neurologic findings.

Diagnostic paracentesis shows an ascitic neutrophil count of 80/µL. Blood and urine cultures are pending, and chest radiograph is normal.

Sodium134 mEq/L
Potassium3.6 mEq/L
Glucose112 mg/dL
Creatinine1.0 mg/dL
Hemoglobin10.8 g/dL (stable)
GI-018.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?

choices.A: Lactulose titrated to 2–3 soft stools daily

GI-018.explain_html:
Correct answer: A Hepatic encephalopathy

This is overt hepatic encephalopathy (grade 2) triggered by constipation. She has no infection (SBP excluded), bleeding, hypoglycemia or electrolyte disturbance — but always look for these.

Lactulose is first-line. It is metabolized by colonic bacteria to acids that convert ammonia (NH₃) to ammonium (NH₄⁺), which is trapped in the colon and excreted; it is also a laxative. Titrate to 2–3 soft bowel movements daily (orally or by NG tube; enemas if unable to take oral).

After a recurrence, add rifaximin to lactulose for secondary prevention — it reduces recurrence and hospitalization.

Ammonia levels do not need to be checked to diagnose or monitor HE; HE is a clinical diagnosis.

Why not the others

  • (B) Rifaximin alone — Rifaximin is an add-on to lactulose for recurrence prevention, not a replacement for initial therapy.
  • (C) Protein restriction to 20 g/d — Protein restriction worsens sarcopenia and malnutrition. Patients with cirrhosis need 1.2–1.5 g/kg/d of protein.
  • (D) Neomycin — Neomycin is nephrotoxic and ototoxic and is no longer recommended.
  • (E) Flumazenil — Flumazenil reverses benzodiazepines; she has taken none, and it has only transient effects in HE.
🧠 Mnemonic

HE precipitants — "HEPATICS": Hemorrhage, Electrolytes (low K⁺, low Na⁺), Protein load/constipation, Alkalosis, Tablets (benzodiazepines, opioids), Infection, Constipation, Shunt (TIPS).

🎯 Educational objective

Treat overt hepatic encephalopathy with lactulose titrated to 2–3 soft stools daily after identifying the precipitant, and add rifaximin for secondary prevention.

GI-019.stem_html:
A 61-year-old man with compensated cirrhosis from hepatitis C was cured with direct-acting antiviral therapy 2 years ago. He has no ascites, encephalopathy or variceal bleeding. He feels well and works full time. He takes carvedilol.

On physical examination, there is no jaundice or ascites. Liver tests and platelet count are stable.
GI-019.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate surveillance for hepatocellular carcinoma?

choices.B: No further surveillance because hepatitis C is cured
choices.D: Abdominal ultrasonography with or without α-fetoprotein every 6 months
choices.E: Contrast CT of the abdomen every 3 months

GI-019.explain_html:
Correct answer: D Hepatocellular carcinoma surveillance

Patients with cirrhosis from any cause have an annual HCC risk of about 1–4% — high enough to justify surveillance. Curing hepatitis C reduces but does not eliminate the risk once cirrhosis is established; surveillance must continue indefinitely.

AASLD recommends abdominal ultrasonography, with or without AFP, every 6 months. Six months reflects the tumor doubling time. Surveillance detects tumors at an early, curable stage (resection, ablation, transplantation).

Who needs surveillance:

  • Everyone with cirrhosis (Child-Pugh A–B, or C if a transplant candidate)
  • Chronic hepatitis B without cirrhosis in high-risk groups: Asian men >40, Asian women >50, Africans/African Americans, family history of HCC, HDV coinfection

If ultrasound visualization is poor (obesity, MASLD), use abbreviated MRI or CT.

Why not the others

  • (A) α-Fetoprotein alone every 12 months — AFP alone is insensitive and is not recommended as the only test.
  • (B) No further surveillance because hepatitis C is cured — The HCC risk persists after SVR in patients with cirrhosis.
  • (C) Liver biopsy every 2 years — Biopsy is not a surveillance tool.
  • (E) Contrast CT of the abdomen every 3 months — CT every 3 months adds radiation and contrast exposure without proven benefit and is not a surveillance strategy.
🎯 Educational objective

Perform HCC surveillance with ultrasonography, with or without AFP, every 6 months in all patients with cirrhosis, including after hepatitis C cure.

GI-020.stem_html:
A 55-year-old man with alcohol-associated cirrhosis and refractory ascites is hospitalized with rising creatinine. Diuretics were stopped on admission 48 hours ago, and he received IV albumin, 1 g/kg/d, for 2 days. There is no shock, and he has not received nephrotoxic drugs or contrast.

On physical examination, blood pressure is 98/58 mm Hg and pulse rate is 90/min. Tense ascites is present.

Creatinine2.6 mg/dL (0.9 mg/dL 2 weeks ago; 2.4 mg/dL on admission)
Sodium128 mEq/L
Urine sodium<10 mEq/L
Urinalysisno protein, blood or casts
Kidney ultrasonographynormal
Ascitic fluid neutrophil count40/µL
GI-020.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?

choices.A: Transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt (TIPS) as first-line therapy
choices.E: Continue intravenous albumin alone for 3 more days

GI-020.explain_html:
Correct answer: D Hepatorenal syndrome

He has hepatorenal syndrome–AKI (HRS-AKI): cirrhosis with ascites, AKI by ICA criteria, no improvement after 2 days of diuretic withdrawal and albumin, no shock, no nephrotoxins, and no structural kidney disease (bland urine, normal ultrasound). Low urine sodium reflects intense renal vasoconstriction.

Pathophysiology: portal hypertension → splanchnic vasodilation → low effective arterial volume → activation of RAAS, sympathetic system and vasopressin → renal vasoconstriction.

Treatment reverses the splanchnic vasodilation:

  • Terlipressin (vasopressin analogue) plus albumin — first-line (CONFIRM trial). Avoid if hypoxemic (SpO₂ <90%) or volume overloaded — risk of respiratory failure.
  • Alternatives: norepinephrine + albumin (ICU) or midodrine + octreotide + albumin (less effective).
  • Definitive treatment: liver transplantation.

Why not the others

  • (A) Transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt (TIPS) as first-line therapy — TIPS may help selected patients but is not first-line for HRS-AKI and can precipitate encephalopathy.
  • (B) Furosemide infusion — Diuretics worsen effective arterial underfilling and kidney perfusion.
  • (C) Hemodialysis — Dialysis is a bridge to transplantation for refractory cases or standard indications, not first-line therapy.
  • (E) Continue intravenous albumin alone for 3 more days — He has already failed a 48-hour albumin challenge; continuing albumin alone without a vasoconstrictor will not reverse HRS.
🎯 Educational objective

Treat hepatorenal syndrome–AKI with terlipressin (or norepinephrine) plus intravenous albumin after diuretic withdrawal and an albumin challenge have failed.

GI-021.stem_html:
A 52-year-old man with alcohol-associated cirrhosis is brought to the emergency department after vomiting bright red blood twice. He has had no previous bleeding.

On physical examination, blood pressure is 96/58 mm Hg, pulse rate is 118/min, and respiration rate is 20/min. He is alert. There are spider angiomas, palmar erythema and moderate ascites.

Two large-bore IV lines are placed, and a crystalloid infusion is started.

Hemoglobin7.2 g/dL
Platelet count72,000/µL
INR1.7
GI-021.lead: In addition to transfusion to a hemoglobin of 7 g/dL, which of the following is the most appropriate management before endoscopy?

choices.E: Fresh frozen plasma to correct the INR to below 1.5

GI-021.explain_html:
Correct answer: D Acute variceal hemorrhage

Suspected acute variceal hemorrhage in cirrhosis. The bundle:

  1. Restrictive transfusion — target hemoglobin 7–8 g/dL. Over-transfusion raises portal pressure and rebleeding.
  2. Vasoactive drug — octreotide (or terlipressin) started before endoscopy and continued 2–5 days.
  3. Antibiotic prophylaxis — ceftriaxone 1 g/d for up to 7 days. Bacterial infection is common and antibiotics reduce rebleeding and mortality.
  4. Upper endoscopy within 12 hours with band ligation.
  5. Pre-emptive TIPS within 72 hours for high-risk patients (Child-Pugh C 10–13, or B >7 with active bleeding).

PPIs are often started until endoscopy shows the source, but they are not the key therapy for varices.

Why not the others

  • (A) Platelet transfusion to more than 100,000/µL — There is no evidence-based platelet target in variceal bleeding; routine transfusion is not recommended.
  • (B) Nonselective beta-blocker (propranolol) — Nonselective beta-blockers are for primary and secondary prophylaxis. They are held during acute bleeding with hypotension because they blunt the compensatory tachycardia.
  • (C) Intravenous pantoprazole alone — PPIs treat peptic ulcer bleeding. Varices need a vasoactive drug and antibiotics.
  • (E) Fresh frozen plasma to correct the INR to below 1.5 — The INR does not reflect bleeding risk in cirrhosis (rebalanced hemostasis). FFP adds volume, raises portal pressure and does not reduce bleeding.
🧠 Mnemonic

Variceal bleed = "BOAT" — Banding, Octreotide, Antibiotics, Transfuse low (Hb 7).

🎯 Educational objective

In suspected acute variceal hemorrhage, give a vasoactive drug and antibiotic prophylaxis before endoscopy, with restrictive transfusion and band ligation within 12 hours.

GI-022.stem_html:
A 41-year-old woman is evaluated for 1 year of progressive difficulty swallowing both solids and liquids, regurgitation of undigested food at night and a 5-kg (11-lb) weight loss. She drinks large amounts of water to "push food down". She has no heartburn. She was born in the United States and has not traveled to Central or South America.

Examination is normal.

Upper endoscopy shows a dilated esophagus with retained food and a "puckered" gastroesophageal junction that the scope passes with a gentle "pop". There is no mass or stricture.
GI-022.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate next diagnostic test?
GI-022.explain_html:
Correct answer: C Achalasia

Dysphagia to solids and liquids from the start suggests a motility disorder (mechanical obstruction typically affects solids first, then progresses). Regurgitation of undigested food, weight loss and a dilated esophagus with a tight GEJ → achalasia.

High-resolution manometry is the gold standard: incomplete relaxation of the lower esophageal sphincter (elevated integrated relaxation pressure) and absent peristalsis. It also gives the Chicago classification subtype (type II responds best to treatment). A barium esophagram shows a "bird's beak".

Endoscopy is required first to exclude pseudoachalasia from a tumor at the GEJ (suspect in older patients with rapid weight loss); here the scope passed easily and no mass was seen.

Treatment: pneumatic dilation, laparoscopic Heller myotomy with fundoplication, or peroral endoscopic myotomy (POEM); botulinum toxin for poor surgical candidates.

Why not the others

  • (A) 24-hour esophageal pH monitoring — pH monitoring evaluates reflux. She has no heartburn, and achalasia patients can have false-positive pH studies from food fermentation.
  • (B) Repeat endoscopy with dilation — Repeat dilation without a confirmed diagnosis is inappropriate; standard dilation does not treat achalasia (pneumatic dilation does, after diagnosis).
  • (D) Esophageal biopsies for eosinophils — Eosinophilic esophagitis causes solid-food dysphagia and food impactions in young atopic men, with rings and furrows on endoscopy.
  • (E) CT scan of the chest — CT is used when pseudoachalasia from malignancy is suspected; it does not confirm achalasia.
🎯 Educational objective

Confirm suspected achalasia with high-resolution esophageal manometry after endoscopy excludes a mechanical cause.

GI-023.stem_html:
A 24-year-old man is evaluated after an episode of food impaction with steak that required endoscopic removal. He has had intermittent difficulty swallowing solid foods for 3 years and chews his food carefully. He has asthma and seasonal allergic rhinitis. He has no heartburn.

Examination is normal.

Upper endoscopy at the time of impaction showed concentric rings, longitudinal furrows and white exudates in the esophagus.
GI-023.lead: Which of the following is the most likely to confirm the diagnosis?

choices.B: Esophageal biopsies showing ≥15 eosinophils per high-power field

GI-023.explain_html:
Correct answer: B Eosinophilic esophagitis

A young man with atopy, solid-food dysphagia and food impaction, and the classic endoscopic findings — rings ("trachealization"), linear furrows and white plaques — has eosinophilic esophagitis (EoE), a chronic, type 2 (allergic) immune disease.

The diagnosis requires esophageal biopsies (at least 6, from proximal and distal esophagus) showing ≥15 eosinophils per high-power field, plus symptoms of esophageal dysfunction and exclusion of other causes.

Treatment (any of three "D"s): Drugs — high-dose PPI or swallowed topical steroids (budesonide, fluticasone), or dupilumab; Diet — empiric elimination (dairy, wheat first); Dilation — for strictures.

Why not the others

  • (A) Esophageal manometry — Manometry evaluates motility disorders such as achalasia; it is not diagnostic for EoE.
  • (C) Skin-prick testing for food allergens — Skin-prick testing performs poorly at identifying EoE food triggers and is not used to diagnose the disease.
  • (D) Barium esophagram — A barium study may show a narrow-caliber esophagus or rings, but it cannot confirm EoE.
  • (E) Serum IgE level — Serum IgE may be elevated in atopic patients but is neither sensitive nor specific for EoE.
🎯 Educational objective

Confirm eosinophilic esophagitis with esophageal biopsies showing at least 15 eosinophils per high-power field.

HE-001.topic: Iron deficiency anemia in an older man
HE-001.stem_html:
A 67-year-old man comes to the office because of 3 months of fatigue and shortness of breath when climbing stairs. He has no abdominal pain, change in bowel habits, black stools, hematochezia, hematuria or weight loss. He eats meat several times a week. He takes aspirin 81 mg daily for primary prevention. His last colonoscopy was 12 years ago and was normal.

Pulse is 92/min. The conjunctivae are pale. Abdominal examination is normal. Rectal examination shows brown stool.

Hemoglobin10.1 g/dL
Mean corpuscular volume74 fL
RDW17.8%
Platelets410,000/µL
Ferritin8 ng/mL
Transferrin saturation6%
Tissue transglutaminase IgA (with normal total IgA)negative
HE-001.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.B: Oral iron and recheck hemoglobin in 3 months

HE-001.explain_html:
Correct answer: A Iron deficiency anemia in an older man

A ferritin of 8 ng/mL confirms iron deficiency (ferritin <45 ng/mL is the AGA threshold in anemic patients). In a man or a postmenopausal woman, iron deficiency anemia is gastrointestinal blood loss — possibly from cancer — until proven otherwise.

The evaluation is bidirectional endoscopy (colonoscopy + upper endoscopy), which finds a cause in a large share of patients; colorectal cancer, gastric cancer, peptic ulcer disease and angioectasias are leading causes. Celiac disease (iron malabsorption) should also be tested — done here.

Replace iron too — but iron is not a substitute for finding the source.

Iron studies Iron deficiency Anemia of inflammation
Ferritin Low Normal or high
Transferrin saturation Low Low–normal
TIBC High Low

Why not the others

  • (B) Oral iron and recheck hemoglobin in 3 months — Treating with iron alone may mask an occult GI cancer. Endoscopic evaluation is required.
  • (C) Bone marrow biopsy — Iron studies already explain the anemia; marrow examination is not needed.
  • (D) Capsule endoscopy — Capsule endoscopy evaluates the small bowel after a negative bidirectional endoscopy.
  • (E) Fecal immunochemical test — A negative stool test does not exclude a GI cause because bleeding is intermittent; it has no role in evaluating established iron deficiency anemia.
🎓 ABIM pearl

Platelets are often mildly high in iron deficiency (reactive thrombocytosis) — it does not point to a myeloproliferative neoplasm.

🎯 Educational objective

Iron deficiency anemia in men and postmenopausal women requires bidirectional endoscopy (and celiac testing) to find a gastrointestinal source, especially cancer.

HE-002.stem_html:
A 54-year-old man comes for follow-up 6 weeks after a proximal deep venous thrombosis of the left femoral vein. It was diagnosed 3 weeks after an elective left total knee arthroplasty, while he was still using crutches. He has been taking apixaban without bleeding. He now walks normally and has returned to work. He has no history of venous thromboembolism or cancer, and age-appropriate cancer screening is up to date.

The left calf is minimally swollen and nontender.
HE-002.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate duration of anticoagulation?
HE-002.explain_html:
Correct answer: A Provoked deep venous thrombosis — duration

This DVT was provoked by a major transient risk factor — surgery (and immobility) — which has now resolved. The risk of recurrence after stopping anticoagulation is low (about 1% per year), lower than the bleeding risk of continuing.

Treat a provoked proximal DVT or PE for 3 months, then stop. Longer or indefinite therapy is for unprovoked VTE (low bleeding risk), persistent risk factors (active cancer, antiphospholipid syndrome) or recurrent VTE.

VTE type Duration
Provoked by surgery or major transient factor 3 months
Provoked by minor transient factor (estrogen, travel, minor injury) 3 months (consider longer case by case)
Unprovoked, low–moderate bleeding risk Extended (indefinite), reassess yearly; reduced-dose DOAC is an option after 6 months
Active cancer Extended while cancer is active

Why not the others

  • (B) Indefinite — Indefinite therapy is for unprovoked or recurrent VTE or persistent risk factors.
  • (C) 12 months — Twelve months adds bleeding risk without meaningful benefit for a surgically provoked clot.
  • (D) 6 weeks — Six weeks is too short for a proximal DVT; it raises recurrence risk. (Isolated distal DVT has different rules.)
  • (E) Decide after a thrombophilia panel — Thrombophilia testing does not change management after a clearly provoked first VTE and is not recommended.
🎓 ABIM pearl

Do not test for thrombophilia while the patient is acutely ill or on anticoagulants — heparin lowers antithrombin, warfarin lowers proteins C and S, and DOACs interfere with clotting-based assays.

HE-003.stem_html:
A 66-year-old woman is evaluated on postoperative day 7 after a total knee replacement. She has received subcutaneous unfractionated heparin for VTE prophylaxis since surgery. Today she has new left calf swelling and pain.

On physical examination, the left calf is swollen and tender. There is no bleeding.

Platelet count62,000/µL (238,000/µL on postoperative day 1)
Duplex ultrasonographyacute left popliteal vein thrombosis
Creatinine0.9 mg/dL
Liver testsnormal
HE-003.lead: In addition to stopping heparin, which of the following is the most appropriate immediate management?

choices.A: Begin argatroban (or fondaparinux or a DOAC) without waiting for test results
choices.E: Wait for PF4 antibody and serotonin release assay results before anticoagulating

HE-003.explain_html:
Correct answer: A Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia

Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT) — antibodies against platelet factor 4 (PF4)–heparin complexes activate platelets, causing thrombocytopenia and thrombosis (venous more than arterial).

Her 4T score is high (8): platelets fell >50% (2), onset day 5–10 (2), new thrombosis (2), no other cause (2). With intermediate or high probability:

  1. Stop all heparin (including flushes and heparin-coated catheters).
  2. Start a non-heparin anticoagulant immediately — argatroban (hepatic clearance; good in kidney failure), bivalirudin, fondaparinux, or a DOAC (increasingly used in stable patients).
  3. Send a PF4/heparin immunoassay; confirm a positive with a functional assay (serotonin release assay).
  4. Anticoagulate 3 months for HIT with thrombosis (4–6 weeks without thrombosis).

Why not the others

  • (B) Platelet transfusion — Platelet transfusion is avoided in HIT unless there is serious bleeding; it may fuel thrombosis.
  • (C) Begin warfarin — Starting warfarin during acute HIT can cause venous limb gangrene and skin necrosis (protein C depletion). Start it only after the platelet count recovers to ≥150,000/µL, overlapping with a parenteral agent.
  • (D) Begin enoxaparin — LMWH cross-reacts with HIT antibodies and is contraindicated.
  • (E) Wait for PF4 antibody and serotonin release assay results before anticoagulating — With a high pretest probability, waiting for tests leaves her at high risk for new thrombosis.
🧠 Mnemonic

4 Ts: Thrombocytopenia (>50% fall), Timing (day 5–10), Thrombosis, oTher causes absent.

🎯 Educational objective

When HIT is suspected with intermediate or high probability, stop all heparin and start a non-heparin anticoagulant before laboratory confirmation.

HE-004.stem_html:
A 34-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department with 2 days of confusion, headache and easy bruising. She has no diarrhea. She takes no medications.

On physical examination, temperature is 37.8 °C (100.0 °F), blood pressure is 136/82 mm Hg. She is confused but has no focal deficits. There are scattered petechiae on her legs.

Hemoglobin7.6 g/dL
MCV88 fL
Platelet count14,000/µL
Reticulocyte count9%
Lactate dehydrogenase1,240 U/L
Haptoglobinundetectable
Total bilirubin3.1 mg/dL (indirect 2.6 mg/dL)
Peripheral smearmany schistocytes
Direct antiglobulin testnegative
PT and aPTTnormal
Creatinine1.1 mg/dL
Pregnancy testnegative
HE-004.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?

choices.A: Therapeutic plasma exchange, glucocorticoids and caplacizumab
choices.B: Wait for ADAMTS13 activity before starting therapy

HE-004.explain_html:
Correct answer: A Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura

Microangiopathic hemolytic anemia (MAHA) — schistocytes, high LDH, low haptoglobin, negative DAT — plus severe thrombocytopenia, neurologic symptoms, fever, and normal coagulation tests (unlike DIC) = thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP) until proven otherwise. Kidney injury is usually mild (severe AKI suggests HUS).

Acquired TTP is caused by autoantibodies against ADAMTS13, the protease that cleaves ultra-large von Willebrand factor multimers. Without it, vWF strings trap platelets and form microthrombi. Untreated mortality is ~90%.

Her PLASMIC score is high (platelets <30k, hemolysis, no cancer, no transplant, MCV <90, INR <1.5, creatinine <2) → start treatment immediately after drawing ADAMTS13 (activity <10% confirms):

  • Therapeutic plasma exchange (removes antibodies, replaces ADAMTS13)
  • Glucocorticoids
  • Caplacizumab (anti-vWF nanobody) and often rituximab

Why not the others

  • (B) Wait for ADAMTS13 activity before starting therapy — ADAMTS13 results take days; delaying plasma exchange increases mortality.
  • (C) Intravenous immune globulin — IVIG is used for ITP; it is not effective for TTP.
  • (D) Platelet transfusion — Platelet transfusions are relatively contraindicated in TTP (may worsen thrombosis) except for life-threatening bleeding.
  • (E) Eculizumab — Eculizumab (anti-C5) treats atypical HUS (complement-mediated TMA), which usually causes more severe kidney injury.
🎓 ABIM pearl

TTP classic pentad (fever, MAHA, thrombocytopenia, neurologic and kidney findings) is present in fewer than 10% of patients — MAHA + thrombocytopenia is enough to act.

🎯 Educational objective

Treat suspected TTP (microangiopathic hemolysis with severe thrombocytopenia and normal coagulation tests) immediately with plasma exchange, glucocorticoids and caplacizumab.

HE-005.stem_html:
A 28-year-old woman is evaluated for 1 week of easy bruising and gum bleeding when brushing her teeth. She takes no medications or supplements. She had a viral upper respiratory infection 3 weeks ago.

On physical examination, vital signs are normal. There are petechiae on her legs and a few bruises on her arms. There is no lymphadenopathy or splenomegaly.

Hemoglobin13.2 g/dL
Leukocyte count6,800/µL (normal differential)
Platelet count8,000/µL
Peripheral smearlarge platelets; no schistocytes; normal red and white cells
PT and aPTTnormal
HIV and hepatitis C antibodiesnegative
HE-005.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?

choices.D: Platelet transfusion as the main treatment

HE-005.explain_html:
Correct answer: E Immune thrombocytopenia

Isolated thrombocytopenia with large platelets, normal other cell lines and smear, no splenomegaly, and no other cause = immune thrombocytopenia (ITP) — a diagnosis of exclusion. Check HIV and HCV (and H. pylori where relevant) in all adults.

Treat newly diagnosed adult ITP when the platelet count is <30,000/µL or there is significant bleeding (ASH 2019):

  • First-line: glucocorticoids — prednisone 1 mg/kg/d (≤6 weeks total) or dexamethasone 40 mg/d × 4 days.
  • Add IVIG (or anti-D in Rh+, non-splenectomized patients) when a rapid rise is needed (severe bleeding, before procedures).
  • Platelet transfusion only for life-threatening bleeding (with IVIG and steroids).
  • Second-line for persistent ITP: TPO receptor agonists (eltrombopag, romiplostim), rituximab, fostamatinib, or splenectomy (usually after 12 months).

Why not the others

  • (A) Bone marrow biopsy before treatment — Bone marrow examination is not needed in typical ITP; it is for atypical features (other cytopenias, abnormal smear, age >60 with systemic symptoms, or failure to respond).
  • (B) Observation without treatment — Observation is appropriate for platelet counts ≥30,000/µL without bleeding; at 8,000/µL with mucosal bleeding she needs treatment.
  • (C) Splenectomy — Splenectomy is a second-line option for persistent or chronic ITP, not initial therapy.
  • (D) Platelet transfusion as the main treatment — Transfused platelets are destroyed rapidly in ITP; transfusion is reserved for life-threatening bleeding.
🎯 Educational objective

Treat newly diagnosed ITP in adults with a platelet count below 30,000/µL or bleeding with glucocorticoids, adding IVIG when a rapid response is needed.

HE-006.stem_html:
A 68-year-old man with type 2 diabetes treated with metformin for 12 years is evaluated for 4 months of fatigue and tingling in his feet. He also takes omeprazole for reflux. He eats a varied diet.

On physical examination, there is reduced vibration sense and proprioception in both feet, and the Romberg test is positive. Ankle reflexes are absent.

Hemoglobin11.4 g/dL
MCV106 fL
Peripheral smearmacro-ovalocytes and hypersegmented neutrophils
Vitamin B₁₂248 pg/mL (reference, 200–900)
Folatenormal
TSHnormal
HE-006.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate next diagnostic test?
HE-006.explain_html:
Correct answer: D Vitamin B₁₂ deficiency

Macrocytic anemia with hypersegmented neutrophils, plus dorsal column findings (loss of vibration and proprioception, positive Romberg), in a patient on long-term metformin and a PPI (both reduce B₁₂ absorption) → vitamin B₁₂ deficiency.

His serum B₁₂ is low-normal (200–350 pg/mL) — a gray zone where the level does not exclude deficiency. Measure methylmalonic acid (MMA) (± homocysteine):

  • B₁₂ is a cofactor for methylmalonyl-CoA mutase and methionine synthase.
  • B₁₂ deficiency → high MMA and high homocysteine.
  • Folate deficiency → high homocysteine, normal MMA.

Treat with intramuscular B₁₂ (or high-dose oral 1,000–2,000 µg/d) — neurologic symptoms may be permanent if treatment is delayed. Check for pernicious anemia (intrinsic factor antibodies). Monitor B₁₂ periodically in patients on long-term metformin (ADA).

Why not the others

  • (A) MRI of the spine — Spinal MRI may show dorsal column T2 hyperintensity but does not confirm the cause.
  • (B) Bone marrow biopsy — Bone marrow biopsy is not needed when the smear and labs point to megaloblastic anemia from B₁₂ deficiency.
  • (C) Schilling test — The Schilling test is obsolete and no longer available.
  • (E) Nerve conduction studies — Nerve conduction studies characterize neuropathy but do not confirm B₁₂ deficiency.
🎯 Educational objective

When serum vitamin B₁₂ is low-normal but deficiency is suspected, measure methylmalonic acid (elevated in B₁₂ deficiency, normal in folate deficiency).

HE-007.stem_html:
A 61-year-old woman is evaluated for 3 weeks of fatigue, exertional dyspnea and dark urine. She has chronic lymphocytic leukemia that has been under observation.

On physical examination, blood pressure is 118/68 mm Hg and pulse rate is 104/min. There is scleral icterus and mild splenomegaly.

Hemoglobin7.4 g/dL
MCV104 fL
Reticulocyte count12%
Lactate dehydrogenase680 U/L
Haptoglobin<10 mg/dL
Indirect bilirubin3.2 mg/dL
Peripheral smearmany spherocytes; no schistocytes
Platelet count186,000/µL
HE-007.lead: Which of the following tests is most likely to confirm the diagnosis?
HE-007.explain_html:
Correct answer: D Warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia

Hemolytic anemia (high reticulocytes, LDH and indirect bilirubin; low haptoglobin) with spherocytes in a patient with CLL → warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia (AIHA). (The high MCV reflects reticulocytosis — reticulocytes are larger.)

Confirm with the direct antiglobulin test (DAT, Coombs): positive for IgG (± C3) in warm AIHA. IgG-coated red cells lose membrane in the spleen and become spherocytes.

Warm AIHA Cold agglutinin disease
Antibody IgG, 37 °C IgM, binds complement
DAT IgG ± C3 C3 only
Site Extravascular (spleen) Intravascular + liver
Causes Idiopathic, CLL, lymphoma, SLE, drugs Mycoplasma, EBV, lymphoma, Waldenström
Treatment Glucocorticoids → rituximab Avoid cold; rituximab, sutimlimab

Why not the others

  • (A) Hemoglobin electrophoresis — Hemoglobin electrophoresis evaluates hemoglobinopathies such as sickle cell disease and thalassemia.
  • (B) Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase activity — G6PD deficiency causes episodic hemolysis after oxidant stress (drugs, infection, fava beans) with bite cells and Heinz bodies.
  • (C) Osmotic fragility test — Osmotic fragility (or EMA binding) tests for hereditary spherocytosis, which is DAT negative and begins early in life.
  • (E) ADAMTS13 activity — ADAMTS13 testing is for TTP, which causes schistocytes and thrombocytopenia; her platelets are normal and the smear shows spherocytes.
🎯 Educational objective

Confirm warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia (hemolysis with spherocytes, often with CLL or SLE) with a positive direct antiglobulin test for IgG.

HE-008.topic: Acute chest syndrome in sickle cell disease
HE-008.stem_html:
A 24-year-old man with sickle cell anemia (HbSS) is hospitalized with a vaso-occlusive pain crisis in his back and legs. On hospital day 2 he develops fever, cough and right-sided chest pain.

On physical examination, temperature is 38.7 °C (101.7 °F), pulse rate is 112/min, and respiration rate is 26/min. Oxygen saturation is 88% breathing ambient air. There are crackles at the right base.

Chest radiograph shows a new right lower lobe infiltrate.

Hemoglobin6.8 g/dL (baseline 8.2 g/dL)
Reticulocyte count9%
Leukocyte count18,200/µL
HE-008.lead: In addition to oxygen, analgesia, incentive spirometry and empiric antibiotics, which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?

choices.E: Intravenous fluids at twice the maintenance rate

HE-008.explain_html:
Correct answer: B Acute chest syndrome in sickle cell disease

A new pulmonary infiltrate plus fever, respiratory symptoms, chest pain or hypoxemia in sickle cell disease = acute chest syndrome (ACS), the leading cause of death in adults with SCD. It often follows a pain crisis (fat embolism from infarcted marrow, infection, hypoventilation from splinting and opioids).

Treatment:

  • Oxygen, analgesia, incentive spirometry.
  • Empiric antibiotics: a third-generation cephalosporin plus a macrolide (atypicals).
  • Red blood cell transfusion — simple transfusion for hypoxemia or a hemoglobin ≥1 g/dL below baseline (target Hb ~10 g/dL; do not exceed this — hyperviscosity). Exchange transfusion for severe or rapidly progressing disease (multilobar, worsening hypoxemia, need for ventilation).
  • Cautious IV fluids (avoid overload).

After recovery, start or continue hydroxyurea (reduces ACS and pain crises).

Why not the others

  • (A) Begin hydroxyurea only — Hydroxyurea prevents future ACS but takes weeks to act; it does not treat an acute episode.
  • (C) Intravenous furosemide — Diuretics have no role unless volume overloaded and may promote sickling through dehydration.
  • (D) Prednisone, 60 mg/d — Glucocorticoids may shorten hospital stay but cause rebound pain crises and readmission; they are not standard.
  • (E) Intravenous fluids at twice the maintenance rate — Aggressive fluids can cause pulmonary edema and worsen ACS; use euvolemic hydration.
🎯 Educational objective

Treat acute chest syndrome in sickle cell disease with oxygen, antibiotics (cephalosporin plus macrolide), incentive spirometry and red cell transfusion (exchange transfusion if severe).

HE-009.stem_html:
A 30-year-old woman of Greek descent is evaluated for a mild anemia found on a pre-employment blood test. She feels well. Her menstrual periods are normal. She has taken an iron supplement for 3 months, prescribed by another clinician, without change in her blood counts.

Hemoglobin11.2 g/dL
Erythrocyte count5.9 million/µL (elevated)
MCV62 fL
Red cell distribution widthnormal
Ferritin98 ng/mL
Peripheral smearmicrocytes and target cells
HE-009.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate next diagnostic test?

choices.A: Bone marrow aspiration with iron stain

HE-009.explain_html:
Correct answer: D Thalassemia trait versus iron deficiency

Microcytosis out of proportion to the anemia, a high red cell count, normal RDW, target cells, normal ferritin and Mediterranean ancestry → thalassemia trait.

The Mentzer index (MCV ÷ RBC count in millions) helps: <13 suggests thalassemia, >13 suggests iron deficiency. Here: 62 ÷ 5.9 ≈ 10.5.

Hemoglobin electrophoresis distinguishes the types:

  • β-thalassemia trait → elevated HbA₂ (>3.5%) ± high HbF.
  • α-thalassemia trait (one or two gene deletions) → normal electrophoresis; diagnosis is by exclusion or DNA testing.

Thalassemia trait needs no treatment, but she should stop iron (risk of iron overload) and receive genetic counseling, since a partner with trait could have a child with thalassemia major.

Iron deficiency Thalassemia trait
RBC count Low High/normal
RDW High Normal
Ferritin Low Normal/high
Mentzer >13 <13

Why not the others

  • (A) Bone marrow aspiration with iron stain — Bone marrow examination is unnecessary; ferritin reliably excludes iron deficiency here.
  • (B) Intravenous iron trial — Her ferritin is normal, and she did not respond to oral iron; more iron would risk overload.
  • (C) Colonoscopy — She has no iron deficiency, so a GI source of blood loss is not suggested.
  • (E) Serum lead level — Lead poisoning causes microcytic anemia with basophilic stippling and neurologic or GI symptoms; it does not cause an elevated RBC count.
🎯 Educational objective

Suspect thalassemia trait in microcytosis with a high RBC count, normal RDW, normal ferritin and a Mentzer index below 13, and confirm with hemoglobin electrophoresis.

HE-010.stem_html:
A 68-year-old man is evaluated for 2 months of low back pain and fatigue. He has no history of trauma.

On physical examination, there is tenderness over the lumbar spine. Neurologic examination is normal.

Hemoglobin9.4 g/dL
Calcium11.4 mg/dL
Creatinine2.1 mg/dL
Total protein9.8 g/dL
Albumin3.2 g/dL
Peripheral smearrouleaux formation
Urinalysis (dipstick)negative for protein
Radiograph of the lumbar spinelytic lesion in L3
HE-010.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate next diagnostic test?

choices.A: Serum protein electrophoresis with immunofixation and serum free light chains
choices.C: Urine dipstick for protein repeated in 1 week

HE-010.explain_html:
Correct answer: A Multiple myeloma — diagnosis

Bone pain with a lytic lesion, anemia, hypercalcemia, kidney injury, a large protein gap (total protein − albumin = 6.6 g/dL; >4 is high), and rouleaux = multiple myeloma until proven otherwise ("CRAB").

Initial testing: serum protein electrophoresis (SPEP) with immunofixation plus serum free light chain (FLC) assay (and/or 24-h urine protein electrophoresis with immunofixation). This combination detects a monoclonal protein in >97% of myeloma.

Diagnosis is confirmed by bone marrow biopsy (≥10% clonal plasma cells) plus a myeloma-defining event (CRAB, or ≥60% plasma cells, FLC ratio ≥100, >1 focal lesion on MRI). Skeletal survey is replaced by whole-body low-dose CT, PET-CT or MRI.

The negative urine dipstick is a classic trap: dipsticks detect albumin, not light chains (Bence Jones protein).

Why not the others

  • (B) Kidney biopsy — Kidney biopsy may later show cast nephropathy, but noninvasive testing for a monoclonal protein comes first.
  • (C) Urine dipstick for protein repeated in 1 week — A dipstick cannot detect light chains; repeating it would add nothing.
  • (D) Bone scan (technetium scintigraphy) — Bone scans detect osteoblastic activity; myeloma lesions are purely lytic and are often missed.
  • (E) Prostate-specific antigen — PSA is reasonable when prostate cancer metastases are suspected, but prostate metastases are usually blastic and the protein gap and rouleaux point to myeloma.
🧠 Mnemonic

Myeloma CRAB: hyperCalcemia, Renal failure, Anemia, Bone lesions.

🎯 Educational objective

Evaluate suspected multiple myeloma with serum protein electrophoresis with immunofixation and serum free light chains.

HE-011.stem_html:
A 66-year-old woman is evaluated after an SPEP done for an elevated total protein showed a monoclonal IgG κ protein of 0.8 g/dL. She feels well. She has no bone pain.

Hemoglobin13.6 g/dL
Calcium9.4 mg/dL
Creatinine0.8 mg/dL
Serum free light chain ratio (κ/λ)1.4 (normal)
Low-dose whole-body CTno lytic lesions
HE-011.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

choices.D: Repeat SPEP and laboratory tests in 6 months, then annually if stable

HE-011.explain_html:
Correct answer: D MGUS — follow-up

She has monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance (MGUS): M protein <3 g/dL, <10% marrow plasma cells, and no CRAB features or other end-organ damage. MGUS is present in about 3% of adults >50.

MGUS progresses to myeloma or a related disorder at about 1% per year, lifelong. Risk factors for progression (Mayo model):

  • M protein ≥1.5 g/dL
  • Non-IgG isotype (IgA, IgM)
  • Abnormal free light chain ratio

She has none → low-risk MGUS (lifetime risk ~5%). A bone marrow biopsy is not required for low-risk IgG MGUS. Repeat SPEP, CBC, calcium and creatinine at 6 months, then annually (or less often — some stop surveillance in very low-risk older patients).

MGUS is never treated with chemotherapy. MGUS can still cause organ damage ("MGRS" — monoclonal gammopathy of renal significance), neuropathy (IgM), and increases fracture risk.

Why not the others

  • (A) Autologous stem cell transplantation — Transplantation is for multiple myeloma, not MGUS.
  • (B) Bone marrow biopsy now — Bone marrow biopsy is not needed in low-risk MGUS (IgG <1.5 g/dL, normal FLC ratio) without CRAB features.
  • (C) Lenalidomide and dexamethasone — MGUS is not treated; therapy is for myeloma.
  • (E) No follow-up is needed — Lifelong risk of progression justifies follow-up.
🎯 Educational objective

Monitor low-risk MGUS (IgG <1.5 g/dL, normal free light chain ratio) with repeat SPEP and laboratory tests at 6 months, then annually, without bone marrow biopsy.

HE-012.stem_html:
A 58-year-old man is evaluated for headaches and itching after hot showers. He has never smoked and does not have sleep apnea symptoms. He takes no testosterone.

On physical examination, blood pressure is 146/88 mm Hg. He has facial plethora. The spleen tip is palpable.

Hemoglobin19.2 g/dL
Hematocrit58%
Leukocyte count13,400/µL
Platelet count612,000/µL
Oxygen saturation98% breathing ambient air
Serum erythropoietinlow
HE-012.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate next diagnostic test?

choices.E: Abdominal CT to look for an erythropoietin-secreting tumor

HE-012.explain_html:
Correct answer: D Polycythemia vera

Erythrocytosis with aquagenic pruritus, plethora, splenomegaly, high WBC and platelets, normal oxygen saturation and a low erythropoietin → polycythemia vera (PV), a myeloproliferative neoplasm. Secondary erythrocytosis (hypoxia, smoking, OSA, testosterone, EPO-secreting tumors) has normal or high EPO.

JAK2 V617F is present in ~95% of PV (exon 12 mutations in most of the rest). A JAK2 mutation plus hemoglobin >16.5 g/dL in men (>16 g/dL in women) meets WHO criteria; bone marrow biopsy completes the diagnosis.

Treatment: phlebotomy to hematocrit <45% (CYTO-PV) plus low-dose aspirin for all; cytoreduction (hydroxyurea, interferon) for high-risk patients (age ≥60 or prior thrombosis). Thrombosis — including Budd-Chiari syndrome — is the main cause of morbidity.

Why not the others

  • (A) Red cell mass measurement — Red cell mass measurement is rarely available and is not needed when hemoglobin is this high and JAK2 testing is available.
  • (B) BCR-ABL1 fusion testing — BCR-ABL1 defines chronic myeloid leukemia, which presents with marked leukocytosis with left shift and basophilia, not isolated erythrocytosis.
  • (C) Polysomnography — OSA causes secondary erythrocytosis with a normal or high EPO; he has no symptoms and EPO is low.
  • (E) Abdominal CT to look for an erythropoietin-secreting tumor — A low EPO argues against an EPO-secreting tumor (renal cell carcinoma, hepatoma, cerebellar hemangioblastoma), which raises EPO.
🎯 Educational objective

In a patient with erythrocytosis and a low erythropoietin level, test for the JAK2 V617F mutation to diagnose polycythemia vera.

HE-013.stem_html:
A 42-year-old woman is evaluated for 1 week of fatigue, gum bleeding and large bruises. She had a nosebleed that lasted 2 hours yesterday.

On physical examination, temperature is 37.4 °C (99.3 °F), pulse rate is 104/min. There are ecchymoses on her arms and legs and oozing from her gums.

Hemoglobin8.1 g/dL
Leukocyte count2,800/µL
Platelet count22,000/µL
PT18 seconds; INR 1.6
Fibrinogen84 mg/dL (low)
D-dimermarkedly elevated
Peripheral smearabnormal promyelocytes with multiple Auer rods ("faggot cells")
HE-013.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate immediate treatment, before genetic confirmation is available?

choices.C: Observation until t(15;17) PML-RARA results are available
choices.E: All-trans retinoic acid (ATRA) and blood product support

HE-013.explain_html:
Correct answer: E Acute promyelocytic leukemia

Pancytopenia, abnormal promyelocytes with multiple Auer rods (faggot cells) and DIC with low fibrinogen and bleeding = acute promyelocytic leukemia (APL), caused by t(15;17) producing the PML-RARA fusion protein, which blocks myeloid differentiation at the promyelocyte stage.

APL is a medical emergency — early death is from hemorrhage (intracranial, pulmonary). Start all-trans retinoic acid (ATRA) immediately on suspicion, without waiting for genetic confirmation. ATRA forces promyelocytes to differentiate and rapidly corrects the coagulopathy.

Supportive care: cryoprecipitate to keep fibrinogen >150 mg/dL, platelets >30,000–50,000/µL, FFP for high INR. Definitive treatment: ATRA + arsenic trioxide (cures >90% of standard-risk patients).

Watch for differentiation syndrome (fever, dyspnea, pulmonary infiltrates, edema, AKI) → dexamethasone.

Why not the others

  • (A) Heparin infusion for DIC — Heparin is not recommended for APL-associated DIC; it increases bleeding risk.
  • (B) Rituximab — Rituximab targets CD20 on B cells; it has no role in APL.
  • (C) Observation until t(15;17) PML-RARA results are available — Delaying ATRA increases the risk of fatal hemorrhage; genetic confirmation can follow.
  • (D) Tranexamic acid alone — Antifibrinolytics are not recommended in APL; they may increase thrombosis and do not treat the leukemia.
🎯 Educational objective

Start all-trans retinoic acid immediately when acute promyelocytic leukemia is suspected, along with aggressive blood product support for coagulopathy.

On physical examination, temperature is 37.4 °C (99.3 °F), pulse rate is 104/min. There are ecchymoses on her arms and legs and oozing from her gums. Which of the following is the most appropriate immediate treatment, before genetic confirmation is available?

HE-014.stem_html:
A 71-year-old man is evaluated after a routine CBC showed lymphocytosis. He feels well, with no fevers, night sweats or weight loss.

On physical examination, there are several small (1–1.5 cm), nontender cervical lymph nodes. There is no hepatosplenomegaly.

Hemoglobin14.1 g/dL
Leukocyte count21,400/µL (absolute lymphocyte count 16,800/µL)
Platelet count198,000/µL
Peripheral smearsmall mature lymphocytes and smudge cells
Flow cytometryclonal B cells expressing CD5, CD19, CD20 (dim) and CD23
HE-014.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

choices.C: Observation with CBC and examination every 3–6 months
choices.E: Radiation therapy to the cervical nodes

HE-014.explain_html:
Correct answer: C Early-stage chronic lymphocytic leukemia

Absolute lymphocytosis (clonal B cells ≥5,000/µL) with CD5+, CD23+ B cells and smudge cells = chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL). He has early-stage disease (Rai stage I — lymphadenopathy; Binet A) with no symptoms and normal hemoglobin and platelets.

Early, asymptomatic CLL is managed with "watch and wait" — early treatment does not improve survival, even with modern targeted therapies.

Treat when there is "active disease" (iwCLL):

  • Progressive marrow failure (hemoglobin <10 g/dL or platelets <100,000/µL)
  • Massive or progressive splenomegaly or lymphadenopathy
  • Lymphocyte doubling time <6 months
  • Constitutional symptoms (fevers, night sweats, weight loss >10%, fatigue)
  • Autoimmune cytopenias not responding to steroids

Modern first-line therapy is BTK inhibitors (ibrutinib, acalabrutinib, zanubrutinib) or venetoclax + obinutuzumab.

Also: vaccinate (non-live), watch for infections (hypogammaglobulinemia), AIHA/ITP, and skin cancers.

Why not the others

  • (A) Allogeneic stem cell transplantation — Transplantation is for high-risk relapsed disease in fit patients, not early CLL.
  • (B) Bendamustine and rituximab — Chemoimmunotherapy has been largely replaced by targeted therapy, and treatment is not indicated in early asymptomatic disease.
  • (D) Ibrutinib — BTK inhibitors are first-line when treatment is indicated; he does not meet criteria.
  • (E) Radiation therapy to the cervical nodes — Localized radiation is not used for CLL lymphadenopathy unless bulky and symptomatic.
🎯 Educational objective

Observe asymptomatic early-stage CLL without treatment until indications for therapy such as cytopenias, symptoms or rapid progression develop.

HE-015.stem_html:
A 24-year-old woman is evaluated before a planned wisdom-tooth extraction because of a history of bleeding. She has had heavy menstrual periods since menarche, needing to change pads every hour on heavy days. She had prolonged bleeding after a tonsillectomy at age 8. She bruises easily and has frequent nosebleeds. Her mother also has heavy menses. She takes no medications.

Examination is normal except for a few small bruises.

Hemoglobin11.4 g/dL
MCV76 fL
Platelet count228,000/µL
PTnormal
aPTTnormal to mildly prolonged (36 s; reference 25–35 s)
HE-015.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate next diagnostic test?

choices.A: Mixing study for a lupus anticoagulant
choices.D: Von Willebrand factor antigen, activity (ristocetin cofactor or GPIb binding) and factor VIII activity

HE-015.explain_html:
Correct answer: D Von Willebrand disease

Mucocutaneous bleeding — menorrhagia since menarche, epistaxis, easy bruising, bleeding after tonsillectomy — with a family history, normal platelets, normal PT and normal or slightly prolonged aPTT → von Willebrand disease (VWD), the most common inherited bleeding disorder (~1% of people; usually type 1, autosomal dominant).

VWF does two jobs: platelet adhesion (bridges platelets to collagen via GPIb) and carrying factor VIII (protects it from clearance) — which is why the aPTT may be slightly prolonged.

Initial panel: VWF antigen, VWF activity (ristocetin cofactor or GPIbM assay), factor VIII activity. VWF levels rise with stress, estrogen, pregnancy and inflammation — repeat if borderline. Blood type O has lower VWF levels.

Treatment: desmopressin (DDAVP) releases stored VWF (type 1), VWF-containing concentrates for major surgery or nonresponders, and tranexamic acid for mucosal bleeding and menorrhagia (plus hormonal therapy). Treat her iron deficiency.

Why not the others

  • (A) Mixing study for a lupus anticoagulant — A lupus anticoagulant prolongs the aPTT in vitro but causes thrombosis, not bleeding.
  • (B) Platelet function analyzer only — The PFA-100 is neither sensitive nor specific enough to diagnose or exclude VWD.
  • (C) Bone marrow biopsy — Bone marrow biopsy has no role in evaluating an inherited bleeding disorder with normal blood counts.
  • (E) Factor IX activity — Hemophilia B (factor IX deficiency) is X-linked, presents in males with joint and muscle bleeds and a prolonged aPTT.
🎓 ABIM pearl

Platelet-type bleeding (mucosal, petechiae, immediate bleeding) → VWD or platelet disorders. Factor-type bleeding (joints, muscles, delayed bleeding) → hemophilia.

🎯 Educational objective

Evaluate lifelong mucocutaneous bleeding with VWF antigen, VWF activity and factor VIII activity to diagnose von Willebrand disease.

ID-001.stem_html:
A 32-year-old man comes to the office with 3 days of fever, productive cough and right-sided pleuritic chest pain. He has no medical problems, takes no medications and has not taken antibiotics in the past year. He has no drug allergies. He does not smoke or drink alcohol heavily.

Temperature is 38.6 °C (101.5 °F), blood pressure is 124/76 mm Hg, pulse is 98/min, respirations are 20/min and oxygen saturation is 97% on room air. Crackles and bronchial breath sounds are heard at the right base. He is alert and drinking fluids well.

Chest radiograph shows right lower lobe consolidation. Blood urea nitrogen is 12 mg/dL.
ID-001.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?

choices.E: Hospital admission for intravenous ceftriaxone and azithromycin

ID-001.explain_html:
Correct answer: C Community-acquired pneumonia — outpatient

He has community-acquired pneumonia with CURB-65 = 0 (no confusion, BUN <20, RR <30, BP normal, age <65) → treat at home.

For an outpatient without comorbidities or MRSA/Pseudomonas risk factors, ATS/IDSA recommends high-dose amoxicillin (1 g three times daily), which covers Streptococcus pneumoniae, the most common and most lethal bacterial cause. Doxycycline is an alternative. A macrolide alone is used only where pneumococcal macrolide resistance is <25%, which is not true in most of the US.

Outpatient CAP Regimen (5 days minimum, until stable)
No comorbidities Amoxicillin 1 g TID, or doxycycline, or macrolide (if local resistance <25%)
Comorbidities (heart, lung, liver, kidney disease, diabetes, alcohol use disorder, cancer, asplenia) Amoxicillin–clavulanate or a cephalosporin plus macrolide or doxycycline, or a respiratory fluoroquinolone alone

Why not the others

  • (A) Azithromycin — Macrolide monotherapy fails against resistant pneumococci; US resistance rates are well above 25%.
  • (B) Levofloxacin — Respiratory fluoroquinolones are reserved for patients with comorbidities or beta-lactam allergy because of tendon rupture, aortic aneurysm, QT prolongation, C. difficile and resistance concerns.
  • (D) Amoxicillin–clavulanate plus azithromycin — Combination therapy is for outpatients with comorbidities. He has none.
  • (E) Hospital admission for intravenous ceftriaxone and azithromycin — CURB-65 of 0 and normal oxygenation support outpatient care.
🧠 Mnemonic

CURB-65: Confusion, Urea (BUN) >19 mg/dL, Respiratory rate ≥30, BP <90 systolic or ≤60 diastolic, age ≥65. 0–1 → home; 2 → consider admission; ≥3 → hospital, think ICU.

🎓 ABIM pearl

Treat for at least 5 days and until afebrile for 48–72 hours with stable vital signs. A follow-up chest film is not routinely needed if he recovers.

🎯 Educational objective

Treat outpatient community-acquired pneumonia in a healthy adult without risk factors with high-dose amoxicillin (or doxycycline); reserve fluoroquinolones and combination therapy for patients with comorbidities.

ID-002.stem_html:
A 27-year-old woman comes to the office with 2 days of painful urination, urgency and frequency. She has no fever, chills, flank pain, vaginal discharge or itching. Her last menstrual period was 2 weeks ago and a urine pregnancy test is negative. She had one similar episode 3 years ago. She has no drug allergies.

Temperature is 36.9 °C (98.4 °F). There is mild suprapubic tenderness and no costovertebral angle tenderness.

Urine dipstick is positive for leukocyte esterase and nitrite.
ID-002.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?

choices.A: No antibiotic until urine culture results are available

ID-002.explain_html:
Correct answer: E Acute uncomplicated cystitis

Dysuria and frequency without vaginal symptoms in a nonpregnant woman has a >90% probability of acute uncomplicated cystitis. No culture is needed before treatment for a typical first or infrequent episode.

First-line choices (IDSA) are agents with low resistance and little collateral damage to gut flora:

First-line Course
Nitrofurantoin monohydrate/macrocrystals 100 mg BID 5 days
Trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole DS BID 3 days (if local resistance <20%)
Fosfomycin 3 g single dose
Pivmecillinam 3–5 days

Nitrofurantoin reaches high concentrations only in urine, so do not use it for pyelonephritis or when creatinine clearance is very low.

Why not the others

  • (A) No antibiotic until urine culture results are available — Waiting for culture delays relief. Cultures are for recurrent, complicated or atypical cases, or suspected pyelonephritis.
  • (B) Amoxicillin for 7 days — E. coli resistance to amoxicillin is high; aminopenicillins alone are not recommended for empiric cystitis therapy.
  • (C) Ciprofloxacin for 3 days — Fluoroquinolones work but are reserved for pyelonephritis or when first-line agents cannot be used, because of serious adverse effects and resistance.
  • (D) Ceftriaxone intramuscularly once — Parenteral ceftriaxone is unnecessary for lower-tract infection in an outpatient who can take oral medication.
🎓 ABIM pearl

Fever, flank pain or CVA tenderness → pyelonephritis: get a urine culture and use a fluoroquinolone or TMP-SMX (if susceptible), often after one IV dose of ceftriaxone.

🎯 Educational objective

Treat acute uncomplicated cystitis empirically with nitrofurantoin for 5 days (or TMP-SMX, fosfomycin, or pivmecillinam); reserve fluoroquinolones for pyelonephritis.

ID-003.stem_html:
A 52-year-old man comes for a routine health visit. He feels well. He has no chronic medical conditions, does not smoke and takes no medications. He received a tetanus–diphtheria–pertussis (Tdap) vaccine 5 years ago and an influenza vaccine this fall. He has never received a pneumococcal vaccine.

Examination is normal.
ID-003.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate pneumococcal vaccination for this patient?

choices.B: PPSV23 now and PCV20 in 1 year
choices.C: A single dose of 20-valent pneumococcal conjugate vaccine (PCV20) now
choices.E: 15-valent pneumococcal conjugate vaccine (PCV15) now and no further doses

ID-003.explain_html:
Correct answer: C Adult pneumococcal vaccination

Since late 2024, CDC recommends pneumococcal vaccination for all adults aged 50 years and older (and for younger adults with risk conditions), regardless of health.

For adults who have never received a conjugate vaccine, give one dose of PCV20 or PCV21 — that completes the series. Alternatively, give PCV15 followed by PPSV23 one year later.

Conjugate vaccines link the polysaccharide to a protein carrier, which recruits T-cell help and produces memory and better immunogenicity than plain polysaccharide vaccines.

Why not the others

  • (A) 23-valent pneumococcal polysaccharide vaccine (PPSV23) now — PPSV23 alone is no longer recommended as the first or only vaccine; it gives weaker, shorter immunity than conjugate vaccines.
  • (B) PPSV23 now and PCV20 in 1 year — Starting with PPSV23 is the outdated sequence; when both are needed, the conjugate vaccine goes first.
  • (D) No pneumococcal vaccine until age 65 — The age threshold for routine vaccination was lowered from 65 to 50 years.
  • (E) 15-valent pneumococcal conjugate vaccine (PCV15) now and no further doses — PCV15 must be followed by PPSV23 (usually ≥1 year later) to complete the series.
🧠 Mnemonic

"Twenty at fifty" — PCV20 (or PCV21) once at 50+ and you are done.

🎓 ABIM pearl

He is also due for recombinant zoster vaccine (2 doses, 2–6 months apart) — recommended for all adults ≥50, even with a prior shingles episode.

🎯 Educational objective

All adults aged 50 years or older who have not received a pneumococcal conjugate vaccine should get a single dose of PCV20 or PCV21 (or PCV15 followed by PPSV23).

ID-004.stem_html:
A 68-year-old man is scheduled for extraction of a fractured molar next week. Four years ago he had a bioprosthetic aortic valve replacement for aortic stenosis. He has hypertension and takes lisinopril and aspirin. He has no drug allergies and no history of endocarditis.

Examination shows a soft systolic ejection murmur at the right upper sternal border. Echocardiography 6 months ago showed a normally functioning prosthetic valve.
ID-004.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate recommendation before the procedure?

choices.A: Amoxicillin 500 mg three times daily for 7 days after the procedure
choices.B: Clindamycin 600 mg orally before the procedure
choices.C: Amoxicillin 2 g orally 30–60 minutes before the procedure

ID-004.explain_html:
Correct answer: C Infective endocarditis prophylaxis

Antibiotic prophylaxis before dental work is now limited to patients at highest risk of a bad outcome from endocarditis, and only for procedures that manipulate the gingiva or periapical region or perforate the oral mucosa (extractions qualify).

Prosthetic valves of any type (including bioprosthetic and transcatheter valves, and valve repairs with prosthetic material) are a highest-risk condition. The regimen is a single dose of amoxicillin 2 g orally 30–60 minutes before the procedure.

Highest-risk conditions (prophylaxis for dental procedures)
Prosthetic valve or prosthetic material used in valve repair
Previous infective endocarditis
Unrepaired cyanotic congenital heart disease; repaired CHD with residual shunt or defect near prosthetic material
Cardiac transplant with valvulopathy

Why not the others

  • (A) Amoxicillin 500 mg three times daily for 7 days after the procedure — Prophylaxis is a single dose before the procedure; a postprocedure course adds adverse effects without benefit.
  • (B) Clindamycin 600 mg orally before the procedure — Clindamycin is no longer recommended for penicillin-allergic patients because it causes more C. difficile infection; azithromycin, clarithromycin or doxycycline are used instead.
  • (D) Intravenous vancomycin before the procedure — IV vancomycin is unnecessary for an outpatient dental procedure in a patient without penicillin allergy.
  • (E) No antibiotic prophylaxis — A prosthetic valve is one of the few conditions where prophylaxis is still recommended.
🎓 ABIM pearl

Prophylaxis is not recommended for GI or GU procedures (colonoscopy, cystoscopy) in any of these patients, or for mitral valve prolapse, bicuspid aortic valve or native valve regurgitation alone. Good oral hygiene prevents far more endocarditis than antibiotics.

🎯 Educational objective

Give a single preprocedure dose of amoxicillin 2 g before dental procedures involving the gingiva in patients with prosthetic valves, prior endocarditis, or certain congenital heart disease.
