NE-011.stem_html:
A 64-year-old woman with small cell lung cancer is brought to the emergency department after a generalized tonic-clonic seizure at home. Her family says she has been confused and vomiting for 2 days.

On physical examination, blood pressure is 128/76 mm Hg and pulse rate is 88/min. She is drowsy and confused. Mucous membranes are moist and there is no edema.

Sodium116 mEq/L (128 mEq/L 2 weeks ago)
Potassium4.0 mEq/L
Glucose102 mg/dL
Serum osmolality242 mOsm/kg H₂O
Urine osmolality540 mOsm/kg H₂O
Urine sodium62 mEq/L
TSH and morning cortisolnormal
NE-011.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate immediate treatment?

choices.B: 100-mL bolus of 3% saline over 10 minutes, repeated up to two more times as needed

NE-011.explain_html:
Correct answer: B Severe symptomatic hyponatremia

She has severe symptomatic hyponatremia — seizure, vomiting, confusion — from SIADH (small cell lung cancer; euvolemia, low serum osmolality, concentrated urine, urine Na >30, normal thyroid and adrenal function).

Severe symptoms mean cerebral edema: treat immediately with hypertonic (3%) saline — 100–150 mL bolus over 10–20 minutes, repeated up to two more times if symptoms persist. The aim is a quick rise of 4–6 mEq/L, which is enough to stop seizures and reverse herniation.

Then limit the total correction to avoid osmotic demyelination syndrome: ≤8 mEq/L in 24 hours for high-risk patients (hypokalemia, alcohol use, malnutrition, liver disease, Na ≤105) and ≤10–12 mEq/L for others. If correction is too fast, re-lower with D5W and desmopressin.

Long-term SIADH management: fluid restriction, salt tablets plus a loop diuretic, urea, or vaptans; treat the tumor.

Why not the others

  • (A) Oral salt tablets and urea — Salt tablets and urea are chronic therapies, not emergency treatment for seizures.
  • (C) Fluid restriction to 800 mL/d — Fluid restriction is the chronic treatment for SIADH. It acts too slowly to reverse seizure-causing cerebral edema.
  • (D) Oral tolvaptan — Tolvaptan is for chronic, mild-to-moderate SIADH; it is too slow and unpredictable for emergencies.
  • (E) Intravenous 0.9% saline at 150 mL/h — Normal saline (osmolality 308) can worsen hyponatremia in SIADH when urine osmolality is high — the kidney keeps the water and excretes the salt.
🎯 Educational objective

Treat hyponatremia with severe symptoms (seizure, obtundation) with 100–150 mL boluses of 3% saline, aiming for a 4–6 mEq/L rise while limiting 24-hour correction to 8–10 mEq/L.

NE-012.stem_html:
A 34-year-old man with autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD) diagnosed by ultrasonography is evaluated during a routine visit. His mother has ADPKD and started dialysis at age 52. His maternal uncle died of a ruptured intracranial aneurysm at age 45. He has hypertension treated with lisinopril. He has no headache or neurologic symptoms.

On physical examination, blood pressure is 128/80 mm Hg. Both kidneys are palpable.

Creatinine1.3 mg/dL
eGFR70 mL/min/1.73 m²
Total kidney volume (MRI)large for age (Mayo class 1D)
NE-012.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate screening test?

choices.B: Magnetic resonance angiography of the head
choices.C: Echocardiography for mitral valve prolapse every year
choices.E: Testing for PKD1 mutation in his children now

NE-012.explain_html:
Correct answer: B Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease

ADPKD (PKD1 or PKD2 mutations) is the most common inherited kidney disease. Extrarenal manifestations include liver cysts (most common), intracranial aneurysms, mitral valve prolapse, colonic diverticula and abdominal wall hernias.

Intracranial aneurysms occur in about 9–12% of ADPKD patients, rising to ~20% in those with a family history of aneurysm or subarachnoid hemorrhage. Screening with MR angiography (no gadolinium needed; time-of-flight) is recommended for patients with a family history of aneurysm/SAH, a prior aneurysm rupture, high-risk occupations (pilots) or before major surgery.

He is also at high risk of rapid progression (large kidney volume for age, early ESKD in his mother), which makes him a candidate for tolvaptan (a vasopressin V2 antagonist that slows growth of kidney volume and eGFR decline). Control blood pressure (target ≤110/75 mm Hg in young patients with preserved GFR, HALT-PKD) and encourage high water intake.

Why not the others

  • (A) Colonoscopy at age 40 — Diverticulosis is more common, but ADPKD does not change colorectal cancer screening.
  • (C) Echocardiography for mitral valve prolapse every year — MVP is common in ADPKD, but routine annual echocardiography is not recommended in the absence of a murmur or symptoms.
  • (D) Annual CT of the abdomen — Serial CT adds radiation and is not used to monitor ADPKD; MRI-based kidney volume is used for prognosis.
  • (E) Testing for PKD1 mutation in his children now — Genetic testing of asymptomatic children is generally deferred until adulthood or until results would change management.
🎯 Educational objective

Screen patients with ADPKD who have a family history of intracranial aneurysm or subarachnoid hemorrhage with magnetic resonance angiography of the head.

NE-013.stem_html:
A 27-year-old man is evaluated for a painless lump in his left testis that he noticed 3 weeks ago in the shower. He has no dysuria, fever or trauma. He had an undescended right testis repaired as an infant.

On physical examination, there is a firm, nontender 1.5-cm nodule within the left testis that does not transilluminate. The epididymis and spermatic cord are normal. There is no inguinal hernia or lymphadenopathy.
NE-013.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate next diagnostic test?

choices.B: Urine nucleic acid testing for chlamydia and gonorrhea
choices.D: CT of the abdomen and pelvis
choices.E: Trial of antibiotics for epididymitis and reexamination in 2 weeks

NE-013.explain_html:
Correct answer: C Testicular mass

A firm, painless intratesticular mass in a young man is testicular cancer until proven otherwise — the most common solid tumor in men aged 15–35 years. Cryptorchidism raises the risk, including in the contralateral, normally descended testis.

The first test is scrotal ultrasonography: a hypoechoic intratesticular mass is highly suggestive. Then:

  • Serum tumor markers — AFP, β-hCG, LDH (before orchiectomy).
  • Radical inguinal orchiectomy for diagnosis and treatment.
  • Staging CT of the abdomen/pelvis and chest imaging.
  • Discuss sperm banking.

Never biopsy through the scrotum — it can seed tumor into scrotal lymphatics.

Scrotal finding Likely cause
Firm, painless intratesticular mass Testicular cancer
Transilluminating, surrounds testis Hydrocele
"Bag of worms," worse standing Varicocele (left > right; new right-sided → image for mass)
Cystic nodule above testis, transilluminates Spermatocele/epididymal cyst
Painful, fever, positive Prehn sign Epididymitis
Sudden severe pain, high-riding testis, absent cremasteric reflex Torsion — emergency surgery

Why not the others

  • (A) Fine-needle aspiration of the testis — Transscrotal needle aspiration or biopsy risks tumor seeding and is contraindicated.
  • (B) Urine nucleic acid testing for chlamydia and gonorrhea — STI testing is for urethritis or epididymitis, which he does not have.
  • (D) CT of the abdomen and pelvis — CT is used for staging after the diagnosis is made by ultrasound and orchiectomy.
  • (E) Trial of antibiotics for epididymitis and reexamination in 2 weeks — The nodule is painless and intratesticular with a normal epididymis; treating as infection delays a cancer diagnosis.
🎯 Educational objective

Evaluate a painless intratesticular mass with scrotal ultrasonography, followed by tumor markers and radical inguinal orchiectomy if a solid mass is confirmed.

NE-014.stem_html:
A 62-year-old man is evaluated after a routine urinalysis showed blood. He has no dysuria, flank pain or gross hematuria. He smoked one pack of cigarettes daily for 35 years and quit 5 years ago. He worked in a dye manufacturing plant. He does not take anticoagulants.

On physical examination, blood pressure is 128/78 mm Hg. Prostate examination is normal.

Repeat urinalysis with microscopy12 erythrocytes/hpf; normal red cell morphology; no casts; no protein
Urine culturenegative
Creatinine0.9 mg/dL
NE-014.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in evaluation?
NE-014.explain_html:
Correct answer: E Asymptomatic microscopic hematuria

Microscopic hematuria is ≥3 red blood cells per high-power field on microscopy. Confirm with microscopy (dipstick alone gives false positives from myoglobin, hemoglobin), and exclude infection, menstruation, recent exercise and trauma.

Non-glomerular (normal red cell morphology, no casts, no proteinuria) hematuria in an adult raises concern for urothelial cancer. Risk is stratified by the AUA 2020 guideline:

  • High risk: age ≥60 (men), >30 pack-years smoking, >25 RBC/hpf, history of gross hematuria, occupational exposure (aromatic amines — dyes, rubber, leather).
  • High-risk patients → cystoscopy plus CT urography (multiphasic CT of the upper tracts).
  • Intermediate risk → cystoscopy + renal ultrasonography.
  • Low risk → repeat urinalysis in 6 months, or cystoscopy + ultrasound with shared decision-making.

He is high risk (age, heavy smoking, dye exposure).

Why not the others

  • (A) Kidney biopsy — Kidney biopsy is for suspected glomerular disease (dysmorphic RBCs, red cell casts, proteinuria, rising creatinine).
  • (B) Repeat urinalysis in 1 year — Waiting is appropriate only for low-risk patients; he is high risk.
  • (C) Urine cytology alone — Cytology is insensitive for low-grade tumors and does not replace cystoscopy and upper-tract imaging.
  • (D) Prostate-specific antigen measurement — PSA screens for prostate cancer but does not evaluate hematuria.
🎓 ABIM pearl

Anticoagulation does not explain hematuria — patients on warfarin or DOACs with hematuria need the same evaluation.

🎯 Educational objective

Evaluate microscopic hematuria in high-risk patients (older age, heavy smoking, occupational exposures) with cystoscopy and CT urography.

NE-015.stem_html:
A 61-year-old man is evaluated for 1 year of difficulty achieving and maintaining erections. He has hypertension, hyperlipidemia and stable angina. He uses isosorbide mononitrate daily and sublingual nitroglycerin about once a month. His other medications are metoprolol, amlodipine, atorvastatin and aspirin. He has normal morning testosterone.

On physical examination, blood pressure is 126/76 mm Hg. Genitourinary examination is normal.
NE-015.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

choices.A: Begin sildenafil, taken at least 1 hour after his isosorbide dose
choices.B: Stop metoprolol because it is the cause of his erectile dysfunction
choices.C: Begin tadalafil daily and continue all medications
choices.D: Discuss alternatives such as a vacuum erection device or intracavernosal alprostadil, and coordinate with his cardiologist about nitrate therapy

NE-015.explain_html:
Correct answer: D Erectile dysfunction and nitrates

PDE-5 inhibitors (sildenafil, vardenafil, tadalafil) are absolutely contraindicated with any nitrate, at any time interval in a patient taking a daily long-acting nitrate. Both drugs raise cyclic GMP in vascular smooth muscle, and together they can cause profound, refractory hypotension and death. (Avoid nitrates for 24 hours after sildenafil/vardenafil and 48 hours after tadalafil.)

Options for this man:

  • Non-PDE-5 therapies: vacuum erection device, intracavernosal alprostadil or intraurethral alprostadil, penile prosthesis.
  • Ask his cardiologist whether the daily nitrate can be stopped — long-acting nitrates do not improve survival, and other antianginals (ranolazine, beta-blockers, CCBs) may control his symptoms. If the nitrate is stopped (including PRN nitroglycerin, with a plan for chest pain), a PDE-5 inhibitor becomes possible.

Erectile dysfunction is a marker of vascular disease — it often precedes coronary events by 2–5 years.

Why not the others

  • (A) Begin sildenafil, taken at least 1 hour after his isosorbide dose — Timing does not make a PDE-5 inhibitor safe with a daily long-acting nitrate; the combination is contraindicated.
  • (B) Stop metoprolol because it is the cause of his erectile dysfunction — Beta-blockers can contribute to ED, but metoprolol is needed for his angina, and stopping it abruptly is risky. ED in this setting is mostly vascular.
  • (C) Begin tadalafil daily and continue all medications — Daily tadalafil with nitrates carries the same risk of severe hypotension.
  • (E) Begin testosterone therapy — His testosterone is normal; testosterone therapy does not treat ED in eugonadal men.
🎯 Educational objective

Do not prescribe PDE-5 inhibitors to patients taking any nitrate; offer alternatives or coordinate nitrate discontinuation with cardiology.

NR-001.stem_html:
A 66-year-old man is evaluated in the emergency department after a 40-minute episode of weakness of the right hand and slurred speech that began while he was reading. Symptoms resolved completely 2 hours ago. He has hypertension and type 2 diabetes. He takes lisinopril and metformin.

Blood pressure is 158/88 mm Hg and pulse is 76/min, regular. Neurologic examination is normal (NIH Stroke Scale score 0).

Noncontrast head CTno hemorrhage or acute infarct
MRI brain with diffusion-weighted imagingno infarct
CT angiography of head and neck30% stenosis of the left internal carotid artery; no large-vessel occlusion
ECG and 24-hour telemetrysinus rhythm
LDL cholesterol132 mg/dL
NR-001.lead: In addition to a high-intensity statin, which of the following is the most appropriate antithrombotic therapy?

choices.B: Aspirin plus clopidogrel for 21 days, then a single antiplatelet agent

NR-001.explain_html:
Correct answer: B High-risk transient ischemic attack

He had a high-risk TIA: motor weakness and speech disturbance lasting >10 minutes. His ABCD² score is 6 (age ≥60 = 1, BP ≥140/90 = 1, unilateral weakness = 2, duration 10–59 min = 1, diabetes = 1). The 90-day stroke risk is highest in the first 48 hours.

For high-risk TIA (ABCD² ≥4) or minor ischemic stroke (NIHSS ≤3) without a cardioembolic source, dual antiplatelet therapy (aspirin + clopidogrel) started within 24 hours and continued for 21 days, then a single agent, lowers early recurrent stroke (CHANCE, POINT). Longer DAPT adds bleeding without further benefit.

ABCD² Points
Age ≥60 1
BP ≥140/90 at evaluation 1
Clinical: unilateral weakness 2; speech disturbance without weakness 1 1–2
Duration: ≥60 min 2; 10–59 min 1 1–2
Diabetes 1

Why not the others

  • (A) Apixaban — Anticoagulation is for cardioembolic sources such as atrial fibrillation; telemetry showed sinus rhythm. Prolonged monitoring for AF is still reasonable.
  • (C) Intravenous alteplase — Thrombolysis is for a disabling deficit present at treatment; his symptoms resolved.
  • (D) Aspirin alone — Aspirin alone is appropriate for low-risk TIA or after the 21-day DAPT period, but it is less effective early after a high-risk TIA.
  • (E) Aspirin plus clopidogrel indefinitely — Long-term DAPT increases major bleeding without additional stroke prevention.
🎓 ABIM pearl

Symptomatic carotid stenosis 70%–99% (and selected 50%–69%) on the side of symptoms → carotid endarterectomy within 2 weeks. His 30% stenosis does not qualify.

🎯 Educational objective

After a high-risk TIA or minor ischemic stroke, start aspirin plus clopidogrel within 24 hours for 21 days, then continue single antiplatelet therapy with a high-intensity statin.

NR-002.stem_html:
A 34-year-old woman comes to the office because of migraines. She has had migraine without aura since her teens, but over the past year attacks have become more frequent — now about 8 headache days per month — and she has missed work several times. Sumatriptan usually relieves an attack within 2 hours; she uses it 6–8 days a month. She also has hypertension, diagnosed 6 months ago and not yet treated. She uses a copper IUD.

Blood pressure is 142/90 mm Hg on two readings and pulse is 82/min. Neurologic examination, including fundoscopy, is normal.
NR-002.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate preventive treatment?
NR-002.explain_html:
Correct answer: E Migraine prevention

She needs migraine prevention: ≥4 headache days per month with disability (many experts use ≥4 days, or fewer if attacks are severe or acute drugs fail or are overused).

First-line oral preventives include propranolol or metoprolol, topiramate, amitriptyline, venlafaxine and candesartan. Choose by comorbidity: her hypertension makes a β-blocker the natural choice — one drug, two problems. Start low, titrate, and judge benefit after 2–3 months. CGRP-targeting therapies (monoclonal antibodies, gepants) are also accepted first-line options, and are especially useful when oral preventives fail or cause side effects.

Comorbidity Good preventive choice Avoid
Hypertension Propranolol, metoprolol, candesartan —
Depression, insomnia Amitriptyline, venlafaxine —
Obesity Topiramate Amitriptyline, valproate
Asthma Topiramate, candesartan β-blockers
Possible pregnancy — Valproate, topiramate (teratogenic)

Why not the others

  • (A) Verapamil plus daily ibuprofen — Verapamil has weak evidence for migraine, and daily NSAID use (≥15 days a month) causes medication-overuse headache.
  • (B) Butalbital–acetaminophen–caffeine as needed — Butalbital combinations cause medication-overuse headache and dependence and are not recommended for migraine.
  • (C) Daily sumatriptan — Using a triptan ≥10 days a month causes medication-overuse headache; daily use is never a preventive strategy.
  • (D) Oxycodone as needed — Opioids worsen migraine over time, cause medication-overuse headache and carry addiction risk.
🎓 ABIM pearl

Combined hormonal contraception is contraindicated in migraine with aura (stroke risk). She has migraine without aura, but her untreated hypertension would also argue against estrogen.

🎯 Educational objective

Offer migraine prevention for frequent or disabling migraine, selecting the agent by comorbidity (a β-blocker for coexisting hypertension), and avoid frequent acute-drug use that leads to medication-overuse headache.

NR-003.stem_html:
A 68-year-old man is brought to the emergency department 90 minutes after the sudden onset of right arm and leg weakness and difficulty speaking. His wife saw him become symptomatic at breakfast. He has hypertension and takes lisinopril. He takes no anticoagulants and has had no recent surgery, bleeding or head trauma.

On physical examination, blood pressure is 196/108 mm Hg, pulse rate is 82/min and regular. He has expressive aphasia, a right facial droop and right hemiparesis (NIHSS score 12). Glucose is 128 mg/dL.

Noncontrast CT of the head shows no hemorrhage or early ischemic changes. CT angiography shows no large-vessel occlusion. Platelet count and INR are pending.
NR-003.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.A: Give aspirin, 325 mg, and admit to the stroke unit
choices.B: Wait for platelet count and INR before deciding on thrombolysis
choices.C: Give alteplase or tenecteplase now without lowering blood pressure
choices.D: Lower blood pressure to below 185/110 mm Hg with intravenous labetalol or nicardipine, then give thrombolysis

NR-003.explain_html:
Correct answer: D Acute ischemic stroke — thrombolysis

He has a disabling acute ischemic stroke within 4.5 hours of onset, with no hemorrhage on CT. He is a candidate for IV thrombolysis — alteplase (0.9 mg/kg) or tenecteplase (0.25 mg/kg single bolus; noninferior to alteplase in the AcT trial and now used by many centers).

Blood pressure must be <185/110 mm Hg before thrombolysis and <180/105 mm Hg for 24 hours after, to lower the risk of intracranial hemorrhage. Use IV labetalol, nicardipine or clevidipine.

Do not wait for platelets or INR unless there is reason to suspect an abnormality (anticoagulant use, liver disease, known thrombocytopenia). The only test needed before thrombolysis is the glucose (hypoglycemia mimics stroke).

Without thrombolysis, stroke patients may have BP up to 220/120 mm Hg (permissive hypertension) in the first 48–72 hours.

Large-vessel occlusion → mechanical thrombectomy up to 24 hours in selected patients.

Why not the others

  • (A) Give aspirin, 325 mg, and admit to the stroke unit — Aspirin is given 24 hours after thrombolysis, or immediately for patients who are not candidates; it is not a substitute for thrombolysis.
  • (B) Wait for platelet count and INR before deciding on thrombolysis — Waiting for coagulation tests delays treatment without reason when there is no suspicion of coagulopathy; "time is brain".
  • (C) Give alteplase or tenecteplase now without lowering blood pressure — Thrombolysis with BP above 185/110 mm Hg increases the risk of symptomatic intracranial hemorrhage.
  • (E) Start a heparin infusion — Heparin has no role in acute ischemic stroke treatment and increases hemorrhage risk.
🎯 Educational objective

Lower blood pressure below 185/110 mm Hg before giving IV thrombolysis to eligible patients with acute ischemic stroke within 4.5 hours, without waiting for coagulation tests unless coagulopathy is suspected.

NR-004.stem_html:
A 26-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department by her family for 2 weeks of anxiety, insomnia, paranoid thoughts and bizarre behavior, followed by a generalized seizure today. She had a flulike illness 3 weeks ago. She has no psychiatric history and does not use drugs.

On physical examination, temperature is 37.9 °C (100.2 °F), blood pressure is 156/94 mm Hg, and pulse rate is 118/min. She is agitated and confused. There are orofacial dyskinesias (lip-smacking and grimacing) and intermittent choreiform arm movements.

Cerebrospinal fluid34 leukocytes/µL (95% lymphocytes); protein 52 mg/dL; glucose normal
CSF HSV PCRnegative
MRI of the brainnormal
EEGdiffuse slowing with "extreme delta brush" pattern
Urine drug screennegative
NR-004.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate test to confirm the diagnosis and guide further evaluation?

choices.E: Anti-NMDA receptor antibodies in CSF, followed by pelvic imaging

NR-004.explain_html:
Correct answer: E Anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis

A young woman with psychiatric symptoms → seizures → movement disorder (orofacial dyskinesias) → autonomic instability, with CSF lymphocytic pleocytosis, a normal MRI and the "extreme delta brush" EEG pattern = anti–NMDA receptor encephalitis, the most common autoimmune encephalitis.

Confirm with anti-NMDA receptor (GluN1) IgG antibodies in CSF (more sensitive and specific than serum).

About half of women have an ovarian teratoma (which contains neural tissue). Look for it with pelvic MRI or transvaginal ultrasonography; removal improves outcomes. HSV encephalitis can trigger anti-NMDAR encephalitis weeks later.

Treatment: first-line immunotherapy — high-dose glucocorticoids, IVIG or plasma exchange — and tumor removal; rituximab or cyclophosphamide if no response. Start treatment while waiting for antibody results when the picture is typical.

Why not the others

  • (A) Serum ceruloplasmin — Wilson disease causes neuropsychiatric symptoms but with liver disease and Kayser-Fleischer rings, not acute encephalitis with CSF pleocytosis.
  • (B) Repeat MRI in 6 weeks — The MRI is often normal in anti-NMDAR encephalitis; repeating it does not confirm the diagnosis and delays treatment.
  • (C) Brain biopsy — Brain biopsy is rarely needed; antibody testing is diagnostic.
  • (D) Antinuclear antibodies — ANA testing evaluates SLE; neuropsychiatric lupus can cause psychosis and seizures but not this pattern with orofacial dyskinesias.
🎯 Educational objective

Suspect anti–NMDA receptor encephalitis in a young patient with psychiatric symptoms, seizures, dyskinesias and autonomic instability; confirm with CSF antibodies and screen for ovarian teratoma.

NR-005.stem_html:
A 34-year-old woman is evaluated for 2 months of double vision and drooping eyelids that worsen in the evening and after reading. She also has difficulty chewing tough meat by the end of a meal. She has no limb weakness or dyspnea.

On physical examination, there is bilateral asymmetric ptosis that worsens with sustained upgaze for 60 seconds. Extraocular movements show variable weakness. Pupils are normal and reactive. Placing an ice pack over the eyelids for 2 minutes improves the ptosis. Reflexes and sensation are normal.

Acetylcholine receptor binding antibodiespositive
TSHnormal
NR-005.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate next diagnostic test?

choices.C: MRI of the brain with contrast

NR-005.explain_html:
Correct answer: A Myasthenia gravis — diagnosis and thymoma

Fatigable ptosis and diplopia, bulbar fatigue, normal pupils, a positive ice pack test (cold improves neuromuscular transmission) and positive acetylcholine receptor (AChR) antibodies = myasthenia gravis (MG). AChR antibodies block, cross-link and destroy postsynaptic receptors.

Once MG is diagnosed, obtain chest CT (or MRI) for thymoma, present in about 10–15% of patients with MG (and thymic hyperplasia in many more). Thymoma requires resection. Even without thymoma, thymectomy improves outcomes in AChR-positive generalized MG aged 18–65 (MGTX trial).

Treatment: pyridostigmine (acetylcholinesterase inhibitor) for symptoms; immunotherapy (prednisone, azathioprine, mycophenolate; complement inhibitors and FcRn blockers for refractory disease). Avoid drugs that worsen MG: aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones, macrolides, magnesium, β-blockers, neuromuscular blockers, checkpoint inhibitors.

Why not the others

  • (B) Electroencephalography — EEG evaluates seizures; it has no role in MG.
  • (C) MRI of the brain with contrast — Brain MRI is for suspected brainstem lesions; the fatigable pattern with normal pupils and positive antibodies confirms MG.
  • (D) Muscle biopsy — Muscle biopsy is for myopathies; MG is a neuromuscular junction disorder.
  • (E) Lumbar puncture — CSF is normal in MG; lumbar puncture is used for GBS or CNS inflammation.
🎯 Educational objective

After diagnosing myasthenia gravis, obtain chest CT or MRI to look for thymoma.

NR-006.stem_html:
A 42-year-old man is evaluated for 5 days of progressive leg weakness and tingling in his feet and hands. He had diarrhea 2 weeks ago. Today he has trouble climbing stairs and his voice is weaker.

On physical examination, blood pressure is 148/92 mm Hg, pulse rate is 108/min, and respiration rate is 22/min. He has bilateral facial weakness. Strength is 3/5 in the legs and 4/5 in the arms. Reflexes are absent throughout. There is mild distal sensory loss.

Cerebrospinal fluid3 leukocytes/µL; protein 148 mg/dL
Forced vital capacity18 mL/kg (falling from 26 mL/kg 6 hours ago)
Maximal inspiratory pressure−22 cm H₂O
NR-006.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

choices.E: Intravenous immune globulin and transfer to the ICU for elective intubation

NR-006.explain_html:
Correct answer: E Guillain-Barré syndrome

Ascending, symmetric weakness with areflexia after a GI infection (Campylobacter jejuni), with albuminocytologic dissociation (high CSF protein, normal cells) = Guillain-Barré syndrome (GBS).

The key danger is respiratory failure (25–30% need ventilation) and autonomic instability. Monitor FVC and negative inspiratory force. The "20/30/40 rule" signals need for intubation: FVC <20 mL/kg, MIP weaker than −30 cm H₂O, MEP <40 cm H₂O. He meets these and is worsening → ICU and elective intubation before he crashes. Oxygen saturation falls late and is not reliable.

Disease-modifying treatment: IVIG (0.4 g/kg/d × 5 days) or plasma exchange — equally effective, best within 2 weeks of onset. Do not combine them.

Why not the others

  • (A) Oral prednisone and outpatient follow-up — He is rapidly progressing with respiratory compromise and needs inpatient ICU care.
  • (B) High-dose intravenous methylprednisolone — Glucocorticoids do not help GBS and may delay recovery.
  • (C) Pyridostigmine — Pyridostigmine treats myasthenia gravis, not GBS.
  • (D) Repeat lumbar puncture in 1 week — The diagnosis is clear; delaying treatment worsens outcomes.
🧠 Mnemonic

"20/30/40" — FVC <20 mL/kg, MIP >−30 (weaker), MEP <40 → intubate.

🎯 Educational objective

Treat Guillain-Barré syndrome with IVIG or plasma exchange and monitor vital capacity, admitting to the ICU for intubation when FVC falls below 20 mL/kg.

NR-007.stem_html:
A 29-year-old woman is evaluated for 5 days of painful loss of vision in her right eye that is worse with eye movement. A year ago she had 3 weeks of numbness from her waist down that resolved on its own.

On physical examination, visual acuity is 20/200 in the right eye and 20/20 in the left. There is a right relative afferent pupillary defect. Funduscopic examination is normal. Red color desaturation is present on the right. Reflexes are brisk in the legs.
NR-007.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate diagnostic test?

choices.B: MRI of the brain and spinal cord with gadolinium

NR-007.explain_html:
Correct answer: B Multiple sclerosis — diagnosis

Optic neuritis (painful monocular vision loss, worse with eye movement, RAPD, red desaturation; disc often normal — "the patient sees nothing and the doctor sees nothing") in a young woman, with a prior episode of a spinal cord syndrome, suggests multiple sclerosis (MS).

MS is diagnosed by dissemination in space and time (McDonald 2017 criteria). MRI of the brain and spinal cord with gadolinium is the key test: look for T2 lesions in periventricular (Dawson fingers), juxtacortical, infratentorial and spinal cord regions, and simultaneous enhancing and nonenhancing lesions (dissemination in time). CSF oligoclonal bands can substitute for dissemination in time.

Acute optic neuritis is treated with IV methylprednisolone (speeds recovery; does not change final vision). Start disease-modifying therapy early when MS is confirmed.

Also consider NMOSD (aquaporin-4 antibodies) and MOG antibody disease, especially with severe or bilateral optic neuritis or longitudinally extensive myelitis.

Why not the others

  • (A) CT of the head — CT is insensitive for demyelinating lesions.
  • (C) Temporal artery biopsy — Giant cell arteritis causes painless vision loss in patients older than 50 with headache and jaw claudication.
  • (D) Serum vitamin B₁₂ level only — B₁₂ deficiency can cause myelopathy and optic neuropathy, but it is painless and bilateral, and it does not explain this relapsing pattern.
  • (E) Electromyography — EMG evaluates peripheral nerve and muscle disease, not CNS demyelination.
🎯 Educational objective

Evaluate suspected multiple sclerosis after optic neuritis or a prior myelitis with gadolinium-enhanced MRI of the brain and spinal cord to show dissemination in space and time.

NR-008.stem_html:
A 62-year-old man is evaluated for a tremor of both hands that has slowly worsened over 10 years. It makes it hard to drink from a cup or sign his name. The tremor improves after a glass of wine. His mother had a similar tremor. He has asthma treated with an inhaled glucocorticoid.

On physical examination, there is a bilateral postural and action (kinetic) tremor of the hands, worse when he holds his arms outstretched and during finger-to-nose testing. There is a mild head tremor ("no-no"). There is no rest tremor, rigidity or bradykinesia. Gait is normal.
NR-008.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?

choices.A: Deep brain stimulation as first-line therapy

NR-008.explain_html:
Correct answer: D Essential tremor

A slowly progressive, bilateral postural and kinetic tremor of the hands (and head) with a family history and improvement with alcohol = essential tremor, the most common movement disorder.

Essential tremor Parkinson disease
Tremor Action/postural Rest ("pill-rolling")
Body parts Hands, head, voice Hands, legs, jaw (not head)
Symmetry Bilateral Asymmetric at onset
Other signs None Bradykinesia, rigidity
Alcohol Improves No effect

First-line drugs: propranolol or primidone. Propranolol is contraindicated in his asthma (nonselective β-blocker), so primidone is the right choice. Topiramate and gabapentin are second-line. For disabling, refractory tremor: deep brain stimulation or MR-guided focused ultrasound thalamotomy.

Why not the others

  • (A) Deep brain stimulation as first-line therapy — DBS is reserved for disabling tremor that does not respond to medication.
  • (B) Propranolol — Propranolol is first-line for essential tremor, but nonselective β-blockade can cause bronchospasm in asthma.
  • (C) Carbidopa-levodopa — Levodopa treats Parkinson disease; it does not help essential tremor.
  • (E) Trihexyphenidyl — Anticholinergics treat rest tremor in young patients with Parkinson disease or dystonia and cause confusion in older adults.
🎯 Educational objective

Treat essential tremor with propranolol or primidone, choosing primidone when β-blockers are contraindicated (e.g., asthma).

NR-009.stem_html:
A 27-year-old woman is evaluated for 2 months of daily headaches that are worse in the morning and when lying down. She hears a "whooshing" sound in both ears in time with her pulse and has brief episodes of her vision "graying out" when she stands up. She has gained 10 kg (22 lb) in the past year. She takes no medications, including tetracyclines, vitamin A or retinoids.

On physical examination, blood pressure is 124/80 mm Hg. BMI is 38. There is bilateral papilledema. There is a mild left sixth nerve palsy. The remainder of the neurologic examination is normal.

MRI of the brain with MR venography shows no mass, hydrocephalus or venous sinus thrombosis; there is an empty sella and flattening of the posterior globes.
NR-009.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate next diagnostic test?

choices.D: CT angiography of the head and neck
choices.E: Lumbar puncture with opening pressure measurement

NR-009.explain_html:
Correct answer: E Idiopathic intracranial hypertension

A young woman with obesity and recent weight gain, headache, pulsatile tinnitus, transient visual obscurations, papilledema and a sixth nerve palsy (a false-localizing sign of raised ICP), with normal neuroimaging except signs of raised pressure (empty sella, flattened globes) → idiopathic intracranial hypertension (IIH, pseudotumor cerebri).

Confirm with lumbar puncture: opening pressure >25 cm H₂O (measured lateral decubitus, legs extended) with normal CSF composition. Imaging must be done first (mass, hydrocephalus) and must include venography to exclude cerebral venous sinus thrombosis, which can mimic IIH.

The main risk is permanent vision loss — get formal visual fields. Treatment: weight loss (5–10%; GLP-1 agonists and bariatric surgery help), acetazolamide; urgent CSF shunting or optic nerve sheath fenestration for threatened vision.

Why not the others

  • (A) Serum prolactin — Prolactin is checked for a pituitary adenoma; an empty sella here is a sign of chronically raised CSF pressure, not a tumor.
  • (B) Polysomnography — OSA is common in obesity and can worsen IIH, but it does not confirm the diagnosis.
  • (C) Electroencephalography — EEG has no role in raised intracranial pressure without seizures.
  • (D) CT angiography of the head and neck — CTA is used for aneurysm or dissection; venography already excluded venous sinus thrombosis.
🎯 Educational objective

Confirm idiopathic intracranial hypertension with lumbar puncture showing an opening pressure above 25 cm H₂O and normal CSF after MRI with venography excludes other causes.

NR-010.stem_html:
A 32-year-old man is evaluated in the emergency department after a first generalized tonic-clonic seizure witnessed by his wife this morning. It lasted 90 seconds, and he was confused for 20 minutes afterward. He has no history of head trauma, CNS infection or febrile seizures. He drinks alcohol socially and does not use drugs. He slept normally last night. He is now back to his baseline.

On physical examination, vital signs are normal. Neurologic examination is normal. There is a lateral tongue bite.

Glucosesodium, calcium, magnesium, normal
Urine drug screennegative
Noncontrast CT of the headnormal
NR-010.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

choices.A: Begin phenytoin with a loading dose
choices.C: Admit for continuous video EEG monitoring
choices.E: Outpatient EEG and brain MRI, counseling on driving restrictions, and no antiseizure medication for now

NR-010.explain_html:
Correct answer: E First unprovoked seizure

He has had a first unprovoked seizure with a normal examination, labs and CT, and has returned to baseline.

The risk of a second seizure is about 30–40% over 5 years (highest in the first 2 years). Work-up identifies patients at higher risk:

  • EEG — epileptiform discharges raise recurrence risk.
  • MRI of the brain — a structural lesion raises recurrence risk.
  • Nocturnal seizure, prior brain insult.

Immediate antiseizure medication reduces the 2-year recurrence risk by about 35% but does not change the long-term prognosis (remission at 3 years). AAN/AES guidance: individualize; most patients with a first seizure and no risk factors are not started on treatment. If EEG or MRI is abnormal, treatment is reasonable (that is effectively epilepsy).

Counsel on driving (state laws, often 3–12 months seizure-free), and safety (no swimming alone, heights, bathing).

Why not the others

  • (A) Begin phenytoin with a loading dose — Phenytoin has many drug interactions and adverse effects and is not a preferred first-line agent; loading is for status epilepticus.
  • (B) Begin levetiracetam today — Starting medication immediately is reasonable for patients with risk factors but is not required after a first unprovoked seizure with normal evaluation; decisions should follow EEG and MRI.
  • (C) Admit for continuous video EEG monitoring — He is at baseline and does not need inpatient monitoring.
  • (D) Lumbar puncture — LP is indicated for fever, meningismus, immunosuppression or persistent altered mental status; he has none.
🎯 Educational objective

After a first unprovoked seizure with normal examination and imaging, obtain EEG and MRI, counsel on driving, and individualize the decision to start antiseizure medication based on recurrence risk.

OB-001.stem_html:
A 31-year-old woman comes for a routine health visit. Her last cervical cytology (Pap test) was 3 years ago at age 28 and was normal; she has never had an abnormal result. She received the HPV vaccine series as a teenager. She has one male partner and has never been diagnosed with HIV infection or another immunocompromising condition.

Examination, including pelvic examination, is normal.
OB-001.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate cervical cancer screening?

choices.C: High-risk HPV testing now, and every 5 years if negative
choices.D: No screening because she completed HPV vaccination
choices.E: Cervical cytology now and every year

OB-001.explain_html:
Correct answer: C Cervical cancer screening

At 30–65 years, average-risk women can be screened with any of three strategies (USPSTF):

Age Strategy
21–29 Cytology every 3 years
30–65 High-risk HPV (hrHPV) testing alone every 5 years, or cotesting (hrHPV + cytology) every 5 years, or cytology alone every 3 years
>65 Stop if adequate negative prior screening and no CIN2+ in the past 25 years

She is due now (3 years since normal cytology). Primary hrHPV testing finds more precancer than cytology and allows a 5-year interval after a negative result. Many guidelines (ACS, ACOG) now prefer it, and self-collected HPV samples are an accepted option.

Why not the others

  • (A) Cytology now and every 10 years — Cytology alone needs a 3-year interval.
  • (B) Colposcopy — Colposcopy is for abnormal screening results, not routine screening.
  • (D) No screening because she completed HPV vaccination — Vaccination does not cover all oncogenic HPV types; vaccinated women follow the same screening schedule.
  • (E) Cervical cytology now and every year — Annual screening finds no more cancers than 3- or 5-year intervals, and it causes more false positives and unnecessary procedures.
🎓 ABIM pearl

Women with HIV, organ transplant, DES exposure or prior CIN2+ need more frequent screening, and screening continues past 65 for them.

🎯 Educational objective

For average-risk women aged 30–65, screen with primary high-risk HPV testing every 5 years (or cotesting every 5 years, or cytology every 3 years).

OB-002.stem_html:
A 29-year-old woman comes to the office to discuss contraception. She wants to avoid pregnancy for at least 3–4 years. She has migraine with aura — about twice a month she sees zigzag lines for 20 minutes before the headache begins. She does not smoke. She has no history of venous thromboembolism or hypertension. She asks about "the pill" because a friend uses it.

Blood pressure is 116/72 mm Hg. BMI is 24 kg/m². Examination is normal. Urine pregnancy test is negative.
OB-002.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate contraceptive method?

choices.A: Combined oral contraceptive taken continuously without placebo week
choices.C: Combined oral contraceptive with 20 µg ethinyl estradiol

OB-002.explain_html:
Correct answer: B Contraception in migraine with aura

Migraine with aura is a US MEC category 4 condition for combined (estrogen-containing) hormonal contraception — an unacceptable health risk at any age. Estrogen and migraine with aura each raise the risk of ischemic stroke, and together the risk multiplies.

Progestin-only and nonhormonal methods are safe (category 1–2). For someone wanting reliable long-term contraception, a long-acting reversible contraceptive (LARC) — levonorgestrel IUD, copper IUD or etonogestrel implant — is the most effective choice (failure <1% per year). The levonorgestrel IUD also reduces menstrual bleeding and cramping.

Estrogen-containing methods are category 4 with:
Migraine with aura
Age ≥35 and smoking ≥15 cigarettes/day
Current or past VTE (not on anticoagulation), known thrombophilia
BP ≥160/100, vascular disease, complicated valvular disease
Breast cancer (current), decompensated cirrhosis, hepatocellular tumors
<21 days postpartum

Why not the others

  • (A) Combined oral contraceptive taken continuously without placebo week — Continuous use of a combined pill still exposes her to estrogen; it is contraindicated with aura.
  • (C) Combined oral contraceptive with 20 µg ethinyl estradiol — Any estrogen dose, even 20 µg, is contraindicated with migraine with aura because of stroke risk.
  • (D) Contraceptive vaginal ring (etonogestrel–ethinyl estradiol) — The vaginal ring contains ethinyl estradiol and carries the same contraindication.
  • (E) Transdermal contraceptive patch — The patch delivers estrogen (with higher overall exposure than many pills) — also contraindicated.
🎓 ABIM pearl

Migraine without aura is category 2 for combined methods if age <35 (category 3 if ≥35 when starting). The single most important question in a migraine patient wanting the pill: "Do you get an aura?"

🎯 Educational objective

Estrogen-containing contraception is contraindicated in migraine with aura; offer a progestin-only or nonhormonal method, preferably a long-acting reversible contraceptive.

OB-003.stem_html:
A 31-year-old woman at 35 weeks' gestation in her first pregnancy is evaluated in the obstetric triage unit for 1 day of headache and blurred vision. Her blood pressure was normal at prenatal visits through 28 weeks.

On physical examination, blood pressure is 168/112 mm Hg (confirmed 15 minutes later at 164/110 mm Hg), and pulse rate is 96/min. She has right upper quadrant tenderness and brisk reflexes. Fetal heart tones are reassuring.

Platelet count92,000/µL
AST142 U/L
ALT168 U/L
Creatinine1.1 mg/dL
Urine protein-to-creatinine ratio1.8 g/g
OB-003.lead: In addition to intravenous labetalol or hydralazine, which of the following is the most appropriate management?

choices.A: Intravenous magnesium sulfate and continue the pregnancy until 37 weeks
choices.B: Intravenous magnesium sulfate and plan delivery after maternal stabilization
choices.C: Oral nifedipine and outpatient follow-up in 1 week

OB-003.explain_html:
Correct answer: B Preeclampsia with severe features

New hypertension after 20 weeks with proteinuria and severe features = preeclampsia with severe features:

  • BP ≥160/110 mm Hg on two readings
  • New headache or visual disturbance
  • RUQ/epigastric pain, aminotransferases ≥2× normal
  • Platelets <100,000/µL
  • Creatinine >1.1 mg/dL or doubling; pulmonary edema

Her low platelets and liver injury also suggest evolving HELLP syndrome.

Management:

  1. Treat severe hypertension within 30–60 minutes — IV labetalol, IV hydralazine or immediate-release oral nifedipine (target <160/110 mm Hg).
  2. IV magnesium sulfate for seizure (eclampsia) prophylaxis, continued 24 hours postpartum. Watch for toxicity (loss of reflexes → respiratory depression; antidote calcium gluconate).
  3. Delivery — the only cure. With severe features at ≥34 weeks, deliver after stabilization. Before 34 weeks, expectant management with steroids for fetal lung maturity may be considered in stable patients at specialized centers.

Long-term: preeclampsia doubles lifetime cardiovascular risk — counts as an ASCVD risk enhancer.

Why not the others

  • (A) Intravenous magnesium sulfate and continue the pregnancy until 37 weeks — At ≥34 weeks with severe features, continuing the pregnancy increases the risk of eclampsia, stroke, placental abruption and HELLP complications.
  • (C) Oral nifedipine and outpatient follow-up in 1 week — Severe preeclampsia requires inpatient care, magnesium and delivery planning.
  • (D) Intravenous furosemide — Patients with preeclampsia are intravascularly depleted; diuretics are used only for pulmonary edema.
  • (E) Intravenous phenytoin for seizure prophylaxis — Magnesium is superior to phenytoin for preventing and treating eclampsia.
🎯 Educational objective

Treat preeclampsia with severe features at 34 weeks or later with antihypertensives, magnesium sulfate seizure prophylaxis and delivery after maternal stabilization.

OB-004.stem_html:
A 33-year-old woman with chronic hypertension tells you she and her partner plan to start trying to conceive in the next few months. She takes lisinopril, 20 mg/d, and her blood pressure is well controlled. She does not use contraception reliably. She has no kidney disease or diabetes.

On physical examination, blood pressure is 126/80 mm Hg. BMI is 28.

Creatinine0.7 mg/dL
Urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio8 mg/g
OB-004.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

choices.B: Continue lisinopril until pregnancy is confirmed, then stop it
choices.D: Switch lisinopril to labetalol or extended-release nifedipine now
choices.E: Switch lisinopril to hydrochlorothiazide and spironolactone

OB-004.explain_html:
Correct answer: D Chronic hypertension and pregnancy planning

ACE inhibitors, ARBs and direct renin inhibitors are teratogenic — second- and third-trimester exposure causes fetal renal dysgenesis, oligohydramnios, skull hypoplasia, growth restriction and death. First-trimester risk is less clear. Because she is planning pregnancy and not using reliable contraception, switch now.

Preferred antihypertensives in pregnancy:

  • Labetalol
  • Extended-release nifedipine
  • Methyldopa (older, less well tolerated)

In the CHAP trial, treating mild chronic hypertension in pregnancy to <140/90 mm Hg reduced preeclampsia with severe features, preterm birth and other adverse outcomes, so do not stop treatment. She should also start low-dose aspirin (81 mg/d) from 12–28 weeks to reduce preeclampsia risk (chronic hypertension is a high-risk factor) and take folic acid.

Why not the others

  • (A) Stop all antihypertensive medications — Stopping treatment leads to uncontrolled hypertension; CHAP showed benefit from treating chronic hypertension in pregnancy.
  • (B) Continue lisinopril until pregnancy is confirmed, then stop it — Many pregnancies are recognized late; switching before conception avoids fetal exposure and the risks of an abrupt change.
  • (C) Switch lisinopril to losartan — ARBs carry the same fetal risks as ACE inhibitors.
  • (E) Switch lisinopril to hydrochlorothiazide and spironolactone — Spironolactone has antiandrogenic effects on a male fetus, and diuretics are not first-line in pregnancy.
🎯 Educational objective

Switch ACE inhibitors or ARBs to labetalol or extended-release nifedipine in women with hypertension who are planning pregnancy.

OB-005.stem_html: A 32-year-old woman is evaluated at her primary care visit 8 weeks after delivering a healthy baby. Her pregnancy was complicated by gestational diabetes diagnosed at 26 weeks and treated with diet and insulin; she stopped insulin after delivery. She is breastfeeding. Her BMI is 30.
OB-005.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate recommendation?

choices.B: Start metformin for diabetes prevention without testing
choices.C: No further testing because gestational diabetes resolves after delivery
choices.E: 75-g oral glucose tolerance test now, then diabetes screening every 1–3 years for life

OB-005.explain_html:
Correct answer: E Gestational diabetes — postpartum follow-up

Gestational diabetes (GDM) usually resolves after delivery but signals a high lifetime risk of type 2 diabetes — about 50–70% within 10–20 years (about a 10-fold higher risk than women without GDM). GDM is also a cardiovascular risk enhancer.

The ADA and ACOG recommend:

  • A 75-g 2-hour oral glucose tolerance test at 4–12 weeks postpartum, using nonpregnant criteria. The OGTT is preferred over A1c because A1c is unreliable early postpartum (blood loss, pregnancy-related red cell turnover).
  • If normal → screen every 1–3 years for life (A1c, fasting glucose or OGTT).
  • Prediabetes → intensive lifestyle intervention and/or metformin (DPP: both reduced progression in women with prior GDM).

Breastfeeding lowers the risk of type 2 diabetes; encourage it.

Why not the others

  • (A) Fasting glucose in 5 years — Waiting 5 years misses early diabetes and prediabetes, when prevention works.
  • (B) Start metformin for diabetes prevention without testing — Metformin is offered for prediabetes, but testing should come first.
  • (C) No further testing because gestational diabetes resolves after delivery — GDM confers a lifelong high risk of type 2 diabetes; follow-up testing is essential.
  • (D) Hemoglobin A1c now — A1c is less reliable in the early postpartum period and less sensitive than the OGTT in this setting.
🎯 Educational objective

Screen women with gestational diabetes with a 75-g OGTT at 4–12 weeks postpartum and then every 1–3 years for life.

OB-006.stem_html:
A 24-year-old woman is evaluated for irregular periods since menarche, now occurring every 2–4 months, and increased hair on her chin and abdomen. She has gained weight over 3 years. She is not sexually active.

On physical examination, BMI is 32. There is terminal hair on the upper lip, chin and lower abdomen, acne on the jaw line, and acanthosis nigricans on the neck. There is no clitoromegaly, deepening of the voice or rapid virilization.

Urine pregnancy testnegative
TSHnormal
Prolactinnormal
Total testosterone68 ng/dL (mildly elevated)
17-hydroxyprogesterone (morningfollicular phase), normal
DHEA-Snormal
OB-006.lead: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
OB-006.explain_html:
Correct answer: E Secondary amenorrhea — PCOS

Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) is the most common endocrine disorder in reproductive-age women. Rotterdam criteria — 2 of 3:

  1. Oligo- or anovulation (irregular cycles) ✔
  2. Clinical or biochemical hyperandrogenism (hirsutism, acne; elevated testosterone) ✔
  3. Polycystic ovarian morphology on ultrasound (or high AMH in adults)

…after excluding other causes: pregnancy, thyroid disease, hyperprolactinemia, nonclassic CAH (normal 17-OH-progesterone), Cushing syndrome and androgen-secreting tumors (rapid virilization, testosterone >150–200 ng/dL, DHEA-S >700 µg/dL).

PCOS is a metabolic disorder: insulin resistance (acanthosis), obesity, type 2 diabetes, dyslipidemia, MASLD, sleep apnea and endometrial hyperplasia/cancer (unopposed estrogen). Screen with an OGTT or A1c and lipids.

Treatment: lifestyle and weight loss; combined oral contraceptives (cycle control, endometrial protection, hirsutism); spironolactone for hirsutism (with contraception); metformin for metabolic risk; letrozole for ovulation induction.

Why not the others

  • (A) Nonclassic congenital adrenal hyperplasia — Nonclassic CAH (21-hydroxylase deficiency) is excluded by a normal morning 17-hydroxyprogesterone.
  • (B) Cushing syndrome — Cushing syndrome causes proximal myopathy, wide violaceous striae, easy bruising and hypertension.
  • (C) Androgen-secreting ovarian tumor — Ovarian tumors cause rapid virilization (clitoromegaly, voice deepening) with very high testosterone.
  • (D) Functional hypothalamic amenorrhea — Hypothalamic amenorrhea occurs with low weight, stress or excessive exercise and low estrogen, without hyperandrogenism.
🎯 Educational objective

Diagnose PCOS by Rotterdam criteria (two of oligo-anovulation, hyperandrogenism and polycystic ovaries) after excluding pregnancy, thyroid disease, hyperprolactinemia, nonclassic CAH and androgen-secreting tumors.

OB-007.stem_html:
A 51-year-old woman is evaluated for 8 months of frequent, severe hot flashes and night sweats that wake her several times a night and interfere with work. Her last menstrual period was 13 months ago. She has an intact uterus. She has no history of breast cancer, VTE, stroke, coronary disease or liver disease. She does not smoke. Her mother had osteoporosis.

On physical examination, blood pressure is 122/76 mm Hg. BMI is 25. Mammography 6 months ago was normal. Her 10-year ASCVD risk is 2%.
OB-007.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?

choices.A: Gabapentin, because hormone therapy is contraindicated after age 50

OB-007.explain_html:
Correct answer: C Menopausal hormone therapy

Menopausal hormone therapy (MHT) is the most effective treatment for vasomotor symptoms. For healthy women <60 years or within 10 years of menopause, without contraindications, benefits outweigh risks (NAMS/Menopause Society 2022) — the "timing hypothesis" from re-analysis of the WHI.

She has an intact uterus, so estrogen must be combined with a progestogen (or use conjugated estrogens/bazedoxifene) to prevent endometrial hyperplasia and cancer. Transdermal estrogen has a lower VTE and stroke risk than oral estrogen. MHT also prevents bone loss.

MHT contraindications
Breast or endometrial cancer (estrogen-sensitive)
Unexplained vaginal bleeding
VTE, stroke, CAD/MI
Active liver disease
High risk of these (e.g., known thrombophilia)

Nonhormonal options for women who cannot or will not take MHT: fezolinetant (neurokinin-3 receptor antagonist), SSRIs/SNRIs (paroxetine 7.5 mg is FDA-approved), gabapentin, oxybutynin, CBT.

Why not the others

  • (A) Gabapentin, because hormone therapy is contraindicated after age 50 — MHT is not contraindicated by age 50; it is appropriate for healthy women younger than 60 or within 10 years of menopause.
  • (B) Black cohosh — Black cohosh is no better than placebo and has been associated with liver injury.
  • (D) Estrogen alone (unopposed) — Unopposed estrogen in a woman with a uterus causes endometrial hyperplasia and cancer.
  • (E) Vaginal estrogen cream alone — Low-dose vaginal estrogen treats genitourinary syndrome of menopause, not systemic vasomotor symptoms.
🎯 Educational objective

For healthy women younger than 60 or within 10 years of menopause with bothersome vasomotor symptoms, offer menopausal hormone therapy, adding a progestogen if the uterus is intact.

OB-008.stem_html:
A 26-year-old woman calls the clinic because a condom broke during intercourse 4 days ago (about 96 hours). Her last menstrual period began 13 days ago, and her cycles are regular. She wants to avoid pregnancy and is interested in long-term contraception afterward. She has no medical problems. Her BMI is 34.

A urine pregnancy test is negative.
OB-008.lead: Which of the following is the most effective emergency contraception for her?

choices.B: No treatment because more than 72 hours have passed

OB-008.explain_html:
Correct answer: A Emergency contraception

The copper IUD is the most effective emergency contraceptive — >99% effective when inserted within 5 days (120 hours) of unprotected intercourse, regardless of BMI — and it then provides up to 10–12 years of highly effective contraception, which she wants. Levonorgestrel 52-mg IUDs are also effective as emergency contraception (noninferior in a 2021 trial).

Method Window Notes
Copper IUD ≤5 days Most effective; not affected by weight
Ulipristal 30 mg (oral) ≤5 days More effective than levonorgestrel, especially days 3–5 and BMI >30; delay hormonal contraception 5 days
Levonorgestrel 1.5 mg ≤3 days (some effect to 5) Less effective if BMI >30; OTC

She is near ovulation (cycle day 13), at BMI 34, and at day 4 — the setting where oral levonorgestrel works worst. If she declines an IUD, ulipristal is the best oral option.

Why not the others

  • (B) No treatment because more than 72 hours have passed — Effective emergency contraception options exist up to 5 days after intercourse.
  • (C) Mifepristone — Mifepristone is not used for emergency contraception in the United States.
  • (D) Combined oral contraceptive pills (Yuzpe method) — The Yuzpe method is less effective and causes more nausea than dedicated emergency contraceptives.
  • (E) Levonorgestrel 1.5 mg orally — Levonorgestrel is less effective beyond 72 hours and in women with BMI above 30.
🎯 Educational objective

The copper IUD, inserted within 5 days of unprotected intercourse, is the most effective emergency contraceptive and is not affected by body weight.

ON-001.stem_html:
A 42-year-old woman comes for a routine health visit. She feels well and has no breast symptoms. She has never had a mammogram. Menarche was at age 13 and she had her first child at 29. She has no history of chest radiation or breast biopsy. Her maternal aunt had breast cancer at age 68; no other relatives have had breast, ovarian, pancreatic or prostate cancer.

Breast examination is normal.
ON-001.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate breast cancer screening recommendation?

choices.C: Genetic testing for BRCA1 and BRCA2
choices.E: Clinical breast examination alone every year

ON-001.explain_html:
Correct answer: B Breast cancer screening

She is at average risk: no personal history of breast cancer or chest radiation, no known high-risk mutation, and only a second-degree relative diagnosed after menopause.

The USPSTF (2024) recommends biennial screening mammography for all women aged 40–74. Starting at 40 rather than 50 was adopted because breast cancer rates in women in their 40s are rising and screening in this decade prevents deaths — with the most benefit for Black women, who have higher breast cancer mortality.

Risk group Screening
Average risk Mammography every 2 years, ages 40–74 (many groups also accept annual)
Lifetime risk ≥20%, BRCA carrier, chest radiation age 10–30 Annual mammography plus annual MRI, often starting at 25–30
Dense breasts Mammography; evidence for supplemental imaging is insufficient

Why not the others

  • (A) Annual breast MRI starting now — Breast MRI is for high-risk women (lifetime risk ≥20%, known mutation, chest radiation), not average-risk screening.
  • (C) Genetic testing for BRCA1 and BRCA2 — A single second-degree relative with postmenopausal breast cancer does not meet criteria for genetic testing.
  • (D) Begin mammography at age 50 — Starting at 50 is the older (2016) recommendation; screening now begins at 40.
  • (E) Clinical breast examination alone every year — Clinical breast examination alone is not a substitute for mammography.
🎓 ABIM pearl

Use a familial risk tool (for example, the USPSTF-recommended BRCA risk tools) when a family history includes breast cancer before 50, ovarian cancer, male breast cancer, multiple relatives, or Ashkenazi Jewish ancestry.

🎯 Educational objective

Average-risk women should have screening mammography every 2 years from age 40 to 74.

ON-002.stem_html:
A 58-year-old man comes for a routine health visit. He smoked 1 pack of cigarettes per day from age 24 to age 49 (25 pack-years) and quit 9 years ago. He feels well, has no cough, hemoptysis or weight loss, and is active. He has hypertension controlled with lisinopril.

Examination is normal.
ON-002.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate lung cancer screening recommendation?

choices.A: Annual low-dose CT of the chest
choices.B: No screening because he quit smoking more than 5 years ago
choices.D: A single low-dose CT of the chest now

ON-002.explain_html:
Correct answer: A Lung cancer screening

The USPSTF (2021) recommends annual low-dose CT (LDCT) for adults who:

  • are 50–80 years old,
  • have ≥20 pack-years of smoking, and
  • currently smoke or quit within the past 15 years.

He meets all three (58 years, 25 pack-years, quit 9 years ago). LDCT screening reduced lung cancer mortality by 20% in NLST and about 24% in NELSON. Screening stops when the person has not smoked for 15 years, develops a condition that limits life expectancy, or would not want or be fit for curative surgery.

Start with shared decision-making about benefits, false positives, overdiagnosis and radiation.

Why not the others

  • (B) No screening because he quit smoking more than 5 years ago — The cutoff is 15 years since quitting, not 5.
  • (C) Annual chest radiography — Chest radiography does not reduce lung cancer mortality and is not a screening test.
  • (D) A single low-dose CT of the chest now — Screening is annual; a single scan gives much less benefit.
  • (E) Sputum cytology every year — Sputum cytology misses most early cancers and is not recommended.
🧠 Mnemonic

"50-20-15" — age 50–80, 20 pack-years, quit within 15 years.

🎓 ABIM pearl

The American Cancer Society (2023) no longer uses the years-since-quitting limit — it recommends screening former smokers with ≥20 pack-years regardless of quit date. Payers usually follow USPSTF.

🎯 Educational objective

Screen adults aged 50–80 with ≥20 pack-years who smoke or quit within 15 years with annual low-dose CT.

ON-003.stem_html:
A 68-year-old man with metastatic prostate cancer to bone comes to the emergency department with 2 weeks of worsening mid-back pain that is worse lying down and wakes him at night. Since yesterday his legs feel heavy and he stumbled twice. He has not had urinary retention or incontinence.

Vital signs are normal. There is tenderness over the T9–T10 spinous processes. Strength is 4/5 in hip flexors and knee extensors bilaterally. Pinprick sensation is reduced below the umbilicus. Knee reflexes are brisk and plantar responses are extensor.
ON-003.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.A: Intravenous dexamethasone and emergency MRI of the entire spine
choices.C: Plain radiographs of the thoracic spine
choices.D: Oral oxycodone and outpatient MRI within 1 week

ON-003.explain_html:
Correct answer: A Malignant spinal cord compression

New back pain in a patient with cancer, worse lying down, plus leg weakness, a sensory level (T10 = umbilicus) and upper motor neuron signs = metastatic epidural spinal cord compression — an oncologic emergency. Function at the time of treatment predicts function afterward: patients who walk into treatment usually keep walking.

Steps, without delay:

  1. Dexamethasone IV (commonly 10 mg load, then 4 mg every 6 hours) to reduce vasogenic edema — give it as soon as the diagnosis is suspected in a patient with deficits.
  2. Emergency MRI of the entire spine with and without contrast — metastases are often at more than one level.
  3. Definitive therapy within hours: surgical decompression + radiation for selected patients (single-level compression, instability, good prognosis), otherwise radiation therapy.

Why not the others

  • (B) Lumbar puncture — Lumbar puncture does not diagnose cord compression and can worsen herniation of a compressed cord.
  • (C) Plain radiographs of the thoracic spine — Radiographs miss epidural disease and delay MRI.
  • (D) Oral oxycodone and outpatient MRI within 1 week — Neurologic deficits make this an emergency; waiting a week risks permanent paralysis.
  • (E) Whole-body bone scan — A bone scan shows bone metastases but not the epidural space or cord.
🧠 Mnemonic

Cancers that most often compress the cord — "Lung, Breast, Prostate" (each ~15%–20%), then renal cell, lymphoma and myeloma.

🎓 ABIM pearl

Thoracic spine is the most common level (~60%). Back pain that worsens when lying flat or with Valsalva in a cancer patient deserves an MRI even before deficits appear.

🎯 Educational objective

Suspected malignant spinal cord compression with neurologic deficits requires immediate dexamethasone, emergency whole-spine MRI and urgent radiation or surgery.

ON-004.stem_html:
A 34-year-old man with newly diagnosed Burkitt lymphoma and bulky abdominal disease received his first cycle of chemotherapy 36 hours ago. He was given IV fluids and allopurinol beforehand. He now reports muscle cramps and has had low urine output for 6 hours.

On physical examination, blood pressure is 142/88 mm Hg and pulse rate is 96/min. Chvostek sign is positive.

Potassium6.1 mEq/L
Phosphorus8.4 mg/dL
Calcium6.8 mg/dL
Uric acid13.6 mg/dL
Creatinine2.6 mg/dL (0.9 mg/dL before chemotherapy)
ECGpeaked T waves; QRS 100 ms
G6PD activitynormal
ON-004.lead: In addition to treating hyperkalemia, which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?

choices.B: Intravenous calcium gluconate to correct the calcium to normal
choices.D: Sodium bicarbonate infusion to alkalinize the urine
choices.E: Stop IV fluids to avoid volume overload

ON-004.explain_html:
Correct answer: A Tumor lysis syndrome

Clinical tumor lysis syndrome (TLS): after chemotherapy for a highly proliferative, bulky tumor (Burkitt, ALL, AML with high WBC), cell breakdown releases potassium, phosphate and nucleic acids (→ uric acid). Phosphate binds calcium → hypocalcemia. Uric acid and calcium phosphate crystals cause AKI.

Rasburicase (recombinant urate oxidase) converts uric acid to soluble allantoin and lowers uric acid within hours. Allopurinol only prevents new uric acid formation and does nothing for uric acid that is already there. Check G6PD first — rasburicase causes hemolysis and methemoglobinemia in G6PD deficiency.

Other measures: aggressive IV fluids (target urine output 80–100 mL/m²/h), treat hyperkalemia, phosphate binders, and early dialysis for refractory hyperkalemia, volume overload or worsening AKI.

Why not the others

  • (B) Intravenous calcium gluconate to correct the calcium to normal — Treat hypocalcemia only if symptomatic (tetany, arrhythmia) — giving calcium with a high phosphate promotes calcium phosphate precipitation in the kidneys and tissues.
  • (C) Increase the allopurinol dose — Allopurinol blocks new uric acid production but does not lower existing levels quickly; it also increases xanthine, which can crystallize.
  • (D) Sodium bicarbonate infusion to alkalinize the urine — Urine alkalinization is no longer recommended — it promotes calcium phosphate and xanthine crystal deposition.
  • (E) Stop IV fluids to avoid volume overload — IV fluids are the cornerstone of TLS treatment; stop only if overload develops despite diuretics, in which case dialysis is needed.
🧠 Mnemonic

TLS labs — "three highs and a low": high K⁺, phosphate, uric acid, low calcium.

🎯 Educational objective

Treat established tumor lysis syndrome with hyperuricemia using rasburicase (after excluding G6PD deficiency), IV fluids and electrolyte management.

ON-005.stem_html:
A 58-year-old man asks whether he should have a "PSA test". He feels well and has no urinary symptoms. His father was diagnosed with prostate cancer at age 78. He is not of African descent and has no known BRCA mutation. He has never had a PSA test.

Examination is normal.
ON-005.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate response?

choices.A: Discuss the benefits and harms of PSA screening and decide together
choices.B: Order a PSA and a digital rectal examination every year
choices.C: Recommend against screening because the harms outweigh the benefits at any age
choices.D: Order an MRI of the prostate
choices.E: Screening is not appropriate until age 70

ON-005.explain_html:
Correct answer: A Prostate cancer screening

The USPSTF recommends individual decision-making about PSA screening for men aged 55–69 years (Grade C), and against screening men ≥70 (Grade D).

Benefit: screening prevents about 1 prostate cancer death per 1,000 men screened over 13 years and reduces metastatic disease. Harms: false positives, biopsy complications (pain, infection, bleeding), and overdiagnosis of indolent cancers → treatment with risks of erectile dysfunction and urinary incontinence.

Shared decision-making is the recommended approach — his values decide. Men at higher risk (Black men, BRCA2 carriers, father or brother diagnosed before 65) may benefit more and start earlier (some guidelines: age 40–45). His father was diagnosed at 78, which raises his risk only slightly.

A DRE adds little and is not recommended as a screening test by the USPSTF. If the PSA is elevated, MRI before biopsy reduces unnecessary biopsies.

Why not the others

  • (B) Order a PSA and a digital rectal examination every year — Screening should follow an informed discussion; routine yearly PSA plus DRE without discussion is not recommended, and DRE is not a recommended screening test.
  • (C) Recommend against screening because the harms outweigh the benefits at any age — For men 55–69, screening is a choice, not a recommendation against; the recommendation against applies at ≥70.
  • (D) Order an MRI of the prostate — MRI is used after an abnormal PSA, not as an initial screening test.
  • (E) Screening is not appropriate until age 70 — The USPSTF recommends against screening at 70 and older, not starting there.
🎯 Educational objective

For men aged 55 to 69 years, PSA-based prostate cancer screening is an individual decision made after discussing benefits and harms.

ON-006.stem_html: A 38-year-old woman has a right colectomy for adenocarcinoma of the ascending colon. Immunohistochemistry of the tumor shows loss of MLH1 and PMS2 expression; the tumor is microsatellite instability–high and has no BRAF V600E mutation, and MLH1 promoter is not hypermethylated. Her mother had endometrial cancer at age 46 and her maternal uncle had colon cancer at age 50.
ON-006.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

choices.A: Annual CA-125 and transvaginal ultrasonography only
choices.B: Germline genetic testing for Lynch syndrome
choices.E: No further evaluation because sporadic MSI-high tumors are common

ON-006.explain_html:
Correct answer: B Lynch syndrome

All colorectal and endometrial cancers should be tested for mismatch repair (MMR) deficiency (IHC or MSI). Loss of MLH1/PMS2 can be sporadic (MLH1 promoter hypermethylation, often with BRAF V600E) or germline.

Here: MSI-high, MLH1 loss, no BRAF mutation, no promoter hypermethylation, young age and a family history of colon and endometrial cancer → high probability of Lynch syndrome (autosomal dominant germline mutation in MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, PMS2 or EPCAM). Next step: germline testing (with genetic counseling).

If confirmed:

  • Colonoscopy every 1–2 years (start at 20–25 for MLH1/MSH2).
  • Endometrial and ovarian cancer risk reduction: hysterectomy and bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy after childbearing (~age 40); daily aspirin reduces colorectal cancer risk (CAPP2).
  • Cascade testing of first-degree relatives.

MSI-high/MMR-deficient tumors also respond to immune checkpoint inhibitors.

Why not the others

  • (A) Annual CA-125 and transvaginal ultrasonography only — Gynecologic screening alone is insufficient and of uncertain benefit; diagnosis should be confirmed first, and surgery is the main risk reduction.
  • (C) Total proctocolectomy for her siblings — Relatives need germline testing first; prophylactic colectomy is not standard for Lynch syndrome.
  • (D) Colonoscopy every 10 years — Lynch syndrome requires colonoscopy every 1–2 years, not 10.
  • (E) No further evaluation because sporadic MSI-high tumors are common — Sporadic MSI-high tumors are usually explained by MLH1 hypermethylation or BRAF mutation, which are absent here.
🧠 Mnemonic

Lynch cancers — "CEO" + more: Colon, Endometrium, Ovary, plus stomach, small bowel, urinary tract (ureter/renal pelvis), biliary, brain, skin (sebaceous).

🎯 Educational objective

Refer patients with MMR-deficient colorectal cancer without BRAF mutation or MLH1 promoter hypermethylation for germline testing for Lynch syndrome.

ON-007.stem_html:
A 63-year-old postmenopausal woman is starting anastrozole after lumpectomy and radiation for a stage I, estrogen receptor–positive, HER2-negative breast cancer. She has no history of fractures. She takes no other medications.

Examination is normal.
ON-007.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate baseline evaluation?

choices.C: Annual CT of the chest, abdomen and pelvis

ON-007.explain_html:
Correct answer: E Aromatase inhibitor–associated bone loss

Aromatase inhibitors (anastrozole, letrozole, exemestane) block peripheral conversion of androgens to estrogen. In postmenopausal women, this drops estrogen to very low levels and accelerates bone loss (2–3% per year) and fracture risk. They also cause arthralgias and hypercholesterolemia.

Obtain a baseline DXA scan before starting, and repeat every 1–2 years. Give calcium, vitamin D and weight-bearing exercise. Start bisphosphonates (or denosumab) for osteoporosis or high fracture risk; adjuvant bisphosphonates also reduce breast cancer recurrence in bone in postmenopausal women.

Tamoxifen (SERM) Aromatase inhibitor
Use Pre- and postmenopausal Postmenopausal (or premenopausal + ovarian suppression)
Bone Protects (postmenopausal) Loss, fractures
Uterus Endometrial cancer, polyps No effect
Clots VTE, stroke Less
Joints — Arthralgias

Why not the others

  • (A) Echocardiogram — Echocardiography is needed before trastuzumab or anthracyclines, not aromatase inhibitors.
  • (B) Endometrial biopsy — Endometrial evaluation is for tamoxifen users with abnormal bleeding; aromatase inhibitors do not stimulate the endometrium.
  • (C) Annual CT of the chest, abdomen and pelvis — Routine imaging after curative-intent treatment of early breast cancer does not improve survival; surveillance is history, examination and annual mammography.
  • (D) Serum CA 15-3 every 3 months — Tumor markers are not recommended for surveillance of early-stage breast cancer.
🎯 Educational objective

Obtain a baseline DXA scan in women starting an aromatase inhibitor because of accelerated bone loss and fracture risk.

ON-008.stem_html:
A 66-year-old man with metastatic melanoma began ipilimumab plus nivolumab 6 weeks ago. He now has 4 days of 8 watery stools daily above his baseline, abdominal cramping and blood in the stool.

On physical examination, temperature is 37.8 °C (100.0 °F), blood pressure is 112/70 mm Hg, and pulse rate is 104/min. The abdomen is diffusely tender without rebound.

Leukocyte count11,800/µL
C-reactive protein82 mg/L
Stool C. difficile PCR and enteric pathogen panelnegative
CT of the abdomendiffuse colonic wall thickening without perforation
ON-008.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?

choices.C: Hold immunotherapy and start intravenous methylprednisolone, 1–2 mg/kg/d

ON-008.explain_html:
Correct answer: C Immune checkpoint inhibitor colitis

Immune checkpoint inhibitors (anti–CTLA-4 ipilimumab, anti–PD-1 nivolumab/pembrolizumab, anti–PD-L1) remove the brakes on T cells and can cause immune-related adverse events (irAEs) in any organ — colitis, hepatitis, pneumonitis, endocrinopathies, dermatitis, myocarditis. Combination CTLA-4 + PD-1 therapy has the highest risk.

He has grade 3 colitis (≥7 stools/day over baseline, with systemic symptoms). Infection is excluded. Management:

  • Hold the checkpoint inhibitor.
  • High-dose glucocorticoids — IV methylprednisolone 1–2 mg/kg/d, then a slow taper over 4–6 weeks.
  • If no response in 48–72 hours: infliximab or vedolizumab.
  • Endoscopy helps grade severity.
Grade Stools over baseline Action
1 <4 Continue ICI; antidiarrheals, fluids
2 4–6 Hold; oral prednisone 1 mg/kg
3–4 ≥7, severe/life-threatening Hold (stop CTLA-4); IV steroids; infliximab/vedolizumab if refractory

Why not the others

  • (A) Emergency colectomy — Surgery is for perforation or toxic megacolon; he has neither.
  • (B) Continue immunotherapy and give loperamide — Continuing immunotherapy with antidiarrheals is appropriate only for grade 1 diarrhea; loperamide can mask worsening colitis.
  • (D) Oral budesonide and continue immunotherapy — Budesonide is not adequate for grade 3 colitis, and immunotherapy must be held.
  • (E) Oral vancomycin — C. difficile testing is negative; this is immune-mediated colitis.
🎯 Educational objective

Treat grade 3 or higher immune checkpoint inhibitor colitis by holding immunotherapy and giving high-dose intravenous glucocorticoids, adding infliximab or vedolizumab if refractory.
