ON-009.stem_html:
A 61-year-old man with a 50 pack-year smoking history is evaluated for 3 weeks of progressive facial swelling, a sense of fullness in his head that worsens when he bends forward, and dyspnea. He has no stridor, confusion or syncope.

On physical examination, blood pressure is 138/84 mm Hg, pulse rate is 92/min, and respiration rate is 18/min. Oxygen saturation is 95% breathing ambient air. There is facial and neck swelling, plethora and dilated veins over the upper chest.

CT of the chest with contrast shows a 6-cm right paratracheal mass compressing the superior vena cava, with mediastinal lymphadenopathy. There is no tissue diagnosis.
ON-009.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.B: Tissue diagnosis by bronchoscopy, EBUS or mediastinoscopy
choices.C: Empiric chemotherapy for small cell lung cancer

ON-009.explain_html:
Correct answer: B Superior vena cava syndrome

Superior vena cava (SVC) syndrome today is usually caused by malignancy (non–small cell and small cell lung cancer, lymphoma) and increasingly by intravascular devices (catheters, pacemaker leads).

Most patients are not in immediate danger; collateral veins develop over weeks. Emergencies are stridor (laryngeal edema or airway compression), cerebral edema (confusion, coma) or hemodynamic compromise — these need urgent endovascular stenting (fastest relief) ± radiation.

He has no emergency features, so the priority is a tissue diagnosis before treatment: histology determines therapy. Small cell lung cancer and lymphoma respond rapidly to chemotherapy; NSCLC may need stenting and chemoradiation. Empiric radiation or steroids can obscure the diagnosis (especially lymphoma).

Supportive measures: elevate the head of the bed; steroids only for lymphoma, thymoma or radiation-related edema.

Why not the others

  • (A) Emergency radiation therapy before biopsy — Radiation before biopsy can make histology uninterpretable and is reserved for life-threatening presentations when stenting is unavailable.
  • (C) Empiric chemotherapy for small cell lung cancer — Chemotherapy requires a histologic diagnosis; treating the wrong tumor type causes harm without benefit.
  • (D) Thrombolytic therapy — Thrombolysis is for catheter-related SVC thrombosis, not extrinsic tumor compression.
  • (E) Empiric high-dose dexamethasone — Empiric glucocorticoids may obscure a lymphoma diagnosis and have no proven benefit in most SVC syndromes.
🎯 Educational objective

In SVC syndrome without stridor, cerebral edema or hemodynamic compromise, obtain a tissue diagnosis before starting treatment.

(c) empiric chemotherapy for small cell lung cancer — chemotherapy requires a histologic diagnosis; treating the wrong tumor type causes harm without benefit. (d) thrombolytic therapy — thrombolysis is for catheter-related svc thrombosis, not extrinsic tumor compression. ON-010.stem_html:
A 56-year-old woman receiving chemotherapy for acute myeloid leukemia is evaluated for a temperature of 38.6 °C (101.5 °F). She feels tired but otherwise well. She has a tunneled central venous catheter. She has no allergies.

On physical examination, blood pressure is 118/72 mm Hg, pulse rate is 104/min, and respiration rate is 18/min. Oxygen saturation is 97% breathing ambient air. There is mild oral mucositis. The catheter site is clean. Lungs are clear and the abdomen is soft.

Leukocyte count400/µL
Absolute neutrophil count80/µL
Platelet count22,000/µL
Creatinine0.8 mg/dL
Chest radiographnormal
ON-010.lead: After blood cultures are drawn from the catheter and a peripheral vein, which of the following is the most appropriate empiric antibiotic therapy?

choices.C: Oral ciprofloxacin and amoxicillin-clavulanate as an outpatient

ON-010.explain_html:
Correct answer: B Febrile neutropenia — empiric therapy

Febrile neutropenia: a single temperature ≥38.3 °C (or ≥38.0 °C sustained for 1 hour) with an ANC <500/µL. It is a medical emergency; start IV antibiotics within 60 minutes.

She is high risk (AML induction, profound and prolonged neutropenia expected, inpatient), so she needs inpatient IV monotherapy with an antipseudomonal β-lactam: cefepime, piperacillin-tazobactam, or meropenem/imipenem.

Add vancomycin (or other gram-positive coverage) only for specific indications:

  • Hemodynamic instability
  • Suspected catheter-related infection (site erythema/drainage, tunnel infection)
  • Skin or soft tissue infection
  • Pneumonia
  • Known MRSA colonization
  • Gram-positive cocci in blood culture before identification

She has none of these, so vancomycin is not needed. Mucositis alone is not an indication.

Why not the others

  • (A) Cefepime plus vancomycin — Empiric vancomycin without a specific indication does not improve outcomes and increases toxicity and resistance.
  • (C) Oral ciprofloxacin and amoxicillin-clavulanate as an outpatient — Outpatient oral therapy is only for low-risk patients (MASCC ≥21, expected short neutropenia); AML induction is high risk.
  • (D) No antibiotics until cultures return — Delaying antibiotics in febrile neutropenia increases mortality.
  • (E) Ceftriaxone plus azithromycin — Ceftriaxone does not cover Pseudomonas, the key pathogen in febrile neutropenia.
🎯 Educational objective

Treat high-risk febrile neutropenia with an intravenous antipseudomonal β-lactam such as cefepime within 1 hour, adding vancomycin only for specific indications.

ON-011.topic: Stage III colon cancer — adjuvant therapy
ON-011.stem_html: A 59-year-old man undergoes a sigmoid colectomy for adenocarcinoma. Pathology shows a T3 tumor with 3 of 18 lymph nodes positive and negative margins (stage III). The tumor is mismatch repair proficient. CT of the chest, abdomen and pelvis shows no distant metastases. He has recovered well from surgery and has an ECOG performance status of 0.
ON-011.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.A: Adjuvant radiation therapy to the pelvis
choices.B: Adjuvant chemotherapy with a fluoropyrimidine plus oxaliplatin
choices.E: Resection of the liver as a preventive measure

ON-011.explain_html:
Correct answer: B Stage III colon cancer — adjuvant therapy

In colon cancer, lymph node involvement (stage III) is the main indication for adjuvant chemotherapy. FOLFOX or CAPOX (fluoropyrimidine + oxaliplatin) reduces recurrence and improves survival by about 20–30% relative to surgery alone.

Duration: 3 months of CAPOX is noninferior for low-risk stage III (T1–3, N1) (IDEA collaboration) with much less oxaliplatin neuropathy; 6 months for high-risk (T4 or N2).

Surveillance: CEA every 3–6 months and CT every 6–12 months for 5 years; colonoscopy at 1 year after surgery.

Stage Treatment
I Surgery alone
II Surgery; adjuvant chemo for high-risk features
III Surgery + FOLFOX/CAPOX
IV Systemic therapy; resection of limited liver/lung metastases may be curative

Why not the others

  • (A) Adjuvant radiation therapy to the pelvis — Radiation is used for rectal cancer, not colon cancer above the peritoneal reflection.
  • (C) Observation with colonoscopy in 1 year — Observation alone forgoes the proven survival benefit of chemotherapy in node-positive disease.
  • (D) Immune checkpoint inhibitor therapy — Checkpoint inhibitors are used for MMR-deficient/MSI-high metastatic disease; his tumor is MMR proficient.
  • (E) Resection of the liver as a preventive measure — There is no role for prophylactic liver resection.
🎯 Educational objective

Offer adjuvant fluoropyrimidine plus oxaliplatin chemotherapy after resection of stage III (node-positive) colon cancer.

ON-012.stem_html:
A 64-year-old man with an 80 pack-year smoking history is evaluated for 3 months of difficulty climbing stairs and rising from chairs, dry mouth and constipation. He notices that his legs feel stronger after a few seconds of effort. He has erectile dysfunction.

On physical examination, there is weakness of the hip flexors and shoulder abductors. Deep tendon reflexes are reduced but increase after 10 seconds of maximal voluntary contraction. There is mild bilateral ptosis. Sensation is normal.

Chest CT shows a 3-cm central hilar mass with bulky mediastinal lymphadenopathy.
ON-012.lead: Which of the following antibodies is most likely to be present?
ON-012.explain_html:
Correct answer: E Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome

Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome (LEMS): autoantibodies against presynaptic P/Q-type voltage-gated calcium channels reduce acetylcholine release. About half of cases are paraneoplastic, almost always small cell lung cancer — a likely diagnosis given his smoking history and central mass.

Clinical triad:

  • Proximal leg weakness that improves with repeated effort (facilitation)
  • Reduced reflexes that increase after exercise
  • Autonomic symptoms — dry mouth, constipation, erectile dysfunction

Ocular and bulbar symptoms are milder than in myasthenia gravis. EMG shows a low CMAP amplitude that increases >100% after 10 seconds of exercise (or high-frequency stimulation).

Treat the tumor; amifampridine (3,4-diaminopyridine) prolongs presynaptic depolarization and improves strength.

Myasthenia gravis LEMS
Target Postsynaptic AChR Presynaptic VGCC
Weakness Worse with use; ocular/bulbar Better with use; proximal legs
Reflexes Normal Reduced (↑ after exercise)
Autonomic No Yes
Associated tumor Thymoma Small cell lung cancer

Why not the others

  • (A) Anti-NMDA receptor — Anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis causes psychiatric symptoms, seizures and dyskinesias, often with ovarian teratoma.
  • (B) Anti-Hu (ANNA-1) — Anti-Hu antibodies with SCLC cause sensory neuronopathy and encephalomyelitis, not facilitating proximal weakness.
  • (C) Anti–muscle-specific kinase (MuSK) — MuSK antibodies cause a form of myasthenia gravis with prominent bulbar and neck weakness.
  • (D) Acetylcholine receptor antibodies — AChR antibodies define myasthenia gravis, in which weakness worsens with repeated use and reflexes are preserved.
🎯 Educational objective

Recognize Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome (proximal weakness improving with effort, reduced reflexes, autonomic symptoms) caused by P/Q-type calcium channel antibodies, often with small cell lung cancer.

ON-013.stem_html:
A 72-year-old woman with metastatic pancreatic cancer is evaluated for worsening abdominal and back pain. She takes acetaminophen and ibuprofen, which no longer control her pain (now 8/10). She has never taken opioids. She has had no bowel obstruction. Her kidney function is normal.

You start oral morphine immediate-release, 5 mg every 4 hours as needed.
ON-013.lead: Which of the following should be started at the same time?

choices.A: A stimulant laxative such as senna, taken regularly
choices.B: No bowel regimen until constipation develops

ON-013.explain_html:
Correct answer: A Opioid-induced constipation in cancer pain

Constipation is the most common opioid adverse effect and — unlike nausea and sedation — does not improve with time (no tolerance). Opioids act on μ receptors in the gut to slow motility and increase fluid absorption.

Start a prophylactic bowel regimen with every opioid prescription: a stimulant laxative (senna or bisacodyl), with or without an osmotic laxative (polyethylene glycol). Titrate to a soft bowel movement at least every 1–2 days.

For refractory opioid-induced constipation: peripherally acting μ-opioid receptor antagonists (PAMORAs) — methylnaltrexone, naloxegol, naldemedine — which block gut μ receptors without reversing analgesia (contraindicated in bowel obstruction).

Other cancer pain principles: around-the-clock dosing for constant pain with breakthrough doses (10–20% of the daily dose), consider adjuvants (for this patient: celiac plexus block), and screen for opioid misuse risk.

Why not the others

  • (B) No bowel regimen until constipation develops — Waiting for constipation leads to suffering, poor adherence to analgesia and impaction. Prevention is standard.
  • (C) Loperamide — Loperamide is an antidiarrheal and would worsen constipation.
  • (D) Docusate alone — Docusate (a stool softener) alone is ineffective for opioid-induced constipation.
  • (E) Methylnaltrexone daily — PAMORAs are second-line for constipation that does not respond to standard laxatives; they are not used for prophylaxis.
🎯 Educational objective

Start a scheduled stimulant laxative with every opioid prescription to prevent opioid-induced constipation.

ON-014.stem_html:
A 46-year-old woman is evaluated for a lump in her left breast that she found 2 weeks ago. It has not changed through her menstrual cycle. She has no nipple discharge. Her last screening mammogram 18 months ago was normal. Her aunt had breast cancer at age 65.

On physical examination, there is a 2-cm firm, mobile, nontender mass in the upper outer quadrant of the left breast. There is no skin change or axillary lymphadenopathy.
ON-014.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in evaluation?

choices.B: Reassurance because her last mammogram was normal
choices.E: Repeat clinical breast examination after her next menstrual period only

ON-014.explain_html:
Correct answer: A Palpable breast mass

A new, persistent palpable breast mass needs imaging regardless of a recent normal mammogram — screening mammography misses 10–20% of palpable cancers.

Imaging depends on age:

  • ≥30 years: diagnostic mammography plus targeted ultrasonography.
  • <30 years: ultrasonography first (dense breasts, radiation concerns), then mammography if suspicious.

Then: core needle biopsy of any suspicious lesion (BI-RADS 4–5). A clinically suspicious mass needs biopsy even if imaging is negative ("triple test": examination, imaging, pathology must all agree). A simple cyst on ultrasound can be observed or aspirated.

Why not the others

  • (B) Reassurance because her last mammogram was normal — A normal mammogram 18 months ago does not exclude cancer in a new palpable mass.
  • (C) Screening mammography in 6 months — Screening mammography is for asymptomatic women; a palpable mass needs diagnostic imaging now.
  • (D) Breast MRI — MRI is for high-risk screening, extent of known cancer, or problem-solving after mammography and ultrasound; it is not the first test.
  • (E) Repeat clinical breast examination after her next menstrual period only — Re-examining after menses is reasonable for vague nodularity in a young woman, but a discrete persistent mass in a 46-year-old needs imaging now.
🎯 Educational objective

Evaluate a palpable breast mass in a woman aged 30 years or older with diagnostic mammography and targeted ultrasonography, followed by biopsy if suspicious.

ON-015.stem_html:
A 52-year-old woman with HER2-positive breast cancer is receiving adjuvant trastuzumab after completing doxorubicin and cyclophosphamide. She has mild exertional dyspnea and ankle swelling.

Echocardiogram shows an LVEF of 42% (62% at baseline). She has no chest pain. ECG shows sinus rhythm without ischemic changes.
ON-015.lead: Compared with anthracycline cardiotoxicity, trastuzumab cardiotoxicity is best characterized by which of the following?

choices.B: Cumulative dose-dependent myocyte death that is usually irreversible
choices.C: Myocyte dysfunction without necrosis that is often reversible after stopping the drug

ON-015.explain_html:
Correct answer: C Trastuzumab cardiotoxicity

Two classic chemotherapy cardiotoxicities:

Anthracyclines (doxorubicin) Trastuzumab (anti-HER2)
Mechanism Free radicals, topoisomerase IIβ → myocyte death Blocks HER2 (ErbB2) survival signaling in myocytes → dysfunction ("stunning")
Dose relation Cumulative, risk ↑ above 250–400 mg/m² Not dose-dependent
Histology Vacuolization, myofibrillar loss No necrosis
Reversibility Usually irreversible Usually reversible after holding drug
Timing Can appear years later During treatment

Prior anthracycline exposure increases the risk of trastuzumab cardiotoxicity.

Management: hold trastuzumab when LVEF falls ≥10 points to <50% (or symptomatic HF), start guideline-directed HF therapy (ACE inhibitor/ARB, beta-blocker), recheck LVEF in 3–4 weeks; many patients can resume trastuzumab once function recovers. Monitor LVEF every 3 months during therapy.

Why not the others

  • (A) Constrictive pericarditis — Constrictive pericarditis is a late complication of chest radiation.
  • (B) Cumulative dose-dependent myocyte death that is usually irreversible — Cumulative, irreversible myocyte death describes anthracycline toxicity.
  • (D) Coronary vasospasm causing ischemia — Coronary vasospasm is a toxicity of fluoropyrimidines (5-FU, capecitabine).
  • (E) Restrictive cardiomyopathy from amyloid deposition — Amyloid restrictive cardiomyopathy occurs with AL amyloidosis or transthyretin amyloid, not trastuzumab.
🎯 Educational objective

Trastuzumab cardiotoxicity is a non–dose-dependent, usually reversible myocardial dysfunction, unlike the cumulative, irreversible damage caused by anthracyclines.

She has mild exertional dyspnea and ankle swelling. Echocardiogram shows an LVEF of 42% (62% at baseline). She has no chest pain. ECG shows sinus rhythm without ischemic changes. Compared with anthracycline cardiotoxicity, trastuzumab cardiotoxicity is best characterized by which of the following?

OP-001.stem_html:
A 66-year-old woman comes to the emergency department 2 hours after the sudden onset of severe pain in her right eye, blurred vision, halos around lights, frontal headache, nausea and vomiting. Symptoms began while she was watching a movie in a dark theater. She is farsighted. She took an over-the-counter cold remedy containing diphenhydramine this morning.

Visual acuity is counting fingers in the right eye and 20/25 in the left. The right eye shows conjunctival injection most intense around the cornea, a hazy cornea and a mid-dilated pupil that reacts poorly to light. The right globe feels hard on gentle palpation.
OP-001.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

choices.A: Dilate the pupil with tropicamide to examine the fundus
choices.D: Topical ocular hypotensive drops and acetazolamide, with emergency ophthalmology evaluation
choices.E: Topical prednisolone acetate and follow-up with ophthalmology in 1 week

OP-001.explain_html:
Correct answer: D Acute angle-closure glaucoma

This is acute angle-closure glaucoma — an emergency that can cause permanent vision loss within hours. In a predisposed eye (farsighted, shallow anterior chamber, older age), pupillary dilation (darkness, anticholinergic or sympathomimetic drugs) pushes the iris against the trabecular meshwork. Aqueous humor cannot drain and intraocular pressure rises sharply (often >40–50 mm Hg).

Treat immediately to lower pressure, then fix the anatomy:

  • Aqueous suppressants: topical timolol, an α₂-agonist (apraclonidine/brimonidine), and acetazolamide 500 mg IV or orally.
  • Pilocarpine (miotic) once pressure starts falling, to pull the iris away from the angle.
  • Hyperosmotic agents (IV mannitol) if pressure remains very high.
  • Emergency ophthalmology for laser peripheral iridotomy — the definitive treatment — and usually prophylactic iridotomy of the other eye.

Why not the others

  • (A) Dilate the pupil with tropicamide to examine the fundus — Dilating the pupil worsens angle closure — the cause of this attack.
  • (B) Topical moxifloxacin — Antibiotic drops treat bacterial conjunctivitis or keratitis; vision loss, a hard eye and a fixed pupil are not infection.
  • (C) Noncontrast CT of the head — Head imaging delays sight-saving treatment; the eye findings explain the headache and vomiting.
  • (E) Topical prednisolone acetate and follow-up with ophthalmology in 1 week — Glucocorticoid drops treat inflammation (for example anterior uveitis) but do not lower the pressure, and a 1-week delay risks blindness.
🧠 Mnemonic

Red-eye red flags — "VIP-PC": Vision loss, Intense pain, Photophobia, Pupil abnormal, Corneal haze. Any one → same-day ophthalmology.

🎓 ABIM pearl

The headache and vomiting can mimic migraine, subarachnoid hemorrhage or an abdominal process — always look at the eye in an older adult with sudden headache and nausea.

🎯 Educational objective

Acute angle-closure glaucoma presents with a painful red eye, halos, a cloudy cornea and a mid-dilated fixed pupil; lower intraocular pressure immediately and arrange emergency laser iridotomy.

OP-002.stem_html:
A 42-year-old man is evaluated for 2 days of left-sided neck pain and headache that began after a vigorous chiropractic neck manipulation. Today his wife noticed that his left eyelid droops.

On physical examination, blood pressure is 134/82 mm Hg. There is left ptosis (mild) and a smaller left pupil. The anisocoria is greater in dim light, and the left pupil dilates slowly after the lights are turned off. Both pupils react to light. Extraocular movements are full. There is no facial weakness, limb weakness or sensory loss. Facial sweating is normal.
OP-002.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate next diagnostic test?

choices.D: CT or MR angiography of the head and neck

OP-002.explain_html:
Correct answer: D Painful Horner syndrome — carotid dissection

Ptosis + miosis (anisocoria worse in the dark, with dilation lag) = Horner syndrome (loss of sympathetic input to the eye). With acute ipsilateral neck pain and headache after neck manipulation, this is internal carotid artery dissection until proven otherwise. The sympathetic fibers run along the internal carotid artery wall. Sweating is spared because facial sweat fibers travel with the external carotid.

CT angiography or MR angiography of the head and neck urgently — dissection is a leading cause of stroke in young adults. Treatment: antiplatelet or anticoagulant therapy (similar outcomes in CADISS/TREAT-CAD).

Anisocoria rules: | Anisocoria worse in | Abnormal pupil | Causes | |---|---|---| | Dark | Small pupil can't dilate | Horner (dissection, Pancoast tumor, stroke), physiologic | | Light | Large pupil can't constrict | CN III palsy (aneurysm — "down and out," ptosis), Adie tonic pupil, pharmacologic (scopolamine) |

A painful third-nerve palsy with a dilated pupil = posterior communicating artery aneurysm → emergency CTA.

Why not the others

  • (A) Edrophonium test — Edrophonium testing is for myasthenia gravis, which causes ptosis without pupillary changes.
  • (B) Chest radiograph only — A chest radiograph or CT looks for a Pancoast tumor in chronic Horner syndrome with arm pain or smoking history; this acute painful presentation needs vascular imaging.
  • (C) Reassurance and follow-up in 1 month — Painful acute Horner syndrome is an emergency because of stroke risk.
  • (E) MRI of the orbits — Orbital MRI does not assess the carotid artery along the sympathetic pathway.
🎯 Educational objective

Acute painful Horner syndrome with neck pain requires urgent CT or MR angiography of the head and neck to exclude carotid artery dissection.

OP-003.stem_html:
A 71-year-old man is evaluated for sudden, painless, complete loss of vision in his right eye that began 2 hours ago. He has hypertension, hyperlipidemia and type 2 diabetes, and smokes. He has no headache, jaw pain or scalp tenderness.

On physical examination, blood pressure is 158/92 mm Hg and pulse rate is 88/min and irregularly irregular. Visual acuity is hand motion in the right eye. There is a right relative afferent pupillary defect. Funduscopy shows a pale, whitened retina with a cherry-red spot at the fovea and a refractile plaque at an arteriolar bifurcation.

ESR14 mm/h
C-reactive proteinnormal
OP-003.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.A: Emergency referral to a stroke center for evaluation as an acute ischemic stroke
choices.B: Ocular massage at home and outpatient ophthalmology follow-up in 1 week

OP-003.explain_html:
Correct answer: A Central retinal artery occlusion

Sudden painless monocular vision loss with a cherry-red spot (the fovea retains its choroidal blood supply while the surrounding ischemic retina turns white) and an embolic Hollenhorst plaque = central retinal artery occlusion (CRAO) — a stroke of the eye.

CRAO is a neurologic emergency: the risk of cerebral stroke is highest in the first week. AHA 2021 recommends immediate referral to an emergency department or stroke center:

  • Consider IV thrombolysis within 4.5 hours at stroke centers (evidence emerging).
  • Urgent stroke work-up: brain MRI (silent infarcts in ~25%), carotid imaging, ECG/telemetry (his irregular pulse suggests atrial fibrillation), echocardiography, lipids, A1c.
  • Exclude giant cell arteritis in patients >50 (ESR/CRP; here normal and no symptoms).

Older "conservative" therapies (ocular massage, paracentesis, lowering intraocular pressure) have no proven benefit.

Why not the others

  • (B) Ocular massage at home and outpatient ophthalmology follow-up in 1 week — Ocular massage is unproven, and outpatient follow-up misses the window for stroke prevention.
  • (C) Outpatient carotid ultrasonography in 2 weeks — Carotid imaging is needed, but urgently as part of an inpatient or emergency stroke evaluation.
  • (D) High-dose oral prednisone — Glucocorticoids are for arteritic CRAO from giant cell arteritis; his inflammatory markers are normal and he has no GCA symptoms.
  • (E) Topical timolol drops — Lowering intraocular pressure does not restore retinal perfusion in CRAO.
🎯 Educational objective

Treat central retinal artery occlusion as an acute ischemic stroke with emergency referral to a stroke center and an urgent stroke evaluation.

PS-001.stem_html:
A 45-year-old man comes to the office because he wants help to stop drinking. He drinks 8–10 beers daily and has failed to cut down several times. He finished a supervised outpatient withdrawal 1 week ago and has not had a drink since. He has opioid use disorder in remission and has taken buprenorphine–naloxone daily for 3 years. He attends weekly counseling.

Vital signs are normal. There is no tremor, jaundice or stigmata of chronic liver disease.

ALT48 U/L
AST66 U/L
Bilirubin, total0.8 mg/dL
Albumin4.1 g/dL
Creatinine0.9 mg/dL (eGFR >90 mL/min/1.73 m²)
PS-001.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate medication to help him maintain abstinence from alcohol?
PS-001.explain_html:
Correct answer: A Alcohol use disorder — pharmacotherapy

Medications for alcohol use disorder (AUD) are underused even though they reduce relapse. The two first-line drugs are naltrexone and acamprosate; the choice depends on the patient.

He takes buprenorphine, an opioid. Naltrexone is an opioid antagonist — it would block buprenorphine's effect and can precipitate opioid withdrawal, risking relapse to opioid use. Acamprosate (a glutamate modulator that eases protracted withdrawal) has no opioid interaction and is cleared by the kidneys, not the liver — a good fit for him.

Drug Best when Avoid when
Naltrexone (oral or monthly IM) Reducing heavy drinking; craving Any opioid use, acute hepatitis or liver failure
Acamprosate Maintaining abstinence after withdrawal; liver disease CrCl ≤30; reduce dose CrCl 30–50
Disulfiram Highly motivated, supervised dosing Heart disease, psychosis, poor adherence
Gabapentin, topiramate Second line —

Why not the others

  • (B) Naltrexone — Naltrexone is contraindicated with ongoing opioid therapy such as buprenorphine.
  • (C) No medication; counseling alone — Combining medication with counseling works better than counseling alone; he should be offered pharmacotherapy.
  • (D) Disulfiram — Disulfiram works only with supervised adherence and has weaker evidence; it is not first-line.
  • (E) Diazepam daily — Benzodiazepines treat acute withdrawal; long-term use is addictive and dangerous with alcohol and buprenorphine (respiratory depression).
🎓 ABIM pearl

Mild aminotransferase elevation (AST > ALT, as here) is not a reason to avoid naltrexone in other patients — the risk is in acute hepatitis or decompensated cirrhosis.

🎯 Educational objective

Offer naltrexone or acamprosate to patients with alcohol use disorder; choose acamprosate when the patient takes opioids (including buprenorphine) and avoid it in severe kidney disease.

PS-002.stem_html:
A 31-year-old woman comes to the office because she "can't turn her brain off." For the past 8 months she has worried almost every day about her job, finances and her parents' health, even when things are going well. She feels restless and tense, has trouble concentrating, tires easily and lies awake worrying. She has no panic attacks, no thoughts of self-harm and no prior psychiatric treatment. She drinks one glass of wine on weekends and does not use other substances. She does not plan pregnancy and uses an IUD.

Vital signs and examination are normal. Her GAD-7 score is 15 (moderate–severe). PHQ-9 score is 6.

TSH1.6 µU/mL
Complete blood count and metabolic panelnormal
PS-002.lead: In addition to referral for cognitive behavioral therapy, which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?

choices.D: Hydroxyzine nightly as the only medication

PS-002.explain_html:
Correct answer: E Generalized anxiety disorder

Excessive, hard-to-control worry about many things on most days for ≥6 months, with restlessness, fatigue, poor concentration, muscle tension and insomnia, is generalized anxiety disorder (GAD). Hyperthyroidism and substances are excluded.

First-line treatment is cognitive behavioral therapy and/or an SSRI or SNRI (sertraline, escitalopram, venlafaxine XR, duloxetine). Start at a low dose (anxious patients feel early activation side effects), increase after 1–2 weeks, and allow 4–6 weeks for effect. Continue for 6–12 months after response before tapering.

Why not the others

  • (A) Alprazolam as needed — Benzodiazepines relieve anxiety quickly but cause dependence, tolerance, falls and cognitive effects, and do not treat co-occurring depression; they are at most a short-term bridge, never first-line.
  • (B) Propranolol — Propranolol blunts physical symptoms of performance anxiety but does not treat GAD.
  • (C) Quetiapine — Atypical antipsychotics have some efficacy but cause weight gain, metabolic syndrome and other adverse effects; they are not first-line.
  • (D) Hydroxyzine nightly as the only medication — Hydroxyzine is a second-line option with sedation and anticholinergic effects; on its own it is not the preferred first treatment.
🧠 Mnemonic

GAD — "Worried WARRIORS": Worry, Anxious, Restless, Reduced concentration, Irritability, On edge/muscle tension, Rest disturbed (sleep), Six months.

🎓 ABIM pearl

Screen all adults for anxiety (USPSTF 2023 recommends screening adults <65 years) and always ask about suicidal thoughts when starting an antidepressant in young adults.

🎯 Educational objective

Treat generalized anxiety disorder with CBT and/or an SSRI or SNRI; avoid benzodiazepines as first-line therapy.

(b) propranolol — propranolol blunts physical symptoms of performance anxiety but does not treat gad. (c) quetiapine — atypical antipsychotics have some efficacy but cause weight gain, metabolic syndrome and other adverse effects; they are not first-line. (d) hydroxyzine nightly as the only medication — hydroxyzine is a second-line option with sedation and anticholinergic effects; on its own it is not the preferred first treatment. 🧠 mnemonic gad — "worried warriors" : w orry, a nxious, r estless, r educed concentration, i rritability, o n edge/muscle tension, r est disturbed (sleep), s ix months. 🎓 abim pearl screen all adults for anxiety (uspstf 2023 recommends screening adults <65 years) and always ask about suicidal thoughts when starting an antidepressant in young adults. 🎯 educational objective treat generalized anxiety disorder with cbt and/or an ssri or snri; avoid benzodiazepines as first-line therapy. 📚 read more in wardology 🌧️ depression & anxiety in primary care → references {'us preventive services task force. screening for anxiety disorders in adults': 'recommendation statement. jama 2023;329:2163.'} demartini j, et al. generalized anxiety disorder. ann intern med 2019;170:itc49.  generalized anxiety disorder

PS-003.topic: Depression — screen for bipolar disorder before an antidepressant
PS-003.stem_html:
A 31-year-old woman is evaluated for 6 weeks of low mood, loss of interest, poor sleep, low energy and difficulty concentrating. Her PHQ-9 score is 18. She has no suicidal thoughts. She asks to start "an antidepressant, like my sister takes".

On further questioning, she describes a period 2 years ago when she slept only 3 hours a night for a week without feeling tired, started several business projects, spent $8,000 on clothes and talked so fast that friends could not keep up. She did not seek care.

Examination, TSH and CBC are normal.
PS-003.lead: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

choices.A: Bipolar I disorder, current episode depressed

PS-003.explain_html:
Correct answer: A Depression — screen for bipolar disorder before an antidepressant

She meets criteria for a major depressive episode now. Her past history shows a manic episode: ≥1 week of decreased need for sleep, grandiosity/increased goal-directed activity, excessive spending and pressured speech with marked impairment. A single lifetime manic episode = bipolar I disorder.

Why it matters: antidepressant monotherapy in bipolar disorder can trigger mania, mixed states and rapid cycling. Always screen for prior mania or hypomania (and family history of bipolar disorder) before starting an antidepressant — e.g., with the Mood Disorder Questionnaire.

Bipolar depression is treated with quetiapine, lurasidone, lumateperone, cariprazine or lamotrigine, or a mood stabilizer (lithium), not an SSRI alone.

Mania (bipolar I) Hypomania (bipolar II)
Duration ≥7 days (or hospitalization) ≥4 days
Impairment Marked, may have psychosis No marked impairment

Why not the others

  • (B) Cyclothymic disorder — Cyclothymic disorder involves milder hypomanic and depressive symptoms for ≥2 years that never meet full criteria for an episode.
  • (C) Major depressive disorder — Major depressive disorder requires that there has never been a manic or hypomanic episode.
  • (D) Persistent depressive disorder (dysthymia) — Dysthymia is chronic, milder depression for ≥2 years.
  • (E) Borderline personality disorder — Borderline personality disorder causes mood shifts lasting hours, with unstable relationships and self-image, not week-long episodes of decreased need for sleep.
🎯 Educational objective

Screen for a history of mania or hypomania before prescribing an antidepressant; one lifetime manic episode establishes bipolar I disorder.

PS-004.stem_html:
A 58-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder that has been stable on lithium for 10 years is brought to the emergency department with 3 days of nausea, diarrhea, coarse tremor, unsteady gait and confusion. Two weeks ago her primary care physician started hydrochlorothiazide for hypertension.

On physical examination, she is disoriented. There is a coarse tremor, ataxia and hyperreflexia with myoclonic jerks.

Lithium level2.8 mEq/L (therapeutic 0.6–1.2)
Sodium134 mEq/L
Creatinine1.6 mg/dL (baseline 1.0 mg/dL)
PS-004.lead: Which of the following is the most likely mechanism of her lithium toxicity?

choices.A: Decreased distal tubular secretion of lithium
choices.B: Inhibition of lithium metabolism by the liver
choices.C: Increased lithium absorption from the gut
choices.D: Displacement of lithium from plasma proteins
choices.E: Increased proximal tubular reabsorption of lithium due to volume contraction

PS-004.explain_html:
Correct answer: E Lithium toxicity — drug interaction

Lithium is not metabolized or protein-bound — it is handled like sodium by the kidney. About 80% is reabsorbed in the proximal tubule alongside sodium.

Thiazide diuretics cause mild volume and sodium depletion → the proximal tubule reabsorbs more sodium — and lithium → levels rise 25–40%. The same happens with ACE inhibitors/ARBs, NSAIDs, dehydration (vomiting, diarrhea, heat) and low-salt diets. Her vomiting and diarrhea made things worse.

Chronic lithium toxicity affects the brain: tremor, ataxia, confusion, hyperreflexia, myoclonus, seizures; also nausea, diarrhea and AKI. Long-term toxicity: nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, CKD, hypothyroidism, hyperparathyroidism.

Treatment: stop lithium, isotonic saline, and hemodialysis for severe toxicity (level >4.0 mEq/L, or >2.5 mEq/L with neurologic symptoms or kidney impairment) — she qualifies. Loop diuretics affect lithium the least.

Why not the others

  • (A) Decreased distal tubular secretion of lithium — Lithium is reabsorbed, not secreted, and the thiazide effect is mainly on proximal reabsorption.
  • (B) Inhibition of lithium metabolism by the liver — Lithium is not metabolized by the liver.
  • (C) Increased lithium absorption from the gut — Thiazides do not affect gut absorption of lithium.
  • (D) Displacement of lithium from plasma proteins — Lithium is not protein-bound, so drugs cannot displace it.
🧠 Mnemonic

Drugs that raise lithium — "NSAIDs, ACE, Thiazides" = "No ACTion" for safe lithium levels.

🎯 Educational objective

Thiazides, ACE inhibitors, ARBs, NSAIDs and volume depletion raise lithium levels by increasing proximal tubular reabsorption along with sodium.

PS-005.stem_html:
A 28-year-old man with schizophrenia is evaluated in the primary care clinic. His psychiatrist started olanzapine 3 months ago, and his psychotic symptoms have improved. He has gained 7 kg (15.4 lb). He smokes one pack of cigarettes daily.

On physical examination, blood pressure is 134/86 mm Hg. BMI is 31 (27 before olanzapine). Waist circumference is 104 cm.

Fasting glucose118 mg/dL
Triglycerides260 mg/dL
HDL cholesterol34 mg/dL
PS-005.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate recommendation regarding his risk?

choices.C: Discuss switching to a lower-risk antipsychotic with his psychiatrist, address smoking, and monitor weight, glucose and lipids
choices.E: Continue olanzapine without monitoring because benefit outweighs risk

PS-005.explain_html:
Correct answer: C Second-generation antipsychotics — metabolic monitoring

He has developed metabolic syndrome (abdominal obesity, high triglycerides, low HDL, impaired fasting glucose, elevated BP) on olanzapine. People with serious mental illness die 10–20 years earlier than the general population, mostly from cardiovascular disease — antipsychotic metabolic effects and smoking are major contributors.

Metabolic risk of second-generation antipsychotics:

  • Highest: clozapine, olanzapine
  • Intermediate: quetiapine, risperidone, paliperidone
  • Lowest: aripiprazole, ziprasidone, lurasidone, brexpiprazole, cariprazine

ADA/APA monitoring: weight/BMI at baseline, monthly for 3 months, then quarterly; glucose/A1c and lipids at baseline, 12 weeks, then annually; BP at baseline, 12 weeks, annually.

Management: coordinate with psychiatry about switching to a lower-risk agent if psychiatrically safe; metformin reduces antipsychotic-induced weight gain; lifestyle; smoking cessation (varenicline is safe and effective in schizophrenia). Statins and antihypertensives as indicated.

Why not the others

  • (A) Switch to clozapine — Clozapine has the highest metabolic risk and requires ANC monitoring for agranulocytosis; it is reserved for treatment-resistant schizophrenia.
  • (B) Begin insulin — His glucose is in the prediabetes range; insulin is not indicated.
  • (D) Stop olanzapine immediately — Abrupt discontinuation risks psychotic relapse; any change should be planned with psychiatry.
  • (E) Continue olanzapine without monitoring because benefit outweighs risk — Monitoring is required with all second-generation antipsychotics; ignoring metabolic effects risks premature cardiovascular death.
🎯 Educational objective

Monitor weight, glucose, lipids and blood pressure in patients taking second-generation antipsychotics, and consider switching to lower-risk agents when metabolic complications develop.

PS-006.stem_html:
A 34-year-old man is hospitalized with cellulitis of the left forearm from injection drug use. He injects heroin and fentanyl several times a day. He has tried to stop on his own twice but relapsed within days because of withdrawal and cravings. He wants help to stop.

On hospital day 2, he has yawning, rhinorrhea, sweating, dilated pupils, gooseflesh, abdominal cramps and anxiety. His last use was 18 hours ago. His Clinical Opiate Withdrawal Scale (COWS) score is 14 (moderate withdrawal).

His liver tests are mildly elevated. He is not pregnant.
PS-006.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?

choices.A: Treat withdrawal with oxycodone and taper over 5 days
choices.B: Wait until he is discharged and refer to a methadone clinic
choices.D: Clonidine alone, followed by outpatient referral
choices.E: Begin buprenorphine now and continue it after discharge

PS-006.explain_html:
Correct answer: E Opioid use disorder — buprenorphine

He has opioid use disorder (OUD), now in moderate withdrawal (COWS ≥8–12). Hospitalization is an important opportunity to start medication for OUD (MOUD).

Buprenorphine (partial μ agonist with very high receptor affinity) and methadone (full agonist) reduce overdose deaths by ~50%, reduce HIV/HCV transmission and improve retention in care. Detoxification alone (withdrawal management without maintenance) leads to relapse in most patients and increases overdose risk (lost tolerance).

Buprenorphine must be started when the patient is in moderate withdrawal — otherwise its high affinity displaces full agonists and causes precipitated withdrawal. With fentanyl, which lingers in fat tissue, waiting longer or using low-dose ("micro") induction or high-dose induction helps. No special waiver is required to prescribe it (X-waiver eliminated 2023).

Also: naloxone kit at discharge, HIV/HCV testing, vaccination, and linkage to outpatient care.

Why not the others

  • (A) Treat withdrawal with oxycodone and taper over 5 days — A short opioid taper (detox) does not treat OUD, and relapse with lost tolerance increases overdose death.
  • (B) Wait until he is discharged and refer to a methadone clinic — Delaying treatment misses the opportunity; buprenorphine can be started in the hospital and continued, and methadone can be started in hospital and bridged to a clinic.
  • (C) Begin oral naltrexone today — Naltrexone requires 7–10 days of abstinence before starting (or it precipitates severe withdrawal), and it has lower retention than buprenorphine.
  • (D) Clonidine alone, followed by outpatient referral — Clonidine relieves autonomic withdrawal symptoms but does not treat OUD or reduce overdose risk.
🎯 Educational objective

Start buprenorphine (or methadone) for opioid use disorder during hospitalization once the patient is in moderate withdrawal, and continue it after discharge.

PS-007.stem_html:
A 78-year-old man with mild Alzheimer dementia is hospitalized with an infected diabetic foot ulcer. The surgeon recommends a below-knee amputation because of osteomyelitis and gangrene. The patient refuses.

When asked, he correctly explains that his foot has a serious infection, that without surgery the infection may spread and kill him, and that surgery would mean he could not walk without a prosthesis. He says, "I've lived a good life. I would rather die with both legs than live without one. My wife died last year, and I don't want to be in a nursing home." His answers are the same when asked again the next day. He is oriented to person and place but not to the date. His MoCA score is 19/30.

His daughter insists that "he has dementia, so he can't decide" and asks you to proceed with surgery.
PS-007.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

choices.A: Respect his refusal because he has decision-making capacity for this choice
choices.B: Proceed with surgery with the daughter's consent because he has dementia
choices.C: Sedate him and proceed with surgery as an emergency
choices.D: Request psychiatry to declare him incompetent
choices.E: Obtain a court order for surgery

PS-007.explain_html:
Correct answer: A Decision-making capacity

Decision-making capacity is a clinical judgment, made by the treating physician, about a specific decision at a specific time. It is different from competence, a legal determination by a court.

The four elements (Appelbaum):

  1. Communicate a choice — consistently ✔
  2. Understand the relevant information ✔
  3. Appreciate how it applies to his own situation ✔
  4. Reason — weigh options in line with his values ✔

A diagnosis of dementia does not by itself remove capacity, nor does a low MoCA or disorientation to date. A choice that others disagree with — even one that may lead to death — is not evidence of incapacity if the reasoning is consistent with the patient's values. Capacity is assessed on a sliding scale: high-stakes decisions require more certainty, and he meets that standard.

Respect his informed refusal, explore his fears (nursing home, loss of independence), offer alternatives (antibiotics, palliative care), document carefully, and support the daughter.

Why not the others

  • (B) Proceed with surgery with the daughter's consent because he has dementia — Surrogates decide only when the patient lacks capacity.
  • (C) Sedate him and proceed with surgery as an emergency — Forced treatment of a patient with capacity is battery.
  • (D) Request psychiatry to declare him incompetent — Any physician can assess capacity; psychiatry may help in difficult cases, but competence is a legal determination, and his capacity is clear.
  • (E) Obtain a court order for surgery — Courts are involved when capacity is in doubt and there is unresolvable conflict; he clearly has capacity.
🧠 Mnemonic

Capacity = "CURA" — Communicate a choice, Understand, Reason, Appreciate.

🎯 Educational objective

Assess decision-making capacity for each specific decision using the ability to communicate a choice, understand, appreciate and reason; a diagnosis of dementia alone does not remove capacity.

PS-008.stem_html:
A 45-year-old woman with depression treated with sertraline is brought to the emergency department with 6 hours of agitation, sweating, diarrhea and shaking. Two days ago she was given tramadol for back pain, and this morning she took dextromethorphan cough syrup.

On physical examination, temperature is 38.9 °C (102.0 °F), blood pressure is 162/96 mm Hg, pulse rate is 124/min. She is agitated and diaphoretic. Pupils are dilated. Bowel sounds are hyperactive. There is inducible ankle clonus, ocular clonus and hyperreflexia, more prominent in the legs. There is no lead-pipe rigidity.
PS-008.lead: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
PS-008.explain_html:
Correct answer: B Serotonin syndrome

Serotonin syndrome: within hours of adding serotonergic drugs (SSRI + tramadol + dextromethorphan), the triad of:

  • Neuromuscular hyperactivity — clonus (inducible, spontaneous, ocular), hyperreflexia (legs > arms), tremor
  • Autonomic instability — hyperthermia, tachycardia, hypertension, diaphoresis, mydriasis, diarrhea/hyperactive bowel sounds
  • Altered mental status — agitation

The Hunter criteria (serotonergic drug + clonus or hypertonia/hyperthermia) are the most accurate.

Treat: stop serotonergic drugs, supportive care, benzodiazepines, and cyproheptadine (5-HT2A antagonist) for moderate cases; severe hyperthermia (>41 °C) → sedation, paralysis and intubation. Antipyretics do not help (muscle-generated heat).

Serotonin syndrome NMS
Drug Serotonergic Dopamine antagonist (or stopping levodopa)
Onset Hours Days
Muscles Clonus, hyperreflexia Lead-pipe rigidity, bradyreflexia
GI Diarrhea Normal
Treatment Cyproheptadine, benzos Dantrolene, bromocriptine

Why not the others

  • (A) Anticholinergic toxicity — Anticholinergic toxicity causes dry skin, urinary retention, decreased bowel sounds and no clonus ("dry as a bone").
  • (C) Malignant hyperthermia — Malignant hyperthermia follows volatile anesthetics or succinylcholine.
  • (D) Neuroleptic malignant syndrome — NMS develops over days after dopamine antagonists, with lead-pipe rigidity and slow reflexes, not clonus.
  • (E) Sympathomimetic toxicity — Sympathomimetics (cocaine, amphetamines) cause agitation, mydriasis, sweating and tachycardia, but not clonus or hyperreflexia.
🎯 Educational objective

Recognize serotonin syndrome by clonus, hyperreflexia, autonomic instability and agitation shortly after adding serotonergic drugs, and distinguish it from neuroleptic malignant syndrome.

PS-009.stem_html:
A 52-year-old woman is evaluated for 8 months of difficulty falling asleep and staying asleep at least 4 nights a week, with daytime fatigue and irritability. She lies in bed worrying about sleep, watches TV in bed and naps in the afternoon. She drinks two cups of coffee in the morning. She does not snore and has no leg discomfort at night. She is perimenopausal without hot flashes. PHQ-9 and GAD-7 scores are low.

Examination is normal.
PS-009.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate initial treatment?
PS-009.explain_html:
Correct answer: B Chronic insomnia

Chronic insomnia disorder: difficulty initiating or maintaining sleep ≥3 nights per week for ≥3 months, with daytime impairment, despite adequate opportunity. Contributing behaviors here: watching TV in bed, napping, worrying in bed (conditioned arousal).

The ACP and AASM recommend cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia (CBT-I) as first-line for all adults — including older adults. It has durable benefits that outlast medications. Components:

  • Sleep restriction (limit time in bed to actual sleep time)
  • Stimulus control (bed only for sleep and sex; get up if not asleep in 20 minutes)
  • Cognitive therapy (catastrophic thoughts about sleep)
  • Sleep hygiene and relaxation

Digital CBT-I programs work. Medications (low-dose doxepin, orexin antagonists like suvorexant/daridorexant, short-term Z-drugs) are second-line and short-term.

Why not the others

  • (A) Polysomnography — Polysomnography is for suspected sleep apnea, periodic limb movements or parasomnias, not routine insomnia.
  • (C) Zolpidem nightly for 1 year — Long-term hypnotics carry risks (complex sleep behaviors, falls) and do not address the underlying behaviors; CBT-I comes first.
  • (D) Diphenhydramine at bedtime — Diphenhydramine is anticholinergic, causes next-day sedation and confusion, and has little evidence for chronic insomnia.
  • (E) Lorazepam at bedtime — Benzodiazepines cause dependence, falls, cognitive impairment and tolerance.
🎯 Educational objective

Treat chronic insomnia disorder with cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia as first-line therapy.

PS-010.stem_html:
A 22-year-old woman with anorexia nervosa is hospitalized for medical stabilization. Her BMI is 13.8. She has eaten very little for 3 weeks. Nutrition support with oral feeds was started 3 days ago.

Today she has new weakness, shortness of breath, leg edema and confusion.

On physical examination, pulse rate is 118/min and respiration rate is 26/min. There is bilateral pitting edema and crackles at the lung bases.

Phosphorus0.9 mg/dL (3.4 mg/dL on admission)
Potassium2.8 mEq/L
Magnesium1.2 mg/dL
Glucose168 mg/dL
PS-010.lead: Which of the following is the primary mechanism of her electrolyte abnormalities?

choices.B: Insulin-driven intracellular shift of phosphate, potassium and magnesium
choices.D: Increased urinary losses from diuretic abuse

PS-010.explain_html:
Correct answer: B Refeeding syndrome in anorexia nervosa

Refeeding syndrome: in prolonged starvation, total-body phosphate, potassium and magnesium are depleted, though serum levels can be normal. When carbohydrates are reintroduced, insulin surges, driving glucose — and with it phosphate, potassium and magnesium — into cells. Phosphate is consumed to make ATP and 2,3-DPG for glycolysis. Thiamine is used up too.

Severe hypophosphatemia (<1 mg/dL) causes respiratory muscle weakness, heart failure, arrhythmias, rhabdomyolysis, hemolysis, seizures and delirium. Sodium and fluid retention (insulin effect) add edema and heart failure.

Prevention (NICE/ASPEN): identify high-risk patients (BMI <16, little intake >10 days, low baseline K/P/Mg), start feeding slowly (10–20 kcal/kg/d) and advance gradually, give thiamine before feeding, and monitor and replace phosphate, potassium and magnesium daily for the first 3–7 days.

Why not the others

  • (A) Gastrointestinal losses from self-induced vomiting — Vomiting causes hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis but not severe hypophosphatemia timed to refeeding.
  • (C) Primary hyperparathyroidism — Primary hyperparathyroidism causes hypercalcemia with mild hypophosphatemia, not an acute fall after nutrition.
  • (D) Increased urinary losses from diuretic abuse — Diuretic abuse causes hypokalemia and metabolic alkalosis but does not explain the sharp fall in phosphate after refeeding began.
  • (E) Vitamin D deficiency — Vitamin D deficiency causes slowly developing hypophosphatemia, not acute symptomatic depletion in days.
🎯 Educational objective

Refeeding syndrome results from insulin-driven intracellular shifts of phosphate, potassium and magnesium in previously starved patients; prevent it with slow feeding, thiamine and close electrolyte replacement.

📚 Read more in Wardology🪫 Hypophosphatemia →

PU-001.stem_html:
A 67-year-old man with COPD comes for follow-up. He quit smoking 3 years ago after 45 pack-years. He uses tiotropium once daily and albuterol as needed; his inhaler technique is good. He gets short of breath walking about 100 meters on level ground. In the past year he had two exacerbations treated with oral prednisone and antibiotics, without hospitalization. He completed pulmonary rehabilitation last year.

Oxygen saturation is 94% on room air. There are scattered expiratory wheezes and a prolonged expiratory phase.

Post-bronchodilator FEV₁/FVC0.52
Post-bronchodilator FEV₁48% of predicted
Blood eosinophil count340/µL
PU-001.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate change to his maintenance therapy?

choices.A: Switch to a long-acting β₂-agonist–long-acting muscarinic antagonist–inhaled glucocorticoid (triple) inhaler
choices.E: Add an inhaled glucocorticoid alone to tiotropium

PU-001.explain_html:
Correct answer: A Stable COPD — escalating inhaled therapy

He has COPD with persistent dyspnea and ≥2 moderate exacerbations a year despite a LAMA. GOLD escalation depends on the blood eosinophil count, a marker of who benefits from inhaled glucocorticoids:

On LAMA or LABA, still exacerbating Escalate to
Eosinophils <100/µL LABA + LAMA
Eosinophils ≥300/µL (or ≥100 on LABA+LAMA) LABA + LAMA + ICS (single inhaler)
Still exacerbating on triple Add roflumilast (FEV₁ <50% + chronic bronchitis) or azithromycin (former smokers); consider dupilumab/mepolizumab if eosinophils ≥300

With eosinophils of 340/µL, triple therapy reduces exacerbations and, in trials, all-cause mortality compared with dual bronchodilators.

Why not the others

  • (B) Add daily oral prednisone 5 mg — Chronic systemic glucocorticoids cause serious harm (osteoporosis, diabetes, myopathy, infection) without benefit in stable COPD.
  • (C) Add roflumilast — Roflumilast is a later add-on for patients who still exacerbate on triple therapy, with FEV₁ <50% and chronic bronchitis.
  • (D) Add daily azithromycin — Azithromycin is also a later add-on after triple therapy (best in former smokers); it can prolong QT and cause hearing loss and resistance.
  • (E) Add an inhaled glucocorticoid alone to tiotropium — ICS should be given with a LABA, not as LAMA + ICS alone. ICS without a LABA is not a recommended COPD combination.
🎓 ABIM pearl

ICS raises pneumonia risk. Avoid or withdraw ICS when eosinophils are <100/µL, with repeated pneumonia, or with mycobacterial infection.

🎯 Educational objective

In COPD with exacerbations despite a long-acting bronchodilator, escalate to triple therapy (LABA + LAMA + ICS) when blood eosinophils are ≥300/µL, and to LABA + LAMA when they are low.

PU-002.stem_html:
A 26-year-old woman comes to the office because she uses her albuterol inhaler 2–3 times per week for cough, chest tightness and wheezing, especially with exercise and in cold air. She has not woken at night because of asthma and has never needed oral glucocorticoids or emergency care. She has allergic rhinitis.

Examination is normal.

SpirometryFEV₁ 88% of predicted; FEV₁/FVC 0.74
After bronchodilatorFEV₁ increases by 15% (420 mL)
PU-002.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
PU-002.explain_html:
Correct answer: E Mild asthma

She has mild asthma (symptoms less than daily, no night waking, normal FEV₁, a significant bronchodilator response).

The biggest change in asthma care: SABA-only treatment is no longer recommended. Even mild asthma carries a risk of severe and fatal attacks, and SABA alone does nothing for airway inflammation. As-needed low-dose ICS–formoterol (budesonide–formoterol) gives anti-inflammatory therapy every time she treats symptoms; it cuts severe exacerbations by about 60% compared with SABA alone, using far less steroid than daily ICS. Formoterol works within minutes, so it works as a reliever.

(Daily low-dose ICS with a SABA reliever is an acceptable alternative pathway.)

Why not the others

  • (A) Oral prednisone for 5 days — She is not having an exacerbation. Systemic glucocorticoids are for acute attacks.
  • (B) Salmeterol twice daily — LABA without ICS increases asthma-related deaths. Never give salmeterol alone in asthma.
  • (C) Montelukast daily — Leukotriene receptor antagonists are less effective than ICS and carry an FDA boxed warning for neuropsychiatric effects.
  • (D) Continue albuterol as needed only — SABA monotherapy increases the risk of severe exacerbations and death and is no longer recommended at any step.
🧠 Mnemonic

"Every puff gets a steroid." In asthma, the reliever should carry ICS.

🎓 ABIM pearl

Before stepping up any asthma therapy, check inhaler technique, adherence, triggers (smoke, allergens, NSAIDs, β-blockers) and comorbidities (rhinitis, GERD, obesity, OSA).

🎯 Educational objective

Treat mild asthma with as-needed low-dose ICS–formoterol (or daily low-dose ICS); SABA-only therapy and LABA monotherapy are not recommended.

PU-003.stem_html:
A 52-year-old woman had a CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis in the emergency department for right flank pain, which showed a 4-mm obstructing ureteral stone that later passed. The lung bases on the scan showed a 7-mm solid nodule with smooth margins in the right lower lobe. She has never smoked, has no history of cancer and no known exposures to asbestos or radon. She feels well and has no cough, hemoptysis or weight loss.

Examination is normal. There is no prior chest imaging.
PU-003.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

choices.B: CT of the chest in 6–12 months
choices.E: CT of the chest in 3 months

PU-003.explain_html:
Correct answer: B Incidental pulmonary nodule

The Fleischner Society guidelines apply to incidental nodules in adults ≥35 years (not to lung cancer screening, known cancer or immunosuppression). Management depends on size, type (solid vs subsolid) and patient risk.

For a single solid nodule 6–8 mm in a low-risk patient (never-smoker, no other risk factors, smooth margins), get a CT at 6–12 months, then consider another at 18–24 months. A solid nodule that is unchanged for 2 years is considered benign.

Single solid nodule Low risk High risk
<6 mm No routine follow-up Optional CT at 12 months
6–8 mm CT at 6–12 months, then consider 18–24 months CT at 6–12 months and 18–24 months
>8 mm CT at 3 months, PET-CT or tissue sampling Same

Why not the others

  • (A) PET-CT now — PET-CT is unreliable below about 8 mm (false negatives) and is reserved for larger solid nodules.
  • (C) CT-guided needle biopsy — Biopsy of a 7-mm low-risk nodule is high-risk and low-yield.
  • (D) No further follow-up — "No follow-up" applies to nodules <6 mm in low-risk patients.
  • (E) CT of the chest in 3 months — A 3-month CT is for nodules >8 mm.
🎓 ABIM pearl

Subsolid (ground-glass) nodules grow slowly — follow them longer (up to 5 years). A growing solid component is the most worrisome change.

🎯 Educational objective

A single incidental 6–8-mm solid lung nodule in a low-risk patient needs a follow-up chest CT at 6–12 months (Fleischner Society).

PU-004.stem_html:
A 50-year-old man comes to discuss the results of a sleep study. His wife reports loud snoring and pauses in his breathing. He falls asleep while watching television and once nodded off at a red light. He has hypertension treated with amlodipine and lisinopril. He drinks 1–2 beers on weekends and takes no sedatives.

Blood pressure is 146/90 mm Hg. BMI is 34 kg/m² and neck circumference is 45 cm (17.7 in). The oropharynx is crowded.

A home sleep apnea test shows an apnea–hypopnea index of 32 events/hour with oxygen saturation nadir of 81%.
PU-004.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
PU-004.explain_html:
Correct answer: E Obstructive sleep apnea

He has severe obstructive sleep apnea (AHI ≥30) with excessive daytime sleepiness — including drowsy driving — and hypertension.

CPAP is first-line therapy for moderate–severe OSA. It splints the upper airway open, abolishes apneas, improves sleepiness and quality of life, lowers motor-vehicle crash risk and modestly lowers blood pressure. Success depends on adherence (≥4 hours per night): mask fitting, humidification and early follow-up matter.

Weight loss is recommended for everyone with OSA and obesity; GLP-1-based therapy can reduce AHI in obesity-related OSA and can be added to, not substituted for, CPAP when sleepiness is dangerous.

AHI (events/h) Severity
5–14 Mild
15–29 Moderate
≥30 Severe

Why not the others

  • (A) Zolpidem at bedtime — Sedative-hypnotics can worsen apneas and oxygen desaturation.
  • (B) Mandibular advancement oral appliance — Oral appliances are an option for mild–moderate OSA or for patients who cannot tolerate CPAP; they are less effective in severe OSA.
  • (C) Modafinil — Modafinil treats residual sleepiness in patients already adherent to CPAP; it does not treat apneas or hypoxemia.
  • (D) Uvulopalatopharyngoplasty — Upper-airway surgery has modest, unpredictable success and is reserved for selected patients who fail or cannot use CPAP.
🧠 Mnemonic

STOP-BANG screen: Snoring, Tired, Observed apneas, Pressure (hypertension), BMI >35, Age >50, Neck >40 cm, Gender male. ≥5 = high risk.

🎓 ABIM pearl

Use in-lab polysomnography rather than a home test when the patient has significant cardiopulmonary disease, neuromuscular weakness, chronic opioid use, prior stroke or suspected hypoventilation.

🎯 Educational objective

CPAP is first-line treatment for moderate–severe obstructive sleep apnea, especially with daytime sleepiness; oral appliances are for mild–moderate disease or CPAP intolerance.

PU-005.topic: Suspected pulmonary embolism — low pretest probability
PU-005.stem_html:
A 34-year-old woman is evaluated in the emergency department for 1 day of left-sided pleuritic chest pain that began after a long day of moving furniture. She has no dyspnea, hemoptysis or leg swelling. She takes no medications, including estrogen. She has no history of venous thromboembolism, recent surgery or cancer.

On physical examination, temperature is 37.0 °C (98.6 °F), blood pressure is 122/76 mm Hg, pulse rate is 82/min, and respiration rate is 16/min. Oxygen saturation is 99% breathing ambient air. There is point tenderness over the left fifth rib that reproduces the pain. Legs are normal. ECG and chest radiograph are normal.
PU-005.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in evaluation?

choices.A: No further testing for pulmonary embolism

PU-005.explain_html:
Correct answer: A Suspected pulmonary embolism — low pretest probability

The first step in suspected PE is estimating the pretest probability (clinical gestalt, Wells or Geneva score). She has a low probability: young, normal vital signs, no risk factors, reproducible chest wall pain.

In low-probability patients, apply the PERC rule. If all 8 criteria are met, the probability of PE is <2% and no further testing is needed — not even a D-dimer:

PERC — all must be "no"
Age ≥50
Heart rate ≥100/min
SpO₂ <95%
Unilateral leg swelling
Hemoptysis
Recent surgery or trauma (≤4 weeks)
Prior VTE
Estrogen use

She is PERC-negative. Over-testing (D-dimer → CT) leads to false positives, contrast exposure and incidental findings.

If PERC is positive: D-dimer (age-adjusted if >50: age × 10 µg/L) for low/intermediate probability → CTPA if positive. High probability → CTPA directly.

Why not the others

  • (B) CT pulmonary angiography — CTPA is for high pretest probability or a positive D-dimer. It is not appropriate in a PERC-negative patient.
  • (C) Lower-extremity duplex ultrasonography — Leg ultrasonography is used when CT is contraindicated or leg symptoms are present; she has neither.
  • (D) Ventilation-perfusion scan — A V/Q scan is an alternative to CTPA in pregnancy or contrast allergy, not a test for PERC-negative patients.
  • (E) D-dimer measurement — D-dimer is the next test for low-probability patients who are not PERC-negative; she meets all PERC criteria.
🎯 Educational objective

In a patient with low clinical probability of pulmonary embolism who meets all PERC criteria, no further testing for PE is needed.

📚 Read more in Wardology🩸 Pulmonary embolism →

  2. Kline JA, et al. Prospective multicenter evaluation of the pulmonary embolism rule-out criteria. J Thromb Haemost 2008;6:772.

PU-006.stem_html:
A 58-year-old man is evaluated on postoperative day 6 after a laparoscopic colectomy for sudden dyspnea and lightheadedness. He was receiving enoxaparin prophylaxis.

On physical examination, blood pressure is 78/50 mm Hg (persisting after a 1-L fluid bolus), pulse rate is 128/min, and respiration rate is 30/min. Oxygen saturation is 86% on 6 L/min oxygen. Jugular venous pressure is elevated. His surgical wounds are healing, with no bleeding.

Bedside echocardiogram shows a dilated, hypokinetic right ventricle with a flattened septum. CT pulmonary angiography shows bilateral main pulmonary artery emboli.

Troponin Televated
Lactate4.2 mmol/L
PU-006.lead: In addition to anticoagulation with unfractionated heparin, which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?

choices.E: Additional intravenous fluid boluses of 3 L

PU-006.explain_html:
Correct answer: C High-risk (massive) pulmonary embolism

High-risk (massive) PE: acute PE with sustained hypotension (SBP <90 mm Hg for ≥15 minutes or needing vasopressors) or obstructive shock. In-hospital mortality is >25%.

The acute RV fails because it cannot handle a sudden rise in afterload. Treatment:

  • Anticoagulation with unfractionated heparin (short half-life, reversible, compatible with thrombolysis or procedures).
  • Reperfusion — systemic thrombolysis (alteplase 100 mg over 2 hours) is recommended unless contraindicated.
  • His surgery was 6 days ago — recent surgery is a relative contraindication; in a patient in shock the benefit generally outweighs bleeding risk. If thrombolysis is contraindicated or fails: catheter-directed therapy or surgical embolectomy.
  • Supportive care: cautious fluids (≤500 mL; more can overdistend the RV), norepinephrine, avoid intubation if possible (positive pressure can cause collapse).
PE risk Definition Treatment
High Hypotension/shock Anticoagulation + thrombolysis
Intermediate-high RV dysfunction + troponin, normotensive Anticoagulation, monitor; rescue lysis if deteriorates
Low Normal RV, normal troponin, sPESI 0 Anticoagulation; consider outpatient

Why not the others

  • (A) Wait 24 hours and repeat echocardiography — Delaying reperfusion in shock increases mortality.
  • (B) Switch to apixaban — Oral anticoagulants are for stable patients and do not treat obstructive shock.
  • (D) Inferior vena cava filter placement — IVC filters are for patients who cannot be anticoagulated; they do not treat existing obstruction or shock.
  • (E) Additional intravenous fluid boluses of 3 L — Large fluid volumes worsen RV dilation and septal shift, decreasing LV filling.
🎯 Educational objective

Treat high-risk pulmonary embolism with hemodynamic instability with anticoagulation plus systemic thrombolysis, unless contraindicated.

PU-007.stem_html:
A 64-year-old woman with metastatic colon adenocarcinoma receiving chemotherapy is found to have segmental pulmonary emboli on a staging CT scan. She has mild dyspnea on exertion. Her primary tumor was resected 6 months ago; she has no GI bleeding or luminal tumor. She is not taking interacting drugs.

On physical examination, blood pressure is 132/78 mm Hg, pulse rate is 88/min, and oxygen saturation is 96% breathing ambient air.

Hemoglobin11.8 g/dL
Platelet count162,000/µL
Creatinine0.8 mg/dL
PU-007.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
PU-007.explain_html:
Correct answer: B Cancer-associated venous thromboembolism

Cancer-associated VTE carries high rates of recurrence and bleeding. Options for initial and long-term treatment:

  • DOACs — apixaban, rivaroxaban, edoxaban — are recommended over LMWH (ASCO, ASH, CHEST). In trials (Caravaggio, SELECT-D, Hokusai-VTE Cancer), they reduced recurrent VTE as well as or better than dalteparin. Rivaroxaban and edoxaban raised GI/GU bleeding in luminal GI and GU cancers; apixaban did not increase major bleeding in Caravaggio.
  • LMWH remains preferred when there is a luminal GI/GU tumor in place, significant drug interactions, or poor oral intake.

Duration: at least 6 months, and indefinitely while the cancer is active or under treatment.

Why not the others

  • (A) Anticoagulation for 6 weeks — Cancer-associated VTE requires at least 6 months of therapy, continued while cancer is active.
  • (C) Warfarin with enoxaparin bridge — Warfarin is inferior to LMWH and DOACs in cancer (more recurrence, unstable INR with chemotherapy and poor intake).
  • (D) Inferior vena cava filter — An IVC filter is only for patients with acute VTE who cannot be anticoagulated.
  • (E) Aspirin — Aspirin is far less effective than anticoagulation for treating VTE.
🎯 Educational objective

Treat cancer-associated VTE with a DOAC (or LMWH, preferred for unresected luminal GI/GU tumors) for at least 6 months and as long as the cancer is active.

PU-008.stem_html:
A 72-year-old man with HFrEF (LVEF 30%) is admitted with dyspnea and a large right pleural effusion. He has been receiving IV furosemide for 3 days with improvement in edema but the effusion persists. He has a 50 pack-year smoking history.

Diagnostic thoracentesis is performed.

Serum
Total protein6.4 g/dL
Lactate dehydrogenase210 U/L (upper limit of normal, 222)
Albumin3.2 g/dL
Pleural fluid
Total protein3.4 g/dL
Lactate dehydrogenase120 U/L
Albumin1.8 g/dL
Glucose110 mg/dL
Cell count600/µL (80% lymphocytes)
PU-008.lead: Which of the following is the most likely cause of the effusion?
PU-008.explain_html:
Correct answer: B Pleural fluid — Light criteria

By Light criteria, the fluid is an exudate if any one is met:

  • Pleural/serum protein >0.5 → 3.4/6.4 = 0.53 ✔
  • Pleural/serum LDH >0.6 → 120/210 = 0.57 ✘
  • Pleural LDH >2/3 of the upper limit of normal serum LDH → 120 vs 148 ✘

He barely meets one protein criterion. Light criteria are very sensitive for exudates and misclassify about 25% of transudates as exudates — especially after diuresis, which concentrates pleural protein.

The fix: calculate the serum-to-pleural albumin gradient. A gradient >1.2 g/dL means the fluid is really a transudate. Here: 3.2 − 1.8 = 1.4 g/dL → transudate from heart failure. (A serum-to-pleural protein gradient >3.1 g/dL or a high pleural NT-proBNP also helps.)

Why not the others

  • (A) Pulmonary embolism — PE-related effusions are usually small exudates and often bloody.
  • (C) Malignancy — Malignant effusions are true exudates (often with high LDH and lymphocytes); the albumin gradient shows this is a transudate.
  • (D) Tuberculosis — Tuberculous effusions are lymphocytic exudates with high protein and adenosine deaminase.
  • (E) Parapneumonic effusion — Parapneumonic effusions are neutrophil-predominant exudates, often with low glucose and pH.
🧠 Mnemonic

Light criteria "0.5 – 0.6 – ⅔". Diuresed heart failure patient with a "borderline exudate"? Check the albumin gradient (>1.2 = transudate).

🎯 Educational objective

In patients with heart failure on diuretics, an effusion that marginally meets Light criteria for exudate is a transudate when the serum-to-pleural albumin gradient exceeds 1.2 g/dL.

PU-009.stem_html:
A 52-year-old man is hospitalized with right lower lobe pneumonia. After 3 days of IV ceftriaxone and azithromycin, he still has fever and right-sided pleuritic pain.

On physical examination, temperature is 38.6 °C (101.5 °F), pulse rate is 104/min. There is dullness to percussion and decreased breath sounds at the right base.

Chest ultrasonography shows a moderate free-flowing effusion with a few septations. Thoracentesis yields cloudy, nonpurulent fluid.

Pleural fluid pH7.05
Pleural fluid glucose38 mg/dL
Pleural fluid LDH1,450 U/L
Pleural fluid Gram stainno organisms
PU-009.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.C: Video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery as the first intervention
choices.D: Change antibiotics to piperacillin-tazobactam and observe

PU-009.explain_html:
Correct answer: A Complicated parapneumonic effusion

He has a complicated parapneumonic effusion: pH <7.20, glucose <60 mg/dL, high LDH and septations. Bacteria have invaded the pleural space even though the Gram stain is negative. These effusions will not resolve with antibiotics alone and progress to empyema and fibrothorax.

Effusion Findings Management
Uncomplicated pH ≥7.20, glucose ≥60, no organisms Antibiotics alone
Complicated pH <7.20, glucose <60, LDH >1000, or positive Gram stain/culture Chest tube drainage + antibiotics
Empyema Frank pus Chest tube + antibiotics

If drainage is incomplete because of loculations, give intrapleural tPA plus DNase (MIST-2); refer for VATS if that fails. Broaden antibiotics to cover anaerobes (e.g., ampicillin-sulbactam) for 2–6 weeks.

Why not the others

  • (B) Repeat thoracentesis in 1 week — Delay allows loculation and empyema to develop.
  • (C) Video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery as the first intervention — Surgery is reserved for failure of tube drainage and fibrinolytics, or for organized empyema.
  • (D) Change antibiotics to piperacillin-tazobactam and observe — Changing antibiotics alone does not drain an infected pleural space.
  • (E) Add intravenous glucocorticoids — Glucocorticoids have no role in parapneumonic effusion.
🎯 Educational objective

Drain a parapneumonic effusion with a chest tube when the pleural fluid pH is below 7.20, glucose is below 60 mg/dL, or the Gram stain or culture is positive.

PU-010.stem_html:
A 22-year-old man is evaluated for sudden right-sided chest pain and mild shortness of breath that began 3 hours ago while he was sitting at his desk. He smokes cigarettes and marijuana. He has no lung disease. This is his first episode.

On physical examination, blood pressure is 124/76 mm Hg, pulse rate is 92/min, and respiration rate is 18/min. Oxygen saturation is 96% breathing ambient air. He is tall and thin. Breath sounds are decreased on the right. The trachea is midline.

Chest radiograph shows a right apical pneumothorax with a 2.5-cm interpleural distance at the hilum. There is no mediastinal shift.
PU-010.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

choices.C: Large-bore (28 F) chest tube and admission
choices.D: Observation or needle aspiration, with outpatient follow-up and smoking cessation

PU-010.explain_html:
Correct answer: D Primary spontaneous pneumothorax

Primary spontaneous pneumothorax (PSP) occurs in tall, thin young men who smoke, without known lung disease, from rupture of apical blebs. He is stable, with few symptoms.

Current guidance (BTS 2023) favors conservative management for stable PSP:

  • Minimal symptoms → observation alone, even for larger pneumothoraces (the PSP trial showed conservative care was noninferior with fewer complications and recurrences).
  • Significant symptoms → needle aspiration or a small-bore (≤14 F) drain/ambulatory device.
  • Large-bore chest tubes are rarely needed.

Smoking cessation (tobacco and cannabis) greatly reduces recurrence. Advise no flying until resolved and no scuba diving unless definitive surgery is done.

Surgery (VATS bullectomy + pleurodesis) is for recurrence, persistent air leak (>3–5 days), bilateral pneumothorax, or high-risk occupations (pilots, divers).

Why not the others

  • (A) Video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery with pleurodesis — Surgery is not indicated for a first episode of PSP without complications or special occupational needs.
  • (B) Emergency needle decompression — Needle decompression is for tension pneumothorax (hypotension, tracheal deviation, hypoxemia), which he does not have.
  • (C) Large-bore (28 F) chest tube and admission — Large-bore tubes are more painful and have no advantage over conservative care or small drains in PSP.
  • (E) Admission for 100% oxygen for 1 week — Supplemental oxygen speeds resorption slightly, but prolonged hospitalization for oxygen alone is not appropriate.
🎯 Educational objective

Manage a stable, first primary spontaneous pneumothorax conservatively (observation or needle aspiration/small-bore drainage) and advise smoking cessation.
