PU-011.stem_html:
A 71-year-old man is evaluated for 18 months of progressive exertional dyspnea and a dry cough. He is a former smoker (30 pack-years). He worked as an accountant and has no birds, mold exposure or relevant medications. He has no joint pain, rash or Raynaud phenomenon.

On physical examination, oxygen saturation is 94% at rest, falling to 86% after walking. There are bibasilar inspiratory "Velcro" crackles and digital clubbing.

High-resolution CT shows subpleural, basal-predominant reticulation with honeycombing and traction bronchiectasis, without ground-glass opacity (usual interstitial pneumonia pattern). Autoimmune serologies are negative. Pulmonary function tests show FVC 64% predicted and DLCO 42% predicted.
PU-011.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?

choices.A: No treatment until FVC falls below 50% predicted

PU-011.explain_html:
Correct answer: D Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis

Older ex-smoker, progressive dyspnea, Velcro crackles, clubbing, a restrictive pattern with low DLCO, definite UIP pattern on HRCT and no exposures or connective tissue disease = idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF). With a typical clinical picture and definite UIP on HRCT, lung biopsy is not needed.

IPF is fibrosis, not inflammation. Antifibrotics — nintedanib or pirfenidone — slow FVC decline by about 50% and are recommended for patients with IPF at diagnosis. Newer agents such as nerandomilast (a PDE4B inhibitor) are adding options.

Supportive care: supplemental oxygen for exertional desaturation, pulmonary rehabilitation, vaccinations, treat reflux symptoms, and early lung transplant referral.

Why not the others

  • (A) No treatment until FVC falls below 50% predicted — Antifibrotics slow decline regardless of disease severity; waiting allows irreversible loss of lung function.
  • (B) Mycophenolate mofetil — Mycophenolate is used for connective tissue disease–associated ILD (e.g., scleroderma), not IPF.
  • (C) Prednisone, 60 mg/d — Glucocorticoids do not help IPF and cause harm; they are used only for acute exacerbations (weak evidence).
  • (E) Azathioprine, prednisone and N-acetylcysteine — Triple therapy with azathioprine, prednisone and NAC increased mortality in IPF (PANTHER-IPF) and is contraindicated.
🎯 Educational objective

Treat idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis with an antifibrotic agent (nintedanib or pirfenidone) and avoid glucocorticoid-based immunosuppression.

PU-012.stem_html:
A 32-year-old woman is evaluated for 2 weeks of painful red bumps on her shins, ankle pain and swelling on both sides, and low-grade fevers. She has no cough or dyspnea.

On physical examination, temperature is 37.8 °C (100.0 °F). There are tender, warm, erythematous nodules on both anterior shins. Both ankles are swollen and tender with periarticular erythema. Lungs are clear.

Chest radiograph shows bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy without parenchymal opacities.

Calcium9.6 mg/dL
Creatinine0.7 mg/dL
Antistreptolysin Onormal
Interferon-γ release assaynegative
Pulmonary function testsnormal
PU-012.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
PU-012.explain_html:
Correct answer: A Löfgren syndrome (acute sarcoidosis)

The combination of erythema nodosum, bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy, acute polyarthritis (classically periarticular ankle inflammation) and fever is Löfgren syndrome, an acute form of sarcoidosis.

The clinical picture is so specific that biopsy is not needed (ATS 2020) once TB, lymphoma, fungal infection and streptococcal infection are reasonably excluded. Löfgren syndrome has an excellent prognosis: more than 90% of patients have spontaneous remission within 1–2 years.

Treatment is supportive — NSAIDs for joint pain and erythema nodosum. Short-course glucocorticoids are used only for severe symptoms. Monitor with clinical follow-up and chest imaging; screen all sarcoidosis patients for eye involvement, cardiac involvement (ECG), hypercalcemia and kidney function.

Why not the others

  • (B) Prednisone, 40 mg/d for 6 months — Prolonged high-dose glucocorticoids are for organ-threatening sarcoidosis (symptomatic lung impairment, heart, eye, CNS, hypercalcemia); Löfgren syndrome resolves on its own.
  • (C) Endobronchial ultrasound–guided lymph node biopsy — Biopsy is not required for a classic Löfgren presentation; tissue is needed when the presentation is atypical.
  • (D) Methotrexate — Methotrexate is a glucocorticoid-sparing drug for chronic, symptomatic sarcoidosis.
  • (E) Mediastinoscopy — Mediastinoscopy is more invasive than EBUS and unnecessary here.
🎯 Educational objective

Diagnose Löfgren syndrome clinically (erythema nodosum, hilar adenopathy, ankle arthritis, fever) and treat with NSAIDs and observation without biopsy.

PU-013.stem_html:
A 56-year-old woman is evaluated for 6 months of cough and exertional dyspnea. She has never smoked. She notices that her symptoms improve when she travels for a week but return after she comes home. She keeps three pet parakeets in her living room and uses a down comforter.

On physical examination, there are fine inspiratory crackles and inspiratory squeaks. There is no clubbing.

High-resolution CT shows ground-glass opacities and centrilobular nodules in the upper and mid lungs, with mosaic attenuation and air trapping on expiratory images. Pulmonary function tests show a mild restrictive pattern with a reduced DLCO.
PU-013.lead: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
PU-013.explain_html:
Correct answer: A Hypersensitivity pneumonitis

Hypersensitivity pneumonitis (HP) is an immune reaction (type III and IV) to an inhaled antigen — here, bird proteins ("bird fancier's lung"; feather bedding counts too). Symptoms that improve away from home point to a home exposure.

HRCT findings typical of HP:

  • Centrilobular nodules and ground-glass opacities (upper/mid zones)
  • Mosaic attenuation with air trapping on expiration (small airway involvement)
  • The "three-density" pattern (normal lung, ground glass, air-trapped lung)

Without significant fibrosis (no reticulation or honeycombing), this is nonfibrotic HP, which has a good prognosis. BAL lymphocytosis (>30%) supports the diagnosis.

The most important treatment is antigen avoidance — remove the birds and feather bedding. Glucocorticoids are used for persistent or severe disease. Fibrotic HP behaves more like IPF.

Why not the others

  • (B) Chronic eosinophilic pneumonia — Chronic eosinophilic pneumonia shows peripheral consolidation ("photographic negative of pulmonary edema") and blood/BAL eosinophilia.
  • (C) Sarcoidosis — Sarcoidosis typically shows hilar lymphadenopathy and perilymphatic nodules, not centrilobular nodules with air trapping.
  • (D) Fibrotic hypersensitivity pneumonitis — Fibrotic HP shows reticulation, traction bronchiectasis or honeycombing; these are absent.
  • (E) Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis — IPF shows basal, subpleural reticulation with honeycombing and no air trapping or centrilobular nodules, and does not improve away from home.
🎯 Educational objective

Recognize hypersensitivity pneumonitis by exposure history, centrilobular nodules, ground glass and mosaic attenuation with air trapping, and treat with antigen avoidance.

On physical examination, there are fine inspiratory crackles and inspiratory squeaks. There is no clubbing. PU-013.search: a 56-year-old woman is evaluated for 6 months of cough and exertional dyspnea. she has never smoked. she notices that her symptoms improve when she travels for a week but return after she comes home. she keeps three pet parakeets in her living room and uses a down comforter. on physical examination, there are fine inspiratory crackles and inspiratory squeaks. there is no clubbing. high-resolution ct shows ground-glass opacities and centrilobular nodules in the upper and mid lungs, with mosaic attenuation and air trapping on expiratory images. pulmonary function tests show a mild restrictive pattern with a reduced dlco. correct answer: a hypersensitivity pneumonitis hypersensitivity pneumonitis (hp) is an immune reaction (type iii and iv) to an inhaled antigen — here, bird proteins ( "bird fancier's lung" ; feather bedding counts too). symptoms that improve away from home point to a home exposure. hrct findings typical of hp: centrilobular nodules and ground-glass opacities (upper/mid zones) mosaic attenuation with air trapping on expiration (small airway involvement) the "three-density" pattern (normal lung, ground glass, air-trapped lung) without significant fibrosis (no reticulation or honeycombing), this is nonfibrotic hp , which has a good prognosis. bal lymphocytosis (>30%) supports the diagnosis. the most important treatment is antigen avoidance — remove the birds and feather bedding. glucocorticoids are used for persistent or severe disease. fibrotic hp behaves more like ipf. why not the others (b) chronic eosinophilic pneumonia — chronic eosinophilic pneumonia shows peripheral consolidation ("photographic negative of pulmonary edema") and blood/bal eosinophilia. (c) sarcoidosis — sarcoidosis typically shows hilar lymphadenopathy and perilymphatic nodules, not centrilobular nodules with air trapping. (d) fibrotic hypersensitivity pneumonitis — fibrotic hp shows reticulation, traction bronchiectasis or honeycombing; these are absent. (e) idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis — ipf shows basal, subpleural reticulation with honeycombing and no air trapping or centrilobular nodules, and does not improve away from home. 🎯 educational objective recognize hypersensitivity pneumonitis by exposure history, centrilobular nodules, ground glass and mosaic attenuation with air trapping, and treat with antigen avoidance. 📚 read more in wardology 🕸️ interstitial lung disease & sarcoidosis → references {'raghu g, et al. diagnosis of hypersensitivity pneumonitis in adults': 'an official ats/jrs/alat clinical practice guideline. am j respir crit care med 2020;202:e36.'}  hypersensitivity pneumonitis

PU-014.stem_html:
A 61-year-old woman is evaluated for 2 years of chronic morning cough with sputum and gradually worsening dyspnea when climbing stairs. She has smoked one pack of cigarettes daily for 40 years. A clinician prescribed an albuterol inhaler last year, which she uses twice a day with some relief.

On physical examination, there is prolonged expiration and scattered wheezes. Oxygen saturation is 95% breathing ambient air.
PU-014.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate diagnostic test?

choices.D: Spirometry before and after a bronchodilator

PU-014.explain_html:
Correct answer: D Diagnosing COPD — spirometry

COPD is suspected in anyone with dyspnea, chronic cough or sputum and risk factors (tobacco, biomass, occupational dust). The diagnosis requires spirometry: a post-bronchodilator FEV₁/FVC ratio <0.70 confirms persistent airflow obstruction. Severity (GOLD 1–4) is graded by FEV₁ % predicted, while treatment is guided by symptoms and exacerbation history (GOLD groups A, B, E).

Many patients are labeled with COPD — and treated — without spirometry; up to a third of them do not have airflow obstruction.

Once COPD is confirmed: smoking cessation (with long-term oxygen for resting hypoxemia, one of the few interventions that lowers mortality), vaccinations, a long-acting bronchodilator, pulmonary rehabilitation, and alpha-1 antitrypsin testing once for all patients with COPD.

Why not the others

  • (A) CT of the chest — CT can show emphysema and screen for lung cancer, but it does not establish airflow obstruction.
  • (B) Peak expiratory flow measurement — Peak flow is useful for monitoring asthma but is not sensitive or specific enough to diagnose COPD.
  • (C) Arterial blood gas — A blood gas assesses gas exchange in severe or acute disease; it does not diagnose COPD.
  • (E) Chest radiograph — A chest radiograph may show hyperinflation but cannot confirm or exclude COPD.
🎯 Educational objective

Confirm COPD with spirometry showing a post-bronchodilator FEV₁/FVC ratio below 0.70 in a symptomatic patient with risk factors.

PU-015.stem_html:
A 67-year-old man with severe COPD (FEV₁ 38% predicted) is brought to the emergency department with 3 days of increased dyspnea, cough and purulent sputum. He uses tiotropium-olodaterol.

On physical examination, temperature is 37.6 °C (99.7 °F), pulse rate is 108/min, and respiration rate is 28/min. He uses accessory muscles and speaks in short phrases. Oxygen saturation is 84% breathing ambient air. There are diffuse wheezes. He is alert and follows commands.

Chest radiograph shows hyperinflation without infiltrate.

Arterial pH7.29
Arterial Pco₂64 mm Hg
Arterial Po₂50 mm Hg
PU-015.lead: In addition to inhaled bronchodilators and controlled oxygen to a saturation of 88–92%, which of the following is the most appropriate management?

choices.A: High-flow oxygen by nonrebreather mask to an SpO₂ of 100%
choices.C: Intravenous methylprednisolone 125 mg every 6 hours for 14 days
choices.D: Antibiotics, prednisone 40 mg/d for 5 days and noninvasive positive-pressure ventilation

PU-015.explain_html:
Correct answer: D COPD exacerbation — hospital management

An acute COPD exacerbation with acute-on-chronic hypercapnic respiratory failure (pH 7.29, Pco₂ 64). The bundle:

  1. Controlled oxygen to SpO₂ 88–92% — excess oxygen worsens hypercapnia (V/Q mismatch, Haldane effect).
  2. Short-acting bronchodilators (albuterol ± ipratropium).
  3. Systemic glucocorticoids — prednisone 40 mg for 5 days (REDUCE trial: as good as 14 days).
  4. Antibiotics when sputum is purulent plus increased dyspnea or volume, or when ventilatory support is needed (e.g., amoxicillin-clavulanate, doxycycline, azithromycin).
  5. Noninvasive ventilation (BiPAP) for pH ≤7.35 and Pco₂ >45 — reduces intubation and mortality.

Intubate if NIV fails, or if the patient cannot protect the airway, is obtunded, has hemodynamic instability or copious secretions.

Why not the others

  • (A) High-flow oxygen by nonrebreather mask to an SpO₂ of 100% — Uncontrolled high-flow oxygen raises Pco₂ and worsens acidosis in hypercapnic COPD.
  • (B) Endotracheal intubation now — He is alert and cooperative, so NIV should be tried first; it reduces the need for intubation and mortality.
  • (C) Intravenous methylprednisolone 125 mg every 6 hours for 14 days — High-dose, prolonged IV glucocorticoids add side effects without better outcomes than 5 days of oral prednisone.
  • (E) Intravenous theophylline — Theophylline has a narrow therapeutic window and adds toxicity without benefit in exacerbations.
🧠 Mnemonic

COPD flare = "ABCDO" — Antibiotics, Bronchodilators, Corticosteroids, Delivery of NIV, Oxygen 88–92%.

🎯 Educational objective

Treat a COPD exacerbation with hypercapnic acidosis with bronchodilators, 5 days of prednisone, antibiotics for purulent sputum, controlled oxygen and noninvasive ventilation.

PU-016.stem_html:
A 69-year-old woman with severe COPD is evaluated 6 weeks after hospitalization for an exacerbation. She now feels at her baseline and has stopped smoking. She uses budesonide-glycopyrrolate-formoterol daily.

On physical examination, she is at rest. Oxygen saturation is 87% breathing ambient air (confirmed on two readings 3 weeks apart). There is mild ankle edema.

Arterial Po₂ (ambient airat rest), 54 mm Hg
Hematocrit49%
Echocardiogrammild right ventricular dilation
PU-016.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

choices.A: No oxygen because she is no longer in an exacerbation
choices.D: Long-term supplemental oxygen for at least 15 hours per day

PU-016.explain_html:
Correct answer: D Long-term oxygen therapy in COPD

Long-term oxygen therapy (LTOT) is one of the few treatments that prolongs survival in COPD (NOTT and MRC trials) — when given for ≥15 hours per day (continuous is best).

Indications (resting, stable, ≥30 days after an exacerbation, on ambient air):

  • Pao₂ ≤55 mm Hg or SpO₂ ≤88%, or
  • Pao₂ 56–59 mm Hg or SpO₂ 89% with cor pulmonale (edema, RV dysfunction) or hematocrit >55%

She qualifies on the first criterion. Titrate to SpO₂ ≥90% at rest, during exertion and sleep.

In contrast, the LOTT trial found no survival benefit for oxygen in moderate resting or exercise-induced desaturation (SpO₂ 89–93%).

Why not the others

  • (A) No oxygen because she is no longer in an exacerbation — Her hypoxemia persists in the stable state (more than 30 days after the exacerbation), which is the indication for LTOT.
  • (B) Phlebotomy — Her hematocrit is only mildly raised; secondary polycythemia improves with oxygen, and phlebotomy is not indicated.
  • (C) Oxygen only during exertion — Exertional oxygen alone does not provide the survival benefit of continuous oxygen in resting hypoxemia.
  • (E) Nocturnal oxygen only — Nocturnal oxygen alone did not improve survival in NOTT; patients with resting hypoxemia need ≥15 h/day.
🎯 Educational objective

Prescribe long-term oxygen for at least 15 hours daily to stable patients with COPD with resting Pao₂ ≤55 mm Hg or SpO₂ ≤88% (or 56–59 mm Hg with cor pulmonale or erythrocytosis).

PU-017.stem_html:
A 44-year-old man is evaluated for 2 years of progressive exertional dyspnea. He smoked 10 cigarettes a day for 15 years and quit 5 years ago. His father died of "emphysema and liver disease" at age 55.

On physical examination, there is reduced breath sounds and prolonged expiration. Oxygen saturation is 94% breathing ambient air.

Spirometry shows a post-bronchodilator FEV₁/FVC ratio of 0.52 and an FEV₁ of 48% predicted. Chest radiograph shows hyperlucency at the lung bases.
PU-017.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate next diagnostic test?

choices.B: Serum alpha-1 antitrypsin level (with phenotype or genotype)

PU-017.explain_html:
Correct answer: B Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency

Early-onset emphysema (age <45), modest smoking history, basilar-predominant (panlobular) emphysema and a family history of emphysema and liver disease → alpha-1 antitrypsin (AAT) deficiency.

AAT, made in the liver, protects the lung against neutrophil elastase. In the PiZZ genotype, misfolded protein is trapped in hepatocytes (→ cirrhosis, HCC) and too little reaches the lung (→ emphysema).

Test with a serum AAT level plus phenotype or genotype. Guidelines recommend testing every patient with COPD once, regardless of age or smoking history, and people with unexplained liver disease, bronchiectasis or necrotizing panniculitis.

For severe deficiency with emphysema: IV augmentation therapy (pooled AAT), absolute avoidance of smoking, standard COPD care, and screening of family members.

Why not the others

  • (A) Methacholine challenge — A methacholine challenge tests for asthma in patients with normal spirometry; he already has fixed obstruction.
  • (C) Sweat chloride test — Sweat chloride testing is for cystic fibrosis, which presents with bronchiectasis, sinusitis and pancreatic insufficiency, not basilar emphysema.
  • (D) High-resolution CT for bronchiectasis — Bronchiectasis can occur in AAT deficiency, but the key diagnostic test is the AAT level.
  • (E) Serum IgE level — IgE helps evaluate allergic asthma or ABPA, not early emphysema.
🎯 Educational objective

Test for alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency in all patients with COPD, especially those with early-onset, basilar-predominant emphysema or a family history.

PU-018.stem_html:
A 46-year-old woman with asthma is evaluated for frequent exacerbations: she has needed oral prednisone four times in the past year. She uses high-dose fluticasone-salmeterol twice daily and tiotropium, with confirmed good inhaler technique and adherence. She has nasal polyps. She does not smoke. GERD and obesity have been addressed.

On physical examination, there are scattered expiratory wheezes.

Blood eosinophil count620/µL
Total IgE80 IU/mL
FEV₁62% predicted with 18% bronchodilator response
PU-018.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate addition to her therapy?

choices.C: An anti–IL-5 or anti–IL-5 receptor monoclonal antibody

PU-018.explain_html:
Correct answer: C Severe eosinophilic asthma — biologic therapy

She has severe asthma: uncontrolled despite high-dose ICS–LABA plus a LAMA (GINA step 5), with adherence, technique and comorbidities addressed. Her blood eosinophils ≥300/µL, nasal polyps and frequent exacerbations mark a type 2 eosinophilic phenotype.

Anti–IL-5 / IL-5R biologics (mepolizumab, reslizumab, benralizumab) reduce exacerbations by about 50% and cut oral steroid use in eosinophilic asthma. Dupilumab (anti–IL-4Rα) and tezepelumab (anti-TSLP, works regardless of eosinophils) are also options; dupilumab is attractive with nasal polyps.

Biologic Target Best fit
Omalizumab IgE Allergic asthma, IgE 30–700 with perennial sensitization
Mepolizumab, benralizumab, reslizumab IL-5 / IL-5R Eosinophils ≥150–300
Dupilumab IL-4Rα Eosinophilic or allergic; nasal polyps, eczema
Tezepelumab TSLP Broad, incl. low eosinophils

Why not the others

  • (A) Theophylline — Theophylline is a weak bronchodilator with a narrow therapeutic window and is rarely used.
  • (B) Daily oral prednisone, 10 mg — Maintenance oral glucocorticoids cause cumulative toxicity (osteoporosis, diabetes, cataracts, infection) and are the last resort.
  • (D) Montelukast as the next step — Montelukast adds little at step 5 and carries a boxed warning for neuropsychiatric effects.
  • (E) Omalizumab — Omalizumab is for allergic asthma with a documented sensitization and appropriate IgE; her phenotype is eosinophilic with a low IgE.
🎯 Educational objective

Add an anti–IL-5/IL-5R biologic (or another type 2 biologic) for severe eosinophilic asthma uncontrolled on high-dose ICS–LABA and LAMA.

PU-019.stem_html:
A 38-year-old man with asthma since childhood is evaluated for worsening control over the past year. He has had three courses of prednisone. He coughs up brownish mucus plugs. His asthma improved each time he received prednisone.

On physical examination, there are scattered wheezes.

High-resolution CT shows central (proximal) bronchiectasis with mucus plugging in the upper lobes.

Blood eosinophil count1,100/µL
Total serum IgE2,800 IU/mL
Aspergillus fumigatus–specific IgEelevated
Aspergillus precipitins (IgG)positive
PU-019.lead: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
PU-019.explain_html:
Correct answer: D Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis

Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis (ABPA) is a hypersensitivity (type I and III) reaction to Aspergillus colonizing the airways of patients with asthma or cystic fibrosis.

Clues: poorly controlled asthma, brown mucus plugs, central bronchiectasis, very high total IgE (>1,000 IU/mL), Aspergillus-specific IgE, eosinophilia and precipitating IgG antibodies.

Treatment: oral glucocorticoids for flares plus an azole (itraconazole or voriconazole) to reduce the fungal burden and steroid needs. Biologics (omalizumab, mepolizumab, dupilumab) are steroid-sparing options. Follow total IgE to monitor activity.

Why not the others

  • (A) Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis — EGPA causes asthma and eosinophilia but also vasculitis (neuropathy, purpura, kidney disease) and is often p-ANCA positive; it does not cause high Aspergillus-specific IgE.
  • (B) Cystic fibrosis — Cystic fibrosis can coexist with ABPA but presents in childhood with pancreatic insufficiency and recurrent infections.
  • (C) Invasive aspergillosis — Invasive aspergillosis occurs in severely immunocompromised patients (neutropenia, transplant) with nodules and a halo sign.
  • (E) Chronic cavitary pulmonary aspergillosis — Chronic cavitary aspergillosis occurs in patients with structural lung disease (prior TB, COPD) and causes cavities and aspergillomas, not central bronchiectasis with high IgE.
🎯 Educational objective

Recognize ABPA in a patient with asthma, central bronchiectasis, mucus plugs, very high total IgE and Aspergillus-specific IgE, and treat with glucocorticoids plus an azole.

PU-020.stem_html:
A 54-year-old woman is intubated for septic shock from pneumonia. She is 165 cm (65 in) tall and weighs 110 kg (243 lb). Her predicted body weight is 57 kg.

Ventilator settings are volume control, tidal volume 700 mL, respiration rate 16/min, PEEP 5 cm H₂O and Fio₂ 0.8.

Chest radiograph shows bilateral diffuse alveolar opacities. Echocardiogram shows normal left ventricular function.

Arterial pH7.32
Arterial Pco₂42 mm Hg
Arterial Po₂72 mm Hg
Plateau pressure34 cm H₂O
PU-020.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate ventilator change?

choices.A: Decrease tidal volume to 340 mL (6 mL/kg of predicted body weight) and increase PEEP
choices.B: Decrease tidal volume to 660 mL (6 mL/kg of actual body weight)
choices.C: Keep current settings and increase Fio₂ to 1.0
choices.D: Increase tidal volume to 800 mL to improve oxygenation
choices.E: Decrease PEEP to 0 cm H₂O to lower plateau pressure

PU-020.explain_html:
Correct answer: A ARDS — lung-protective ventilation

She has ARDS (Berlin definition): acute onset, bilateral opacities not explained by heart failure, and Pao₂/Fio₂ = 72/0.8 = 90 → severe (<100).

Lung-protective ventilation (ARDSNet) saves lives:

  • Tidal volume 4–8 mL/kg (target 6) of PREDICTED body weight — based on height and sex, not actual weight (lungs don't grow with obesity). 6 × 57 ≈ 340 mL. Her 700 mL ≈ 12 mL/kg PBW — the volume that increased mortality in the ARDSNet trial.
  • Plateau pressure ≤30 cm H₂O.
  • Higher PEEP for moderate–severe ARDS, using a PEEP/Fio₂ table.
  • Accept permissive hypercapnia (pH ≥7.20–7.25).

For severe ARDS (P/F <150): prone positioning ≥12–16 h/day (PROSEVA, lowered mortality), and consider neuromuscular blockade or ECMO in refractory cases. Use a conservative fluid strategy once shock resolves.

Why not the others

  • (B) Decrease tidal volume to 660 mL (6 mL/kg of actual body weight) — Tidal volume must be calculated from predicted body weight; using actual weight in obesity gives dangerously large volumes.
  • (C) Keep current settings and increase Fio₂ to 1.0 — Raising Fio₂ without reducing tidal volume leaves injurious ventilation in place and risks oxygen toxicity.
  • (D) Increase tidal volume to 800 mL to improve oxygenation — Larger tidal volumes cause volutrauma and increase mortality.
  • (E) Decrease PEEP to 0 cm H₂O to lower plateau pressure — Removing PEEP causes alveolar collapse (atelectrauma) and worsens hypoxemia.
🎯 Educational objective

Ventilate ARDS with a tidal volume of about 6 mL/kg of predicted body weight, a plateau pressure of 30 cm H₂O or less and adequate PEEP.

PU-021.stem_html:
A 36-year-old woman is evaluated for 1 year of progressive exertional dyspnea and two episodes of near-syncope while climbing stairs. She has no history of lung disease, VTE or connective tissue disease. She used an appetite suppressant (fenfluramine-phentermine) for weight loss 10 years ago.

On physical examination, there is a loud P₂, a right ventricular heave and a holosystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border that increases with inspiration. There is mild ankle edema. Lungs are clear.

Transthoracic echocardiogram shows a dilated right ventricle, estimated pulmonary artery systolic pressure 68 mm Hg and normal left ventricular size and function. Pulmonary function tests and HRCT of the chest are normal. Ventilation-perfusion scan is normal.
PU-021.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate next diagnostic test?
PU-021.explain_html:
Correct answer: E Pulmonary hypertension — diagnosis

Echocardiography suggests pulmonary hypertension (PH), but it only estimates pressures. The diagnosis requires right heart catheterization (RHC):

  • Mean pulmonary artery pressure >20 mm Hg
  • Pre-capillary PH (group 1, 3, 4): PAWP ≤15 mm Hg and PVR >2 Wood units

The work-up looks for the group first:

Group Cause Test
1 PAH — idiopathic, heritable, drugs (fenfluramine, methamphetamine), CTD, HIV, portal hypertension RHC (+ vasoreactivity testing)
2 Left heart disease (most common) Echo
3 Lung disease / hypoxia PFTs, HRCT, sleep study
4 CTEPH V/Q scan (the screening test)
5 Unclear/multifactorial —

Her left heart, lungs and V/Q scan are normal, so group 1 PAH (here likely drug-associated) is most likely; RHC confirms it, measures severity and includes vasoreactivity testing (responders can be treated with calcium channel blockers).

Why not the others

  • (A) CT pulmonary angiography — The normal V/Q scan already excludes CTEPH, and it is more sensitive than CTPA for chronic thromboembolic disease.
  • (B) Cardiac MRI — Cardiac MRI assesses RV function and prognosis but does not measure pulmonary pressures or PVR.
  • (C) Polysomnography — Sleep apnea causes mild PH; her pressures and drug history point elsewhere, and RHC is still needed for diagnosis.
  • (D) Exercise echocardiography — Exercise echocardiography does not establish the diagnosis of PH.
🎯 Educational objective

Confirm suspected pulmonary hypertension with right heart catheterization after evaluating for left heart disease, lung disease and CTEPH (with a V/Q scan).

📚 Read more in Wardology📈 Pulmonary hypertension →

PU-022.stem_html:
A 26-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department after being found unresponsive at a party. Her friends say she took "a handful of pills". She has a respiration rate of 6/min with shallow breaths. Pupils are pinpoint.

Her lungs are clear and chest radiograph is normal.

Arterial pH (ambient air)7.21
Arterial Pco₂70 mm Hg
Arterial Po₂58 mm Hg
Fio₂0.21 at sea level
PU-022.lead: Which of the following is the most likely mechanism of her hypoxemia?
PU-022.explain_html:
Correct answer: D Hypoxemia — A–a gradient

Calculate the alveolar–arterial (A–a) oxygen gradient:

PAo₂ = Fio₂ × (760 − 47) − Pco₂/0.8 = 0.21 × 713 − 70/0.8 = 150 − 87.5 = 62.5 mm Hg

A–a gradient = 62.5 − 58 = 4.5 mm Hg — normal (normal is <10–15 mm Hg in young adults; roughly age/4 + 4).

A normal A–a gradient with hypoxemia means the lungs are exchanging gas normally; the problem is getting air in. With a high Pco₂, slow respirations and pinpoint pupils, the cause is hypoventilation from opioid overdose. Treat with naloxone and ventilatory support.

Mechanism A–a gradient Corrects with O₂?
Hypoventilation Normal Yes
Low inspired O₂ (altitude) Normal Yes
V/Q mismatch (COPD, PE, pneumonia) ↑ Yes
Shunt (ARDS, AVM, intracardiac) ↑ Poorly
Diffusion limitation (ILD) ↑ Yes

Why not the others

  • (A) Low inspired oxygen — Low inspired oxygen occurs at altitude; she is at sea level breathing room air.
  • (B) Right-to-left shunt — Shunt widens the A–a gradient and responds poorly to supplemental oxygen.
  • (C) Ventilation-perfusion mismatch — V/Q mismatch, the most common cause of hypoxemia, widens the A–a gradient.
  • (E) Diffusion impairment — Diffusion impairment (e.g., ILD) increases the A–a gradient and is worsened by exercise.
🎯 Educational objective

Hypoxemia with a normal A–a gradient and hypercapnia indicates hypoventilation, as in opioid overdose.

PU-023.stem_html:
A 55-year-old man with COPD and hypertension wants to quit smoking. He smokes 25 cigarettes daily and has his first cigarette within 5 minutes of waking. He tried nicotine patches alone 2 years ago and relapsed after a month. He has no history of seizures, eating disorders or psychiatric illness. He had a myocardial infarction 3 years ago and is now stable.

On physical examination, blood pressure is 132/80 mm Hg.
PU-023.lead: Which of the following is the most effective pharmacotherapy?
PU-023.explain_html:
Correct answer: B Tobacco cessation pharmacotherapy

Varenicline (a partial agonist at the α4β2 nicotinic receptor) is the most effective single drug for smoking cessation. It reduces cravings and blunts the reward of smoking. The ATS 2020 guideline recommends varenicline over nicotine patch and over bupropion for tobacco-dependent adults.

Key facts for the boards:

  • Safe in stable cardiovascular disease and in psychiatric illness — EAGLES found no significant increase in neuropsychiatric events, and the FDA removed the boxed warning in 2016.
  • Start 1 week before the quit date (or use a flexible quit approach); continue for 12 weeks or longer; side effects are nausea and vivid dreams.
  • Combination NRT (patch + short-acting gum/lozenge) is about as effective as varenicline and is a strong alternative; varenicline + patch is even more effective.
  • Always combine with behavioral counseling.

Why not the others

  • (A) Nortriptyline — Nortriptyline is a second-line agent with anticholinergic and cardiac side effects, a poor choice after MI.
  • (C) Bupropion alone — Bupropion is less effective than varenicline; it also lowers the seizure threshold.
  • (D) Electronic cigarettes as first-line therapy — E-cigarettes may help some smokers quit, but they are not FDA-approved cessation aids and are not recommended as first-line therapy over proven drugs.
  • (E) Nicotine gum alone, as needed — As-needed gum alone is less effective than varenicline or combination NRT, especially in heavy, highly dependent smokers.
🎯 Educational objective

Varenicline is the most effective single pharmacotherapy for tobacco cessation and is safe in patients with stable cardiovascular disease.

RH-001.stem_html:
A 66-year-old man comes to the office with 1 day of severe pain, redness and swelling of his right first metatarsophalangeal joint. He had two similar episodes last year. Allopurinol 100 mg daily was started 4 months ago and increased to 200 mg daily 6 weeks ago. He also has hypertension and chronic kidney disease. Medications are allopurinol, amlodipine and losartan. He stopped taking the colchicine prescribed with allopurinol after 2 months.

Temperature is 37.4 °C (99.3 °F). The right first MTP joint is red, warm, swollen and too tender to touch. No tophi are seen.

Creatinine1.8 mg/dL (eGFR 38 mL/min/1.73 m²)
Serum urate7.4 mg/dL
Leukocyte count9,600/µL
RH-001.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

choices.A: Continue allopurinol and start oral prednisone for a short course
choices.B: Increase allopurinol to 600 mg daily as the only change
choices.C: Stop allopurinol until the flare resolves; start indomethacin
choices.D: Stop allopurinol and switch to febuxostat

RH-001.explain_html:
Correct answer: A Gout flare during urate-lowering therapy

Flares are common in the first months of urate-lowering therapy (ULT) — falling urate levels mobilize crystals from tissue deposits. That is a reason to keep ULT going, treat the flare, and use prophylaxis.

Treat the flare with any of the three anti-inflammatory options, choosing by comorbidities. With CKD stage 3b, NSAIDs are a poor choice, so a short oral glucocorticoid course (prednisone 30–40 mg/day, then taper over 7–10 days) is best. Low-dose colchicine is an alternative with renal dose adjustment and no interacting drugs.

Then:

  • Restart prophylaxis (low-dose colchicine or low-dose prednisone) for 3–6 months after starting ULT.
  • Titrate allopurinol upward every few weeks — even in CKD — to a serum urate <6 mg/dL.

Why not the others

  • (B) Increase allopurinol to 600 mg daily as the only change — Allopurinol should be titrated, but raising the dose does not treat the current flare.
  • (C) Stop allopurinol until the flare resolves; start indomethacin — Stopping ULT during a flare is unnecessary and causes urate swings that prolong flares; NSAIDs are also risky with CKD.
  • (D) Stop allopurinol and switch to febuxostat — Febuxostat is no more effective here and carries a boxed warning for cardiovascular death; the problem is the flare and an unmet urate target, not allopurinol failure.
  • (E) Continue allopurinol and start indomethacin — Continuing allopurinol is correct, but NSAIDs such as indomethacin can worsen kidney function with an eGFR of 38.
🧠 Mnemonic

"Start low, go slow, aim below 6" — allopurinol 100 mg (50 mg in CKD), increase by 100 mg every 2–5 weeks, target urate <6.

🎓 ABIM pearl

Before allopurinol, test for HLA-B*58:01 in patients of Southeast Asian (Han Chinese, Korean, Thai) or African American ancestry — carriers have a high risk of severe cutaneous reactions (SJS/TEN, DRESS).

🎯 Educational objective

Continue urate-lowering therapy during a gout flare, treat the flare according to comorbidities (glucocorticoids when NSAIDs are unsafe), add prophylaxis, and titrate to a serum urate below 6 mg/dL.

RH-001.search: a 66-year-old man comes to the office with 1 day of severe pain, redness and swelling of his right first metatarsophalangeal joint. he had two similar episodes last year. allopurinol 100 mg daily was started 4 months ago and increased to 200 mg daily 6 weeks ago. he also has hypertension and chronic kidney disease. medications are allopurinol, amlodipine and losartan. he stopped taking the colchicine prescribed with allopurinol after 2 months. temperature is 37.4 °c (99.3 °f). the right first mtp joint is red, warm, swollen and too tender to touch. no tophi are seen. creatinine 1.8 mg/dl (egfr 38 ml/min/1.73 m²) serum urate 7.4 mg/dl leukocyte count 9,600/µl correct answer: a gout flare during urate-lowering therapy flares are common in the first months of urate-lowering therapy (ult) — falling urate levels mobilize crystals from tissue deposits. that is a reason to keep ult going , treat the flare, and use prophylaxis. treat the flare with any of the three anti-inflammatory options, choosing by comorbidities. with ckd stage 3b , nsaids are a poor choice, so a short oral glucocorticoid course (prednisone 30–40 mg/day, then taper over 7–10 days) is best. low-dose colchicine is an alternative with renal dose adjustment and no interacting drugs. then: restart prophylaxis (low-dose colchicine or low-dose prednisone) for 3–6 months after starting ult. titrate allopurinol upward every few weeks — even in ckd — to a serum urate <6 mg/dl . why not the others (b) increase allopurinol to 600 mg daily as the only change — allopurinol should be titrated, but raising the dose does not treat the current flare. RH-002.stem_html:
A 42-year-old woman comes to the office with 3 months of pain and swelling in both hands and wrists. Her hands are stiff for about 90 minutes every morning. She has trouble opening jars and typing at work. Ibuprofen helps partly. She does not plan pregnancy and uses a levonorgestrel IUD.

There is symmetric swelling and tenderness of the 2nd and 3rd metacarpophalangeal and proximal interphalangeal joints of both hands and both wrists. The distal interphalangeal joints are spared. There are no rashes, nail changes or nodules.

Rheumatoid factorpositive (high titer)
Anti–cyclic citrullinated peptide antibodiespositive (high titer)
C-reactive protein2.4 mg/dL
Complete blood countnormal
ALT18 U/L
Creatinine0.7 mg/dL
Hepatitis B surface antigen and core antibody; hepatitis C antibodynegative
Hand radiographsperiarticular osteopenia; no erosions
RH-002.lead: In addition to a short course of low-dose prednisone, which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?

choices.D: Continue ibuprofen alone and reassess in 6 months

RH-002.explain_html:
Correct answer: C Early rheumatoid arthritis

Symmetric small-joint polyarthritis with prolonged morning stiffness, high-titer RF and anti-CCP and elevated CRP is rheumatoid arthritis with moderate–high disease activity. Anti-CCP is highly specific (~95%) and predicts erosive disease.

The window to prevent joint damage is early. Start a conventional synthetic DMARD now — methotrexate is the anchor drug (start ~15 mg weekly, increase to 20–25 mg weekly, with daily folic acid). Treat to target (remission or low disease activity), reassess every 1–3 months, and add a biologic or targeted synthetic DMARD if the target is not reached in 3–6 months.

Before methotrexate, check CBC, liver tests, creatinine, hepatitis B and C serologies and a chest radiograph; counsel to limit alcohol and use contraception (methotrexate is teratogenic).

Why not the others

  • (A) Adalimumab — TNF inhibitors are added when methotrexate fails to reach target. Monotherapy as the first DMARD is not preferred, and they cost far more.
  • (B) Hydroxychloroquine — Hydroxychloroquine is used for low disease activity or in combination. It is not enough for moderate–high activity RA.
  • (D) Continue ibuprofen alone and reassess in 6 months — NSAIDs relieve symptoms but do not stop erosions. Delaying a DMARD for 6 months risks irreversible damage.
  • (E) Tofacitinib — JAK inhibitors are reserved for inadequate response to methotrexate and carry warnings for VTE, MACE and malignancy (especially age ≥50 with risk factors).
🎓 ABIM pearl

RA spares the DIP joints. DIP involvement points to osteoarthritis (Heberden nodes) or psoriatic arthritis (with nail pitting).

🎯 Educational objective

Start methotrexate (with folic acid) promptly for newly diagnosed moderate–high activity rheumatoid arthritis, using a short glucocorticoid bridge if needed, and escalate by treat-to-target.

RH-003.stem_html:
A 74-year-old woman comes to the office with 3 weeks of a new headache over her right temple. Combing her hair hurts, and her jaw aches after chewing for a minute. She also has aching and stiffness of her shoulders and hips for 1 hour each morning. She has lost 3 kg (6.6 lb) and has had low-grade fevers. Her vision is normal.

Temperature is 37.8 °C (100.0 °F) and blood pressure is 138/80 mm Hg in both arms. The right temporal artery is tender and nodular with a reduced pulse. Visual acuity is 20/25 in both eyes; fundi are normal. Shoulder range of motion is limited by pain; strength is normal.

Erythrocyte sedimentation rate88 mm/h
C-reactive protein6.9 mg/dL
Hemoglobin11.1 g/dL
Platelets468,000/µL
RH-003.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.A: Prednisone 40–60 mg daily now, then temporal artery biopsy or ultrasound
choices.B: Temporal artery biopsy, and start prednisone if the biopsy is positive

RH-003.explain_html:
Correct answer: A Giant cell arteritis

New headache after 50, scalp tenderness, jaw claudication, a tender temporal artery, polymyalgia symptoms and very high inflammatory markers = giant cell arteritis (GCA) until proven otherwise.

The feared complication is sudden, permanent vision loss from anterior ischemic optic neuropathy. So: start high-dose glucocorticoids immediately (prednisone 40–60 mg/day; IV methylprednisolone if vision is affected), then confirm with temporal artery biopsy or vascular ultrasound. Biopsy stays diagnostic for at least 1–2 weeks after steroids start.

Add tocilizumab to allow a faster steroid taper (fewer relapses and less steroid toxicity).

Why not the others

  • (B) Temporal artery biopsy, and start prednisone if the biopsy is positive — Waiting for biopsy before treating risks blindness; biopsy findings persist for weeks after steroids start.
  • (C) Aspirin alone — Aspirin is not a substitute for glucocorticoids; its role in preventing ischemic events in GCA is uncertain.
  • (D) Prednisone 15 mg daily — 15 mg is the dose for isolated polymyalgia rheumatica. GCA needs high-dose glucocorticoids.
  • (E) MRI of the brain — Brain MRI does not diagnose GCA and delays treatment. (MRI or CT angiography of the aorta can assess large-vessel GCA later.)
🧠 Mnemonic

GCA red flags — "JAW HuRTS": Jaw claudication, Age >50, Worse vision, Headache (new), Rheumatica (PMR), Tender Scalp.

🎓 ABIM pearl

About half of patients with GCA have PMR, and about 15% of patients with PMR develop GCA. Ask every PMR patient about headache, jaw claudication and vision at every visit.

🎯 Educational objective

When giant cell arteritis is suspected, start high-dose glucocorticoids immediately and confirm the diagnosis with temporal artery biopsy or ultrasound afterward.

RH-004.stem_html:
A 38-year-old man who works in a warehouse comes to the office with 5 days of low back pain that began after lifting a heavy box. The pain is in the lower lumbar area and right buttock and does not travel below the knee. It is worse with bending and better lying still. He has no fever, weight loss, history of cancer, injection drug use, bowel or bladder changes, or numbness in the groin.

Temperature is 36.8 °C (98.2 °F). There is right paraspinal muscle tenderness and limited flexion due to pain. Straight-leg raise is negative bilaterally. Strength, sensation and reflexes in both legs are normal.
RH-004.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

choices.B: Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug and advice to stay active

RH-004.explain_html:
Correct answer: B Acute low back pain

This is acute nonspecific (mechanical) low back pain with no red flags and a normal neurologic examination. More than 90% of patients improve within 4–6 weeks regardless of treatment.

Management:

  • No imaging for the first 6 weeks without red flags — imaging finds incidental degenerative changes, does not improve outcomes, and leads to more procedures.
  • Stay active; return to normal activity as tolerated.
  • First-line treatments: superficial heat, massage, acupuncture or spinal manipulation; if medication is needed, an NSAID or a short course of a skeletal muscle relaxant.
Red flags → image early Concern
Cancer history, unexplained weight loss Metastasis
Fever, injection drug use, recent infection, immunosuppression Epidural abscess, osteomyelitis
Saddle anesthesia, urinary retention, bilateral leg weakness Cauda equina syndrome
Progressive or severe neurologic deficit Cord or root compression
Osteoporosis, glucocorticoid use, older age with trauma Compression fracture

Why not the others

  • (A) Lumbar spine radiographs — Radiographs expose the patient to radiation and add nothing without red flags.
  • (C) MRI of the lumbar spine — MRI without red flags does not change management and often shows disk bulges unrelated to symptoms. Reserve it for red flags or persistent radiculopathy in a surgical or injection candidate.
  • (D) Bed rest for 1 week — Bed rest slows recovery compared with staying active.
  • (E) Oxycodone for 2 weeks — Opioids are no better than NSAIDs for acute low back pain and carry risks of dependence and harm.
🎓 ABIM pearl

Sciatica (pain below the knee with a positive straight-leg raise) without deficits is also treated conservatively first; most cases improve within 6 weeks.

🎯 Educational objective

Acute low back pain without red flags needs no imaging; treat with activity, heat and NSAIDs or a short muscle-relaxant course.

RH-005.stem_html:
A 54-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes mellitus comes to the office with 4 months of gradually worsening pain and stiffness of her left shoulder. She now cannot reach behind her back to fasten her bra or reach a high shelf. The pain wakes her at night when she rolls onto that side. She recalls no injury.

There is no shoulder swelling or warmth. Active and passive range of motion are both markedly reduced in all planes, most severely in external rotation. Strength is normal within the available range. Shoulder radiographs are normal.
RH-005.lead: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
RH-005.explain_html:
Correct answer: A Adhesive capsulitis

The key finding is loss of both active AND passive motion, worst in external rotation, with normal radiographs. That is adhesive capsulitis ("frozen shoulder") — inflammation and fibrosis of the glenohumeral capsule. It is much more common in diabetes and thyroid disease and after periods of immobility.

It runs in phases — freezing (painful), frozen (stiff), thawing — over 1–3 years. Treatment: physical therapy with stretching, NSAIDs, and an intra-articular glucocorticoid injection for pain in the early phase.

Active ROM Passive ROM Clue
Rotator cuff tendinopathy / impingement Painful arc Normal Pain on 60–120° abduction
Rotator cuff tear Reduced, weak Normal Drop-arm sign
Adhesive capsulitis Reduced Reduced External rotation worst, normal X-ray
Glenohumeral OA Reduced Reduced Joint space loss, osteophytes on X-ray

Why not the others

  • (B) Glenohumeral osteoarthritis — Osteoarthritis also limits both active and passive motion, but radiographs would show joint-space narrowing and osteophytes.
  • (C) Rotator cuff tear — A rotator cuff tear limits active motion and strength, but the examiner can move the arm passively through a normal range.
  • (D) Biceps tendinopathy — Biceps tendinopathy causes anterior shoulder pain with tenderness in the bicipital groove and does not restrict passive motion.
  • (E) Subacromial impingement syndrome — Impingement causes a painful arc with preserved passive motion.
🎓 ABIM pearl

If passive motion is lost after a fall in an older adult, get an axillary view — a posterior shoulder dislocation is easily missed and also blocks external rotation.

🎯 Educational objective

Loss of both active and passive shoulder motion, especially external rotation, with normal radiographs indicates adhesive capsulitis, which is associated with diabetes.

RH-006.stem_html:
A 26-year-old woman with systemic lupus erythematosus diagnosed 2 years ago is evaluated for new leg swelling and foamy urine. Her lupus has been managed with hydroxychloroquine. She has had joint pains and a facial rash in the past month.

On physical examination, blood pressure is 148/94 mm Hg. There is a malar rash, synovitis of the wrists and 2+ pitting edema of both legs.

Creatinine1.3 mg/dL (0.8 mg/dL 6 months ago)
Urinalysis3+ protein; 20–30 erythrocytes/hpf with dysmorphic red cells and red cell casts
Urine protein-to-creatinine ratio2.8 g/g
Anti–double-stranded DNA antibodieselevated
C3 and C4low
RH-006.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.C: Begin an ACE inhibitor and repeat urinalysis in 3 months

RH-006.explain_html:
Correct answer: A Lupus nephritis

Active SLE (rash, arthritis, high anti-dsDNA, low complement) with proteinuria >0.5 g/day, an active urine sediment (red cell casts, dysmorphic RBCs) and rising creatinine → lupus nephritis.

Kidney biopsy is indicated for any patient with SLE and proteinuria ≥0.5 g/day, especially with active sediment or a fall in GFR. The ISN/RPS class and activity/chronicity drive treatment; clinical findings cannot predict the class reliably.

Class Pattern Treatment
I–II Mesangial Usually none beyond SLE care
III–IV Focal / diffuse proliferative Glucocorticoids + mycophenolate or low-dose IV cyclophosphamide, often + belimumab or voclosporin
V Membranous (nephrotic) Immunosuppression ± ACEi/ARB
VI Advanced sclerosis Prepare for kidney replacement

All patients continue hydroxychloroquine and get RAAS blockade for proteinuria.

Why not the others

  • (B) Increase hydroxychloroquine dose — Hydroxychloroquine is continued in all SLE but does not treat active proliferative nephritis; the dose is capped at 5 mg/kg/d to limit retinal toxicity.
  • (C) Begin an ACE inhibitor and repeat urinalysis in 3 months — An ACE inhibitor treats proteinuria but waiting 3 months without classifying the lesion risks permanent kidney loss.
  • (D) Begin rituximab — Rituximab is used in refractory cases; induction should be chosen after biopsy confirms the class.
  • (E) Kidney ultrasonography only — Ultrasonography shows kidney size but cannot determine the class or activity of nephritis.
🎯 Educational objective

Perform kidney biopsy in patients with SLE and proteinuria of 0.5 g/day or more, especially with an active sediment or declining kidney function, to guide treatment.

Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

(c) begin an ace inhibitor and repeat urinalysis in 3 months — an ace inhibitor treats proteinuria but waiting 3 months without classifying the lesion risks permanent kidney loss. (d) begin rituximab — rituximab is used in refractory cases; induction should be chosen after biopsy confirms the class. (e) kidney ultrasonography only — ultrasonography shows kidney size but cannot determine the class or activity of nephritis. 🎯 educational objective perform kidney biopsy in patients with sle and proteinuria of 0.5 g/day or more, especially with an active sediment or declining kidney function, to guide treatment. 📚 read more in wardology 🦋 lupus & antiphospholipid syndrome → 🧫 glomerular disease — nephritic & nephrotic → references kdigo 2024 clinical practice guideline for the management of lupus nephritis. kidney int 2024;105:s1. {'fanouriakis a, et al. eular recommendations for the management of sle': '2023 update. ann rheum dis 2024;83:15.'}  lupus nephritis

RH-007.stem_html:
A 39-year-old woman is evaluated 1 week after hospitalization for an unprovoked left femoral deep venous thrombosis. She had a stroke at age 35 that was attributed to "a small-vessel event". She had two miscarriages in the first trimester. She is currently receiving enoxaparin.

On physical examination, there is livedo reticularis on both thighs. The left leg is mildly swollen.

Platelet count118,000/µL
aPTTprolonged; does not correct with mixing
Lupus anticoagulantpositive (repeated after 12 weeks, positive)
Anticardiolipin IgG80 GPL (high)
Anti–β₂-glycoprotein I IgGhigh
RH-007.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate long-term anticoagulant?

choices.D: Warfarin with a target INR of 2.0–3.0

RH-007.explain_html:
Correct answer: D Antiphospholipid syndrome — anticoagulation

Arterial (stroke) and venous thrombosis, pregnancy morbidity, livedo, mild thrombocytopenia and persistently positive antiphospholipid antibodies (≥12 weeks apart) = antiphospholipid syndrome (APS). She is triple positive (lupus anticoagulant + anticardiolipin + anti-β₂GPI) — the highest-risk profile. The prolonged aPTT that does not correct is the lupus anticoagulant (an in-vitro artifact; she clots, not bleeds).

Treatment is lifelong warfarin, target INR 2–3. DOACs should be avoided, especially in triple-positive or arterial APS — rivaroxaban and apixaban caused more arterial events (strokes) than warfarin (TRAPS, ASTRO-APS).

In pregnancy, warfarin is replaced by LMWH + low-dose aspirin.

Why not the others

  • (A) Dabigatran — Dabigatran has no supporting evidence in APS and is not recommended.
  • (B) Rivaroxaban — Rivaroxaban was inferior to warfarin in triple-positive APS (TRAPS), with excess arterial thrombosis.
  • (C) Apixaban — Apixaban was associated with more strokes than warfarin in APS (ASTRO-APS).
  • (E) Aspirin alone — Aspirin alone is inadequate after a thrombotic event in APS; it may be used for primary prevention in asymptomatic antibody carriers.
🎯 Educational objective

Treat thrombotic antiphospholipid syndrome with long-term warfarin (INR 2–3) and avoid DOACs, especially in triple-positive patients or after arterial events.

RH-008.stem_html:
A 48-year-old woman with diffuse cutaneous systemic sclerosis diagnosed 1 year ago is evaluated for 3 days of headache and blurred vision. Her skin thickening has progressed rapidly over the past 6 months. Two months ago she started prednisone, 20 mg/d, for arthritis. She is positive for anti–RNA polymerase III antibodies.

On physical examination, blood pressure is 192/112 mm Hg (usually 118/70 mm Hg) and pulse rate is 92/min. Funduscopic examination shows flame hemorrhages and cotton-wool spots. There is diffuse skin thickening of the arms, chest and face.

Hemoglobin9.6 g/dL with schistocytes on peripheral smear
Platelet count96,000/µL
Creatinine2.2 mg/dL (0.8 mg/dL 1 month ago)
Urinalysis1+ protein, few erythrocytes
RH-008.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
RH-008.explain_html:
Correct answer: D Scleroderma renal crisis

Scleroderma renal crisis (SRC): abrupt malignant hypertension, acute kidney injury and often thrombotic microangiopathy (schistocytes, low platelets) in early diffuse cutaneous SSc. Classic risk factors: rapidly progressive skin disease, anti–RNA polymerase III antibodies and glucocorticoids (prednisone >15 mg/d).

The mechanism is intimal proliferation of renal arterioles → renal ischemia → massive renin release. ACE inhibitors transformed survival: before them, SRC was almost uniformly fatal. Use a short-acting ACE inhibitor (captopril), titrated every few hours to lower blood pressure by about 20 mm Hg/day, and continue it even if creatinine rises or dialysis is needed — many patients recover kidney function months later.

Add a calcium channel blocker if BP stays high. Avoid high-dose glucocorticoids in SSc.

Why not the others

  • (A) Intravenous labetalol — Labetalol may be added but does not block the renin-angiotensin system that drives the crisis.
  • (B) Plasma exchange — Plasma exchange is for TTP. The TMA here is driven by SRC and responds to ACE inhibition.
  • (C) Intravenous methylprednisolone — Glucocorticoids are a risk factor for SRC and would worsen it.
  • (E) Intravenous nitroprusside — Nitroprusside lowers BP but does not address the renin-mediated mechanism and does not improve kidney survival.
🎓 ABIM pearl

ARBs are not an adequate substitute for ACE inhibitors in SRC. And prophylactic ACE inhibitors do not prevent SRC — they may even worsen outcomes when it occurs.

🎯 Educational objective

Treat scleroderma renal crisis with an ACE inhibitor (captopril) titrated rapidly, continuing it even if dialysis is required.

RH-009.stem_html:
A 44-year-old woman with diffuse cutaneous systemic sclerosis diagnosed 6 months ago is evaluated during a routine visit. She has Raynaud phenomenon and skin thickening of her hands, forearms and chest. She has no cough or dyspnea and walks 2 miles a day. Her anti–topoisomerase I (anti–Scl-70) antibody is positive.

On physical examination, oxygen saturation is 98% breathing ambient air. There are fine bibasilar "Velcro" crackles. Chest radiograph is normal.
RH-009.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate next diagnostic test?

choices.E: High-resolution CT of the chest and pulmonary function tests with DLCO

RH-009.explain_html:
Correct answer: E Systemic sclerosis–associated interstitial lung disease

Interstitial lung disease (ILD) is the leading cause of death in systemic sclerosis. Highest risk: diffuse cutaneous disease, anti–Scl-70 (topoisomerase I) antibodies, early disease (first 5 years), Black race and male sex.

All patients with SSc should be screened for ILD at diagnosis with high-resolution CT (HRCT) — plus PFTs (FVC, DLCO). Chest radiographs and lung examination miss early disease, and symptoms appear late. HRCT typically shows nonspecific interstitial pneumonia (NSIP): basal ground-glass and reticulation with traction bronchiectasis.

Monitor with PFTs every 3–6 months in early disease. Treatment for progressive or significant ILD: mycophenolate, tocilizumab, cyclophosphamide, rituximab, or the antifibrotic nintedanib.

Also screen for pulmonary arterial hypertension annually (echocardiography, PFTs with DLCO, NT-proBNP) — more common in limited cutaneous SSc (anti-centromere).

Why not the others

  • (A) Surgical lung biopsy — Biopsy is rarely needed when the HRCT pattern fits in a patient with known SSc.
  • (B) Six-minute walk test only — A six-minute walk test measures functional capacity but does not detect or characterize ILD.
  • (C) Bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage — Bronchoscopy is not needed to diagnose SSc-ILD; it is used to exclude infection when suspected.
  • (D) Repeat chest radiograph in 1 year — Chest radiographs are insensitive for early ILD; her crackles already suggest disease.
🧠 Mnemonic

SSc antibodies — Scl-70 = Scarring lungs (diffuse, ILD); centromere = CREST (limited, PAH); RNA polymerase III = Renal crisis (and cancer).

🎯 Educational objective

Screen all patients with systemic sclerosis for interstitial lung disease with high-resolution CT and pulmonary function tests including DLCO.

RH-010.stem_html:
A 56-year-old woman with primary Sjögren disease diagnosed 8 years ago is evaluated for persistent painless swelling of the left parotid gland for 4 months. She has longstanding dry eyes and dry mouth managed with artificial tears and pilocarpine. She has had recurrent palpable purpura on her legs.

On physical examination, the left parotid gland is firm, nontender and enlarged. There is no fever. There is a palpable left cervical lymph node.

Anti-Ro/SSApositive
Anti-La/SSBpositive
Rheumatoid factorhigh titer
C4low
Serum protein electrophoresismonoclonal IgM κ spike
Cryoglobulinspositive
RH-010.lead: This patient is at greatest risk for which of the following?

choices.C: Squamous cell carcinoma of the oral cavity

RH-010.explain_html:
Correct answer: E Sjögren disease — lymphoma risk

Primary Sjögren disease raises the risk of non-Hodgkin lymphoma about 15–20 times — the highest of any autoimmune disease. Most are extranodal marginal zone (MALT) lymphomas of the salivary glands. Chronic B-cell stimulation in the inflamed gland drives clonal expansion.

Red flags for lymphoma in Sjögren:

  • Persistent salivary gland (parotid) enlargement
  • Palpable purpura / cryoglobulinemic vasculitis
  • Low C4
  • Monoclonal gammopathy, high-titer RF
  • Lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly, cytopenias

She has almost all of them. The next step is imaging and biopsy of the parotid gland.

Why not the others

  • (A) Bacterial parotitis — Bacterial parotitis is painful, tender and febrile with purulent discharge; her swelling is painless and persistent.
  • (B) Hepatocellular carcinoma — Hepatocellular carcinoma is not linked to Sjögren disease.
  • (C) Squamous cell carcinoma of the oral cavity — Dry mouth increases dental caries and candidiasis but is not a major cause of oral squamous cell carcinoma.
  • (D) Primary biliary cholangitis — PBC is associated with Sjögren disease, but it does not explain a parotid mass with a monoclonal protein and low C4.
🎯 Educational objective

Patients with Sjögren disease have a high risk of MALT lymphoma; persistent parotid enlargement, purpura, low C4 and a monoclonal protein are warning signs.

RH-011.stem_html:
A 61-year-old woman is evaluated for 2 months of progressive difficulty climbing stairs, getting up from a chair and lifting her arms to wash her hair. She has noticed a rash on her face and hands.

On physical examination, there is a violaceous rash on the upper eyelids with periorbital edema, scaly violaceous papules over the metacarpophalangeal and interphalangeal joints, and erythema over the upper chest and back. Strength is 4/5 in the hip flexors and deltoids. Distal strength is normal.

Creatine kinase2,400 U/L
Aldolaseelevated
Anti–TIF1-γ antibodypositive
RH-011.lead: In addition to treating the muscle disease, which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

choices.D: Comprehensive evaluation for occult malignancy, including CT of the chest, abdomen and pelvis and pelvic ultrasonography

RH-011.explain_html:
Correct answer: D Dermatomyositis and malignancy

Heliotrope rash (eyelids), Gottron papules (knuckles), shawl-sign erythema and proximal muscle weakness with high CK = dermatomyositis.

Dermatomyositis is a paraneoplastic disease in up to 20–25% of adults, most often within 3 years of diagnosis — ovarian, lung, pancreatic, stomach, colorectal and non-Hodgkin lymphoma. Risk is highest with anti–TIF1-γ and anti–NXP2 antibodies, older age, rapid onset and cutaneous necrosis.

In a high-risk patient, guidelines (IMACS 2023) recommend enhanced screening: CT of the chest, abdomen and pelvis, plus pelvic/transvaginal ultrasonography and CA-125 in women, mammography, colonoscopy, PSA in men, and consider PET-CT. Repeat screening annually for 3 years in high-risk patients.

Treatment: glucocorticoids plus a steroid-sparing agent (methotrexate, azathioprine, mycophenolate); IVIG is effective for refractory disease.

Why not the others

  • (A) No further evaluation — The association with cancer is strong; omitting evaluation can miss a treatable tumor.
  • (B) Muscle biopsy every 6 months — Serial biopsies are not used to monitor dermatomyositis; CK and strength testing are.
  • (C) Genetic testing for muscular dystrophy — Muscular dystrophies are inherited and do not cause heliotrope rash or Gottron papules.
  • (E) Age-appropriate cancer screening only — Routine screening alone is not enough for a high-risk patient (older age, anti–TIF1-γ).
🎯 Educational objective

Screen adults with dermatomyositis for occult malignancy, with enhanced screening (including CT of the chest, abdomen and pelvis) for high-risk patients such as those with anti–TIF1-γ antibodies.

RH-012.stem_html:
A 27-year-old man is evaluated for 1 year of low back and buttock pain. The pain is worst in the morning, with 1 hour of stiffness, wakes him in the second half of the night and improves with exercise. Rest makes it worse. He had an episode of a painful red eye 6 months ago that was treated with eye drops.

On physical examination, there is tenderness over both sacroiliac joints and reduced lumbar forward flexion (modified Schober test, 3 cm).

C-reactive protein18 mg/L
HLA-B27positive
MRI of the sacroiliac jointsbilateral bone marrow edema (active sacroiliitis)
RH-012.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate initial treatment?

choices.D: Naproxen at full dose, plus a physical therapy and exercise program

RH-012.explain_html:
Correct answer: D Axial spondyloarthritis

Inflammatory back pain — onset before 40, insidious, morning stiffness, better with exercise, worse with rest, night pain — plus anterior uveitis, HLA-B27 and MRI sacroiliitis = axial spondyloarthritis (ankylosing spondylitis).

First-line: full-dose NSAIDs (continuously when the disease is active) plus exercise and physical therapy. NSAIDs relieve symptoms in most patients.

If disease stays active after two different NSAIDs over 4 weeks, escalate to a biologic: TNF inhibitor (preferred, especially with uveitis or IBD — use a monoclonal antibody, not etanercept) or IL-17 inhibitor (secukinumab, ixekizumab), or a JAK inhibitor.

Conventional synthetic DMARDs (methotrexate, sulfasalazine) do not work for axial disease; sulfasalazine may help peripheral arthritis only.

Why not the others

  • (A) Methotrexate — Methotrexate does not improve axial symptoms or progression.
  • (B) Oral prednisone — Systemic glucocorticoids are not effective for axial spondyloarthritis and are not recommended for long-term use.
  • (C) Sulfasalazine — Sulfasalazine helps peripheral arthritis, not axial disease.
  • (E) TNF inhibitor as first-line therapy — Biologics are for disease that remains active despite at least two NSAID trials; they are not first-line.
🎯 Educational objective

Treat axial spondyloarthritis first with full-dose NSAIDs and exercise, escalating to a TNF or IL-17 inhibitor if disease remains active.

RH-013.stem_html:
A 68-year-old man with rheumatoid arthritis is evaluated for 2 days of a hot, swollen, very painful right knee. He cannot bear weight. He takes methotrexate and adalimumab. He has had no trauma.

On physical examination, temperature is 38.3 °C (100.9 °F), blood pressure is 128/76 mm Hg, and pulse rate is 102/min. The right knee is warm, red and has a large effusion; any movement causes severe pain. Other joints show no active synovitis.

Leukocyte count14,200/µL
C-reactive protein186 mg/L
Serum urate7.8 mg/dL
RH-013.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.B: Arthrocentesis with synovial fluid cell count, Gram stain, culture and crystal analysis
choices.D: Increase methotrexate for an RA flare

RH-013.explain_html:
Correct answer: B Septic arthritis

An acute hot, swollen joint is septic arthritis until proven otherwise. He has major risk factors: RA (damaged joints), immunosuppression (TNF inhibitor, methotrexate), and older age. Septic arthritis destroys cartilage within days and has a mortality of up to 10%.

Arthrocentesis is the single most important test — do it before antibiotics:

  • Synovial WBC >50,000/µL (often >100,000) with >90% neutrophils suggests infection (lower in immunosuppressed patients).
  • Gram stain and culture (and blood cultures).
  • Crystal analysis — but crystals do not exclude infection; gout and sepsis can coexist.

His serum urate is irrelevant to the decision: it can be high without gout and normal during a gout flare.

Then start empiric IV antibiotics (vancomycin ± ceftriaxone depending on Gram stain) and arrange joint drainage (needle, arthroscopic or open).

Why not the others

  • (A) Intra-articular glucocorticoid injection — Injecting glucocorticoids into an infected joint is dangerous; infection must be excluded first.
  • (C) Begin colchicine for presumed gout — Treating presumed gout without aspirating risks missing a septic joint; a high urate does not establish gout.
  • (D) Increase methotrexate for an RA flare — A single acutely inflamed joint with fever in an immunosuppressed patient is not a typical RA flare and must be aspirated first.
  • (E) MRI of the knee — MRI can show effusion and osteomyelitis, but it cannot distinguish infection from crystals, and it delays the essential test.
🎯 Educational objective

Aspirate an acute hot joint for cell count, Gram stain, culture and crystals before starting treatment, because septic arthritis must be excluded.

RH-014.stem_html:
A 76-year-old woman is evaluated on postoperative day 3 after a hip replacement for acute pain and swelling of her right wrist. She has hypothyroidism and osteoarthritis.

On physical examination, temperature is 37.9 °C (100.2 °F). The right wrist is warm, swollen and tender, with limited motion.

Wrist radiograph shows a linear calcification of the triangular fibrocartilage. Arthrocentesis is performed.

Synovial fluid leukocyte count22,000/µL (80% neutrophils)
Synovial fluid Gram stainno organisms (culture pending)
Polarized microscopyrhomboid-shaped, weakly positively birefringent crystals
RH-014.lead: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
RH-014.explain_html:
Correct answer: D Calcium pyrophosphate deposition (pseudogout)

Acute CPP crystal arthritis (pseudogout): an older patient with an acutely inflamed wrist or knee, often triggered by surgery or acute illness, with chondrocalcinosis on radiographs and rhomboid, weakly positively birefringent crystals (blue when parallel to the compensator).

Gout (monosodium urate) CPPD
Crystal shape Needle Rhomboid
Birefringence Strongly negative (yellow when parallel) Weakly positive (blue when parallel)
Typical joints 1st MTP, ankle, knee Knee, wrist
Radiograph Punched-out erosions with overhanging edges Chondrocalcinosis

In patients <60 or with polyarticular disease, look for associated metabolic disorders: hemochromatosis, hyperparathyroidism, hypomagnesemia, hypophosphatasia ("the 4 Hs").

Treat with joint aspiration, intra-articular glucocorticoids (once infection is excluded), NSAIDs or colchicine.

Why not the others

  • (A) Gout — Gout crystals are needle-shaped and strongly negatively birefringent.
  • (B) Rheumatoid arthritis — RA is a symmetric polyarthritis of the small joints; it does not cause a monoarthritis with CPP crystals.
  • (C) Osteoarthritis flare — Osteoarthritis causes a noninflammatory effusion (WBC <2,000/µL) without crystals.
  • (E) Reactive arthritis — Reactive arthritis is an asymmetric oligoarthritis of the lower limbs after GI or GU infection, without crystals.
🧠 Mnemonic

"P for Pseudogout, Positive and Parallelogram (rhomboid)." Gout = Needles, Negative.

🎯 Educational objective

Diagnose acute CPP crystal arthritis by rhomboid, weakly positively birefringent crystals in synovial fluid, often with chondrocalcinosis on radiographs.

RH-015.stem_html:
A 66-year-old woman is evaluated for 2 years of right knee pain that is worse with walking and stairs and better with rest. Morning stiffness lasts less than 15 minutes. She has hypertension and stage 3a chronic kidney disease (eGFR 52 mL/min/1.73 m²). Acetaminophen has not helped.

On physical examination, BMI is 32. There is bony enlargement and crepitus of the right knee with a small cool effusion. There is no warmth or erythema.

Radiographs show medial joint space narrowing and osteophytes.
RH-015.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?

choices.E: Topical diclofenac and an exercise and weight-loss program

RH-015.explain_html:
Correct answer: E Knee osteoarthritis

Activity-related knee pain, brief morning stiffness, bony enlargement, crepitus and medial joint space narrowing in an older adult = knee osteoarthritis.

The core treatments (ACR 2019) are exercise (strengthening, aerobic, tai chi) and weight loss (≥5–10% of body weight improves pain and function), plus self-management education.

For drug therapy, topical NSAIDs are recommended first for the knee — they work nearly as well as oral NSAIDs with far less systemic exposure. They are the best choice in older adults and those with CKD, hypertension or GI risk, where oral NSAIDs are risky. Intra-articular glucocorticoid injections give short-term relief for flares. Total knee replacement is for end-stage disease when conservative care fails.

Why not the others

  • (A) Intra-articular hyaluronic acid injection — Hyaluronic acid injections have little benefit over placebo and are conditionally recommended against.
  • (B) Oral tramadol — Tramadol has modest benefit with risks of dependence, falls and serotonin syndrome; it is conditionally recommended only when other options fail.
  • (C) Oral glucosamine and chondroitin — Glucosamine and chondroitin are no better than placebo and are not recommended.
  • (D) Arthroscopic débridement — Arthroscopic débridement and lavage do not help degenerative knee osteoarthritis and are not recommended.
🎯 Educational objective

Treat knee osteoarthritis with exercise, weight loss and topical NSAIDs, particularly in older adults or patients with chronic kidney disease.

RH-016.stem_html: A 52-year-old man of Han Chinese descent is evaluated after his third gout flare in a year. He has tophi on both elbows. He has hypertension and chronic kidney disease (eGFR 48 mL/min/1.73 m²). His serum urate is 9.4 mg/dL. You plan to start urate-lowering therapy.
RH-016.lead: Which of the following should be done before starting allopurinol?
RH-016.explain_html:
Correct answer: E Allopurinol hypersensitivity — HLA-B*58:01

Allopurinol hypersensitivity syndrome — including DRESS and SJS/TEN — is rare but carries a mortality of up to 25%. The strongest risk factor is HLA-B*58:01, which is common in people of Han Chinese, Korean, Thai and African descent. CKD and starting at high doses also raise the risk.

ACR 2020 recommends testing for HLA-B*58:01 before starting allopurinol in patients of Southeast Asian (e.g., Han Chinese, Korean, Thai) or African American descent. If positive, choose febuxostat instead.

Other allopurinol rules:

  • Start low (≤100 mg/d; ≤50 mg/d in CKD stage 4+) and titrate to serum urate <6 mg/dL — higher doses are fine in CKD once titrated slowly.
  • Give anti-inflammatory prophylaxis (colchicine, NSAID or low-dose prednisone) for 3–6 months when starting.

Why not the others

  • (A) No testing is needed — His ancestry calls for HLA-B*58:01 testing to avoid a potentially fatal reaction.
  • (B) Liver biopsy — Liver biopsy has no role in starting urate-lowering therapy.
  • (C) 24-hour urine uric acid — A 24-hour urine uric acid is rarely needed and does not affect the safety of allopurinol.
  • (D) Thiopurine methyltransferase (TPMT) activity — TPMT testing is done before azathioprine or mercaptopurine. It matters for allopurinol only because allopurinol interacts with those drugs.
🎯 Educational objective

Test for HLA-B*58:01 before starting allopurinol in patients of Southeast Asian or African American descent to reduce the risk of severe hypersensitivity.

RH-017.stem_html:
A 72-year-old woman is evaluated for 6 weeks of aching and stiffness of both shoulders and hips, worst in the morning for about 2 hours. She has trouble getting out of bed and combing her hair. She has no headache, jaw pain with chewing, scalp tenderness or visual symptoms.

On physical examination, there is reduced active range of motion of both shoulders because of pain; passive motion is better. Strength is normal when tested despite the pain. There is no synovitis of the hands. Temporal arteries are normal.

Erythrocyte sedimentation rate64 mm/h
C-reactive protein38 mg/L
Creatine kinasenormal
Rheumatoid factor and anti-CCPnegative
TSHnormal
RH-017.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?

choices.E: Temporal artery biopsy before any treatment

RH-017.explain_html:
Correct answer: B Polymyalgia rheumatica

An older adult with bilateral shoulder and hip girdle aching and morning stiffness, raised inflammatory markers, normal CK and no features of another disease → polymyalgia rheumatica (PMR).

PMR responds dramatically to low-dose glucocorticoids: prednisone 12.5–25 mg/d (EULAR/ACR 2015). Improvement within days is so typical that a poor response should make you question the diagnosis. Taper slowly over at least 1 year to the lowest effective dose. Add methotrexate (or tocilizumab) for relapses or high risk of glucocorticoid toxicity.

About 15–20% of PMR patients have giant cell arteritis — always ask about headache, jaw claudication, scalp tenderness and vision. If present, high-dose prednisone (40–60 mg) is needed. She has none.

Why not the others

  • (A) Naproxen alone — NSAIDs may help briefly but are inadequate for PMR and add GI and kidney risk in older adults.
  • (C) Methotrexate alone — Methotrexate is a glucocorticoid-sparing add-on, not initial monotherapy.
  • (D) Prednisone, 60 mg/d — High-dose prednisone is for giant cell arteritis. Uncomplicated PMR responds to low doses, and higher doses cause more toxicity.
  • (E) Temporal artery biopsy before any treatment — Temporal artery biopsy is for suspected GCA. She has no cranial or visual symptoms.
🎯 Educational objective

Treat polymyalgia rheumatica with low-dose prednisone (12.5–25 mg/d) and screen for symptoms of giant cell arteritis.

(c) methotrexate alone — methotrexate is a glucocorticoid-sparing add-on, not initial monotherapy.
